2.5

Sorting, Binary Search & Selection

highverified
Roles: all

Topic overview

Sorting converts an unordered collection into an order that supports merging, grouping, range queries, deterministic output, and binary search. Binary search is broader than exact lookup: it finds a boundary in a monotonic predicate, provided the invariant and interval convention are correct. Selection algorithms and bounded heaps can answer kth-element or top-k questions without fully sorting all input. This chapter derives comparison-sort limits, contrasts stable and unstable algorithms, explains Python's key-based stable sorting, traces lower-bound binary search with duplicates, and distinguishes O(log n) search from O(n) insertion into an array. It also covers partial selection, external sorting, non-comparison sorting assumptions, floating-point and missing-value order, and concurrent mutation. You will implement stable merge sort and a left-bound search, use `sorted`, `bisect`, and `heapq`, and verify permutation, ordering, stability, and boundary properties. The engineering goal is to choose the least work that satisfies the actual output contract while making ordering, tie, key, memory, and determinism semantics explicit.

Prerequisites

  • big-o
  • stacks-queues-heaps

Learning objectives

  • Compare sorting algorithms by comparison count, stability, memory, adaptivity, and data-movement behavior.
  • Implement binary search with a stated half-open invariant and handle duplicates, insertion points, and monotonic predicates.
  • Choose full sort, heap top-k, partition selection, counting/radix methods, or external sort from the output and system constraints.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Comparison sorting generally requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Stable sorting preserves the input order of equal keys, which matters for multi-key workflows. Binary search reduces boundary lookup in a sorted or otherwise monotonic domain to O(log n), but the invariant and duplicate policy must be explicit; insertion into a Python list remains O(n). For top-k or kth selection, avoid a full sort when a heap or partition algorithm meets the contract. Production design also considers memory, I/O, determinism, missing values, and concurrent mutation.

What you must know

  • Order contract before algorithm
  • Stable ties preserve prior order
  • Binary search finds a boundary
  • Search O(log n), insertion O(n)
  • Partial answers can avoid full sort

Why this matters

Ordering is a foundational systems operation. Database plans sort for merge joins and grouping, ranking pipelines select candidates, time series require chronological order, and reproducible outputs depend on deterministic ties. A faulty comparator can make results inconsistent; an off-by-one binary search can fail only at empty or duplicate boundaries; sorting an entire billion-row stream to retain one hundred items wastes work and memory. Interviewers probe these topics because the invariants are compact but unforgiving. In production, the algorithm sits within data movement, serialization, spill, and distributed partitioning, so the best asymptotic comparison count may not be the best system plan.

Intuition

Sorting pays once to create structure that later operations exploit. Binary search repeatedly discards a half whose boundary cannot contain the answer. The robust mental model is not 'look for the value' but 'maintain an interval that is guaranteed to contain the first true position.' Selection asks for less information than sorting: if only the largest k are needed, ordering every pair is unnecessary. Match the amount of ordering work to the information the caller will consume.

Ordering contracts, stability, and comparators

A sort needs a total or suitably consistent order over keys. Specify ascending or descending direction, missing and non-finite placement, locale or normalization for text, tie-breaking, and whether output must be stable. A stable algorithm preserves original relative order among records with equal sort keys. This supports multi-key sorting: perform a stable sort by a secondary key, then a stable sort by the primary key, or more clearly supply a composite key.

Python's `sorted` returns a new list and list `.sort` mutates in place; both are stable and accept a key function. Key extraction is normally performed once per item, avoiding repeated expensive comparator work. Prefer key functions to custom pairwise comparison. Do not rely on an unordered source to supply a meaningful tie order; include a deterministic identifier when persistence or distributed reproducibility matters.

A comparator must be consistent. Cyclic or stateful comparisons invalidate algorithm assumptions. Floating NaN is not ordered like an ordinary number, mixed types may be incomparable, and timestamp strings may not reflect chronological order. Normalize into a documented key domain before sorting. Sorting changes representation, not data truth: duplicate records and invalid timestamps need separate policies.

Comparison sorts, lower bounds, and data movement

Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix and shifts an item into place. It is O(n²) in the worst case but adaptive and simple for small or nearly sorted runs. Merge sort divides, recursively sorts halves, and merges in linear work, giving O(n log n) worst-case time and commonly O(n) auxiliary storage; it can be stable. Heap sort gives O(n log n) worst-case time with low auxiliary storage but is generally unstable and has different locality. Quicksort partitions around a pivot, is often fast in memory, and has O(n log n) expected time with randomized or suitable pivots but O(n²) worst cases without safeguards.

In the comparison decision-tree model, n distinct items have n! possible orders. A binary comparison tree needs at least n! leaves, so its height is Omega(log(n!))=Omega(n log n). Algorithms can beat this comparison bound only by using more structure, such as bounded integer keys in counting or radix sorting. Those methods pay in key-domain assumptions, auxiliary storage, and passes.

Comparisons are not the full cost. Large records should often be sorted by compact keys or references to reduce movement. External merge sort creates sorted runs that fit memory and merges them with mostly sequential I/O. Distributed sorting samples partition boundaries, shuffles records, sorts partitions, and must handle skew and global tie semantics. Measure bytes read, written, shuffled, and spilled as well as CPU.

Binary search as boundary finding

Use a half-open interval [lo, hi) containing every possible answer. For lower bound—the first index i where a[i]≥x—start lo=0, hi=n. While lo<hi, set mid=(lo+hi)//2. If a[mid]<x, indexes through mid cannot be the answer, so lo=mid+1; otherwise mid may be the first answer, so hi=mid. Termination lo==hi returns an insertion point from zero through n. This handles empty input and duplicates without post-hoc patches.

Upper bound finds the first element greater than x by changing the predicate. Exact membership checks whether the returned lower-bound index is in range and equal. Binary search only requires a monotonic predicate: false values followed by true values. It can find the smallest capacity that meets an SLA, the first timestamp at or after a cutoff, or a feasible numeric threshold. The predicate cost multiplies the logarithmic number of evaluations.

Python `bisect_left` and `bisect_right` expose insertion-point semantics. Their search is O(log n), but inserting into a list shifts elements and is O(n); the official performance note makes that distinction explicit. The sequence must remain sorted and must not be concurrently mutated during search. For numeric answer search, define termination tolerance, overflow behavior, and monotonicity; floating search is not identical to discrete index search.

Selection, top-k, and system choices

If only the smallest or largest k items are needed, a bounded heap scans n items in O(n log k) time and O(k) state. It suits streaming and small k. Partition selection, including randomized quickselect, finds a kth order statistic in expected O(n) time and can partition top candidates without ordering them; worst-case safeguards or deterministic selection are available when guarantees matter. `heapq.nsmallest` and `nlargest` choose practical strategies, but their exact implementation policy is not the contract.

A full sort remains appropriate when all items must be ordered, many subsequent range operations reuse the order, or k is close to n. Selection output is often unordered; sorting the retained k costs O(k log k). Define ties at the boundary: exactly k records, all equal-score records, or deterministic IDs. Ranking metrics can change if tie handling is accidental.

Production pipelines need schema and order versioning. Monitor input size, key extraction failures, spill volume, skewed partitions, comparator errors, and end-to-end latency. Use stable secondary keys for reproducibility, protect untrusted sort sizes, and avoid materializing an infinite source. A database index or search engine may maintain order incrementally, while repeated `insort` into a large array pays linear movement. Choose the system primitive, not only the textbook algorithm.

Math / formal view

Any comparison sort on n distinct inputs needs at least log2(n!)=Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Merge sort satisfies T(n)=2T(n/2)+Theta(n)=Theta(n log n). Binary search performs O(log n) predicate evaluations over n discrete candidates. Heap top-k costs O(n log k) time and O(k) state.

Find the first timestamp at or after a cutoff

Setup

A sorted event-time array may be empty and may contain duplicate timestamps. The caller needs the leftmost eligible index for a range scan.

Maintain [lo,hi) as the set of possible insertion points. When `times[mid] < cutoff`, discard through mid; otherwise keep mid by moving hi. Return lo, which can equal len(times) when no event qualifies. Verify that every index before lo is less than the cutoff and every index from lo is greater than or equal. Compare the implementation with `bisect_left` over empty, singleton, duplicate, all-before, and all-after cases. The binary lookup is logarithmic, but inserting a late event at that point into an array remains linear.

Conclusion

Boundary invariants eliminate ambiguous duplicate behavior and make the returned index useful for both membership and range scans.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build stable merge sort and lower-bound binary search, then verify ordering, permutation, stability, duplicates, and boundary invariants.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def merge_sort(items, key=lambda x: x):
    if len(items) <= 1: return list(items)
    middle = len(items)//2
    left = merge_sort(items[:middle], key); right = merge_sort(items[middle:], key)
    out=[]; i=j=0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if key(left[i]) <= key(right[j]): out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else: out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]

def lower_bound(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo+hi)//2
        if a[mid] < x: lo = mid+1
        else: hi = mid
    return lo
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from bisect import bisect_left
from heapq import nlargest
records = [('b', 2), ('a', 1), ('c', 2)]
ordered = sorted(records, key=lambda row: row[1])
first_two = bisect_left([1,2,2,4], 2)
top = nlargest(2, records, key=lambda row: row[1])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version key and tie semantics, test non-finite and duplicate boundaries, measure memory/spill and key cost, add deterministic secondary keys, and select external or distributed execution when inputs exceed one process.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
items=[('first',2),('second',1),('third',2)]
out=merge_sort(items,key=lambda x:x[1])
assert [x[1] for x in out] == [1,2,2]
assert [x[0] for x in out if x[1]==2] == ['first','third']
for a in [[],[1],[1,2,2,4]]:
    for x in [0,1,2,3,5]:
        i=lower_bound(a,x)
        assert i == bisect_left(a,x)
        assert all(v < x for v in a[:i])
        assert all(v >= x for v in a[i:])
assert first_two == 1 and len(top) == 2

Common mistakes

  • Binary search returns an arbitrary matching duplicate.

    A generic implementation might, but lower/upper-bound variants define the first or after-last boundary and should be chosen explicitly.

  • `bisect.insort` inserts in O(log n).

    Finding the position is logarithmic; shifting the list to insert is O(n) and dominates.

  • Top-k always requires sorting all n items.

    A bounded heap uses O(n log k), and partition selection can use expected O(n) when only a partial order is required.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why must comparison sorting take Omega(n log n)?

    There are n! possible distinct orders and a binary comparison decision tree needs at least that many leaves, requiring height Omega(log n!).

  • What does stable sort guarantee?

    Records with equal comparison keys retain their relative input order; it does not define that input order or automatically make ties deterministic across unordered sources.

  • How do you binary-search an answer rather than an array?

    Define a monotonic feasibility predicate and search for its first true boundary, accounting for predicate cost and domain termination.

Production / system-design connection

Define key normalization, missing placement, direction, stability, tie policy, and deterministic secondary keys. Choose partial selection when it satisfies the output, and external or distributed sort when data exceeds memory. Monitor records, bytes, comparisons or key-extraction cost, spill, shuffle skew, and latency. Keep inputs immutable during binary search, validate monotonic predicates, cap untrusted workloads, and regression-test boundary and duplicate behavior.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What does `bisect_left` return when every element is less than x?

    Show solution

    It returns len(a), the valid insertion point after the final element.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Choose an algorithm to retain the largest 50 scores from an unknown-length stream.

    Show solution

    Use a min-heap capped at 50 for O(n log 50) time and O(50) state, then sort the final heap if presentation order is required.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A stable sort gives different tie order across two runs fed from a set. Why?

    Show solution

    Stability preserves source order among ties, but the set did not supply the required deterministic source order. Add an explicit secondary key.

2.6

Sampling & Streaming Algorithms

highverified
Roles: de, mle, ds

Topic overview

Streaming algorithms process items in one or a few passes while keeping state far smaller than the complete history. They are necessary when input is unbounded, arrives faster than storage queries can respond, or is simply too large to materialize. This chapter begins with exact one-pass aggregates, then derives reservoir sampling for a uniform fixed-size sample from an unknown-length stream. It explains how approximate sketches trade memory for controlled error, using count-min sketch as the main example and distinguishing one-sided frequency overestimation from unbiased sampling. You will learn how mergeability supports partitioned processing, why randomness and hash independence assumptions must be stated, how windows change the problem, and why a compact structure is not automatically correct under deletions or concept drift. A worked stream monitor maintains exact totals, a reservoir, and approximate heavy-hitter counts while preserving checkpointable state. Production sections cover event identity, ordering, late data, replay, deduplication, seed/version management, overflow, adversarial keys, accuracy audits, and fallback. The goal is to choose an explicit error and retention contract, not to use approximation merely because it sounds scalable.

Prerequisites

  • big-o
  • hash-tables
  • python-generators
  • probability-basics

Learning objectives

  • Derive reservoir sampling's inclusion probability and implement a reproducible fixed-size sample from an unknown-length stream.
  • Explain count-min sketch update, query, overestimation, width/depth trade-offs, and merge requirements.
  • Design streaming state with explicit windows, replay, identity, checkpoint, numerical, adversarial, and accuracy-audit policies.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A streaming algorithm updates a bounded summary in one or few passes rather than storing all items. Reservoir sampling keeps k uniform positions from a stream of unknown length by retaining item t with probability k/t and replacing a random reservoir position. Count-min sketch uses multiple hashed counter rows; query returns the minimum counter, so it never underestimates nonnegative insertion-only frequency but can overestimate through collisions. These guarantees depend on randomness, hash, update, and window assumptions, and production needs replay-safe checkpoints and accuracy monitoring.

What you must know

  • Bounded state changes the problem
  • Reservoir gives uniform positions
  • Sketches expose explicit error
  • Merge only compatible summaries
  • Window, replay, and identity are semantics

Why this matters

Telemetry, clickstreams, logs, network events, and model inference traffic can exceed memory and grow without a known endpoint. Exact storage and repeated full scans may be too costly, yet operators still need samples, counts, distinct estimates, quantiles, and heavy hitters. Streaming algorithms supply useful summaries with bounded state, but their guarantees are narrow. Reservoir sampling is not representative when event positions are not the target population; count-min sketch does not support arbitrary negative updates under the same simple guarantee. In production, replay can double-count and incompatible seeds can make summaries impossible to merge. Interviews test the derivation; engineering requires lifecycle, accuracy, and recovery design.

Intuition

A reservoir gives every arriving position a chance to displace one of k current representatives. Early items begin with an advantage but face replacement at every later step, exactly balancing their final inclusion probability. A count-min sketch lays several small counter tables over the same keys. Collisions add extra mass; taking the smallest row estimate chooses the least-contaminated view. Both structures save memory by discarding information, so they must expose what question remains answerable and how wrong the answer can be.

The streaming model and exact bounded aggregates

A stream algorithm receives items sequentially, usually cannot revisit arbitrary history, and maintains state bounded independently of total length or growing sublinearly. State the model: insertion-only or updates/deletions, one pass or multiple, ordered or partitioned, finite window or all history, and whether approximation or random failure probability is allowed. These choices determine which summaries are valid.

Some queries are exactly streamable with constant state: count, sum, minimum, maximum, and online mean. Welford-style recurrences compute variance more stably than subtracting two large accumulated quantities. Grouped exact counts are not constant state when the number of keys grows. Exact deduplication over unbounded unique IDs requires unbounded information in the general case. A bounded dictionary does not solve this without eviction semantics.

Windows make old information expire. Tumbling and sliding event-time windows require time, ordering, lateness, and revision policies. A summary for all history cannot answer an arbitrary recent window unless it retains decomposable window state. Exponential decay answers a different weighted-history question. Define the population and query before selecting the data structure.

Reservoir sampling and uniform inclusion

For reservoir size k, store the first k stream items. At one-based position t>k, choose a random integer j uniformly from 1 through t. If j≤k, replace reservoir position j. The new item is included with probability k/t. For any earlier item already in the reservoir before step t, its survival probability is 1-(k/t)(1/k)=1-1/t=(t-1)/t. Inductively, every one of the t positions has final inclusion probability k/t.

The guarantee is uniform over stream positions, not necessarily users, sessions, time, or a target distribution. High-activity users occupy more positions and therefore appear more often. For user-uniform sampling, sample users or use a design consistent with that estimand. Weighted reservoir variants solve other explicit inclusion goals. Use a well-defined pseudorandom generator, record its seed/state when replay reproducibility matters, and avoid modulo-biased home-grown randomness.

A single reservoir is not merged by simply concatenating partition reservoirs and resampling equally when partitions have different counts. Correct merging must account for each partition's population size or use mergeable priority-based sampling. Preserve item count and compatible sampling metadata. Test statistically across many runs in addition to deterministic invariant tests; one sample cannot demonstrate uniformity.

Count-min sketch and approximate frequency

A count-min sketch has d rows and w counters per row, each with an independently seeded hash. Updating key x by nonnegative amount c increments one counter in every row. Querying x returns the minimum of those counters. Every true update to x reaches all its counters, while collisions add nonnegative counts, so the estimate cannot be below the true insertion-only frequency. The minimum limits collision contamination to the best row.

With conventional parameterization, width scales as about e/epsilon and depth as about ln(1/delta), giving additive error roughly epsilon times total stream mass with probability at least 1-delta under the hash assumptions. Constants and exact theorem statements depend on the construction. Counters can overflow, hashes can be attacked, and negative updates break the simple one-sided guarantee. Conservative update can reduce overcount in practice but changes the algorithm.

Sketches with identical dimensions, hash functions, seeds, counter semantics, and domain normalization can be merged by elementwise addition for disjoint stream partitions. Incompatible sketches must not be silently combined. Heavy-hitter discovery also needs candidate generation because a count-min sketch answers queries for supplied keys; it does not list keys it discarded. Pair it with a candidate structure and verify candidates against exact samples or logs when consequences matter.

Distributed operation, recovery, and accuracy governance

Stream processing adds delivery and state semantics. At-least-once replay duplicates updates unless the computation is idempotent or deduplicated within a defined scope. Exactly-once claims are end-to-end protocol claims involving sources, state checkpoints, and sinks, not a property of a sketch. Checkpoint the item count, reservoir or counters, RNG state or deterministic sampling identity, hash seeds, schema version, and window metadata atomically enough for the recovery contract.

Partitioning can skew load and accuracy. Hot keys concentrate counters and work; repartitioning changes ownership. Merge only compatible summaries and avoid counting overlapping partitions twice. Late events may revise event-time windows; decide whether results update, drop, or side-output them. Backpressure and bounded input buffers remain necessary because a bounded summary does not bound transport queues.

Audit approximation continuously. Compare sketch estimates with exact counts on sampled keys or periodic bounded windows, measure overestimation distribution and heavy-hitter precision/recall, and alert on saturation or incompatible configuration. Protect hash functions and key sizes at trust boundaries. Provide a fallback to exact computation for high-impact decisions or when error budgets are exceeded. Approximation should be versioned and observable like a model.

Math / formal view

Reservoir sampling: at time t>k, include the new item with probability k/t and replace a uniform reservoir slot. An earlier item survives step t with probability (t-1)/t, yielding inclusion k/t by induction. Count-min sketch query is min_r C[r,h_r(x)]; for nonnegative insertion-only updates it is at least f(x), with additive-error probability controlled by width and depth under stated hash assumptions.

Monitor an unknown-length event stream

Setup

An operations service needs total volume, a uniform sample of 1,000 event positions, and approximate counts for candidate error signatures.

Maintain an exact total and online mean payload size, a reservoir updated with a dedicated RNG, and a count-min sketch with versioned dimensions and seeds. Candidate signatures come from a bounded heap or separate tracker; the sketch estimates their frequency. Checkpoint all state consistently with the consumed source offset. On replay, restore both offset and state rather than applying events twice. Periodically compute exact counts for a sampled bounded interval and compare error. Document that the reservoir is event-uniform, not customer-uniform, and that the sketch covers insertion-only counts in the current window policy.

Conclusion

Each summary answers a different question and carries its own population, error, and recovery contract; combining them does not create a generic compressed database.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build reservoir sampling and count-min sketch, then verify size, reproducibility, no-underestimation, merge compatibility, and approximate uniformity.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import random

def reservoir(items, k, seed=0):
    rng=random.Random(seed); sample=[]; count=0
    for count,item in enumerate(items,1):
        if count <= k: sample.append(item)
        else:
            j=rng.randrange(count)
            if j < k: sample[j]=item
    return sample,count

class CountMin:
    def __init__(self,width,depth,seeds):
        self.width=width; self.seeds=tuple(seeds); self.rows=[[0]*width for _ in range(depth)]
    def _index(self,key,seed): return hash((seed,key)) % self.width
    def add(self,key,count=1):
        if count < 0: raise ValueError('insertion-only')
        for row,seed in zip(self.rows,self.seeds): row[self._index(key,seed)] += count
    def estimate(self,key): return min(row[self._index(key,seed)] for row,seed in zip(self.rows,self.seeds))
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
sample,n=reservoir(range(1000),20,seed=7)
sketch=CountMin(200,4,[11,23,37,53])
exact={}
for key in ['a']*50 + ['b']*20 + ['c']*5:
    sketch.add(key); exact[key]=exact.get(key,0)+1
estimates={key:sketch.estimate(key) for key in exact}

Checkpoint RNG/hash configuration and state with source offsets, define window and population, validate compatible merges, audit approximation against exact samples, monitor saturation/backpressure, and provide an exact fallback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions

hits=[0]*20
for seed in range(2000):
    s,_=reservoir(range(20),1,seed)
    hits[s[0]] += 1

Common mistakes

  • A reservoir sample is automatically representative of users.

    It is uniform over stream positions. Users producing more events receive more positions unless the sampling design changes.

  • Count-min sketch returns exact counts for frequent items.

    It can overestimate any queried key through collisions; width/depth control probabilistic additive error, not exactness.

  • Any two sketches of the same shape can be merged.

    They also need identical hash functions/seeds, counter semantics, normalization, window, and nonoverlapping input accounting.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does reservoir sampling keep every position with probability k/n?

    The new item enters with k/t; each retained earlier item survives each later step with factor (t-1)/t, whose product yields k/n.

  • Why does count-min use the minimum counter?

    Each row contains the true count plus nonnegative collision mass; the minimum selects the least-contaminated row while retaining no-underestimate behavior.

  • Can exact distinct count use bounded memory for an unbounded universe?

    Not generally. Exact membership information grows with distinct values; bounded-memory systems use a finite window, external state, or approximation such as HyperLogLog.

Production / system-design connection

Version population, window, normalization, hash/RNG seeds, dimensions, and error guarantees. Checkpoint summaries with source progress, make replay behavior explicit, and merge only compatible nonoverlapping state. Monitor saturation, estimated error against exact audits, heavy-hitter quality, late events, and backpressure. Bound counters and queues, defend against adversarial keys, and provide an exact verification path for high-impact decisions or breached error budgets.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    At stream position 100 with reservoir size 10, what is the new item's inclusion probability?

    Show solution

    10/100=0.1; if included, it replaces one of the ten slots uniformly.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Can you merge two count-min sketches with different hash seeds?

    Show solution

    No. Corresponding counters represent different key mappings; retain separate queries or rebuild with compatible configuration.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A restored stream job doubles every approximate count after a crash. What likely failed?

    Show solution

    The checkpointed summary state and source offset were inconsistent, so already-applied events were replayed into retained state. Restore them under one recovery contract or make updates replay-idempotent.

3.1

SQL Joins

very highverified
Roles: ds, de, mle, da

Topic overview

A SQL join combines rows according to a predicate, but its most important property is cardinality: how many output rows each input key can produce. This chapter develops joins from Cartesian product and filtering, then covers inner, left, right, full, cross, self, semi, and anti semantics; NULL and three-valued logic; duplicate multiplication; key normalization; and physical nested-loop, hash, and merge join strategies. You will learn to state table grain before joining, place predicates correctly for outer joins, enforce one-to-one or many-to-one expectations with constraints and tests, and reconcile measures after combination. A worked customer-order example preserves customers without orders while distinguishing structural absence from unknown amounts. The performance section connects logical SQL to optimizer choices, indexes, statistics, memory, spill, skew, and join order without assuming a particular plan from query text. The objective is not merely to recall join syntax. It is to predict the output population, prove which unmatched rows survive, catch unintended many-to-many expansion, and operate joins safely as data distributions and schemas change.

Prerequisites

  • hash-tables
  • normalization-db

Learning objectives

  • Predict output grain, matched multiplicity, and unmatched-row behavior for every major join type.
  • Explain NULL predicate behavior and distinguish semi/anti existence tests from value-producing joins.
  • Validate join correctness and diagnose physical plans using keys, constraints, statistics, indexes, memory, and skew.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A join pairs rows whose predicate evaluates true. Inner join keeps matches; left join also preserves unmatched left rows with NULL-extended right columns; full join preserves unmatched rows from both sides. Cardinality depends on key multiplicities: a key appearing a times on the left and b times on the right contributes a×b inner matches. Define each table's grain, validate key uniqueness and match rates, and be careful placing right-side filters after a left join because `WHERE` can remove NULL-extended rows. The optimizer may implement the same logic with nested-loop, hash, or merge join.

What you must know

  • Declare row grain first
  • Multiplicity determines output rows
  • Outer joins preserve one side
  • NULL makes predicates unknown
  • Logical join differs from physical algorithm

Why this matters

Joins reconstruct business entities from normalized or separately produced tables. They also cause some of the most expensive silent data errors: duplicated dimension keys multiply facts, unmatched entities disappear under an inner join, filters collapse an outer join, and inconsistent IDs create false misses. In ML, row multiplication can overweight users or leak labels; in analytics, it can inflate revenue. Interview questions test syntax, but experienced reviewers ask for expected row counts, uniqueness, unmatched policy, and reconciliation. Production systems must additionally manage skewed keys, stale statistics, memory spills, indexes, and changing upstream contracts.

Intuition

Write a sentence for one row in each input. A customer row represents one customer; an order row represents one order. Joining on customer ID creates one row per matching customer-order pair, not automatically one row per customer. Outer joins add placeholder rows for an input that found no partner. This pair-making model makes duplicate multiplication and filter placement predictable before any SQL executes.

Logical join semantics and grain

Conceptually, an inner join starts from candidate row pairs and retains those for which the ON predicate is true. A cross join retains the Cartesian product. A left outer join also emits one NULL-extended result for each left row with no true match; right and full joins extend the analogous sides. A self-join aliases one relation into distinct roles, such as employee and manager. SQL is bag-based by default, so duplicate input rows remain and duplicate matches multiply.

State grain and keys before querying. If R has a_k rows and S has b_k rows for join key k, an equality inner join contributes a_k b_k rows. A many-to-one enrichment requires at most one right row for each key. Primary, unique, and foreign-key constraints make part of this contract executable, but historical or staged data may violate it before constraints are applied. Measure row counts, distinct keys, maximum multiplicity, and unmatched keys.

A semi join asks whether a match exists and returns each qualifying left row once; `EXISTS` expresses it. An anti join returns left rows for which no match exists using `NOT EXISTS`. Joining solely to filter can duplicate left rows when multiple matches exist, so existence queries are semantically safer. `DISTINCT` after a wrong join hides evidence and can discard legitimate duplicate facts.

NULL, predicates, and outer-join filters

SQL uses three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL usually produce UNKNOWN rather than true or false. Join matching retains only TRUE predicates, so two NULL keys do not ordinarily match under equality. If missing-key equivalence is required, use a dialect-supported null-safe comparison and document why; coalescing to a sentinel risks colliding with real data.

Predicate location matters with outer joins. A right-table condition in the ON clause restricts which right rows match while retaining unmatched left rows. The same condition in a WHERE clause runs after NULL extension; UNKNOWN rows fail the filter and the query can behave like an inner join for that condition. This is not a performance trick but a change in result semantics.

`NOT IN` is dangerous when its subquery can contain NULL: comparisons can become UNKNOWN and return no rows unexpectedly. `NOT EXISTS` states the anti-join intent and handles correlation explicitly. Also distinguish `COUNT(*)`, which counts NULL-extended rows, from `COUNT(right.key)`, which ignores NULL and can count actual matches. Test empty tables, NULL keys, duplicate keys, and unmatched rows with tiny fixtures.

Nested-loop, hash, and merge join algorithms

The optimizer chooses a physical algorithm for equivalent logical semantics. A nested-loop join scans or probes the inner side for outer rows. It is effective when the outer side is small and an index makes each inner lookup cheap; without an index, scanning a large inner relation repeatedly can be disastrous. A hash join builds a hash table on one equality-join side and probes it with the other. It suits equijoins and depends on build-side size, memory, hash distribution, and spill behavior.

A merge join consumes both inputs in join-key order, advancing through sorted groups. It can handle large sorted inputs and range-like predicates in some engines, but obtaining order may require sorts. Duplicate groups require emitting all matching combinations. Physical details vary by system, so use the actual plan rather than inferring the algorithm from SQL syntax.

Join order has a large search space and intermediate cardinality determines cost. Optimizers estimate selectivity from statistics and constraints; correlated columns, stale statistics, or skewed hot keys can cause severe estimation errors. Push selective filters when semantics allow, project unused columns, index relevant lookup keys, and refresh statistics. Do not force a plan before understanding why estimates differ from actual rows.

Correctness checks and production operation

Turn expected relationships into checks. Before a many-to-one merge, assert right-key uniqueness. Compare input and output row counts under the declared grain. Use match indicators or grouped counts to quantify left-only, right-only, and matched keys. Reconcile additive measures: if an enrichment should not duplicate facts, total amount before and after should agree. Inspect the highest-multiplicity keys rather than averaging away skew.

Normalize key types, whitespace, case, Unicode, and timezone only according to domain rules. Preserve raw identifiers for audit. Define late-arriving dimension behavior, effective-date joins for slowly changing dimensions, and whether missing dimension records fail, quarantine, or produce an unknown member. Temporal joins must prevent using attributes that became known after an event or prediction time.

In production, monitor duplicate rates, unmatched rates, row expansion factor, reconciliation differences, plan shape, estimated-versus-actual rows, spill, and latency. Version contracts and outputs, make jobs idempotent, and retain a rollback dataset. Apply access controls because joining two permitted datasets can create a more sensitive combined view.

Math / formal view

For equality key k with multiplicities a_k in R and b_k in S, inner-join cardinality is Σ_k a_k b_k. A left join adds one output for each left row whose key has b_k=0. A many-to-one left enrichment requires b_k≤1 and therefore preserves the left row count.

Enrich customers with order aggregates

Setup

Customers are one row per customer. Orders are one row per order, and customers with no orders must remain.

Validate customer IDs as unique. Aggregate valid orders to customer grain before joining, producing total spend and order count. Left-join aggregates to customers. Put order eligibility predicates inside the aggregation or ON semantics rather than filtering right columns after NULL extension. Assert output rows and unique customer IDs equal the customer input, inspect match categories, fill a missing aggregate with zero only when it structurally means no qualifying orders, and reconcile total spend with the aggregate input. A missing amount within a matched order remains a data-quality state, not zero.

Conclusion

Pre-aggregation and explicit cardinality keep the output at customer grain, while separate missingness policies preserve meaning.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Model join cardinality with tiny tables and verify preservation, unmatched, duplication, and reconciliation invariants.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def inner_join(left,right,key):
    out=[]
    for lrow in left:
        for rrow in right:
            if lrow.get(key) is not None and lrow.get(key)==rrow.get(key):
                out.append({**lrow,**rrow})
    return out

def left_join(left,right,key):
    out=[]
    right_fields=set().union(*(r.keys() for r in right)) if right else set()
    for lrow in left:
        matches=[r for r in right if lrow.get(key) is not None and lrow.get(key)==r.get(key)]
        if matches:
            out.extend({**lrow,**r} for r in matches)
        else:
            out.append({**{f:None for f in right_fields if f not in lrow},**lrow})
    return out
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE customer(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount REAL); INSERT INTO customer VALUES (1),(2),(3); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,5),(11,1,7),(12,2,3);')
rows=con.execute('SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id), COALESCE(SUM(o.amount),0) FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id').fetchall()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Translate these invariants into warehouse tests: key uniqueness, row expansion, unmatched rates, temporal validity, measure reconciliation, plan regression, and rollback-ready outputs.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert rows == [(1,2,12.0),(2,1,3.0),(3,0,0)]
assert len(rows)==3 and len({r[0] for r in rows})==3
assert sum(r[2] for r in rows)==15.0
dup=con.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id').fetchone()[0]
assert dup==3

Common mistakes

  • A left join always preserves exactly the left row count.

    It preserves every left row but can multiply it when multiple right rows match. Exact preservation also needs a many-to-one contract.

  • Move every filter to WHERE for readability.

    For outer joins, moving a right-side predicate from ON to WHERE can remove NULL-extended unmatched rows and change semantics.

  • Use DISTINCT to fix duplicate join output.

    It hides the cardinality error and may remove legitimate facts. Diagnose key multiplicity and choose an explicit duplicate policy.

Likely follow-ups

  • When is `EXISTS` better than a join?

    When the question is whether a right-side match exists and no right columns are needed; it avoids multiplying left rows by match count.

  • Why can a hash join spill?

    The build-side hash state and buffers exceed available memory, often because cardinality was large or underestimated.

  • How do you debug a join that became slow without SQL changes?

    Compare current and prior plans, statistics, cardinalities, key skew, indexes, spill, and estimated-versus-actual rows.

Production / system-design connection

Declare grain, keys, multiplicity, NULL and unmatched policies, and temporal validity. Enforce constraints where possible and test row counts, uniqueness, match categories, expansion factor, and measure reconciliation. Monitor plan changes, estimate error, hot keys, spill, and latency. Keep statistics and indexes healthy, secure the combined data, and publish versioned idempotent outputs with rollback.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    A key appears 3 times left and 4 times right. How many inner matches?

    Show solution

    Twelve, because every matching left row pairs with every matching right row.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Return customers having at least one failed payment without duplicating customers.

    Show solution

    Use a correlated `EXISTS` subquery or a semi-join pattern rather than joining all failed payments into the customer rows.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A left join loses customers after adding `WHERE orders.status='paid'`. Why?

    Show solution

    Unmatched rows have NULL status, so the WHERE predicate is UNKNOWN and removes them. Put qualifying-order logic in ON or a prefiltered/aggregated relation.

3.2

GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregation

highverified
Roles: ds, de, mle, da

Topic overview

SQL aggregation changes row grain by partitioning input rows into groups and computing one result per group. This chapter explains the logical order from WHERE filtering through GROUP BY, aggregate evaluation, HAVING, SELECT, and final ORDER BY. It distinguishes `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(expression)`, distinct counts, conditional aggregates, and NULL behavior; covers grouping sets, rollups, and the danger of mixing metrics at incompatible grains; and connects exact results to hash and sort aggregation plans. You will learn to declare the output grain, make denominators explicit, avoid integer and divide-by-zero errors, separate row filters from group filters, and reconcile summaries against base data. A worked daily product metric example computes orders, customers, revenue, and failure rate without accidentally weighting joined rows. The production material covers incremental recomputation, late data, slowly changing definitions, approximate distinct counting, spill, skew, data quality, and metric governance. The goal is to make an aggregate a trustworthy semantic contract rather than a compact query whose population and NULL rules are implicit.

Prerequisites

  • sql-joins

Learning objectives

  • Predict grouped output grain and logical clause order for row filters, aggregates, HAVING, and final projection.
  • Choose correct count, distinct, conditional, NULL, denominator, and grouping-set semantics for a metric.
  • Validate and operate aggregations using reconciliation, incremental-window, late-data, plan, spill, and governance controls.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

`GROUP BY` partitions filtered input rows by key and returns one result row per observed group; aggregate functions summarize rows within each group. `WHERE` filters rows before grouping, while `HAVING` filters groups after aggregates. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values, and distinct or conditional metrics must be explicit. Always state the output grain and denominator, because joins or duplicate inputs can change weighting. Physical execution may use hash or sort aggregation and can spill when state exceeds memory.

What you must know

  • Aggregation changes grain
  • WHERE rows, HAVING groups
  • COUNT variants differ
  • Denominators are contracts
  • Reconcile grouped totals

Why this matters

Dashboards, features, experiments, finance, and monitoring depend on aggregates. A plausible number can be wrong because a join duplicated facts, NULLs were skipped, an average averaged averages, or a denominator included the wrong population. Aggregates also concentrate state: millions of high-cardinality groups can exhaust memory or create skew. Interviewers ask GROUP BY syntax, but senior reasoning states the metric grain, eligibility, numerator, denominator, missingness, and validation. Production work adds late arrivals, correction windows, incremental idempotency, and definition versioning so the same metric remains interpretable over time.

Intuition

Imagine sorting eligible rows into labeled buckets. Every grouping-key combination creates a bucket, and each aggregate inspects that bucket. The output has bucket grain, not input-row grain. WHERE decides which cards reach the buckets; HAVING decides which completed buckets are shown. If an earlier join copied a card three times, the aggregate faithfully counts it three times—aggregation cannot repair an incorrect input population.

Output grain and logical query processing

Start by writing 'one output row per ...'. Every selected non-aggregate expression must be functionally determined by the grouping keys under the database's rules. Without GROUP BY, aggregates treat eligible rows as one group and commonly return one row even for empty input; specific aggregate results on empty sets differ, with count returning zero while many others return NULL.

A useful logical order is FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, aggregate computation, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, and LIMIT, though optimizers may physically reorder equivalent work. WHERE cannot reference the aggregate result at its query level because grouping has not occurred. HAVING can. Use a subquery when a later row-level stage must filter a derived aggregate alias.

Grouping by too many columns preserves a finer grain than intended; grouping by too few combines populations. Selecting an arbitrary representative column is unsafe even if a permissive dialect allows it. Functional dependencies and keys can justify omitted columns, but portability and clarity often favor explicit grouping or a dimension join after aggregation.

Counts, NULLs, conditional metrics, and denominators

`COUNT(*)` counts input rows in the group, including rows whose individual columns are NULL. `COUNT(x)` counts rows where x is non-NULL. `COUNT(DISTINCT x)` counts distinct non-NULL x values, which can be expensive and has dialect-specific multi-column forms. `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, and `MAX` generally ignore NULL inputs and may return NULL for an empty eligible set. Decide whether NULL means unknown, not applicable, or structural absence before coalescing.

Conditional aggregation expresses multiple metrics over one population through `FILTER (WHERE ...)` where supported or `CASE` expressions. For a rate, explicitly define eligible denominator and qualifying numerator, cast to an appropriate numeric type, and protect zero denominators with `NULLIF` or a policy. A NULL rate for no eligible observations is often more honest than zero.

Avoid averaging precomputed group averages unless groups should receive equal weight. To recover the overall mean, combine sum and count or use a weighted average. Ratios are especially sensitive to grain: sum numerators and denominators at the correct base grain, then divide, rather than averaging row-level or subgroup ratios accidentally.

Distinctness, rollups, windows, and compatible grains

`GROUPING SETS`, `ROLLUP`, and `CUBE` produce multiple aggregation grains in one query. Their subtotal NULLs may represent 'all values' rather than a missing key, so use grouping metadata to distinguish them. These constructs can be efficient and consistent but require clear labels and downstream grain awareness.

An aggregate collapses rows; a window aggregate retains one output per current row. Use GROUP BY for one row per group and a window function when a group statistic must align back to detail rows. Joining multiple independently aggregated tables can create a fanout if they are not first reduced to compatible keys. Aggregate each fact source to the target grain before combining metrics.

Exact distinct counts require state proportional to observed values in a straightforward plan. Approximate structures can trade controlled error for bounded memory at large scale, but the metric must be labeled approximate and its merge/window guarantees documented. Deduplicating before aggregation needs an explicit identity and survivor policy; `DISTINCT` is not a substitute for event-idempotency design.

Execution, incremental updates, and metric governance

Hash aggregation maintains a table of group states and is effective when groups fit memory. Sort aggregation orders rows by grouping keys and scans runs; it may exploit existing order and spill through external sorting. High-cardinality or skewed groups affect memory, parallel balance, and spill. Plans and implementation vary, so inspect actual nodes, estimates, memory, and disk use.

Incremental aggregation must define source watermark, correction window, and idempotency. Appending a recomputed day can duplicate results; merge/upsert by a stable grain and version. Late or corrected facts require recomputing affected partitions or supporting retractions. Distinct-state mergeability and non-additive metrics complicate incremental rollups. Store additive components such as sum and count where later recombination is expected.

Govern metrics as versioned definitions: owner, grain, eligibility, dimensions, numerator, denominator, timezone, currency/unit, late-data behavior, privacy threshold, and quality checks. Monitor base rows, group cardinality, NULL rates, reconciliation totals, freshness, plan spill, and abrupt distribution changes. Preserve backfills and previous versions for audit and rollback.

Math / formal view

For groups G_k partitioning eligible rows, SUM_k=Σ_{i∈G_k}x_i and AVG_k=SUM_k/N_k over non-NULL eligible x. Overall average across groups is (Σ_k SUM_k)/(Σ_k N_k), not generally the unweighted mean of AVG_k. A rate is Σ indicators(numerator condition)/Σ indicators(denominator eligibility), with explicit zero-denominator policy.

Daily product metrics at product-day grain

Setup

Orders contain product, customer, amount, status, and event date; retries have already been deduplicated by order ID.

Filter to the reporting date and valid event policy, then group by date and product. Compute `COUNT(*)` as order rows, `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` as customers, conditional successful revenue, and failed eligible orders divided by eligible orders using numeric casting and `NULLIF`. Do not join a one-to-many tag table before aggregation unless its fanout is intended. Assert one row per product-date, reconcile total qualifying revenue with the filtered base, test no-order and all-NULL amounts, and record exact distinct cost. Persist the numerator and denominator alongside the rate for audit and later weighted rollup.

Conclusion

The metric remains recomposable and diagnosable because its grain, population, missingness, and additive components are explicit.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute metrics in SQLite and verify grain, NULL, denominator, and reconciliation behavior.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def grouped_sum(rows,key,value):
    out={}
    for row in rows:
        group=row[key]
        if row[value] is not None: out[group]=out.get(group,0)+row[value]
    return out
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE orders(product TEXT, customer TEXT, amount REAL, status TEXT); INSERT INTO orders VALUES ("a","u1",10,"ok"),("a","u2",NULL,"failed"),("b","u1",5,"ok");')
rows=con.execute('SELECT product, COUNT(*) n, COUNT(amount) observed, SUM(CASE WHEN status="ok" THEN amount ELSE 0 END) revenue, 1.0*SUM(status="failed")/NULLIF(COUNT(*),0) fail_rate FROM orders GROUP BY product ORDER BY product').fetchall()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Persist versioned grain plus additive numerator/denominator components, reconcile against base data, handle late corrections idempotently, and monitor group cardinality, NULLs, and spill.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert rows == [('a',2,1,10.0,0.5),('b',1,1,5.0,0.0)]
assert len({row[0] for row in rows}) == len(rows)
assert sum(row[3] for row in rows) == 15.0
assert grouped_sum([{'g':'a','x':1},{'g':'a','x':None},{'g':'b','x':2}],'g','x') == {'a':1,'b':2}

Common mistakes

  • `COUNT(column)` counts table rows.

    It excludes rows where that column is NULL; use `COUNT(*)` for rows and choose distinctness deliberately.

  • WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable filters.

    WHERE filters input rows before grouping; HAVING filters completed groups and can reference aggregates.

  • Average subgroup averages to get the total average.

    That weights every group equally. Combine sums and counts unless equal group weighting is the intended estimand.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does a left join do to `COUNT(*)` for an unmatched left row?

    The NULL-extended joined row still exists, so `COUNT(*)` is one; `COUNT(right.primary_key)` is zero.

  • Why can aggregation spill to disk?

    Group state or sort runs exceed available memory, often due to high cardinality, wide state, or underestimated groups.

  • When should you retain numerator and denominator?

    For audit, correct weighted rollups, uncertainty, and debugging; a stored ratio alone loses information.

Production / system-design connection

Version metric grain, eligibility, dimensions, NULL rules, numerator, denominator, timezone, units, and exact/approximate status. Build idempotent incremental recomputation with late-data correction. Test uniqueness, base-to-summary reconciliation, zero denominators, and fanout. Monitor group cardinality, freshness, NULLs, spill, skew, and definition changes, and retain additive components plus rollback-ready outputs.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    How do `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(amount)` differ?

    Show solution

    The first counts eligible rows; the second counts only rows where amount is non-NULL.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Compute a global rate from per-region successes and trials.

    Show solution

    Sum successes across regions and divide by summed trials. Do not unweightedly average regional rates unless equal region weight is intended.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Revenue doubles after joining product tags before grouping. Why?

    Show solution

    The one-to-many tag join duplicated each order across tags. Aggregate orders first or allocate measures with an explicit multi-tag policy.

3.3

Window Functions

very highverified
Roles: ds, de, mle, da

Topic overview

Window functions calculate across related rows while preserving one output row for each current input row. They power ranking, deduplication, running totals, moving statistics, session comparisons, and change detection without collapsing detail through GROUP BY. This chapter separates partition, ordering, peer groups, and window frame; contrasts `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, and `DENSE_RANK`; explains `LAG`, `LEAD`, and aggregate windows; and shows why default frames can make `LAST_VALUE` or cumulative aggregates surprising. You will learn SQL's logical stage constraints, use a subquery to filter window outputs, make tie ordering deterministic, and prevent future leakage in time-based features. A worked event example selects the latest valid row per entity and verifies ties. The performance sections cover sorts, indexes, partition skew, memory, spill, named windows, and incremental limits. The goal is to reason about the exact row set visible to every function, rather than assuming `PARTITION BY` alone defines the calculation. This framing also makes code review, boundary testing, historical reproducibility, and cross-dialect migration more reliable when defaults differ.

Prerequisites

  • sql-aggregation
  • sorting-searching

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish result partition, peer order, and ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS frame for common window functions.
  • Choose ranking, offset, cumulative, rolling, and deduplication patterns with deterministic ordering and NULL policies.
  • Prevent temporal leakage and diagnose window plans, sorts, skew, spill, and incremental limitations.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A window function computes over rows related to the current row but does not collapse them. `PARTITION BY` resets groups, `ORDER BY` defines sequence and peers, and the frame defines which ordered rows an aggregate-like window sees. `ROW_NUMBER` is unique order, `RANK` leaves gaps across ties, and `DENSE_RANK` does not. Window functions logically run after WHERE, grouping, and HAVING, so filter their results in an outer query. Always specify deterministic tie-breakers and an explicit frame for running or rolling calculations.

What you must know

  • Windows preserve row grain
  • Partition, order, and frame differ
  • Peers affect ranks and RANGE
  • Filter window outputs later
  • Temporal frames must exclude the future

Why this matters

Window functions replace complex self-joins for many analytics and feature tasks, but compact syntax can hide wrong populations. An incomplete ORDER BY makes deduplication nondeterministic. A default peer-aware frame includes tied future-looking rows. A rolling feature can leak later events into training. Large skewed partitions force sorts or spill. Interviews ask ranking differences, while production reviews should also demand stable ordering, event-time availability, frame endpoints, NULL behavior, and validation at partition boundaries.

Intuition

GROUP BY packs each bucket into one summary row. A window keeps every card on the table but lets the current card look sideways at a declared neighborhood. Partition chooses the table section, ordering lines cards up, and frame draws the neighborhood around the current card. Ranking functions mainly use peers and order; aggregate windows use the frame. Confusing those layers is the source of most window bugs.

Partition, order, peers, and frame

The `OVER` clause defines a window. `PARTITION BY` divides result rows into independent partitions; omitting it uses one partition. Window `ORDER BY` defines order inside each partition and identifies peers—rows equal on all ordering expressions. It does not guarantee final display order, which requires query-level ORDER BY. Add a stable unique tie-breaker when row identity or reproducibility matters.

A frame is a subset around the current row, described with `ROWS`, `RANGE`, or `GROUPS` and boundaries such as unbounded preceding, a finite offset, current row, or following. `ROWS` counts physical ordered rows. `RANGE` and `GROUPS` treat peer/order values differently. When ORDER BY is present, default frames in PostgreSQL include rows from the partition start through the current row's last peer, which can surprise aggregate windows.

Ranking and offset functions have function-specific behavior and do not all use frames the same way. Aggregate functions used with OVER aggregate the frame. State all three dimensions even when defaults happen to work. Reuse a named WINDOW clause when several functions need exactly the same partition/order definition, while checking whether their frame needs differ.

Ranking, offsets, and deterministic deduplication

`ROW_NUMBER` assigns consecutive unique positions according to window order; peers still receive different numbers, and their order is nondeterministic without a tie-breaker. `RANK` gives peers the same rank and leaves gaps afterward. `DENSE_RANK` gives peers the same rank without gaps. `NTILE` divides ordered rows into a requested number of buckets, whose sizes may differ. Choose based on product semantics rather than presentation.

`LAG` and `LEAD` access offset rows and are useful for deltas, previous states, and interval boundaries. Define partition, sequence, and what a missing neighbor means. A default value can obscure whether the neighbor was absent or truly had that value. Time difference calculations should use typed timestamps and an event ordering that resolves identical times.

For latest-row deduplication, compute row number partitioned by business ID and ordered by event timestamp descending plus ingestion/version and a unique ID, then keep row number one in an outer query. This encodes a survivor policy. If equal timestamps can represent distinct facts, deduplication may be wrong. Keep metrics for duplicates and conflicting payloads rather than silently dropping them.

Running totals, rolling windows, and leakage

A cumulative sum commonly uses `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` with deterministic order. A finite moving calculation uses a frame such as a number of preceding rows, but 'last seven rows' is not 'last seven days' when events are irregular. Range-based interval frames can express time ranges in supporting dialects, or a calendar spine and explicit join can define expected periods.

`LAST_VALUE` with the default frame often returns the current row or last peer, not the final partition value, because the frame ends at the current peer. Use an explicit full-partition frame when the business question asks for the partition's final row—and ensure using it is not future leakage. Similarly, centered or following frames deliberately see future rows and are invalid for online features unless the prediction timestamp includes them.

For ML and forecasting, define the information cutoff. A feature at time t may include events strictly before t, or through t if the current event is available; the choice affects frame end and tie order. Validate features by simulating historical execution at each cutoff, not only checking the final table.

Logical evaluation and physical execution

Window functions logically run after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING and before final ORDER BY. They can appear in SELECT and ORDER BY at their query level, so filtering on a window result requires a subquery or dialect-specific qualifier. Aggregation can feed a window function in the same query level because grouping occurs first; a window result cannot feed a same-level aggregate.

Execution commonly requires data ordered by partition and order keys. An existing compatible index or earlier plan order may reduce sorting, but filtering, joins, multiple incompatible windows, or cost choices can introduce sorts. Large or skewed partitions consume memory and may spill. Align compatible window specifications, select only required columns, filter eligible rows before the window where semantics allow, and inspect actual plans.

Window results are difficult to maintain incrementally when a late row changes ranks or all subsequent cumulative values. Define correction windows and recomputation boundaries. Monitor partition sizes, peer/tie rates, sort and spill, late events, and nondeterministic conflicts. Version feature/order definitions and preserve source cutoffs for reproducibility.

Math / formal view

Within partition P ordered by key, ROW_NUMBER assigns 1..|P|; RANK(row)=1+number of rows with strictly smaller order key, while DENSE_RANK is 1+number of distinct smaller keys. For explicit cumulative ROWS frame, C_i=Σ_{j=1}^i x_j. A k-row moving frame uses indexes max(1,i-k+1)..i, which is not necessarily a fixed time interval.

Select the latest valid event per entity

Setup

Events may share an event timestamp because of retries; ingestion sequence and event ID provide deterministic resolution.

Filter invalid events first. Compute `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY event_time DESC, ingestion_seq DESC, event_id DESC)`. In an outer query keep row number one. Assert one output row per entity, inspect peer/conflict counts, and test NULL timestamps according to explicit placement. For historical features, restrict eligible events to the prediction cutoff before ranking; otherwise a future correction can become the selected row and leak. Compare results with a grouped maximum plus join only after accounting for duplicate maxima.

Conclusion

The window pattern combines selection and an auditable survivor policy, but temporal eligibility must be applied before the ranking.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Run SQLite window queries and verify ranking ties, latest-row determinism, cumulative frames, and row preservation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def row_number(rows,partition_key,order_key):
    groups={}
    for row in rows: groups.setdefault(row[partition_key],[]).append(row)
    out=[]
    for group in groups.values():
        for number,row in enumerate(sorted(group,key=order_key),1): out.append({**row,'row_number':number})
    return out
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE events(entity TEXT, ts INTEGER, seq INTEGER, value INTEGER); INSERT INTO events VALUES ("a",10,1,5),("a",10,2,7),("a",20,1,3),("b",5,1,4);')
rows=con.execute('SELECT entity,ts,seq,value, ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts DESC,seq DESC) rn, SUM(value) OVER(PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts,seq ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) running FROM events ORDER BY entity,ts,seq').fetchall()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Add deterministic IDs, explicit frame and NULL semantics, cutoff tests, plan/spill monitoring, partition limits, and correction-window recomputation for late data.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert len(rows)==4
latest=[row for row in rows if row[4]==1]
assert {(r[0],r[1],r[2]) for r in latest} == {('a',20,1),('b',5,1)}
a=[r for r in rows if r[0]=='a']
assert [r[5] for r in a] == [5,12,15]
assert len({(r[0],r[4]) for r in rows})==len(rows)

Common mistakes

  • `PARTITION BY` defines a rolling window frame.

    It defines independent partitions. ORDER BY and the frame clause determine ordered neighborhoods within each partition.

  • `ROW_NUMBER` makes duplicate ties deterministic.

    It assigns unique numbers, but peer order is unspecified unless ORDER BY includes a deterministic tie-breaker.

  • Default `LAST_VALUE` returns the final partition value.

    With common default frames it often ends at the current row's peer group. Specify the intended full frame explicitly.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do RANK and DENSE_RANK differ?

    Both share a rank across peers; RANK leaves gaps equal to prior peer-group size, while DENSE_RANK increments by one distinct order value.

  • Why filter window results in a subquery?

    Window evaluation occurs after same-level WHERE and HAVING, so those clauses cannot reference the window result at that level.

  • How can a rolling feature leak?

    A following or full-partition frame, or ranking before the historical cutoff filter, can use events not available at prediction time.

Production / system-design connection

Specify partition, deterministic order, peer policy, frame type/endpoints, NULL placement, and information cutoff. Test empty/singleton partitions, ties, late events, and boundaries. Inspect sorts, compatible windows, partition skew, memory, and spill. Version dedup and feature survivor rules, recompute affected windows on corrections, and monitor conflict/tie rates plus temporal leakage checks.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Scores 100,100,90 receive what RANK and DENSE_RANK values?

    Show solution

    RANK gives 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Write the conceptual frame for a cumulative sum excluding future rows.

    Show solution

    Partition as needed, deterministic ORDER BY, and `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Latest-row selection changes between runs for duplicate timestamps. Why?

    Show solution

    The window order has peers without a unique tie-breaker. Add ingestion/version and stable ID according to a documented survivor policy.
