3.4

CTEs & Subqueries

mediumverified
Roles: ds, de, mle, da

Topic overview

Subqueries and common table expressions (CTEs) name intermediate relational results. They can clarify a complex transformation, express existence and scalar lookup, isolate a change of grain, or recursively traverse a hierarchy. They do not automatically make a query faster, and their evaluation or materialization behavior depends on the database, version, references, volatility, and optimizer. This chapter develops scalar, row, table, correlated, `EXISTS`, `IN`, and derived-table forms; explains NULL-sensitive anti-joins; shows how non-recursive CTEs support readable stage contracts; and traces the anchor-and-recursive-term working-table model. You will learn when correlation creates repeated work, when an optimizer can decorrelate or inline, how to guard scalar cardinality, and how to bound cycles and depth in recursive queries. A worked funnel example computes one row per user at each stage before combining them. Production sections cover plan inspection, repeated references, temporary materialization, recursion safety, transaction snapshots, naming, testing, and portability. The objective is to structure reasoning without treating query syntax as an execution directive.

Prerequisites

  • sql-joins
  • sql-aggregation

Learning objectives

  • Choose scalar, table, correlated, EXISTS, anti-join, derived-table, or CTE form from result cardinality and semantics.
  • Trace recursive CTE anchor and working-table iterations while enforcing termination, cycle, and depth rules.
  • Inspect optimization, inlining, materialization, repeated work, and snapshot behavior instead of assuming syntax determines performance.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A subquery is a query embedded in another expression or table expression; it may be uncorrelated or reference outer rows. `EXISTS` is ideal for semi-join logic, and `NOT EXISTS` for anti-join logic that avoids NULL surprises. A CTE names a query result for the following statement and improves staged reasoning, but whether it is inlined or materialized is engine- and query-dependent. A recursive CTE combines an anchor with a recursive term evaluated against a working table until no new rows remain, so termination and cycle controls are essential.

What you must know

  • Cardinality selects subquery form
  • EXISTS expresses membership
  • CTE names a relational stage
  • Materialization is not guaranteed
  • Recursive queries need termination

Why this matters

Complex analytics often change grain several times: filter facts, aggregate to entity, rank events, and combine metrics. Named stages can make these contracts reviewable. Poor use can instead hide an accidental many-row scalar result, execute a correlated lookup repeatedly, or materialize a huge intermediate. Recursive queries can loop or explode on cyclic or high-branching data. Interview questions often contrast CTEs and subqueries; a strong answer says their logical semantics may be equivalent while physical behavior must be verified in the target engine. Production work adds version-specific optimizer behavior, snapshot consistency, and safety bounds.

Intuition

A subquery is a relation or value-producing question inside another question. Correlation means the inner question receives parameters from each outer row. A CTE gives an intermediate relation a name so the query reads as a pipeline of grain changes. A recursive CTE starts with seed rows, repeatedly expands the newest frontier, and stops when the frontier is empty—similar to graph traversal managed by the database.

Subquery forms, cardinality, and NULL semantics

A scalar subquery appears where one value is expected and must return at most one row; zero rows usually yield NULL, while multiple rows are an error. Make uniqueness or aggregation explicit rather than relying on current data. A table subquery appears in FROM and has a relational schema. Row and array forms are dialect-specific. `IN` compares against a set-like result, while `EXISTS` tests whether at least one row satisfies a correlated condition and does not need to project useful columns.

A correlated subquery references columns from an outer query level. Logically it can be evaluated per outer row, although an optimizer may decorrelate it into a join or other plan. Correlation is expressive for existence, latest-related-value, and conditional logic, but performance depends on available indexes, cardinality, and decorrelation. Inspect the plan and actual loop counts.

For anti-membership, `NOT IN` can return UNKNOWN when its input contains NULL, producing surprising empty results. `NOT EXISTS` with an explicit equality predicate usually states the intent safely. Do not coalesce NULL keys to a sentinel without proving the sentinel cannot be real. Test empty subqueries, NULLs, duplicates, zero-row scalar results, and multi-row scalar violations.

Non-recursive CTEs as stage contracts

A non-recursive `WITH name AS (query)` creates a named relation visible to the following statement. Use names that state grain and meaning, such as `eligible_orders`, `customer_totals`, or `ranked_events`. Select only needed columns and assert the key of each stage mentally or through data tests. This makes fanout and denominator changes easier to review than one deeply nested expression.

A CTE is not inherently a temporary table, cache, or optimization. Current PostgreSQL can fold a side-effect-free, non-recursive, singly referenced CTE into the parent query, while multiple references and explicit materialization controls affect behavior. Other engines differ. Materialization can prevent repeated computation and create a useful boundary, or it can write and scan a large intermediate and block predicate pushdown. Inlining can enable global optimization, or repeat expensive work.

If an intermediate is reused across statements, needs indexes, or is too important to recompute, a temporary or persisted table may be clearer. That introduces lifecycle, transaction, cleanup, statistics, and concurrency concerns. Choose the artifact from its lifetime and reuse contract, not because CTE syntax feels modular.

Recursive CTE evaluation, traversal, and cycles

A recursive CTE has a non-recursive anchor and a recursive term combined by `UNION ALL` or `UNION`. Conceptually the anchor populates a result and working table. Each iteration evaluates the recursive term using the current working rows, appends produced rows, and replaces the working table until it is empty. SQL syntax is recursive while evaluation is iterative.

Hierarchy queries carry node ID, parent/path, depth, and accumulated values. `UNION` removes duplicate whole rows and can sometimes halt repeated states, but it is not a general cycle policy when depth or path differs. Track visited IDs in a path, use engine cycle syntax where available, validate the graph as acyclic when that is a domain invariant, and enforce depth or row limits. A cycle should produce a diagnostic rather than silently truncating if correctness matters.

Search output order is not automatically breadth-first or depth-first; compute an order key and apply final ORDER BY according to the engine's supported pattern. High fanout can grow exponentially even without cycles. Bound roots, depth, total rows, and time for interactive queries. Index the recursive join key and inspect iteration and row growth.

Planning, validation, and production use

Equivalent SQL forms can yield the same optimized plan, and similar-looking forms can differ because of NULL, duplicate, volatility, or cardinality semantics. Compare plans with representative parameters. For correlated work, inspect outer loops and inner rows. For CTEs, check whether materialized, how often scanned, whether predicates push down, and how estimates compare with actual rows. Avoid embedding version-specific optimizer folklore in permanent style rules.

Test every stage's grain, key uniqueness, row counts, and reconciliation. A scalar stage requires zero-or-one proof; an entity aggregate requires one row per entity; an existence stage should not multiply the outer relation. For recursive output, validate maximum depth, unique path semantics, cycle cases, orphan nodes, multiple roots, and deterministic ordering.

Production queries run under a snapshot and transaction context. Repeated separate statements may see different data depending on isolation, while one statement's CTE stages ordinarily share the statement view. Monitor runtime, temporary bytes, repeated scans, recursion rows/depth, and failure limits. Version SQL and expected plans carefully, but alert primarily on resource and correctness regressions rather than exact plan text.

Math / formal view

For a correlated outer relation R, naive logical evaluation can cost Σ_{r∈R} cost(Q(r)); decorrelation may transform this into set-oriented joins. A recursive CTE defines R_0=anchor and R_{i+1}=recursive(R_i); the result is the union of generated iterations until the working set is empty, subject to duplicate and cycle semantics.

Build a conversion funnel from staged entity-grain CTEs

Setup

Raw events contain many rows per user. The report needs one row per user with first view, signup, and purchase times.

Create `eligible_events` with the date and quality policy. Create one CTE per stage grouped to user with minimum timestamp. Start from the intended user population and left-join each one-row-per-user stage. Compute ordering checks so signup must not precede view and purchase must not precede signup. Assert uniqueness at every stage, output row preservation, and stage counts that cannot increase down the funnel. Inspect whether the engine inlines stages; persist a stage only if reuse or cost evidence justifies it. Keep event-time cutoffs explicit to avoid future data in historical cohorts.

Conclusion

Named stages improve review because each changes grain under an explicit contract; they do not remove the need to validate cardinality or examine the plan.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Use SQLite CTEs for staged grain and recursion, verifying uniqueness, anti-join NULL safety, order, and cycle bounds.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def expand(children,roots,max_depth):
    out=[]; frontier=[(root,0,(root,)) for root in roots]
    while frontier:
        node,depth,path=frontier.pop(0); out.append((node,depth))
        if depth==max_depth: continue
        for child in children.get(node,[]):
            if child in path: raise ValueError('cycle')
            frontier.append((child,depth+1,path+(child,)))
    return out
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE edge(parent TEXT, child TEXT); INSERT INTO edge VALUES ("a","b"),("a","c"),("b","d");')
rows=con.execute('WITH RECURSIVE tree(node,depth,path) AS (SELECT "a",0,"/a/" UNION ALL SELECT e.child,t.depth+1,t.path||e.child||"/" FROM tree t JOIN edge e ON e.parent=t.node WHERE t.depth<10 AND instr(t.path,"/"||e.child||"/")=0) SELECT node,depth FROM tree ORDER BY depth,node').fetchall()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Add stage-grain tests, recursion row/depth/time limits, cycle diagnostics, plan and temp-I/O monitoring, and engine-version checks for materialization behavior.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert rows == [('a',0),('b',1),('c',1),('d',2)]
assert expand({'a':['b','c'],'b':['d']},['a'],10)==rows
try: expand({'a':['b'],'b':['a']},['a'],10)
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('cycle must fail')
assert len({node for node,_ in rows})==len(rows)

Common mistakes

  • A CTE always materializes once and is therefore faster.

    Inlining and materialization depend on engine, version, query properties, and references. Verify the actual plan.

  • `NOT IN (subquery)` is equivalent to `NOT EXISTS` in the presence of NULL.

    A NULL in the IN result can make NOT IN comparisons UNKNOWN. Use explicit anti-join semantics and test NULLs.

  • `UNION` automatically makes every recursive hierarchy cycle-safe.

    Rows with the same node but different path/depth remain distinct. Use explicit visited/cycle logic and bounds.

Likely follow-ups

  • When can a correlated subquery be efficient?

    When the outer relation is small, an indexed probe is selective, or the optimizer decorrelates it into an efficient set plan.

  • When would you force or choose materialization?

    When a costly stable intermediate is reused and the materialization cost is lower than repeated work, after checking memory, pushdown, and plan evidence.

  • How do you stop a recursive CTE on cyclic data?

    Track visited nodes/path or use supported cycle syntax, enforce row/depth/time limits, and return cycle diagnostics according to the contract.

Production / system-design connection

Name stages by grain, validate their keys and reconciliation, and treat materialization as an evidence-based physical choice. Guard scalar cardinality, NULL anti-joins, and recursive cycles/depth/row growth. Inspect actual loops, repeated scans, temp bytes, and pushdown on representative data. Version SQL with engine assumptions, maintain indexes/statistics, and bound untrusted recursion with clear incomplete-result semantics.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What happens when a scalar subquery returns two rows?

    Show solution

    It violates scalar cardinality and the statement errors; prove uniqueness or aggregate according to an explicit policy.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Find customers with no orders when order customer IDs may contain NULL.

    Show solution

    Use `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id)` rather than NULL-sensitive NOT IN.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A recursive hierarchy query never finishes after a new parent relation is loaded. What do you inspect?

    Show solution

    Look for a cycle or explosive fanout, add visited/cycle detection and explicit depth/row limits, and validate hierarchy constraints.

3.5

Transactions & Indexes

mediumverified
Roles: de, mle, da

Topic overview

Transactions group database changes into an atomic unit, while indexes maintain additional access paths that accelerate selected reads at the cost of storage and write work. They solve different problems but interact: an index must remain transactionally consistent, updates create index maintenance and locking or versioning work, and query access paths influence how long a transaction holds resources. This chapter introduces ACID properties, commit and rollback, statement errors, savepoints, idempotent retry boundaries, B-tree and hash-style access, multicolumn order, covering/index-only scans, expression and partial indexes, selectivity, and write amplification. It separates index eligibility from optimizer choice and explains why an index can exist yet be slower than a sequential scan. You will design a transfer transaction with invariants and an index set for a time-filtered status query, then verify rollback and plan behavior. Detailed isolation anomalies are deferred to the dedicated isolation chapter; here the focus is transaction boundaries and index design. Production sections cover long transactions, deadlocks, bloat, online builds, monitoring, migrations, and rollback.

Prerequisites

  • sql-joins
  • big-o

Learning objectives

  • Define atomic transaction boundaries and application-level invariants with commit, rollback, savepoint, and retry behavior.
  • Choose B-tree, multicolumn, covering, expression, or partial index designs from predicates, ordering, selectivity, and write workload.
  • Diagnose index usage and transaction/index operational costs through plans, locks, versions, bloat, build strategy, and monitoring.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A transaction makes a set of operations commit or roll back as one unit and preserves database constraints under the chosen isolation and durability mechanisms. An index is a maintained access structure—commonly a B-tree—that can reduce searched pages for selective equality, range, and ordering queries. Indexes consume storage and add work to inserts, updates, deletes, vacuum/maintenance, and concurrency. Composite order, predicate shape, selectivity, and table size determine usefulness; the optimizer may correctly choose a scan even when an index exists.

What you must know

  • Transaction boundary matches invariant
  • Rollback handles all failure paths
  • Indexes trade reads for writes
  • Composite order follows workload
  • Plan evidence beats index folklore

Why this matters

A transfer that debits without crediting corrupts money; a feature publication that exposes partial partitions corrupts training. Transactions provide a correctness boundary, but applications must choose that boundary and safely retry failures. Indexes can turn a point lookup from scanning a table into a shallow tree probe, yet excessive or poorly ordered indexes slow ingestion and occupy memory and disk. Long transactions retain old versions and block maintenance. Interview questions often list ACID and index types; engineering requires invariant, workload, recovery, concurrency, migration, and measurement reasoning.

Intuition

A transaction is a sealed change set: observers should see an allowed before or after state, not a half-applied business action. An index is the database's maintained lookup map. Like a book index, it accelerates questions organized by its leading entries but must be updated whenever indexed content changes. A map for every imaginable question becomes heavier than the book itself, so indexes are selected from real query and write patterns.

Transactions, ACID, and application invariants

Atomicity means a transaction's changes take effect together or not at all. Consistency means committed transitions preserve declared constraints and application invariants; the database cannot infer every business rule. Isolation governs interactions among concurrent transactions and has its own dedicated chapter. Durability means a reported commit survives failures according to the system's persistence and replication contract—not that every replica is instantly current.

Begin a transaction at the smallest boundary that contains one invariant-preserving action. Validate inputs, execute changes, check affected-row counts, and commit; on any error, roll back. Some systems mark a transaction failed until rollback after a statement error. Savepoints permit partial rollback inside a transaction but do not justify swallowing integrity failures casually. Keep network calls outside database transactions when possible because unpredictable waits retain connections, locks, and versions.

Retries must repeat the whole logical transaction when the database reports a retryable concurrency failure. Make external effects idempotent or coordinate them with an outbox/inbox pattern; a database rollback cannot undo an already-sent email or remote charge. Use unique idempotency keys and constraints so a client timeout after commit does not duplicate the operation.

B-tree access and alternative indexes

A B-tree keeps sorted keys in balanced pages, supporting logarithmic-height equality and range navigation plus ordered scans. Leaf entries identify table rows or contain enough data for an index-only path when visibility and engine conditions permit. Equality on leading columns followed by a range/order often fits a composite B-tree. The exact prefix rules and skip-scan capabilities vary, so verify target behavior.

Hash indexes focus on equality in systems that support them. Other specialized structures serve text, spatial, array, JSON, or block-range workloads. Index type must match operator classes and predicates. An expression index can support a normalized or computed predicate such as lowercased email, but the query expression and immutability rules must align. A partial index stores rows satisfying a predicate, reducing size and write cost for a stable selective subset; queries must imply that predicate.

A covering index includes columns needed to answer a query without fetching all base rows, but wider entries reduce fanout and increase maintenance. Clustered or table-order relationships affect locality differently by engine. Avoid treating vendor names as universal semantics. Indexes accelerate access paths; they do not replace uniqueness constraints, data validation, or full-text/vector systems where a different retrieval model is needed.

Composite order, selectivity, and write cost

Design indexes from frequent, important query shapes: equality predicates, range predicates, join keys, ordering, returned columns, and table/cardinality distribution. A composite `(tenant_id, event_time)` index supports tenant equality followed by time range and ordered retrieval. Reversing it may suit global time queries but not isolate one tenant efficiently. Separate single-column indexes are not always equivalent to one composite path, though optimizers can combine indexes in some cases.

Selectivity matters. If a predicate returns a large fraction of rows, sequential access can be cheaper than random index probes plus heap fetches. Small tables may be faster to scan. Parameter values can change the best plan. Functions, implicit casts, collation, NULL conditions, and mismatched expressions can prevent the intended access. Use plans with representative values and inspect actual rows and buffers.

Every index adds storage and update work. Inserting must place entries; updating indexed columns may create new entries; deleting leaves maintenance; cache capacity is divided among structures. Redundant indexes compound write amplification. Track index usage but account for rare critical queries and constraint backing before removal. Consolidate only when semantics and plans remain correct.

Concurrency, maintenance, and safe index changes

Transactions and indexes interact through locks, multiversion visibility, and maintenance. An index lookup can find versions that are not visible to the current snapshot; the engine checks visibility. Long-running transactions can prevent cleanup of old versions, increase bloat, and hold locks. Large updates can generate substantial log, replication lag, and index churn. Deadlocks arise from inconsistent resource ordering and should be handled through consistent access order plus retry of a chosen victim.

Index builds consume CPU, I/O, memory, and locks. Online or concurrent build modes reduce blocking but take longer and have failure/retry semantics. Validate the resulting index and plan before relying on it, then remove old structures in a separate rollback-aware step. Schema migrations must account for application versions that overlap deployment.

Monitor transaction age, lock waits, deadlocks, rollback/retry rate, log volume, replication lag, index size, scan/use counts, cache hit, bloat, and query latency. Set statement and idle-transaction timeouts appropriate to workload. Periodically review indexes against workload evidence. A safe change has capacity estimates, staged rollout, and a reversal path.

Math / formal view

A balanced B-tree with fanout b and n entries has height O(log_b n), often only a few page levels. Total write work includes base-row change plus each affected index entry. A composite index orders lexicographically by its columns; efficient navigable ranges depend on constraints over leading order. Transaction atomicity is all-or-nothing, while isolation guarantees require a separate concurrency model.

Transfer balance and index account history

Setup

A transfer debits one account, credits another, records one immutable transfer ID, and serves recent history by account and time.

Start one transaction, insert the unique idempotency key, lock or conditionally update accounts in a consistent ID order, assert both affected-row counts and nonnegative balance policy, insert ledger rows, then commit. Any failure rolls back all database changes. Retry the entire action only for classified transient errors, using the unique transfer ID to recognize an uncertain prior commit. Create a composite history index on `(account_id, occurred_at DESC)` with only carefully selected included columns. Use an actual plan for representative high- and low-activity accounts, and measure write/replication impact before rollout.

Conclusion

The transaction protects the financial invariant while the index serves one validated access pattern; idempotency and operations complete the design.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Use SQLite to verify transaction rollback, uniqueness/idempotency, and a composite index query plan.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def transfer(con,transfer_id,source,target,amount):
    with con:
        con.execute('INSERT INTO transfer(id) VALUES (?)',(transfer_id,))
        changed=con.execute('UPDATE account SET balance=balance-? WHERE id=? AND balance>=?',(amount,source,amount)).rowcount
        if changed!=1: raise ValueError('insufficient or missing source')
        if con.execute('UPDATE account SET balance=balance+? WHERE id=?',(amount,target)).rowcount!=1: raise ValueError('missing target')
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE account(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,balance INTEGER CHECK(balance>=0)); CREATE TABLE transfer(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE history(account_id INTEGER,occurred_at INTEGER,amount INTEGER); CREATE INDEX history_account_time ON history(account_id,occurred_at DESC); INSERT INTO account VALUES (1,100),(2,0);')
transfer(con,'t1',1,2,30)
plan=con.execute('EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT amount FROM history WHERE account_id=? AND occurred_at>=? ORDER BY occurred_at DESC',(1,0)).fetchall()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Add bounded retries, consistent lock order, idempotency/outbox integration, transaction-age monitoring, representative EXPLAIN ANALYZE checks, and reversible online index rollout.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert con.execute('SELECT SUM(balance) FROM account').fetchone()[0]==100
assert con.execute('SELECT balance FROM account ORDER BY id').fetchall()==[(70,),(30,)]
try: transfer(con,'t2',1,99,10)
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('missing target must fail')
assert con.execute('SELECT balance FROM account ORDER BY id').fetchall()==[(70,),(30,)]
assert any('history_account_time' in str(row) for row in plan)

Common mistakes

  • ACID consistency means every business rule is automatically enforced.

    The database preserves constraints and transaction semantics you declare; application invariants still require correct schema and transaction logic.

  • An index always makes matching queries faster.

    Low selectivity, small tables, random fetches, stale statistics, casts, or wide output can make a scan cheaper.

  • Create a single-column index for every filtered column.

    Indexes cost writes and storage, and workload-shaped composite/partial designs may be more useful. Verify plans before adding or removing.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why can a query ignore an available index?

    The cost estimate favors another path due to selectivity, size, clustering, returned rows, predicate mismatch, statistics, or parameter values.

  • What is an index-only scan?

    A path where required columns are available from the index and visibility conditions let the engine avoid or reduce base-table fetches; it is not guaranteed by merely including columns.

  • How do you handle a serialization or deadlock failure?

    Roll back and retry the whole idempotent transaction with bounded backoff, while investigating contention if rates rise.

Production / system-design connection

Keep transactions short, invariant-scoped, and fully rolled back on failure; classify retries and coordinate external effects with idempotency/outbox patterns. Design indexes from important query shapes and representative plans, balancing read latency against write, storage, cache, maintenance, and replication cost. Monitor transaction age, locks, retries, bloat, index use, log volume, and plan regressions. Roll out builds and removals in separate reversible stages.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Why can `(tenant_id,event_time)` serve a tenant time range better than `(event_time,tenant_id)`?

    Show solution

    Equality on the leading tenant key narrows a contiguous index range before scanning ordered event time.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    A request writes the database then calls a payment API inside the transaction. What risk?

    Show solution

    The remote call holds database resources and cannot be undone by rollback. Use idempotent external workflow/outbox coordination and a short database transaction.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    After adding five indexes, ingestion slows and replication lag rises. Why?

    Show solution

    Every row change maintains more index entries and generates additional I/O/log work. Measure usage and consolidate or remove redundant noncritical indexes safely.

3.6

Stored Procedures & Data Pipelines

mediumverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

Stored functions and procedures execute reusable logic close to database data. They can centralize set-based transformations, enforce a privileged interface, reduce application round trips, and make some migrations atomic. They can also hide dependencies, concentrate load, couple code to one dialect, create security-definer escalation, and become an unobservable scheduler disguised as a routine. This chapter distinguishes SQL functions, procedures, triggers, views, and application jobs; explains parameters, result and transaction semantics, volatility and side effects, dynamic SQL and injection, set-oriented implementation, error handling, idempotent batches, and deployment versioning. You will build a small load procedure contract and compare it with an application-orchestrated pipeline. A key principle is separation of concerns: the routine owns a bounded database transaction or transformation, while an orchestrator owns schedules, retries across systems, lineage, backfills, alerts, and human recovery. Because routine capabilities vary strongly by engine, the chapter uses PostgreSQL documentation for concrete examples while clearly labeling portability boundaries.

Prerequisites

  • transactions-indexes
  • sql-ctes-subqueries

Learning objectives

  • Choose among function, procedure, trigger, view, and application job based on invocation, result, side-effect, and transaction needs.
  • Design set-based, parameterized, privilege-safe routines with explicit errors, idempotency, observability, and bounded transaction scope.
  • Deploy and operate database routines within versioned pipelines that support lineage, backfill, testing, rollback, and cross-system orchestration.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A stored routine is versioned logic executed by the database. Functions usually return a value or relation and can participate in queries under engine rules; procedures are called as commands and may support transaction control depending on engine and call context. They are useful for data-local set operations and controlled database interfaces, but not a replacement for workflow orchestration. Keep routines set-based, parameterized, least-privileged, observable, idempotent where retried, and deployed with compatible application and schema versions.

What you must know

  • Routine type follows side effects
  • Keep data-local work set-based
  • Parameterize dynamic SQL
  • Least privilege and search path
  • Orchestration remains external

Why this matters

Moving data-heavy logic to the database can avoid network transfer and use optimized relational execution. A routine can offer one audited operation instead of broad table privileges. But a slow row-by-row procedure can monopolize connections and locks; an unqualified security-definer routine can be exploited through object resolution; hidden triggers make write behavior surprising; and a scheduled procedure has no cross-system lineage or recovery plan. Interviews may focus on definition syntax. Production design must include ownership, transactional boundaries, deployment compatibility, performance, observability, and what happens after partial external failure.

Intuition

A stored routine is an API whose server happens to be the database. That location is powerful when the work is mostly relational and must share one transaction. It is constraining when logic calls many services, requires rich libraries, or evolves independently. Treat the routine like production code: typed inputs, narrow privileges, predictable side effects, tests, metrics, versioning, and a caller that understands retry semantics.

Functions, procedures, triggers, and views

Capabilities vary by database. In current PostgreSQL, a function is invoked within a query or data-manipulation expression and declares a return type; a procedure is invoked with `CALL`, has no function return value, can use output parameters, and under allowed call context may commit or roll back during execution. Other engines use different terminology and restrictions. Check target documentation rather than transporting assumptions.

A view stores a query definition and behaves like a virtual relation; a materialized view stores results with refresh semantics. A trigger runs implicitly on events and can enforce local invariants or auditing but makes side effects less visible. Prefer constraints for declarative integrity, explicit calls for business workflows, and triggers only when unavoidable automatic coupling is understood.

Define routine contract: schema-qualified name, parameter types and defaults, result columns, NULL behavior, privileges, volatility/side effects, exception behavior, transaction ownership, and supported version. Avoid overloading that creates ambiguous calls. Returning sets can keep work relational; scalar loops that issue a query per row often recreate an N+1 problem inside the database.

Set-based implementation, dynamic SQL, and security

Express transformations as set operations so the optimizer can choose joins, aggregation, indexes, and parallel execution. Procedural control is appropriate for bounded branching, metadata operations, or coordination, but row-by-row loops over large tables multiply execution overhead and lock duration. Stage large changes, batch with deterministic keys, and measure plans for the SQL inside routines.

Use typed parameters for values. When identifiers must be dynamic, construct SQL through engine quoting/format facilities and allowlists; value parameterization cannot substitute table names. Never concatenate untrusted text into executable SQL. Validate range and cardinality inputs to prevent unbounded work. Be clear whether a routine sees caller settings, timezone, locale, and search path.

Invoker-rights routines use caller privileges; security-definer routines use owner privileges and need rigorous hardening: minimal owner rights, trusted schema qualification, controlled search path, revoked public execution where appropriate, and audit. A routine can become an authorization boundary only if object resolution and every reachable operation are safe. Do not log secrets or full sensitive parameters.

Transaction ownership, errors, and idempotency

Decide whether the caller or procedure owns the transaction. Nested transaction behavior is usually savepoint-like or unsupported rather than independent commits. A routine called inside an explicit transaction may not be allowed to commit even if procedures can in other contexts. Hidden commits break caller atomicity. Keep one clear owner and document which failures abort the transaction.

Raise domain-specific errors with enough context for diagnosis but not sensitive data. Check affected-row counts and invariants. Do not catch every exception and return success; rollback and observability depend on accurate failure. Separate retryable concurrency or transient conditions from permanent validation failures. Long routines should support cancellation and avoid holding locks during external calls.

Scheduled and retried loads need idempotency. Use a stable run or partition key, write to staging, validate, and merge or swap atomically. Record run status and source version under a transaction that cannot report success before results are visible. If partial commits are intentional for large batches, checkpoints and restart logic must make the weaker atomicity explicit.

Routines inside data pipelines

A database routine can own the database-local transformation boundary. A workflow orchestrator should own schedule, dependencies across warehouses and services, credentials, retries, backfill ranges, concurrency, lineage, alerting, and manual intervention. Calling one giant procedure from cron is not a complete pipeline: it lacks structured state and may rerun blindly after an uncertain timeout.

Version routine definitions in migrations with review and tests. Coordinate application and schema compatibility through expand-and-contract deployment: add a compatible routine/version, deploy callers, observe, then remove the old interface later. `CREATE OR REPLACE` may not allow every signature change and can alter in-flight behavior. Use explicit versioned names when simultaneous callers require different contracts.

Monitor call rate, duration, rows read/written, lock waits, temp/spill, failures by class, retries, and source/output freshness. Capture query identifiers and plans for expensive internal statements. Test permissions, search path, NULLs, empty data, duplicates, reruns, cancellation, deadlocks, and rollback. Keep an application-side fallback or prior routine version until the new path is proven.

Math / formal view

A routine's useful atomic boundary is a transition S→S' that preserves declared invariants or rolls back. Row-at-a-time execution over n rows can issue Theta(n) statements/round trips inside the engine, while one set-based statement lets the optimizer choose a relational plan. Retry safety requires applying the same logical run identifier more than once without duplicating committed effects.

Load a daily aggregate partition idempotently

Setup

An orchestrator calls a database routine for one business date; retries and late corrections are possible.

Accept a typed date and run ID, reject an unbounded range, and acquire a concurrency guard for that partition. Build results into a staging relation using set-based SQL, validate row grain, counts, and reconciliations, then merge or replace the target partition within one transaction. Record source snapshot, definition version, row counts, and success atomically. A retry with the same run ID returns the existing result or safely recomputes according to policy. The orchestrator supplies schedule, backoff, backfill fan-out, alerts, and lineage across upstream and downstream systems.

Conclusion

The procedure gives a reliable database-local transaction, while orchestration remains visible and recoverable outside it.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Model an idempotent set-based partition load in SQLite and verify rerun, rollback, uniqueness, and reconciliation invariants.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def load_day(con,day,run_id):
    with con:
        prior=con.execute('SELECT status FROM run WHERE run_id=?',(run_id,)).fetchone()
        if prior: return prior[0]
        con.execute('INSERT INTO run(run_id,day,status) VALUES (?,?,"running")',(run_id,day))
        con.execute('DELETE FROM daily WHERE day=?',(day,))
        con.execute('INSERT INTO daily(day,customer,total) SELECT day,customer,SUM(amount) FROM event WHERE day=? GROUP BY day,customer',(day,))
        con.execute('UPDATE run SET status="success" WHERE run_id=?',(run_id,))
        return 'success'
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE event(day TEXT,customer TEXT,amount REAL); CREATE TABLE daily(day TEXT,customer TEXT,total REAL,PRIMARY KEY(day,customer)); CREATE TABLE run(run_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,day TEXT,status TEXT); INSERT INTO event VALUES ("2026-01-01","a",2),("2026-01-01","a",3),("2026-01-01","b",4);')
first=load_day(con,'2026-01-01','run-1'); second=load_day(con,'2026-01-01','run-1')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Add explicit privilege tests, concurrency guard, source snapshot/version, affected-row metrics, cancellation, plan monitoring, orchestrator-owned retries, and expand-contract routine deployment.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert first==second=='success'
assert con.execute('SELECT customer,total FROM daily ORDER BY customer').fetchall()==[('a',5.0),('b',4.0)]
assert con.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM run WHERE run_id="run-1"').fetchone()[0]==1
assert con.execute('SELECT SUM(total) FROM daily').fetchone()[0]==con.execute('SELECT SUM(amount) FROM event').fetchone()[0]

Common mistakes

  • Stored procedures are always faster because they run in the database.

    Data locality can help, but row loops, poor plans, locks, and hidden work can be slower. Measure set-based alternatives and end-to-end cost.

  • A security-definer routine is safe because callers cannot access tables directly.

    Unsafe search path, dynamic SQL, excessive owner rights, or callable helpers can escalate privileges. Harden the whole boundary.

  • A scheduled procedure is a complete data pipeline.

    Cross-system dependencies, lineage, retries, backfills, alerts, and recovery still need orchestration and operational state.

Likely follow-ups

  • Function versus procedure in PostgreSQL?

    Functions return a value/relation and are used in queries; procedures are called with CALL and can have transaction-control capabilities under allowed context.

  • When is a trigger appropriate?

    For tightly local automatic behavior that must accompany writes and whose hidden coupling, ordering, performance, and recursion risks are accepted; prefer constraints or explicit workflows where possible.

  • How do you deploy a breaking routine signature change?

    Add a compatible/versioned interface, migrate callers, observe, and remove the old version later rather than replacing it underneath mixed deployments.

Production / system-design connection

Treat routines as least-privileged versioned APIs. Keep large work set-based, parameterize values, harden dynamic identifiers and search path, define transaction and retry ownership, and make loads idempotent by run/partition key. Let an orchestrator manage cross-system workflow. Monitor duration, rows, locks, spill, error class, freshness, and permissions, and use expand-contract rollout with a tested prior-version fallback.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Why is row-by-row procedural SQL often slow?

    Show solution

    It repeats statement/executor overhead and prevents the optimizer from planning the transformation as one relational operation.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Where should a pipeline's cross-service retries and backfill schedule live?

    Show solution

    In an orchestrator; the routine should own a bounded database-local transformation/transaction with an idempotent interface.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A security-definer routine starts resolving an attacker-created table. What likely failed?

    Show solution

    The routine used an unsafe search path or unqualified object names. Pin trusted schemas and minimize owner privileges.

3.7

Database Normalization: 1NF to 3NF

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

Relational normalization uses keys and functional dependencies to place facts where they can be inserted, updated, and deleted without contradictory copies. First, second, and third normal form are not a ritual of splitting tables; they are tests against a declared meaning of attributes. This chapter defines superkeys, candidate keys, prime attributes, determinants, functional and transitive dependencies, then derives 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF). It explains lossless decomposition and dependency preservation, because individually clean-looking tables can still fail to reconstruct the original relation or enforce a rule locally. You will normalize an order-line relation, identify update, insertion, and deletion anomalies, and preserve historical prices rather than incorrectly deriving them from a current product table. The design section connects normalized operational schemas with foreign keys, temporal validity, generated identifiers, JSON, star schemas, materialized views, performance, and governance. The objective is to model one fact once under the correct key, then denormalize only for a measured read or analytics need with explicit ownership and refresh semantics.

Learning objectives

  • Derive candidate keys and functional dependencies from domain semantics rather than sample coincidences.
  • Normalize a relation through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF while checking lossless join and dependency preservation.
  • Choose deliberate denormalization for operational or analytical workloads with integrity, history, refresh, lineage, and performance controls.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Normalization organizes attributes around keys and functional dependencies to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. 1NF requires atomic relation-valued design in the chosen model; 2NF removes dependencies on only part of a composite candidate key; 3NF removes non-key attributes depending transitively on keys, with a formal dependency condition; BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. A decomposition must also be lossless, and dependency preservation is desirable. Denormalize only for a measured workload and define how duplicate facts stay consistent.

What you must know

  • Dependencies come from semantics
  • Candidate keys may be composite
  • Decomposition must be lossless
  • 3NF and BCNF differ
  • Denormalization creates maintenance duty

Why this matters

A table that repeats customer addresses on every order can disagree with itself after one partial update. A design that stores product price only in the current product row can destroy the price actually charged historically. Normalization makes invariants enforceable with keys and foreign keys and reduces write anomalies. Over-normalization or indiscriminate decomposition can create expensive joins and awkward ownership, while warehouse facts and dimensions intentionally optimize a different workload. Interviews often ask form definitions; engineering requires dependency justification, lossless reconstruction, temporal meaning, and a deliberate boundary between source-of-truth data and derived copies.

Intuition

Each stable fact should have one natural home determined by the thing it describes. Customer email belongs with customer identity; quantity for an order line belongs with the order-product line; the charged unit price belongs with that historical transaction, not merely the current catalog. Functional dependencies are sentences like 'order_id determines customer_id.' Normalization groups facts whose determinants belong together and replaces repeated facts with references.

Keys and functional dependencies

For relation R, a functional dependency X→Y means any two valid rows agreeing on attributes X must agree on Y. It is a domain constraint over all valid states, not a pattern inferred safely from one dataset. A superkey determines every attribute. A candidate key is a minimal superkey; one may be chosen as primary, while alternatives remain meaningful unique constraints. Prime attributes belong to at least one candidate key.

Use attribute closure to reason about keys: begin with X and repeatedly add attributes determined by known dependencies until no change. If closure reaches all R, X is a superkey; test minimality by removing each member. Surrogate IDs simplify references but do not erase natural dependencies. If email is unique by business rule, preserve that constraint even when customer_id is primary.

Dependencies can be full, partial, or transitive. With composite key (order_id, product_id), quantity may depend on the full key while order_date depends only on order_id. If order_id determines customer_id and customer_id determines customer_name, then customer_name is transitively determined by order_id. Record assumptions such as effective time, tenant, locale, or version; dependencies often need those attributes to be true.

1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF

First normal form treats each row/column intersection as a value from its declared domain and avoids repeating groups in one relation. 'Atomic' is model-relative: a timestamp is one value even though it has components. Storing comma-separated IDs prevents constraints and relational operations; a proper child relation models multiple values. JSON can be valid for an opaque document but is not a shortcut when individual elements need relational integrity and queries.

Second normal form applies to relations with composite candidate keys and removes non-prime attributes that depend on a proper subset of a candidate key. Split order-level attributes from order-line attributes. Third normal form can be stated: for every nontrivial X→A, X is a superkey or A is prime. The common intuition removes non-key facts depending on other non-key facts.

BCNF is stricter: every determinant X of a nontrivial dependency must be a superkey. A 3NF relation can violate BCNF when the dependent attribute is prime. BCNF removes more redundancy but may sacrifice dependency preservation; 3NF synthesis is sometimes selected so constraints remain enforceable without joining decomposed tables. Do not claim a form without listing candidate keys and dependencies.

Lossless join, dependency preservation, and anomalies

A decomposition must be lossless: joining decomposed relations on their common attributes must recreate exactly the valid original relation, not add spurious combinations. For a binary decomposition R into R1 and R2, a useful lossless condition under dependencies is that the common attributes functionally determine all of R1 or all of R2. Foreign keys and uniqueness often embody this relationship. Test the theory, not only current sample output.

Dependency preservation means original constraints can be enforced by checking individual decomposed relations without reconstructing them. It reduces enforcement cost and complexity. A BCNF decomposition can be lossless yet fail to preserve a dependency, motivating a 3NF design or an additional constraint mechanism.

Redundancy creates update anomalies when copies disagree, insertion anomalies when one fact cannot be stored without another, and deletion anomalies when deleting one fact accidentally erases the last copy of another. Normalization reduces these structural hazards but transactions, constraints, and application logic still matter. A normalized schema with no foreign keys can still contain orphaned references.

Temporal facts, analytics, and deliberate denormalization

Facts change over time. An order line's charged price is a transaction fact and should remain even if the product catalog price changes. Customer address 'at order time' differs from current address. Model effective dates or immutable snapshots according to the question. A dependency such as product_id→price may be false without effective_time or version. Soft deletion and slowly changing dimensions likewise modify keys and uniqueness scopes.

Operational schemas favor integrity and focused updates; analytical star schemas intentionally denormalize dimensions around fact tables for scan and reporting patterns. This is not failed normalization when the warehouse is a derived, governed model with declared grain, conformed dimensions, history rules, and rebuildable lineage. Materialized views and caches are also duplicate representations and need refresh, invalidation, and reconciliation.

Denormalize only after measuring a workload and identifying the source of truth. Document duplicate columns, owner, sync mechanism, staleness bound, failure behavior, and backfill. Monitor constraint violations, orphan rates, reconciliation, join latency, and refresh lag. Schema evolution should expand compatibly, backfill, validate, switch readers/writers, then contract with rollback available.

Math / formal view

Given functional dependencies F, closure X+ is the set of attributes derivable from X; X is a superkey when X+=R. 3NF requires for every nontrivial X→A that X be a superkey or A be prime. BCNF requires X be a superkey. Binary decomposition R→R1,R2 is lossless under F when (R1∩R2)→R1 or (R1∩R2)→R2 follows from F.

Normalize orders and preserve charged price

Setup

One table repeats order date, customer name, product name, current price, charged price, and quantity for every order line.

Declare `(order_id, product_id, line_number)` or a stable line ID as the order-line key. Dependencies include order_id→customer_id,order_date; customer_id→current customer attributes; product_id→current product attributes under a version; line key→quantity,charged_unit_price. Decompose into customer, product/version, order, and order_line with uniqueness and foreign keys. Keep charged price on order_line because it is determined by the transaction line and must not change with the catalog. Verify the joins are lossless under keys and that revenue reconciles. Test a product-price change and customer deletion policy without mutating historical facts.

Conclusion

Normalization separates current entity facts from immutable transaction facts, reducing contradictions while preserving the history the business actually needs.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Use SQLite constraints to model normalized orders and verify uniqueness, references, historical price stability, and revenue reconciliation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def closure(attributes,dependencies):
    result=set(attributes)
    changed=True
    while changed:
        changed=False
        for left,right in dependencies:
            if set(left)<=result and not set(right)<=result:
                result.update(right); changed=True
    return result
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:'); con.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE customer(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT); CREATE TABLE product(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT,current_price REAL); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customer(id),ordered_at TEXT); CREATE TABLE order_line(order_id INTEGER REFERENCES orders(id),line_no INTEGER,product_id INTEGER REFERENCES product(id),quantity INTEGER CHECK(quantity>0),charged_price REAL CHECK(charged_price>=0),PRIMARY KEY(order_id,line_no)); INSERT INTO customer VALUES(1,"A"); INSERT INTO product VALUES(2,"P",10); INSERT INTO orders VALUES(3,1,"2026-01-01"); INSERT INTO order_line VALUES(3,1,2,2,8); UPDATE product SET current_price=12 WHERE id=2;')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Add schema migrations, natural-key uniqueness, temporal validity, orphan/reconciliation checks, analytics lineage, and expand-contract rollback for every model change.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
deps=[(('order_id',),('customer_id','order_date')),(('customer_id',),('customer_name',)),(('order_id','line_no'),('product_id','quantity','charged_price'))]
assert {'customer_id','customer_name','order_date'} <= closure({'order_id'},deps)
assert con.execute('SELECT charged_price FROM order_line').fetchone()[0]==8
assert con.execute('SELECT current_price FROM product').fetchone()[0]==12
assert con.execute('SELECT SUM(quantity*charged_price) FROM order_line').fetchone()[0]==16

Common mistakes

  • A surrogate primary key makes a table normalized.

    Natural functional dependencies and redundant facts still exist; preserve candidate-key constraints and analyze determinants.

  • 3NF means every table has only an ID and one value.

    Attributes depending directly on the key can coexist. Normalization follows dependencies, not an arbitrary narrow-table rule.

  • Denormalization is always bad design.

    Derived analytics and read models can denormalize deliberately when source ownership, refresh, consistency, lineage, and reconciliation are explicit.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do 3NF and BCNF differ?

    3NF permits X→A when A is prime even if X is not a superkey; BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey.

  • What is lossless decomposition?

    Joining decomposed relations under valid constraints recreates exactly the original relation without missing or spurious rows.

  • Why preserve dependencies?

    So constraints can be enforced locally in decomposed relations instead of requiring expensive joins or procedural checks.

Production / system-design connection

Document grain, candidate keys, dependencies, temporal scopes, constraints, and deletion policy. Validate lossless reconstruction and preserve enforceable dependencies. Treat star schemas, materialized views, caches, and duplicated columns as governed derived products with source ownership, lineage, refresh, staleness, reconciliation, and rollback. Monitor orphans, uniqueness, history integrity, and join/read costs before denormalizing further.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    If `(order_id,product_id)` is a key and order_date depends only on order_id, which form is violated?

    Show solution

    Second normal form, because a non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a composite candidate key.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Where should the price actually charged for an order line live?

    Show solution

    On the order-line transaction fact (or referenced immutable price version), not only in the mutable current product record.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A BCNF decomposition needs a join to validate an original dependency. What property may be lost?

    Show solution

    Dependency preservation; the decomposition can still be lossless while requiring cross-table enforcement.

3.8

Query Plans & SQL Performance

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

A query plan is the database's chosen physical program for a declarative SQL statement. It specifies scans, filters, joins, sorts, aggregates, exchanges, and materialization, with estimated rows and costs derived from statistics and a cost model. This chapter teaches plan reading from leaves to root, distinguishes estimated `EXPLAIN` from execution-producing `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and shows how cardinality errors cascade into bad join order, algorithm, memory, and parallelism choices. It covers sequential and index scans, nested-loop, hash, and merge joins, sorts and spills, hash aggregation, predicate pushdown, projection, sargability, prepared-plan/parameter effects, and why estimated cost is not milliseconds. You will diagnose a slow join by comparing estimates with actual rows and buffers, then fix the underlying distribution, predicate, statistics, index, or query semantics rather than blindly forcing a node. Production sections address safe plan capture, workload baselines, plan changes after upgrades, memory and temp I/O, concurrency, and regression monitoring. The goal is evidence-led optimization without cargo-cult hints.

Prerequisites

  • transactions-indexes
  • sql-joins
  • sql-aggregation

Learning objectives

  • Read physical plans from data sources to root and explain cardinality, loops, rows, cost, buffers, memory, and spill evidence.
  • Connect estimation errors and predicate/index shape to scan, join order, algorithm, aggregation, sorting, and parallel choices.
  • Optimize safely with representative execution evidence, workload-level measurement, reversible changes, and plan-regression monitoring.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The optimizer transforms declarative SQL into a physical operator tree using statistics and a cost model. Read from leaf scans upward, tracking estimated rows, actual rows per loop, join algorithms, filters, sorts, memory, buffers, and spill. `EXPLAIN` estimates without running; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes and can have side effects for writes. Large estimated-versus-actual cardinality errors often cause poor join order or memory choices. Costs are planner units, not milliseconds, so validate with representative runtime and workload impact before changing SQL, indexes, statistics, or configuration.

What you must know

  • Plan is a physical operator tree
  • Cardinality drives choices
  • Actual rows times loops matters
  • Cost units are not time
  • Fix evidence, not node names

Why this matters

A logically correct query can scan too much data, repeat an inner probe millions of times, spill a hash table, or choose a plan based on stale statistics. Index folklore and SQL formatting do not reveal this. Plans explain where rows flow and estimates diverge, making optimization a testable process. Interview questions may ask why an index is unused; production engineers must also account for cache state, concurrent workload, parameter distributions, temp I/O, maintenance, and the risk that a plan change helps one query while harming writes or other tenants.

Intuition

SQL describes the answer; the plan is the execution recipe. Each node consumes rows from children and emits rows upward. Row-count estimates are the recipe's quantities. If the optimizer thinks ten rows will flow where ten million actually do, it may choose a tiny nested-loop or memory allocation that becomes disastrous. Follow the rows, compare predictions with measurements, and find the first meaningful divergence.

Plan anatomy and safe measurement

Plans are trees or DAG-like structures of physical operators. Leaves access tables or indexes; upper nodes filter, join, aggregate, sort, materialize, exchange, or project. Indentation identifies parent/child flow. Estimated startup and total cost are cost-model units for comparing alternatives, accompanied by estimated rows and row width. They are not promises of milliseconds.

`EXPLAIN` obtains a plan without executing it. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the statement and reports actual timing, rows, and loops, so write queries really write unless wrapped and rolled back safely. Timing instrumentation has overhead, and warm cache differs from cold or production concurrency. Add buffer, I/O, memory, and verbose options supported by the engine when needed, while redacting literals and sensitive schema data.

Actual rows reported per loop must be multiplied by loops to understand work. 'Rows removed by filter' shows late discard. A node's inclusive time contains child work, so do not sum every node as independent duration. Identify the longest/resource-heavy branch and earliest estimate divergence, then reproduce with representative parameters and data.

Scans, joins, sorts, and aggregates

A sequential scan reads a table or partition and can be optimal for small tables or predicates returning a large fraction. An index scan navigates an index then retrieves qualifying rows; random base-table access may dominate for many matches. Bitmap paths can combine or batch index locations. Index-only paths depend on covered columns and visibility/engine conditions. Partition pruning and predicate pushdown reduce data only when predicates are compatible and semantics allow.

Nested loops suit a small outer side with cheap inner probes. Hash joins build equality-key state and can spill if build data exceeds memory. Merge joins consume compatible order and handle sorted groups. Sorts may be in-memory or external; top-N methods can reduce work for LIMIT under conditions. Hash aggregation maintains per-group state, while sort aggregation consumes grouped order.

Operators are not inherently good or bad. A nested loop with ten indexed probes is excellent; with ten million full inner scans it is not. A sequential scan can beat an index for bulk retrieval. Judge rows, loops, buffers, locality, memory, spill, and required output—not the presence of a favored node.

Cardinality estimation, statistics, and predicate shape

Optimizers estimate base selectivity from statistics such as row counts, null fractions, distinct values, histograms, and frequent values. Combining predicates often assumes independence unless extended statistics capture dependencies. Correlated columns, skew, rapidly changing tables, expressions, and multi-column relationships create errors. Errors propagate: underestimated filters choose wrong join order and undersized memory; overestimates can avoid useful indexes or parallelize excessively.

Refresh statistics after major distribution changes and increase detail selectively for important skew. Constraints and uniqueness provide stronger information. Compare estimated and actual rows at every node and fix the first consequential mismatch. A bad estimate may also reveal wrong join semantics or hidden casts rather than merely stale statistics.

A predicate is sargable when it can constrain an access method. Applying a function or incompatible cast to an indexed column may prevent a range; rewrite to compare the column directly, add a justified expression index, or normalize at write time. Leading wildcards and arithmetic can have similar effects. Never rewrite in a way that changes timezone, collation, NULL, or boundary semantics just to obtain an index.

A disciplined production optimization loop

Begin with the user-visible symptom and workload: latency percentile, throughput, resource saturation, lock waits, or cost. Capture query identity, parameter distribution, plan, execution counters, and concurrency. Confirm correctness and expected row grain. Remove unnecessary columns/rows, fix fanout, and improve predicate semantics before adding structures. Then consider indexes, statistics, query rewrite, partitioning, materialized results, memory, or architecture.

Test on representative volume and skew, not only a small clone. Measure repeated runs, cold/warm behavior as relevant, write impact, storage, maintenance, and other queries. A new covering index can accelerate one report while slowing ingestion and eviction. Configuration memory is often per operation or connection; multiplying it globally can exhaust a busy server. Hints or forced plans are last-resort, version-sensitive commitments.

Roll out reversibly and monitor plan hash/shape carefully alongside latency, rows, buffers, spill, and error. Plan text can legitimately change after statistics or upgrades, so alert on performance and cardinality regressions rather than any difference. Maintain workload baselines and reevaluate indexes. Document assumptions and a rollback trigger.

Math / formal view

Optimizer chooses plan p minimizing estimated cost C(p|statistics,parameters,configuration). If a nested-loop outer emits N actual rows and inner executes L=N loops at cost q, work is roughly Nq even when estimated N was tiny. Cardinality estimation error ratio actual/estimated propagates multiplicatively through joins and controls algorithm and memory decisions.

Diagnose a slow customer-order join

Setup

A report changed from seconds to minutes after one tenant imported millions of orders; SQL text and indexes did not change.

Capture `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` safely for representative tenant parameters with buffers. Read leaves upward. Find the tenant filter estimated hundreds but returning millions because tenant and date are correlated and statistics are stale/coarse. The underestimated outer side drives repeated nested index probes and later sort spill. Verify join grain, update statistics or extended statistics, consider a workload-shaped composite/partial index, and compare an alternative hash/merge plan without forcing it permanently. Test small and large tenants, ingestion impact, cache, temp I/O, and concurrent load, then deploy with rollback thresholds.

Conclusion

The root cause is distribution and estimation, not that nested loops are universally bad; the fix aligns optimizer evidence with the current workload.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Use SQLite plan output and timing to verify index eligibility, result equivalence, and the difference between selective and broad predicates.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def plan_text(con,sql,params=()):
    return ' '.join(str(row) for row in con.execute('EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN '+sql,params))
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE event(tenant INTEGER,ts INTEGER,value TEXT)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO event VALUES (?,?,?)',((i%10,i,str(i)) for i in range(1000)))
con.execute('CREATE INDEX event_tenant_ts ON event(tenant,ts)')
selective='SELECT value FROM event WHERE tenant=? AND ts>=?'
indexed_plan=plan_text(con,selective,(3,900))
rows=con.execute(selective,(3,900)).fetchall()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Repeat with the production engine's EXPLAIN ANALYZE, representative parameters and concurrency; record rows, loops, buffers, spill, write impact, and rollback thresholds.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert all(int(value[0])>=903 for value in rows)
assert 'event_tenant_ts' in indexed_plan
scan_plan=plan_text(con,'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM event WHERE value LIKE ?',('%9%',))
assert 'SCAN' in scan_plan.upper()
expected=con.execute('SELECT value FROM event').fetchall()
actual=con.execute('SELECT value FROM event WHERE tenant>=0').fetchall()
assert sorted(expected)==sorted(actual)

Common mistakes

  • Planner cost 100 means about 100 milliseconds.

    Costs are engine-specific relative units for plan comparison, not direct wall-clock time.

  • Any sequential scan indicates a missing index.

    Scanning can be optimal for small tables or broad retrieval; compare selectivity, buffers, locality, and actual runtime.

  • Read the first expensive-looking top node and add a hint.

    Trace leaves upward, actual rows and loops, and the earliest estimate divergence; hints can mask changing root causes.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why can estimated and actual rows differ greatly?

    Stale or coarse statistics, correlation, skew, expressions, parameter values, casts, or incorrect semantic assumptions can defeat the estimator.

  • Why might an index scan be slower for many rows?

    Many random base-row fetches and low selectivity can cost more than a sequential read.

  • What is the risk of EXPLAIN ANALYZE on UPDATE?

    It executes the write. Use a safe environment or explicit transaction and rollback while accounting for locks and side effects.

Production / system-design connection

Capture plans and parameters safely, read rows/loops/buffers/memory/spill from leaves upward, and fix semantic or estimation root causes before forcing access paths. Benchmark representative scale, skew, cache, and concurrency plus write/maintenance impact. Roll out indexes/statistics/query changes reversibly and monitor latency, temp I/O, plan regressions, and estimated-versus-actual cardinality over time.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What does loops=1000 on an inner plan node imply?

    Show solution

    The node executed 1,000 times; multiply its per-loop actual rows/time to understand total work.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    A query returns 70% of a table. Should an index scan be assumed faster?

    Show solution

    No. A sequential scan may be cheaper than many index probes and base fetches; inspect the representative plan and buffers.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A date predicate applies `DATE(timestamp_col)` and misses the timestamp index. What can you do?

    Show solution

    Rewrite to a semantically correct timestamp range or create a justified expression index, carefully preserving timezone and boundary meaning.
