3.9

Transactions & Isolation Levels

highverified
Roles: de, mle, da

Topic overview

Transaction isolation defines which concurrent interleavings a database permits and what each transaction may observe. It is not equivalent to atomicity, and level names alone are insufficient because implementations differ. This chapter builds a history-based model, then explains dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew, and serialization anomalies. It covers multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), snapshots, locks, optimistic validation, PostgreSQL's current Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable behavior, serialization failures, deadlocks, and retry design. You will trace an on-call schedule where two individually valid updates violate a cross-row invariant under snapshot-style execution, then prevent it with a serializable transaction or explicit locking/materialized constraint. The operations section addresses transaction scope, deterministic lock order, read-only replicas, connection pools, long snapshots, timeouts, idempotency, metrics, and chaos testing. The objective is to choose the weakest level and explicit controls that actually preserve named invariants, then treat abort and retry as a normal part of concurrent correctness.

Prerequisites

  • transactions-indexes

Learning objectives

  • Classify concurrent histories by dirty read, nonrepeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew, and serialization behavior.
  • Explain snapshot/MVCC visibility and compare target-engine isolation guarantees without relying solely on standard level names.
  • Implement invariant-preserving transactions with locks or serializable validation, bounded idempotent retries, timeouts, and contention monitoring.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Isolation controls how concurrent transactions appear to execute. Read Committed commonly gives each statement a fresh committed snapshot; repeatable/snapshot levels hold a stable transaction view but can still permit write skew in some systems; Serializable aims to make committed outcomes equivalent to some serial order and may abort transactions that threaten that guarantee. MVCC lets readers see versions rather than blocking every writer, but old snapshots have cleanup cost. Choose isolation from the invariant, use explicit locks or constraints where appropriate, and retry serialization failures and deadlocks as whole idempotent transactions.

What you must know

  • Name the invariant first
  • Isolation controls histories
  • MVCC uses version visibility
  • Snapshot can allow write skew
  • Serializable requires retry handling

Why this matters

Two requests can each read a valid state, make disjoint writes, and jointly violate a rule. Inventory becomes negative, one on-call doctor becomes zero, or duplicate jobs are created even though each statement is atomic. Raising isolation blindly can reduce throughput or still miss a target-engine nuance. Holding locks during network calls causes contention, while ignoring serialization aborts turns correct database protection into user errors. Interviewers ask anomalies and levels; production requires a concrete invariant, engine-specific guarantee, transaction design, retries, monitoring, and behavior under replica lag or uncertain commits.

Intuition

Imagine concurrent transactions as proposed edits to shared history. Lower isolation lets more overlapping views proceed. MVCC gives each reader a versioned photograph, allowing readers and writers to overlap. But two photographs can each justify a different disjoint write that would never both happen in any valid serial execution. Serializable mechanisms detect or prevent such dangerous combinations, sometimes by making one proposal retry.

Concurrent histories and anomalies

A history interleaves reads, writes, commits, and aborts from transactions. Serial execution completes one transaction before another. Serializable execution may interleave but has an outcome equivalent to some serial order. Conflict and serialization theory provide formal tests, while applications begin with invariants over rows and predicates.

A dirty read observes uncommitted data that may roll back. A nonrepeatable read sees a row change between reads. A phantom occurs when a predicate query returns a changed set because rows are inserted, deleted, or updated into the predicate. Lost update overwrites another transaction's change based on stale state. Some databases prevent simple lost writes even at common levels, but read-modify-write patterns still need conditional updates or locks.

Write skew occurs when transactions read overlapping predicate state but write different rows, so neither write conflicts directly. Each sees the invariant satisfied and both commits break it. This is the classic limitation of many snapshot-isolation designs. Anomaly labels help, but the real task is to show the forbidden final state and how the chosen mechanism rules it out.

MVCC, snapshots, and engine-specific levels

MVCC stores row versions with visibility metadata so a query can read a consistent snapshot while concurrent updates create newer versions. Readers avoid many writer locks, but updates still coordinate and visibility checks occur through indexes and table storage. Long transactions keep old versions potentially visible, delaying cleanup and increasing bloat or history retention.

In current PostgreSQL, Read Uncommitted behaves as Read Committed. At Read Committed, each statement sees a snapshot as of that statement, so two SELECTs in one transaction can see different committed data. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read uses a transaction snapshot and prevents the standard phantom phenomenon in its documented behavior, yet serialization anomalies such as write skew can remain. Serializable uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation to detect dangerous structures and abort a transaction when needed. Other databases map names differently.

Read-only replicas add another timeline: a locally consistent snapshot may lag the primary. Read-your-writes and monotonic-read requirements need routing or causal/session guarantees. Isolation applies to a database transaction, not automatically to caches, object storage, queues, or external APIs.

Locks, constraints, conditional writes, and serializable execution

Use declarative uniqueness, foreign keys, checks, and exclusion constraints where they encode the invariant; they are enforced under concurrency more reliably than application prechecks. A conditional update such as decrementing inventory only where stock is sufficient combines check and write and verifies affected rows. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks existing rows that will be changed, but predicate invariants involving absence or multiple rows may require range/predicate locking, a materialized guard row, advisory mechanism, or serializable execution.

Acquire locks in a consistent global order to reduce deadlocks. Keep the transaction short and do not wait on users or remote services. Locks protect only the resources and predicates actually covered; locking two doctor rows may preserve an on-call count if every writer follows the same protocol, while an uncoordinated code path can still violate it.

Serializable execution is often the clearest general guard for complex read-then-write invariants, but aborts are expected under contention. The application must retry the entire transaction from a new snapshot. Do not retry only the failed final statement using stale decisions. Bound attempts, add jittered backoff, surface exhaustion, and make external effects idempotent or move them through an outbox after commit.

Deadlocks, retries, and operational controls

A deadlock is a wait cycle among transactions; the database detects it and aborts a victim. It can occur at any isolation level. Consistent lock order, smaller batches, and shorter transactions reduce risk but do not eliminate every dynamic cycle. Lock timeouts and statement timeouts bound waits; distinguish timeout, deadlock, serialization failure, connection loss, and permanent constraint error because retry policy differs.

An uncertain commit occurs when the connection fails after the server may have committed. Retrying without an idempotency key can duplicate effects. Store a unique operation ID and query its outcome, or design the mutation as an idempotent upsert/ledger action. Backoff prevents retry storms, and a retry budget protects latency.

Monitor transaction duration and age, active/idle state, lock waits, deadlocks, serialization abort rate, retries, pool utilization, replica lag, and invariant violations. Load tests must use concurrent workers and adversarial timing; sequential unit tests cannot demonstrate isolation. Document which operations require which level and lock protocol. Review changes that add a read or widen a predicate because they can change conflict patterns and performance.

Math / formal view

A schedule is serializable when its observable outcome is equivalent to some serial ordering of transactions. Snapshot visibility can prevent dirty/nonrepeatable reads while permitting write skew when T1 and T2 read a shared predicate and write disjoint rows. Serializable mechanisms prevent or abort cycles/dangerous structures; aborted transactions are not committed counterexamples and must be retried from the beginning.

Preserve at least one doctor on call

Setup

Two on-call rows are true. Each doctor concurrently checks that another doctor remains and turns their own row off.

Under a stable snapshot, each transaction sees two on-call doctors, updates a different row, and can commit without a direct write conflict, leaving zero—write skew. Options include a serializable transaction with retry; locking a shared schedule guard row before checking/updating; or redesigning the invariant into an enforceable representation. Test with two concurrent connections and a barrier after reads. On serialization/deadlock failure, roll back and retry the whole idempotent action. Keep any notification outside the transaction through an outbox.

Conclusion

Row-level atomic writes are insufficient for a predicate invariant; the design must make concurrent decisions conflict or validate serializability.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate write skew and verify that a shared guard lock/serial critical section preserves the cross-row invariant.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def snapshot_decision(snapshot,self_id):
    if sum(snapshot.values()) < 2: return None
    return self_id

def apply_writes(state,writes):
    for doctor in writes: state[doctor]=False
    return state
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from threading import Lock,Thread
state={'a':True,'b':True}; guard=Lock()
def safe_off(doctor):
    with guard:
        if sum(state.values()) < 2: return False
        state[doctor]=False; return True
results=[]
threads=[Thread(target=lambda d=d: results.append(safe_off(d))) for d in state]
for t in threads:t.start()
for t in threads:t.join()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Implement the invariant with target-database constraints/locking or Serializable transactions, whole-transaction idempotent retries, consistent lock order, timeouts, and monitoring of abort/lock rates.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
snapshot={'a':True,'b':True}
writes=[snapshot_decision(snapshot,'a'),snapshot_decision(snapshot,'b')]
unsafe=apply_writes(dict(snapshot),[w for w in writes if w])
assert sum(unsafe.values())==0
assert sum(state.values())==1
assert sorted(results)==[False,True]
assert all(value in (True,False) for value in state.values())

Common mistakes

  • Atomic transactions automatically prevent every race.

    Atomicity is all-or-nothing for one transaction; isolation determines allowed interactions among concurrent transactions.

  • Repeatable Read always equals serializable.

    Many snapshot implementations preserve a view but permit write skew. Check the target engine's documented guarantees.

  • Retry the last failed statement after a serialization error.

    The transaction's reads and decisions came from an invalidated snapshot; roll back and retry the entire logical transaction.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is write skew?

    Concurrent transactions read overlapping invariant state, write disjoint rows, and jointly violate the invariant without a direct write-write conflict.

  • Why can MVCC create bloat?

    Long snapshots keep old row versions potentially visible, delaying reclamation while updates create new versions.

  • How do deadlock and serialization failure differ?

    A deadlock is a lock wait cycle; serialization failure is an abort to prevent a nonserializable outcome. Both commonly require whole-transaction retry.

Production / system-design connection

Map every critical invariant to constraints, conditional writes, locks, or a documented serializable transaction. Keep transactions short, order locks consistently, classify errors, and use bounded jittered whole-transaction retries with idempotency for uncertain commits. Account for replica lag and external systems. Monitor long transactions, locks, deadlocks, serialization aborts, retries, pools, bloat, and invariant checks, and test true concurrent histories.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What anomaly has two transactions read a shared predicate and update disjoint rows to violate it?

    Show solution

    Write skew, commonly possible under snapshot isolation without serializable validation or an explicit conflict.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    How can you safely decrement inventory?

    Show solution

    Use a conditional atomic update constrained by available stock and check the affected row, or lock the relevant inventory record inside the invariant transaction.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A service duplicates an order after a timeout retry even though transactions are atomic. Why?

    Show solution

    The first commit outcome was uncertain and the retry lacked a unique idempotency key, so it created a second independent transaction.

CHAPTER 04

🏗️ Analytics Engineering & Data Modeling

Warehouses, dimensional modeling, dbt, semantic layers and trustworthy analytical datasets.

7 lessons · 7 deep-complete · 14 visuals
Study order. Learn the interview answer first. Then make sure you can explain every key point without notes. Use the deep sections to understand trade-offs, failure modes, and production implications.
4.1

OLTP vs OLAP

very highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

Online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) describe workload families, not mutually exclusive product labels. OLTP systems serve many short, selective, concurrent state changes whose correctness depends on transactions, constraints, low tail latency, and predictable recovery. OLAP systems scan, join, and aggregate large portions of historical data for reporting, exploration, and model development; they favor columnar storage, vectorized execution, parallelism, compression, and workload isolation. This chapter derives those differences from access patterns, then connects them to row versus column layout, normalized versus dimensional models, indexing, materialized results, replication and change-data capture. You will learn why running an unbounded analytical query on a primary transaction database can harm customer traffic, why copying data introduces freshness and consistency trade-offs, and why a modern system may support both workload types without making their operational requirements identical. A worked commerce design follows an order from a transactional write into an analytical fact model and defines reconciliation, latency, privacy, rollback, and failure behavior. The goal is to choose boundaries from measured workload and correctness requirements rather than repeating that OLTP is simply “rows” and OLAP is simply “columns.”

Prerequisites

  • transactions-indexes
  • sql-aggregation

Learning objectives

  • Classify a database workload from access shape, concurrency, latency, correctness, and freshness requirements.
  • Explain how row/column layout, execution model, indexing, schema design, and isolation support different workloads.
  • Design and operate a transaction-to-analytics path with explicit delivery semantics, reconciliation, privacy, and recovery.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

OLTP handles many short, concurrent reads and writes over a small number of records, so it prioritizes transactions, constraints, selective indexes, low tail latency, and recovery. OLAP handles fewer but heavier scans, joins, and aggregations over large history, so it benefits from columnar compression, vectorized and parallel execution, dimensional models, and workload isolation. These are workload properties rather than strict product categories. Organizations commonly preserve a normalized operational source of truth and propagate committed changes into an analytical store, accepting and monitoring a freshness boundary instead of letting large scans contend with customer transactions.

What you must know

  • Classify the workload, not the vendor
  • Transactions protect state changes
  • Analytics amortizes work over columns and batches
  • Replication creates a freshness boundary
  • Correctness needs reconciliation across systems

Why this matters

A dashboard that scans years of orders can evict useful pages, consume I/O, hold resources, and increase lock or MVCC pressure on the system accepting new orders. Conversely, forcing an analytical warehouse to serve millisecond point updates may create cost and concurrency problems. Data teams therefore separate workloads, but separation creates another system whose state can lag, duplicate, omit, or reinterpret the operational source. Good architecture balances customer-facing correctness with analytical usability and proves that the copy is trustworthy. Interviews test the contrast; engineering requires knowing the failure modes at the boundary.

Intuition

Think of a checkout ledger and an investigation table. Checkout repeatedly finds a few accounts and writes a valid new state before a deadline. An investigation reads millions of historical rows, selects a handful of columns, groups them in several ways, and can tolerate seconds but not inconsistent definitions. A single engine may perform both, yet the physical layout, resource scheduling, schema, and replicas used for each path should follow these different shapes.

Workload shape and service objectives

Classify a workload along several axes. Selectivity asks what fraction of rows and columns a query touches. Mutation granularity asks whether writes affect individual entities or arrive as batches. Concurrency asks how many operations overlap and whether they contend for the same keys. Latency needs include median and tail percentiles, not only average response. Correctness includes atomicity, isolation, durability, constraints, and read-after-write expectations. Analytics adds freshness, reproducibility, and definition consistency. Scale alone does not decide the category: a huge key-value lookup service can remain transactional, while a small laptop scan can be analytical.

Typical OLTP operations insert an order, authorize a payment, or update inventory with narrow predicates and short transactions. Indexes trade write work for selective reads. Normalized schemas reduce duplicated mutable facts and allow constraints to protect relationships. The system must recover without exposing partial state and degrade safely when dependencies fail. Long user or network waits should not occur inside a database transaction.

Typical OLAP queries aggregate history, join multiple subjects, compute windows, or explore unanticipated slices. They often touch many rows but few columns and reuse scans across batches of values. Throughput, bytes scanned, spill, and queue time matter alongside latency. Workload managers, separate compute, caching, summaries, and materialized views prevent one query from monopolizing resources. Interactive BI and batch training are both analytical but may need different queues and freshness targets.

Physical layout and execution

A row-oriented layout keeps values from one record near one another. Fetching or updating an entire customer row can therefore require few page accesses. A columnar layout stores values of a column together within blocks. A query reading three columns from a hundred-column table can avoid the others, and similar adjacent values compress well. Analytical engines commonly execute operators over vectors rather than paying interpretation and function-call overhead per scalar value. Parallel scans and aggregations use multiple cores and partitions.

The labels are tendencies, not guarantees. Transaction engines can use column stores, analytics engines can maintain row-oriented components, and hybrid systems can choose layouts adaptively. Secondary indexes, clustered order, zone maps, partition metadata, and materialized aggregates change how much data is touched. The optimizer still needs accurate cardinality and cost estimates. Columnar storage does not rescue a query that selects every column, misses pruning, explodes a join, or creates severe skew.

Writes expose the opposite trade-off. Updating one logical row scattered across many column segments can be expensive, so column stores may buffer, append deltas, and compact later. Analytical tables often prefer immutable files and batch rewrites. Every design should be evaluated using the actual mix: scanned columns, predicate selectivity, update rate, file sizes, compression, concurrency, and failure recovery—not a synthetic headline benchmark.

Operational and analytical models

Operational schemas organize mutable facts around entities and invariants. Normalization reduces update anomalies, but it does not automatically make a schema understandable for cross-functional analysis. Analytical models publish stable business processes at declared grain. A fact table may record one order line, while dimensions describe customer, product, channel, and calendar context. Denormalization and conformed dimensions simplify repeated group-by queries and centralize metric meaning.

The analytical model is not a careless copy. It chooses event time, processing time, currency conversion, late-arriving behavior, deletion policy, and historical interpretation. Measures must be classified as additive, semi-additive, or non-additive. Surrogate keys can preserve dimension history. Semantic metrics must identify their numerator, denominator, filters, time grain, and eligible population. A warehouse query is reproducible only when inputs and transformation versions are recoverable.

Some use cases should query operational data directly: a customer viewing the order they just placed needs authoritative current state. Others need historical, cross-system context that an OLTP schema should not carry. Operational analytical processing, read replicas, federated queries, and lakehouse engines can narrow the physical separation, but they do not eliminate ownership, freshness, resource, or semantic boundaries. Decide which system is authoritative for each question.

Moving committed state into analytics

Batch extraction periodically snapshots or queries source ranges. Change-data capture (CDC) reads a commit log or equivalent stream and emits ordered row changes. Dual-writing independently from application code is dangerous: one destination can succeed while the other fails. An outbox written in the source transaction or log-based CDC ties publication to committed state more safely. Delivery is commonly at least once, so downstream processing needs stable event identifiers, source positions, idempotent merges, and replay.

A change event can be delivered correctly yet produce a wrong table because schema, ordering, delete, or temporal semantics were misunderstood. Capture inserts, updates, deletes, transaction boundaries where needed, and source schema evolution. Watermarks express progress, not truth. Reconcile source counts and control totals at a stable cutoff. Measure end-to-end freshness from source commit time, backlog, duplicate and reject rates, and silent gaps. Backfills should use the same semantics as incremental processing and must not race with the live stream.

Security follows data. Minimize copied personal data, tokenize identifiers, propagate classification, enforce purpose-based access, and implement deletion across replicas and backups under policy. Recovery needs checkpoints, replayable raw events or snapshots, versioned transformations, quarantines, and a tested rollback or rebuild path. Separation protects workloads only when resource, correctness, and operational ownership are explicit.

Math / formal view

A useful workload vector is W=(s,c,m,q,L,F,I), where s is row selectivity, c is projected-column fraction, m is mutation granularity/rate, q is concurrency, L is a latency distribution, F is required freshness, and I is the isolation/correctness contract. OLTP tends toward small s, high q, fine mutations, tight tail L, and strong I. OLAP tends toward large s, small c, batch mutations, heavier operators, and an explicit F. These tendencies guide design; they are not definitions enforced by a product name.

Orders from checkout to daily revenue

Setup

Checkout must atomically create an order, reserve inventory, and expose the result immediately; finance needs historical daily net revenue by product and region.

The operational transaction writes normalized order, line, inventory, and outbox records under constraints. A log consumer reads only committed changes, deduplicates by source position, and lands immutable raw events. Transformations create an order-line fact at declared grain, join effective customer/product dimension versions, handle cancellations as explicit adjustments, and publish a daily aggregate. A watermark reports the latest complete commit time. At each daily cutoff, row counts, order IDs, gross amount, refunds, and net amount reconcile to source controls. A bad transformation version writes a new table and swaps consumers only after validation; rollback restores the prior version without changing operational orders.

Conclusion

The design protects checkout latency while making the analytical copy observable, replayable, historically meaningful, and financially reconcilable.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compare row-oriented and column-oriented projections with a tiny model, then verify that both produce identical analytical results.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def row_scan(rows, region):
    touched=0; total=0.0
    for row in rows:
        touched += len(row)
        if row['region']==region:
            total += row['amount']
    return total,touched

def column_scan(columns, region):
    touched=0; total=0.0
    for value,amount in zip(columns['region'],columns['amount']):
        touched += 2
        if value==region:
            total += amount
    return total,touched
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
rows=[{'order_id':1,'region':'EU','amount':10.0,'note':'a'},{'order_id':2,'region':'US','amount':7.0,'note':'b'},{'order_id':3,'region':'EU','amount':4.0,'note':'c'}]
columns={key:[row[key] for row in rows] for key in rows[0]}
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE orders(order_id INTEGER,region TEXT,amount REAL,note TEXT)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO orders VALUES(:order_id,:region,:amount,:note)',rows)
sql_total=con.execute("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE region='EU'").fetchone()[0]
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Benchmark representative filters and projections on the target engine, isolate analytical resources, publish freshness and reconciliation metrics, and keep a rollback-ready versioned output.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
row_total,row_touched=row_scan(rows,'EU')
column_total,column_touched=column_scan(columns,'EU')
assert row_total==column_total==sql_total==14.0
assert column_touched < row_touched
assert sum(columns['amount'])==21.0
assert len(rows)==len(columns['order_id'])

Common mistakes

  • OLTP means row storage and OLAP means column storage in every system.

    Those layouts often suit the workload shapes, but hybrid engines exist; classify access, mutation, concurrency, and correctness first.

  • A read replica makes analytics safe automatically.

    Heavy queries can still consume replica resources, lag may violate freshness, and schema/semantic coupling remains.

  • Exactly-once delivery removes the need for reconciliation.

    Transport guarantees cannot prove correct transformation semantics, source coverage, deletes, or business measures.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is columnar storage effective for analytics?

    It reads only projected columns, compresses similar values well, and supports vectorized processing over batches, reducing I/O and per-value overhead.

  • Why avoid application dual writes?

    Independent destinations cannot commit atomically in ordinary application code, so partial failure creates divergent truth. Transactional outbox or log-based CDC couples publication to the source commit.

  • Can one database serve both workloads?

    Yes, but success depends on workload isolation, physical design, concurrency control, freshness, and measured service objectives rather than the hybrid label itself.

Production / system-design connection

Define an owner and service-level objectives for transaction latency, analytical freshness, reconciliation, recovery point, and recovery time. Isolate heavy compute, bound queries, monitor tail latency, locks, MVCC age, queueing, scan/spill, CDC lag, schema failures, and control-total differences. Make ingestion idempotent and replayable, version transformations, test backfills, propagate security classifications and deletion, and retain a tested rollback to the last trusted analytical snapshot.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

4.2

Star Schemas, Facts & Dimensions

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

A star schema publishes a business process as a fact table at one explicit grain surrounded by dimensions that provide descriptive context. Its value is not merely fewer joins: it makes repeated analytical questions predictable, metrics auditable, and filters consistent across tools. This chapter follows the dimensional design sequence—choose a business process, declare grain, identify dimensions, and define facts—then examines transaction, periodic snapshot, and accumulating snapshot facts; additive, semi-additive, and non-additive measures; conformed dimensions; surrogate keys; degenerate dimensions; role-playing dates; unknown members; bridges; and factless facts. You will learn to reject mixed-grain tables, distinguish event time from load time, preserve referential integrity for late-arriving data, and avoid summing ratios or balances across invalid dimensions. A worked order-line mart derives revenue and order metrics without double counting. The production sections cover incremental loading, reconciliation, semantic-layer alignment, access control, schema evolution, cost, and rollback. The aim is to make the grain sentence the executable contract that connects source events, SQL tests, metric definitions, and downstream machine-learning features.

Prerequisites

  • oltp-olap
  • sql-joins
  • sql-aggregation

Learning objectives

  • Design a star schema by declaring business process and grain before selecting dimensions and facts.
  • Classify facts and measures so aggregations remain valid across time, entities, and dimensional filters.
  • Validate and operate a dimensional mart using keys, reconciliation, late-data policy, semantic definitions, and rollback.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A star schema has a central fact table that records a business process at a declared grain and dimension tables that describe the who, what, where, when, and how. Start with the grain—for example, one row per order line—then choose dimensions and numeric facts consistent with it. Use conformed dimensions across facts, surrogate keys when historical dimension versions matter, and classify measures as additive, semi-additive, or non-additive. Validate uniqueness and referential integrity, reconcile source totals, handle late facts and dimensions explicitly, and define metrics above the model so users do not silently aggregate at the wrong grain.

What you must know

  • Declare grain before columns
  • Facts record processes
  • Dimensions provide context
  • Additivity has dimensional limits
  • Conformed dimensions enable consistent drill-across

Why this matters

Analytical teams repeatedly join operational tables, interpret mutable codes, and calculate the same metric differently. A dimensional model moves this logic into a governed publication layer. The wrong design, however, can make errors systematic: an order-level amount repeated on every line inflates revenue, a current customer tier rewrites historical segmentation, and an unmatched dimension can drop facts. Star schemas are valuable when their grain, history, and aggregation contracts are explicit and tested—not because a diagram looks like a star.

Intuition

Treat the fact table as a notebook where every line represents the same kind of occurrence. Dimensions are dictionaries attached to that line. If one notebook line sometimes means an order and sometimes an order item, no grouping can be trusted. Once every line has the same meaning, measures can be summed or counted only along dimensions for which that operation is valid.

Business process, grain, dimensions, and facts

Begin with a measurable business process such as orders, shipments, subscriptions, support interactions, or daily account balances. Do not begin from a source table list or a desired dashboard. Write the grain as a sentence with identifiers and time semantics: one row per order line at acceptance time, or one row per account per calendar day after close. The grain determines which dimensions and facts can coexist without duplication.

Dimensions contain descriptive attributes used to filter, group, label, and navigate: customer, product, store, promotion, date, channel, or status. They usually have one row per dimension entity or historical version. Facts are measurements or event indicators at the declared grain. Foreign keys connect the fact to dimension versions. A degenerate dimension such as order number can remain in the fact when it has identity but no independent descriptive attributes. Role-playing dimensions reuse one date dimension as order date, ship date, and delivery date through separate keys.

Reject columns from a coarser or finer grain unless they are allocated or modeled separately. An order total repeated on each order line is not line-level revenue. Header facts can live in an order fact, while line quantity and extended amount live in an order-line fact. The grain should appear in documentation, uniqueness tests, model names, reviews, and metric contracts.

Fact table and measure types

A transaction fact records an event at its lowest useful grain, such as one scan, click, payment, or order line. It is sparse over time and naturally supports event counts and additive amounts. A periodic snapshot records the state of many entities at regular intervals, such as account balance per day or inventory per product-store-week. An accumulating snapshot tracks milestones of a process on one row, such as order placed, packed, shipped, and delivered, and is updated as the process advances. Factless facts record that an event or coverage relationship occurred even without a numeric measure, such as attendance or promotion eligibility.

An additive measure can be summed across every relevant dimension. Extended sales amount is often additive across product, customer, and time when currency rules are consistent. A semi-additive measure cannot be summed across some dimension: an account balance can be summed across accounts at one instant but not across daily snapshots. A non-additive measure such as a ratio, percentage, or unit price should be recomputed from additive components or summarized with a justified weighting. Distinct counts also require care because group-level distinct values do not add.

Store atomic components when possible: numerator and denominator, local amount and currency, quantity and unit amount. Define null, zero, cancellation, refund, and adjustment semantics. Event time, effective time, and load time answer different questions and should not be collapsed into one ambiguous timestamp.

Conformed dimensions, keys, and historical context

A conformed dimension has consistent keys, attribute meaning, and value domains across multiple fact tables, allowing users to drill across processes such as orders and returns. Conformance is a governance commitment, not merely identical column names. Shared definitions for customer segment or fiscal calendar must have an owner and change policy. Multiple marts can use a bus matrix to show which business processes share which dimensions.

Warehouse surrogate keys decouple analytical identity from mutable or reused source keys and can identify a specific historical version. Keep the durable business key for lineage. A fact should reference the dimension version effective at the event time when historical analysis requires as-was context. Type 1 overwrites current attributes; Type 2 inserts versions. These choices are attribute-specific and driven by questions, not a blanket table setting.

Late-arriving facts may reference a dimension that has not been processed. Options include an explicit unknown or inferred member that is later completed, retry/quarantine, or an ordered dependency. Never silently inner-join the fact away. Unknown, not-applicable, redacted, and lookup-failed states may need distinct members. Enforce one active version per business key, non-overlapping effective intervals, stable surrogate keys, and referential coverage from facts.

Testing, metrics, and production operation

Make the grain executable with uniqueness over its natural key or event identifier. Test fact foreign keys against dimensions, including the intended unknown member policy. Reconcile row counts, quantities, gross amounts, discounts, refunds, and net amounts to source controls at a stable cutoff. Test accepted values and temporal relationships, and inspect the largest unmatched or high-multiplicity keys. Aggregate-level tests should verify important metric identities, not only column nullability.

A semantic layer or governed metric definition sits above physical tables. It declares entity, measure, aggregation, time dimension, filters, and join path. The star makes these definitions easier but does not prevent a BI tool from double counting across a bridge or joining two fact tables directly. Publish supported drill paths and pre-aggregations where cost requires them. Protect sensitive dimension attributes with masking, row policies, and purpose-limited marts; surrogate keys are not anonymization.

Incremental loads need deterministic keys, overlap windows for late data, idempotent merges, and full-refresh equivalence tests. Large facts need appropriate partitioning, clustering, compaction, statistics, and workload budgets. Use versioned build outputs or atomic swaps so readers never see partial tables. Monitor freshness, volume, duplicates, unknown-member rate, reconciliation differences, query cost, and downstream breakage. Retain the previous trusted version for rollback.

Math / formal view

Let fact table F have declared grain key G. Correctness requires G→all non-derived fact attributes within the table and uniqueness of G for a snapshot of the model. A measure m is additive over a set of dimensions D when, for disjoint partitions along D, m(union groups)=sum m(group). Ratios generally violate this property; store additive numerator and denominator and compute their ratio after aggregation.

Order-line sales mart

Setup

Operational orders have headers, items, products, customers, payments, and refunds. Analysts need net revenue, units, and orders by product category, customer segment, and order day.

Declare the fact grain as one row per accepted order line, identified by order_id and line_id. Join the product and customer Type 2 versions effective at order time and role-play the date dimension. Store quantity, gross line amount, allocated discount, refunded amount, and net amount; retain order_id as a degenerate dimension. Do not copy header order total to every line. `SUM(net_amount)` and `SUM(quantity)` are additive; order count is `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` at query time or comes from a separate order fact. Tests enforce key uniqueness, dimension coverage, non-overlapping versions, and `gross-discount-refund=net`. Daily source control totals reconcile at the same timezone cutoff. A late customer uses an explicit inferred member and is re-keyed idempotently when the version arrives.

Conclusion

A precise line grain supports product analysis without inflating header measures, while explicit dimension history preserves as-was segmentation.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build a tiny star schema, calculate line-grain metrics, and verify uniqueness, referential coverage, and reconciliation invariants.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def validate_star(facts, dimensions):
    grain=[(row['order_id'],row['line_id']) for row in facts]
    if len(grain)!=len(set(grain)): raise ValueError('duplicate fact grain')
    product_keys=set(dimensions['product'])
    if any(row['product_key'] not in product_keys for row in facts): raise ValueError('missing product')
    return {
        'gross':sum(row['gross'] for row in facts),
        'net':sum(row['gross']-row['discount']-row['refund'] for row in facts),
        'orders':len({row['order_id'] for row in facts})
    }
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.executescript('CREATE TABLE dim_product(product_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT); CREATE TABLE fact_line(order_id INTEGER,line_id INTEGER,product_key INTEGER,gross REAL,discount REAL,refund REAL,PRIMARY KEY(order_id,line_id),FOREIGN KEY(product_key) REFERENCES dim_product(product_key)); INSERT INTO dim_product VALUES(1,"book"),(2,"game"); INSERT INTO fact_line VALUES(10,1,1,20,2,0),(10,2,2,15,0,5),(11,1,1,8,0,0);')
rows=con.execute('SELECT order_id,line_id,product_key,gross,discount,refund FROM fact_line').fetchall()
facts=[dict(zip(['order_id','line_id','product_key','gross','discount','refund'],row)) for row in rows]
metrics=validate_star(facts,{'product':{1,2}})
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Turn the grain, foreign-key, measure-identity, and source-control checks into CI and production tests; build atomically, monitor unknown members and reconciliation, and keep the prior mart version for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert metrics=={'gross':43.0,'net':36.0,'orders':2}
assert con.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_line').fetchone()[0]==3
assert con.execute('SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM fact_line').fetchone()[0]==2
by_category=dict(con.execute('SELECT p.category,SUM(f.gross-f.discount-f.refund) FROM fact_line f JOIN dim_product p USING(product_key) GROUP BY p.category'))
assert by_category=={'book':26.0,'game':10.0}
assert sum(by_category.values())==metrics['net']

Common mistakes

  • Choose columns first and infer the fact grain afterward.

    Declare the business process and row meaning first; every dimension and measure must be valid at that grain.

  • Every numeric column is safely summable.

    Balances, ratios, prices, and distinct counts have aggregation restrictions; store atomic components and document valid dimensions.

  • Join facts directly because they share dimension keys.

    Two fact tables often have different grains and create fanout. Aggregate each to a compatible conformed grain before combining.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the grain of a fact table?

    The exact real-world meaning of one row, including entity identifiers and time/event semantics. It determines valid keys, dimensions, facts, and aggregations.

  • Why use a surrogate dimension key?

    It separates warehouse row-version identity from mutable source keys and lets a fact reference the historical dimension version effective for the event.

  • What is a conformed dimension?

    A governed dimension with consistent keys and semantics across business processes, enabling compatible filtering and drill-across among facts.

Production / system-design connection

Publish the grain, ownership, freshness, history, and metric contracts. Enforce uniqueness, referential coverage, temporal interval validity, accepted unknown-member behavior, and source reconciliation. Build idempotently into versioned or atomically swapped targets, monitor freshness, volume, fanout, unknown rates, control totals, cost, and sensitive access, and retain a tested rollback version. Require compatible aggregation before combining facts of different grains.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What are the four core dimensional design steps?

    Show solution

    Select a business process, declare its grain, identify dimensions, and identify facts consistent with that grain.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Model daily bank balances for analysis by account and branch.

    Show solution

    Use a periodic snapshot fact at one account per closing day, join account/branch/date dimensions, and mark balance semi-additive: sum across accounts at one date but not across dates.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Revenue doubles after joining orders to items. What likely happened?

    Show solution

    An order-grain amount was repeated across item-grain rows or a dimension key was non-unique. Reassert both grains, inspect multiplicities, and move/allocate the measure appropriately.

4.3

Slowly Changing Dimensions

mediumverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

Slowly changing dimensions (SCDs) are policies for how analytical attributes change and which historical questions remain answerable. Type 1 overwrites an attribute and intentionally presents the latest value for all facts. Type 2 inserts a new dimension version with effective bounds, preserving as-was history and requiring facts or temporal joins to select the correct surrogate key. Type 0 retains the original; Type 3 keeps limited previous state, while hybrid types address specialized reporting needs. This chapter treats SCD choice per attribute and business question rather than as a fashionable table-wide setting. You will learn to define durable business identity, change detection, half-open intervals, current-row invariants, late and out-of-order corrections, inferred members, deletes, and idempotent incremental merges. A worked customer-tier history shows how the same sale is grouped differently under current-state and event-time semantics. The production material covers source replay, hash pitfalls, concurrency, backfills, privacy deletion, bitemporal needs, reconciliation, and rollback. The central lesson is that historical truth has multiple meanings—what was effective, what the system knew, and what has since been corrected—and the model must name which one it preserves.

Prerequisites

  • star-schema
  • sql-window-functions

Learning objectives

  • Choose an SCD policy per attribute from the historical questions and correction semantics it must support.
  • Implement and validate non-overlapping Type 2 versions with deterministic late-data and idempotency behavior.
  • Distinguish valid time, system time, current-state reporting, correction, deletion, and bitemporal requirements.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

SCD techniques define how dimension attribute changes affect historical analysis. Type 1 overwrites and is appropriate when only the corrected or latest value should be shown. Type 2 inserts a new surrogate-keyed row with effective intervals, so facts can retain the version valid at event time. Type 0 retains the original, and Type 3 stores limited prior state. For Type 2, enforce one current row per business key, non-overlapping half-open intervals, deterministic change detection, and idempotent handling of late or repeated events. Choose by attribute and question; not every change deserves preserved history.

What you must know

  • History policy is per attribute
  • Type 1 rewrites interpretation
  • Type 2 versions effective state
  • Intervals must not overlap
  • Late corrections need explicit semantics

Why this matters

If customer region is overwritten, last year's revenue may move between regions each time the customer relocates. Sometimes that is desired current-state reporting; often finance needs the region effective when the sale happened. Preserving every source update without semantics can be equally wrong: typo corrections become fake business transitions, duplicated events create zero-duration versions, and out-of-order changes overlap. SCD design is a temporal data contract, not just an ETL recipe.

Intuition

Imagine a passport for an entity. Type 1 erases and rewrites a field on the same page. Type 2 keeps a sequence of stamped pages, each valid from one instant until the next. A fact either stores the page number that was valid when it occurred or finds that page using event time. A correction may fix an old page rather than create a new real-world period, so the arrival timestamp alone is not enough.

Choose history from the question

Type 0 retains the original attribute and ignores later changes, suitable for an immutable registration cohort when that meaning is intentional. Type 1 overwrites; all historical facts joined through the dimension appear under the newest or corrected value. It is appropriate for error correction, fields where history has no value, or current-state segmentation. Type 2 inserts a version and preserves effective history. Type 3 adds a previous-value column and supports only limited comparison. Types 4 through 7 combine history tables, mini-dimensions, current outriggers, or dual keys for specialized workloads.

Choose at attribute level. A customer name typo may be Type 1 while risk tier is Type 2 and original acquisition channel is Type 0. Group attributes that change together only when their source semantics and query needs align; otherwise one noisy attribute can create excessive versions. State whether a dashboard asks “as it was then,” “as we know now,” or “under the current classification.” These are all legitimate but different.

Some changes are events better modeled as facts rather than dimension versions—for example, subscription status transitions with duration and reason. Rapidly changing attributes can produce dimension explosion and may belong in a mini-dimension, periodic snapshot, or event fact. The label slowly changing describes a modeling pattern, not a performance promise.

Type 2 representation and invariants

A Type 2 row commonly contains a surrogate key, durable business key, tracked attributes, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, and optionally `is_current`. Use half-open intervals `[valid_from, valid_to)` so adjacent versions meet without overlapping and an event exactly at the boundary matches the new version. A high sentinel end date is convenient but must fit every target timestamp type; nullable infinity is another choice. Derive current status from the open interval when possible, or validate the redundant flag.

For each business key, enforce at most one current version, unique surrogate keys, ordered bounds with start before end, and no overlap. Every fact requiring as-was context must match exactly one version at its event timestamp. Facts predating known history may use an explicit unknown version or follow a documented inference policy. Natural/business keys can be reused or merged in source systems, so durable identity mapping needs governance.

Change detection compares the tracked semantic values, not arbitrary serialization. Normalize only according to domain rules. Hashing can reduce comparison width but cannot replace null, collation, type, canonicalization, and collision reasoning. Include the tracked attribute set/version in the hash contract. Ignore changes to untracked operational metadata. Deduplicate source events by a stable ID or sequence before modifying history.

Late data, corrections, and two notions of time

A late effective change can arrive after later versions have already been created. Appending it as current is wrong. The loader must insert it in effective-time order, split or shorten the covering interval, and preserve adjacent versions. An out-of-order correction may update attributes for an existing interval rather than represent a new transition. Define source precedence, tie-breaking, and whether restated source history is authoritative. Reprocessing must be idempotent: the same source event cannot create another version.

Valid time describes when a fact was true in the business world. System time describes when the warehouse learned or recorded it. A standard Type 2 dimension usually preserves valid-time versions as currently understood, but overwriting an old version loses the ability to reproduce what a report showed before correction. Bitemporal modeling records both axes and supports “what was believed on reporting date R about business date V.” It is more complex and justified for audit, regulatory, or model-reproducibility requirements.

Hard deletion conflicts with immutable history. Privacy and retention policy may require erasure or irreversible anonymization across current and historical versions, facts, caches, and backups. Soft delete is not sufficient when deletion is legally required. Record tombstone semantics without retaining prohibited content. Separate business cancellation from physical privacy deletion.

Loading and operating dimension history

A robust incremental flow stages and deduplicates source changes, resolves durable identity, classifies new, unchanged, corrected, and changed records, then applies interval changes atomically. For an in-order Type 2 change, close the current version at the new `valid_from` and insert the new row. Readers must not observe the gap between those writes. Concurrency needs serialization by business key or an atomic merge strategy whose engine semantics are verified. Rerunning a batch should produce the same target state.

Backfills must coexist safely with live ingestion. Use a source cutoff or captured log position, rebuild history deterministically in a shadow table, validate it, catch up changes after the cutoff, then atomically swap. Re-keying facts can be expensive; retaining stable historical surrogate keys or rebuilding dependent facts may be necessary. Type 1 corrections should not accidentally change a Type 2 change hash and create versions.

Monitor version count per key, multiple-current and overlap violations, zero/negative intervals, unknown/inferred member rates, late-event age, duplicate events, fact temporal match cardinality, freshness, and source reconciliation. Retain raw change evidence and code versions. Rollback should restore the prior dimension and dependent fact-key state together; rolling back only one side breaks referential and historical consistency.

Math / formal view

For business key b, Type 2 versions are intervals I_i=[s_i,e_i). Correctness requires s_i<e_i, pairwise disjoint intervals, and at most one interval containing any time t. An as-was fact f with key b and event time t must map to exactly one version v where v.b=b and v.s≤t<v.e, or to an explicit documented unknown policy. System-time intervals add a second axis when prior warehouse beliefs must remain reproducible.

Customer tier changes and a late correction

Setup

Customer C is Bronze from January 1, becomes Gold effective March 1, and a change effective February 10 arrives on April 5 indicating Silver.

Initial history is Bronze `[Jan 1, Mar 1)` and Gold `[Mar 1, infinity)`. The late Silver event cannot be appended. Insert Silver `[Feb 10, Mar 1)` and shorten Bronze to `[Jan 1, Feb 10)`, leaving Gold unchanged. A February 20 sale maps to Silver; a March 20 sale maps to Gold. The current-state view may classify both under Gold, while the as-was view uses their stored/effective surrogate keys. A repeated Silver event is deduplicated and makes no new row. Tests verify contiguous ordered intervals, one current version, and exactly one temporal match for every sale. If the event corrected a typo rather than a real tier transition, the policy would update the affected historical interval instead of inventing a period.

Conclusion

Late arrival changes interval placement, and reporting semantics decide whether facts follow effective history or current classification.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build Type 2 interval insertion, including a late change, and verify non-overlap, one-current, idempotency, and temporal lookup.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
from datetime import date
INF=date.max

def insert_version(rows,key,start,value):
    if any(r['key']==key and r['start']==start and r['value']==value for r in rows): return rows
    same=sorted((r for r in rows if r['key']==key),key=lambda r:r['start'])
    covering=next((r for r in same if r['start']<=start<r['end']),None)
    end=covering['end'] if covering else next((r['start'] for r in same if r['start']>start),INF)
    if covering: covering['end']=start
    rows.append({'key':key,'start':start,'end':end,'value':value})
    return sorted(rows,key=lambda r:(r['key'],r['start']))

def lookup(rows,key,when):
    matches=[r for r in rows if r['key']==key and r['start']<=when<r['end']]
    if len(matches)!=1: raise ValueError('expected one version')
    return matches[0]
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
rows=[]
insert_version(rows,'C',date(2024,1,1),'Bronze')
insert_version(rows,'C',date(2024,3,1),'Gold')
insert_version(rows,'C',date(2024,2,10),'Silver')
before_repeat=[dict(r) for r in rows]
insert_version(rows,'C',date(2024,2,10),'Silver')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use engine-supported atomic merges with verified concurrency semantics, persist source event IDs and effective times, monitor interval invariants and late age, and rebuild/rollback dimensions with dependent facts.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert rows==before_repeat
assert [r['value'] for r in rows]==['Bronze','Silver','Gold']
assert all(a['end']<=b['start'] for a,b in zip(rows,rows[1:]))
assert sum(r['end']==INF for r in rows)==1
assert lookup(rows,'C',date(2024,2,20))['value']=='Silver'
assert lookup(rows,'C',date(2024,3,20))['value']=='Gold'

Common mistakes

  • Make the entire dimension Type 2.

    Choose policy by attribute; volatile or corrective fields can create meaningless versions and excessive storage.

  • Use inclusive start and end bounds for adjacent versions.

    Both versions match at the boundary. Half-open intervals make adjacency and temporal joins unambiguous.

  • Append every late change as the current version.

    Insert by effective time, repair neighboring bounds, and distinguish correction from real transition.

Likely follow-ups

  • When is Type 1 correct?

    When only current/corrected interpretation matters, history has no analytical value, or a prior value was erroneous and should be restated.

  • What invariants define a valid Type 2 history?

    Stable surrogate identity, ordered positive intervals, no overlap, at most one current row per business key, idempotent changes, and exactly one intended temporal match for facts.

  • Why would you need bitemporal data?

    To answer both what was effective in the business world and what the system believed at an earlier reporting time, preserving prior reports after late corrections.

Production / system-design connection

Define history semantics per attribute, durable identity, effective/system timestamps, source precedence, correction and deletion policies. Stage and deduplicate events, apply interval mutations atomically, serialize conflicting business-key updates, and make replay idempotent. Validate overlap, one-current, fact match cardinality, late age, inferred members, and reconciliation. Rebuild in versioned shadow tables and roll back dimensions with dependent facts. Enforce privacy erasure across all historical copies when required.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    How do Type 1 and Type 2 differ?

    Show solution

    Type 1 overwrites an attribute and restates historical joins under the latest value; Type 2 inserts effective-dated versions so facts can retain as-was context.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    A legal-name typo is fixed while customer risk class changes. Choose policies.

    Show solution

    Usually correct the name with Type 1 and preserve risk class with Type 2, assuming historical risk classification is needed.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A fact matches two customer dimension rows at its event time. What failed?

    Show solution

    The versions overlap, boundary comparisons are inconsistent, or identity resolution duplicated the business key. Repair intervals and enforce temporal uniqueness.

4.4

dbt: Transformation-as-Code

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

dbt turns analytical SQL transformations into a version-controlled dependency graph with compilation, environments, tests, documentation, and reusable metadata. The tool does not make a data model correct by itself: engineers still define grain, business semantics, materialization, incremental boundaries, and failure behavior. This chapter explains how `source()` and `ref()` create lineage and execution order; how staging, intermediate, and mart layers move from source-conformed to business-conformed data; and how views, tables, ephemeral models, incremental models, and snapshots trade freshness, cost, persistence, and recoverability. You will learn to separate unit tests of SQL logic from data tests of built relations, use source freshness and model contracts appropriately, design idempotent incremental builds, and use state-aware continuous integration without allowing partial production publication. A worked order mart traces raw inputs through staging and fact models with exact keys and reconciliation. Production guidance covers orchestration, concurrency, slim CI, backfills, artifacts, observability, secrets, warehouse permissions, deployment and rollback. The objective is to treat a dbt project as a governed analytical software system whose compiled SQL and datasets are both production artifacts—not as a folder of ad hoc queries.

Prerequisites

  • star-schema
  • sql-ctes-subqueries
  • sql-window-functions

Learning objectives

  • Structure a dbt dependency graph from source-conformed staging through purpose-built intermediates to business-conformed marts.
  • Choose materializations and incremental strategies from correctness, freshness, cost, rebuild, and late-data requirements.
  • Build a deployment and testing workflow that distinguishes SQL logic, dataset assertions, freshness, contracts, artifacts, and rollback.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

dbt compiles templated SQL models into a directed acyclic graph using declared `source()` and `ref()` dependencies, then builds and tests selected nodes in dependency order. A maintainable project stages source data once, uses focused intermediate transformations, and publishes business-conformed marts with explicit grain and metrics. Materialization is a workload decision: views defer compute, tables precompute, incremental models update a bounded subset and need idempotent late-data logic, and snapshots preserve changing source state. Production quality requires version control, CI against isolated schemas, unit and data tests, contracts for public shapes, source freshness, atomic deployment, artifacts, monitoring, and a tested rollback or full rebuild.

What you must know

  • Dependencies must be declared
  • Staging is source-conformed
  • Marts are business-conformed
  • Incremental logic must equal full refresh
  • Tests and contracts protect different boundaries

Why this matters

When transformations live as copied SQL in schedulers and dashboards, definitions drift, dependencies are implicit, changes are hard to review, and failures leave unclear partial state. dbt makes the graph and compiled artifacts inspectable, but weak projects can still produce tangled models, repeated business logic, expensive view chains, and incremental tables that silently diverge from a full rebuild. The engineering value comes from disciplined modeling, contracts, verification, environment isolation, and operational ownership around the tool.

Intuition

Treat each model as a pure-looking build step with a named input contract and one published output. `ref()` is a typed-looking wire in a circuit: it records dependency and resolves the environment-specific relation. Staging cleans source vocabulary into reliable atoms; intermediate nodes perform one explainable transformation; marts assemble the business entities people query. Materialization decides whether a node is recomputed at read time, build time, or only for changed slices.

The model graph and project structure

A dbt model is usually a SQL select statement plus configuration and properties. `source()` names externally loaded relations and carries freshness or schema metadata. `ref()` names another dbt resource, lets dbt infer an edge, and resolves the correct database/schema identifier for the current target. The resulting directed acyclic graph determines selection, build order, documentation lineage, and impact analysis. Hiding dependencies behind hard-coded relation names or uncontrolled macros breaks these capabilities. Cycles usually reveal mixed responsibilities and must be redesigned.

Official dbt guidance describes an arc from source-conformed to business-conformed data. Staging models are thin, source-oriented atoms: rename, cast, standardize and perform limited cleanup once. They should not embed changing business aggregations or join many domains. Intermediate models combine or reshape those atoms for a clear purpose and can remain private. Marts publish entities, facts, dimensions, and metrics in language consumers understand. Folder and naming conventions should communicate this intent rather than encode arbitrary execution numbers.

Keep models cohesive and avoid both extremes: a thousand one-line pass-through nodes increase cognitive and runtime overhead, while one enormous query hides grain transitions and repeated logic. Declare a grain and primary key for every published relation. Centralize reusable semantic rules without creating macros that generate opaque SQL. Compile and inspect the actual target-dialect SQL; templating is code generation, and what the warehouse runs is the final behavior.

Materializations and incremental correctness

A view stores a query and computes when read. It is simple and fresh with respect to upstream state, but deep view chains can repeat expensive work and expose upstream changes immediately. A table pays compute and storage at build time, then serves predictable reads until refreshed. Ephemeral models inline as common table expressions and reduce persisted clutter, but can make compiled SQL large and are unsuitable as public boundaries. Materialized views and custom materializations are platform-specific and require current adapter documentation.

An incremental model updates only selected records or partitions. Its filter is not an optimization detail; it is a second algorithm that must converge to the same state as a correct full refresh. Choose a unique key and merge/append/overwrite strategy from source semantics. Use source update timestamps only if they are trustworthy and handle equal timestamps, clock behavior, deletes and corrections. An overlap window catches late changes but must be sized and monitored; it does not solve arbitrarily late data. Partition overwrite can be clearer for time-bounded restatement.

Make every run idempotent. A retry cannot duplicate facts or advance a watermark past failed work. Test incremental versus full-refresh equivalence on fixtures containing updates, deletes, duplicates, late events and schema changes. Snapshots are designed to capture changing source records over time; they are not a substitute for event history when the source lacks reliable change semantics. Plan periodic rebuilds when drift risk justifies the cost.

Testing, contracts, and documentation

Unit tests provide static input rows and assert a model's SQL output before materializing production data. They are useful for branches, joins, date boundaries and regression logic. Data tests query built relations and return failing rows: uniqueness, not-null, relationships, accepted values, temporal overlap, reconciliation and business invariants. Generic tests parameterize reusable assertions; singular tests express model-specific rules. A passing set of basic column tests does not prove metric correctness, so add aggregate identities and source control totals where risk warrants them.

Source freshness evaluates whether upstream data arrived within an expectation; downstream model freshness may require separate end-to-end observation. A model contract declares output column names and types and may express constraints, but platform enforcement differs. Contracts protect shape and compatibility; data tests protect content after build. Public, cross-team models benefit most from contracts and versions. Do not assume a declared primary key is enforced by every analytical warehouse—keep the uniqueness test unless the target guarantee is verified.

Descriptions, owners, exposures, tags and semantic metadata make the generated catalog useful only when reviewed with code. Document grain, time semantics, null/unknown behavior, freshness, sensitivity, and supported metrics. Persist dbt artifacts such as the manifest and run results with the code revision and environment. They support lineage, impact analysis, observability and reproducibility, but emitted lineage reflects declared/compiled dependencies and can miss external side effects.

CI, deployment, and operation

Continuous integration should compile the project, validate configuration, run unit tests, and build/test the affected graph in an isolated schema using representative data. State-aware selection can reduce cost, but deferral to production artifacts needs compatible versions and must not hide a changed upstream assumption. Prevent pull requests from overwriting shared relations. Linting and SQL style help review, while query-plan or bytes-scanned budgets catch accidental full scans.

Production orchestration loads sources first, then invokes selected dbt resources with bounded concurrency and warehouse resources. A command succeeding is not enough: capture model and test statuses, timings, adapter responses, freshness, row counts and artifacts. Define behavior for warnings, flaky external sources and partial graph failure. Critical publication can build versioned tables and swap aliases only after downstream tests, or use target-platform transactional mechanisms. Avoid leaving a mixture of old and new mutually dependent marts visible.

For backfills, record the source cutoff, parameters and code revision; isolate compute; use the same business logic; reconcile before promotion; and catch up live changes. Rollback may mean restoring a prior table snapshot, alias, manifest/code release, or rebuilding from trusted raw data. Keep secrets outside the project, grant CI and production service accounts least privilege, restrict developer targets, mask sensitive data in test environments, and audit access. Monitor model duration, queue time, scan cost, freshness, failures, test results, contract changes and downstream incidents.

Math / formal view

Represent a dbt project as DAG G=(V,E), with one model/source/test resource per node and edge u→v when v depends on u. A valid build order is a topological ordering. For an incremental model with source history S_t and target state T_t, correctness requires the incremental transition U(T_t,ΔS)=T_{t+1} to be idempotent and observationally equivalent to a full build F(S_{≤t+1}) for the documented late/update/delete horizon.

Build a tested order mart

Setup

Raw customer, order and item tables land hourly. Analysts need one order-line fact and one customer mart without copying transformation logic into dashboards.

Declare raw tables as sources with freshness expectations. `stg_orders` and `stg_items` rename identifiers, cast timestamps, normalize statuses and retain source update time; no cross-domain joins occur there. An intermediate model allocates order discounts to lines and tests that allocated amounts reconcile to the header. `fct_order_lines` declares one order plus line grain, references effective dimensions and exposes additive amount components. `dim_customers` publishes stable customer attributes. Unit fixtures exercise cancellations, null discounts and boundary timestamps. Data tests enforce fact uniqueness, relationships and reconciliation. The incremental fact merges by line key with a monitored overlap window and delete handling, then a scheduled full-refresh comparison checks equivalence. CI builds the changed node and children in a pull-request schema. Production builds versioned outputs, runs tests, publishes only after success, stores artifacts and retains the prior aliases for rollback.

Conclusion

The graph makes dependencies visible, while grain, tests, materialization and promotion policy make the resulting data trustworthy.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build a minimal dependency-graph executor and verify topological order, isolated relation resolution, cycle rejection and reproducible output.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def topo(graph):
    indegree={node:0 for node in graph}
    children={node:[] for node in graph}
    for node,deps in graph.items():
        for dep in deps:
            if dep not in graph: raise KeyError(dep)
            indegree[node]+=1; children[dep].append(node)
    ready=sorted(node for node,n in indegree.items() if n==0); order=[]
    while ready:
        node=ready.pop(0); order.append(node)
        for child in sorted(children[node]):
            indegree[child]-=1
            if indegree[child]==0: ready.append(child); ready.sort()
    if len(order)!=len(graph): raise ValueError('cycle')
    return order

def relation(target,node):
    return f'{target}__{node}'
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import sqlite3
graph={'stg_orders':[],'stg_items':[],'int_lines':['stg_orders','stg_items'],'fct_lines':['int_lines']}
con=sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
for node in topo(graph):
    con.execute('CREATE TABLE '+relation('pr42',node)+'(built INTEGER)')
    con.execute('INSERT INTO '+relation('pr42',node)+' VALUES(1)')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use dbt's compiled graph and artifacts in real projects; build affected nodes in isolated CI targets, store run evidence, promote tested versions atomically, and retain the prior production relations for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert topo(graph)==['stg_items','stg_orders','int_lines','fct_lines']
assert all(con.execute('SELECT built FROM '+relation('pr42',node)).fetchone()==(1,) for node in graph)
assert relation('prod','fct_lines')!='pr42__fct_lines'
try: topo({'a':['b'],'b':['a']})
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('cycle must fail')

Common mistakes

  • Put business joins and metrics in staging models.

    Keep staging source-conformed and reusable; publish cross-source business semantics in intermediate or mart layers.

  • An incremental filter only affects performance.

    It defines which history can be corrected and can make the target diverge permanently from a full build.

  • A dbt contract proves values are correct.

    Contracts primarily protect output shape/types and supported constraints; content and metric invariants need data/unit tests and reconciliation.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why use `ref()` instead of a hard-coded table name?

    It declares graph lineage, controls build order, supports selection and environment resolution, and enables impact analysis.

  • When should a model be incremental?

    When full rebuild cost or latency is material and the source provides deterministic keys and change/delete semantics that can make incremental results equivalent within a stated horizon.

  • How do unit tests differ from data tests?

    Unit tests validate SQL transformation logic with controlled static inputs; data tests query built relations for failing real records or invariants.

Production / system-design connection

Compile and test every change in isolated schemas, retain manifest/run artifacts, enforce public model contracts and semantic data tests, and verify incremental/full-refresh equivalence. Orchestrate bounded graph runs with least-privilege identities, source and end-to-end freshness, cost/runtime budgets, and explicit partial-failure policy. Promote atomically or through versioned aliases, make backfills reproducible, monitor downstream impact, and keep prior trusted tables and code ready for rollback.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What project arc does current dbt guidance recommend?

    Show solution

    Move from source-conformed staging atoms through purpose-built intermediate transformations to business-conformed marts.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Choose a materialization for a costly daily aggregate read by hundreds of dashboards.

    Show solution

    A table or supported materialized view is a sensible starting point; evaluate freshness, rebuild cost, target capabilities and atomic refresh rather than stacking a costly ordinary view.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    An incremental fact misses corrections older than seven days. Why?

    Show solution

    The overlap horizon is part of the algorithm and excludes those changes. Add reliable change capture or a restatement/backfill strategy, monitor late age, and verify against full refresh.
