4.5

Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

A data contract is a versioned agreement at a producer-consumer boundary: identity, schema, semantics, quality expectations, freshness, ownership, compatibility, security classification and change process. Lineage records how datasets are produced and consumed through jobs and runs so teams can assess impact, trace incidents and understand provenance. Neither is sufficient alone. A schema can remain compatible while the meaning or population changes, and a lineage graph can show edges without proving that the data on them is correct. This chapter separates contracts from tests, service-level objectives and documentation; distinguishes design-time from runtime and column-level lineage; and explains how OpenLineage represents jobs, runs, datasets, events and extensible facets. You will learn to classify additive and breaking changes, evolve public datasets through deprecation and versions, propagate sensitivity, and avoid turning governance into unreviewed YAML. A worked customer mart change follows an identifier type migration through consumers and rollback. Production guidance covers ownership, CI, catalog integration, event delivery, graph completeness, incident response and access control. The outcome is a practical governance system that makes change safe without pretending every producer can guarantee perfect data.

Prerequisites

  • dbt-modeling
  • star-schema

Learning objectives

  • Define a useful data contract spanning structure, semantics, quality, service levels, ownership, security, compatibility and change policy.
  • Interpret design-time, runtime, dataset-, job-, run- and column-level lineage without overstating completeness or correctness.
  • Operate a compatible schema/semantic change using impact analysis, consumer validation, versioning, deprecation, monitoring and rollback.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A data contract is a versioned producer-consumer agreement for a dataset's identity, schema, field semantics, grain, quality expectations, freshness, ownership, security and compatibility policy. Tests measure whether an instance meets parts of that agreement; they are not the agreement itself. Lineage links datasets through jobs and concrete runs, enabling impact and root-cause analysis. Good governance validates contracts in CI and production, captures runtime lineage, assigns owners, classifies breaking changes, versions or dual-publishes incompatible changes, propagates access policy, and monitors both contract violations and missing lineage. Lineage shows provenance, not correctness.

What you must know

  • Contract includes semantics, not only schema
  • Tests observe contract properties
  • Lineage records production relationships
  • Compatibility needs consumer evidence
  • Ownership and change process make metadata operational

Why this matters

A producer can rename a column, change cents to dollars, alter deduplication, or deliver six hours late while all pipelines technically succeed. Consumers discover the change through broken dashboards or model drift. Contracts establish expectations and change protocol; lineage identifies who may be affected and which run introduced a value. Without enforcement and ownership they become stale paperwork. Without humility they promise guarantees the platform cannot enforce. The useful design connects metadata to delivery, monitoring and incident response.

Intuition

Think of a dataset as a public API. Its table and columns are the response shape, grain and meanings are semantics, freshness and quality are service behavior, and ownership/change policy is API governance. Lineage is the distributed trace: it shows which job run read which inputs and produced which outputs. An API schema and a trace help for different reasons, and neither proves the business answer is right.

What a data contract must say

Start with stable dataset identity and owner. Define the row grain, primary or candidate keys, column names and types, nullability, units, domains, timezone, encoding, event/effective/processing timestamps, retention and deletion semantics. For nested or streaming records, define envelope, ordering, partition key and event identity. Semantic examples are often more useful than a type alone: `amount` needs currency and gross/net meaning; `customer_id` needs identity scope and reuse policy.

Quality expectations should be measurable and risk-based: uniqueness, relationship coverage, allowed values, reconciliation, distribution bounds or domain invariants. State evaluation window, threshold, severity and failure behavior. Freshness needs a reference timestamp and percentile or deadline, not “near real time.” Availability, completeness and recovery objectives may differ. Security metadata includes classification, purpose, allowed consumers, masking, residency and retention.

Define compatibility rules and a change process: notification, review, impact evidence, versioning, deprecation window and emergency procedure. A contract cannot guarantee upstream reality; it can state what the producer validates and how violations are surfaced. Separate hard guarantees enforced before publication from monitored objectives that may occasionally breach. Assign consumer responsibilities too, such as not depending on undocumented columns or current physical partition layout.

Compatibility and semantic change

An additive nullable column is often structurally backward compatible, but it can increase cost or leak sensitive information. Removing or renaming a field and narrowing/changing a type are usually breaking. Widening a type can still break code generators or equality behavior. Changing units, grain, population, timestamp meaning, deduplication, default null handling or late-data policy is semantically breaking even when schema is identical. Contract tooling that checks only names and types cannot detect these changes.

Classify compatibility relative to real consumers: backward compatibility lets new data work with old readers; forward compatibility lets old data work with new readers. Evidence comes from the consumer graph, query/code analysis, contract tests and staged execution—not an assumption that no one uses a column. Unknown consumers mean risk, not safety. Publish supported interfaces instead of granting everyone access to internal staging tables.

For an incompatible change, create a new version or parallel field/table, backfill deterministically, dual-publish if necessary, let consumers validate and migrate, monitor adoption, then deprecate and remove on a communicated date. Preserve the old path long enough for rollback. Avoid permanent dual semantics with unclear ownership. Emergency security changes may require immediate restriction; document the exception and provide a safe consumer response.

Design-time and runtime lineage

Lineage can be declared at design time from SQL references, orchestration DAGs and model manifests, or observed at runtime from query plans, logs and instrumented job events. Design lineage answers what should depend on what; runtime lineage answers what a concrete run actually read and wrote. Dynamic SQL, stored procedures, external APIs, file globbing and manual uploads create blind spots. Column-level lineage traces expressions from input fields to output fields but can be ambiguous for filters, joins, aggregation populations and opaque functions.

OpenLineage's core model distinguishes a Job, a Run instance and a Dataset. Runtime run events record lifecycle states and input/output datasets; design-time job and dataset events can publish static metadata. Facets extend entities with schema, source-code location, versions, quality metrics, assertions and other information. Consistent namespaces and names are essential: if two integrations identify the same table differently, the graph fragments. Run IDs must remain stable across events for one execution.

Lineage is evidence, not proof. An edge does not specify business correctness, delivery completeness, transformation version, or whether a failed run published partial data unless those facets/events are captured. Events can arrive late, duplicate or be lost, so the lineage backend needs idempotent ingestion and completeness monitoring. Sensitive SQL and column names may themselves require access control.

Enforcement, incidents, and operating model

Validate proposed contracts as machine-readable artifacts in CI, but also require review of semantic and policy changes. Compile producer code, compare public schemas/contracts with the released version, run unit and data tests, and use lineage/consumer manifests for impact analysis. At publication, enforce supported constraints, quarantine or block severe violations, and emit data-quality and lineage events with the code and dataset versions. Do not silently coerce incompatible rows merely to keep a pipeline green.

A catalog should surface owner, descriptions, contract version, freshness, quality, classifications, lineage and recent incidents in one place. Metadata freshness is itself a service: stale ownership and incomplete graphs damage decisions. Track percentage of public assets with owners/contracts, lineage event completeness, unresolved violations, time to acknowledge, deprecation age and consumer migration. Avoid vanity coverage metrics that reward empty descriptions.

During an incident, identify the first bad dataset version and run, traverse downstream consumers, stop or label publication, notify owners, restore or rebuild a trusted version, and verify business measures. Lineage accelerates this only if runtime versions and ownership are reliable. Access to graph traversal must respect sensitive relationships. Use least-privilege publication identities, signed or authenticated metadata events where appropriate, audit changes, and prevent untrusted producers from claiming another dataset's namespace.

Math / formal view

Model lineage as a directed, version-aware graph G=(D∪J,E), where D are dataset versions and J are job runs. Edges D→J denote reads and J→D denote writes. Impact is a reachability query constrained by environment and version. A contract C_v is a predicate set over dataset metadata and observations plus a compatibility relation K(C_v,C_{v+1}); structural K is necessary but not sufficient for semantic compatibility.

Migrate a public customer identifier

Setup

A public customer mart exposes a 32-bit integer ID. Growth requires a string identifier that also changes identity scope across regions.

The change is not a simple type widening: scope semantics change. Contract v2 adds `customer_global_id` with explicit format, uniqueness domain, lineage to the identity service, security classification and rollout dates while retaining v1 `customer_id`. CI compares contracts, scans consumer manifests and queries, and flags dashboards and feature pipelines using the old field. The producer backfills v2, validates one-to-one mappings and exception counts, dual-publishes versioned outputs, and emits runtime lineage with dataset and code versions. Consumers reconcile results in a shadow environment and migrate. Adoption and old-field reads are monitored. If mapping defects appear, the alias returns to v1 while v2 is repaired from versioned inputs. After the deprecation window and owner approval, v1 is removed and retention policy deletes obsolete mappings.

Conclusion

Schema, identity semantics, lineage, consumer evidence and rollback all participate in a safe public change.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Validate a compact row contract, build a job-dataset lineage graph, and verify that breaking changes and downstream impact are detected.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def validate(rows,contract):
    errors=[]
    for i,row in enumerate(rows):
        for name,spec in contract['columns'].items():
            if name not in row: errors.append((i,name,'missing')); continue
            value=row[name]
            if value is None and not spec['nullable']: errors.append((i,name,'null'))
            if value is not None and not isinstance(value,spec['type']): errors.append((i,name,'type'))
    key=contract['key']; values=[row.get(key) for row in rows]
    if len(values)!=len(set(values)): errors.append((-1,key,'duplicate'))
    return errors

def downstream(edges,start):
    seen=set(); frontier=list(start)
    while frontier:
        node=frontier.pop(0)
        for child in edges.get(node,[]):
            if child not in seen: seen.add(child); frontier.append(child)
    return seen

v1={'key':'customer_id','columns':{'customer_id':{'type':int,'nullable':False},'tier':{'type':str,'nullable':False}}}
rows=[{'customer_id':1,'tier':'gold'},{'customer_id':2,'tier':'silver'}]
edges={'raw.customer':['job.build_customer'],'job.build_customer':['mart.customer'],'mart.customer':['job.dashboard','job.features'],'job.dashboard':['dashboard.revenue'],'job.features':['model.churn']}
impact=downstream(edges,{'mart.customer'})
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use a versioned contract format and OpenLineage-compatible events in production, secure namespaces, persist code/dataset versions, monitor event completeness and violations, and exercise dual-publish plus rollback with real consumers.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert validate(rows,v1)==[]
assert impact=={'job.dashboard','job.features','dashboard.revenue','model.churn'}
bad=rows+[{'customer_id':2,'tier':None}]
assert (-1,'customer_id','duplicate') in validate(bad,v1)
assert (2,'tier','null') in validate(bad,v1)
v2={'key':'customer_id','columns':{'customer_id':{'type':str,'nullable':False},'tier':{'type':str,'nullable':False}}}
assert validate(rows,v2) and validate(rows,v2)[0][2]=='type'

Common mistakes

  • A contract is just a JSON schema.

    Useful contracts also define grain, semantics, quality/service expectations, ownership, security, compatibility and change procedure.

  • Lineage proves the output is correct.

    It shows declared or observed production relationships; correctness still needs tests, reconciliation, versions and domain review.

  • Adding a nullable column is always safe.

    It may change cost, wildcard outputs, serialization, privacy exposure or consumer behavior; compatibility is consumer-relative.

Likely follow-ups

  • How is a contract different from a data test?

    The contract states the expected interface and policy; a test observes whether a dataset instance satisfies one measurable property of it.

  • What is runtime lineage?

    Evidence from a concrete execution linking a run and its actual input/output dataset identities and versions, rather than only declared design dependencies.

  • What is the hardest breaking change to detect?

    Semantic change with unchanged schema—such as unit, grain, population, time or identity meaning—because shape-only tools remain green.

Production / system-design connection

Version public contracts and enforce supported shape/constraint checks before publication; measure quality and freshness with explicit severity and failure policy. Capture authenticated design and runtime lineage with stable namespaces, run IDs, code and dataset versions, and monitor missing events. Require semantic review, consumer impact evidence, dual-publish/version incompatible changes, enforce classification and retention, and maintain owner-driven incident and rollback procedures.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Name four contract elements beyond column type.

    Show solution

    Examples: grain, field semantics/units, keys, quality thresholds, freshness, ownership, classification, retention, compatibility and deprecation policy.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    A producer changes `revenue` from cents to dollars without renaming it. Is the schema compatible?

    Show solution

    Structurally perhaps, semantically no. Version or introduce a clearly named field, backfill, dual-publish, notify and validate consumers, then deprecate the old meaning.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Impact analysis misses a dashboard that broke. What lineage gaps should you inspect?

    Show solution

    Hard-coded relations, direct BI queries, dynamic SQL, mismatched namespaces, lost runtime events, unregistered extracts and external/manual dependencies.

4.6

Columnar Storage, Parquet & Predicate Pushdown

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

Apache Parquet is an open columnar file format for analytical data. A file is divided horizontally into row groups; each row group contains one contiguous column chunk per column, and column chunks contain encoded and compressed pages. That hierarchy lets readers project only required columns and use metadata statistics, dictionaries, page indexes and partition information to skip data that cannot match a predicate. This chapter derives the I/O and compression benefits, explains definition and repetition levels for nested structures, and separates file-format capabilities from query-engine behavior. You will learn why predicate pushdown is not the same as file pruning, how row-group size and sort order affect selectivity, why thousands of tiny files damage planning and throughput, and why a Parquet file alone does not provide table transactions, schema governance or safe concurrent updates. A worked event dataset estimates bytes avoided under projection and time-range pruning. Production guidance covers types, timestamps, nulls, dictionary fallback, compression, encryption, object-store requests, compaction, statistics, corruption, schema evolution and table formats. The aim is to reason from the query and physical layout to measured scan cost instead of assuming the `.parquet` suffix automatically makes analytics fast.

Prerequisites

  • oltp-olap
  • big-o

Learning objectives

  • Explain Parquet's file, row-group, column-chunk and page hierarchy and how it supports projection, encoding, compression and parallel reads.
  • Distinguish partition pruning, row-group/page skipping and predicate pushdown, then diagnose why an intended filter still scans data.
  • Choose and operate file size, row-group layout, sort order, schema, encoding and table metadata from real workloads and reliability needs.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Parquet stores data by column within row groups. Each row group has one contiguous column chunk per field, split into encoded and compressed pages, with footer metadata describing schema and locations and often statistics. Analytical readers can avoid unprojected columns and skip row groups or pages whose metadata proves a predicate cannot match. Similar adjacent values compress effectively through encodings such as dictionary and run-length encoding. Performance still depends on engine support, file and row-group size, sort order, statistics, filter form and object-store requests. Parquet is a file format, not a transaction manager; reliable tables need metadata, atomic commits, schema policy and compaction around the files.

What you must know

  • Row groups partition rows
  • Column chunks make projection cheap
  • Pages carry encoding and compression
  • Statistics can prove non-matches
  • A file format is not a table transaction layer

Why this matters

Analytical workloads often read a few columns from billions of values. Row-oriented interchange wastes I/O and misses compression opportunities. Parquet can reduce bytes read dramatically, but poor layout creates tiny-file overhead, weak pruning, memory pressure or silent type inconsistencies. Teams also confuse storage partition filters with predicate pushdown and assume concurrent file writes form an atomic table. Understanding the physical hierarchy helps explain both speedups and costly surprises.

Intuition

Imagine a library shelf built in horizontal batches. For each batch of records, all timestamps are stored together, all customer IDs together and all amounts together. A query requesting time and amount opens only those compartments. A label on each compartment records minimum and maximum; if the requested date is outside that range, the whole compartment stays closed. Sorting improves labels, while random mixing makes every label span almost everything.

File, row group, column chunk, and page

A Parquet file contains one or more row groups plus file metadata in the footer. A row group is a horizontal slice of rows and is a common unit of parallel scan planning. Within each row group, every leaf column has a contiguous column chunk, so reading a projection can seek to only relevant chunks. Column chunks are divided into pages, the unit for encoding and compression. Page headers and metadata describe how to decode values; optional page indexes can enable finer skipping.

The footer records schema, row groups, column chunk locations, counts, codecs, encodings and available statistics. Reading many remote files requires fetching their metadata, so file count and footer access affect planning. Row groups should be large enough for sequential throughput and compression but small enough for parallelism, memory and useful skipping. Universal magic sizes are misleading because object store latency, engine scheduling, row width and query selectivity differ.

Parquet represents nested records by shredding them into leaf columns plus definition and repetition levels that encode nullability and list/struct structure. A projected nested field may require reading its levels to reassemble records. Logical types annotate physical primitives for dates, decimals, timestamps and strings; writers and readers must agree on precision, timezone and compatibility. Always inspect the actual schema written, not only the dataframe type before serialization.

Encoding, compression, and CPU trade-offs

Encoding changes the representation before compression. Dictionary encoding stores distinct values once and replaces occurrences with smaller indexes, effective for low-to-moderate cardinality columns. Run-length and bit-packed encodings compress repeated indexes and levels. Delta encodings exploit small differences in ordered numbers or lengths. Implementations choose among supported encodings and may fall back when a dictionary grows too large. Compression codecs then reduce encoded page bytes; codec choice trades ratio, CPU, compatibility and splittability at the page/chunk organization.

Columnar locality improves compression because adjacent values share type and often distribution. Sorting by a frequently filtered column creates long runs and narrow min/max ranges, improving both encoding and skipping. But clustering for one query can reduce locality for another and makes writes/compaction more expensive. High-cardinality random identifiers rarely benefit from a dictionary and can make dictionary construction wasteful.

Measure compressed size, write throughput, read CPU, decoded rows, cache behavior and bytes fetched for representative projections. Smaller files may lower first-result latency yet increase metadata requests; large row groups improve sequential I/O but reduce fine-grained skipping. Encryption can protect column data and footer metadata where supported, but key distribution and reader compatibility are operational dependencies. Compression is not access control.

Projection, pruning, and predicate pushdown

Column projection avoids reading chunks for unselected columns. Partition pruning excludes files or directories using table/partition metadata before Parquet scanning. Row-group or page skipping uses column statistics, dictionaries, bloom filters or indexes to prove that a physical block cannot contain a match. Predicate pushdown means the engine passes a filter into the scan so filtering and skipping occur near the reader; a pushed predicate may still read every group if metadata ranges overlap it. These mechanisms should be reported separately.

A predicate must be translatable to the storage reader. Wrapping a column in an unsupported function, implicit casts, timezone conversion, complex disjunction or user-defined function may prevent pushdown. Statistics can be absent, truncated, unreliable for a type, or broad because data is unsorted. Null counts help with `IS NULL`; min/max do not encode arbitrary distributions. Bloom filters can disprove membership probabilistically without false negatives when correctly built, but add storage and CPU and are not universally supported.

Use the query engine's explain/profile output to inspect projected columns, filters, files/row groups selected, rows decoded and bytes read. Compare a direct range predicate with an equivalent transformed predicate. If every row group spans the full date range, rewrite data with useful clustering or partitioning rather than adding more SQL hints. Never infer pruning only from fast execution on a warm cache.

From files to reliable analytical tables

A directory of Parquet files does not by itself define an atomic table version. Readers listing files while writers add or replace them can observe partial batches, duplicates or missing data. Schema can vary across files, deletes require rewriting or side metadata, and partition directories can become inconsistent. Open table formats and managed warehouses add snapshots, manifests, atomic metadata commits, schema and partition evolution, delete semantics and time travel over underlying files.

The small-file problem appears when each task or event creates tiny objects. Planning and object-store request overhead dominate, compression suffers and executors process too little data per task. Compact files under a snapshot-aware transaction so readers never see both old and replacement files. Avoid blind file deletion; metadata may reference a file from an older snapshot needed for rollback. Coordinate retention with time travel and legal requirements.

Validate schema, row counts, control totals, nulls, key uniqueness and file checksums where appropriate. Detect corrupt or unreadable files before promotion. Monitor file and row-group size distributions, file count per partition, compression ratio, scan bytes, pruning effectiveness, footer/request latency, compaction backlog and query spill. Version writer libraries and test cross-engine reads. Preserve raw/replay inputs, publish a new snapshot atomically and roll back metadata to a trusted snapshot when a bad write is discovered.

Math / formal view

For N rows and columns C with compressed chunk sizes b_{g,c} in row group g, a projected scan over P⊆C reads approximately Σ_{g∈G_selected}Σ_{c∈P}b_{g,c} plus metadata and request overhead. Statistics prune group g for predicate x∈[a,b] when its trustworthy interval [min_g,max_g] is disjoint from [a,b]. Overlapping ranges prevent proof of absence even if few rows match.

Time-range event scan

Setup

A daily event dataset has 100 columns but a dashboard reads timestamp, region and amount for one hour.

Write files partitioned by day and sort within each day by event timestamp before forming row groups. The table layer prunes all other day files. Projection requests three leaf column chunks rather than 100. For the selected day, row-group min/max timestamps exclude groups outside the hour; the reader applies the pushed region filter to remaining pages. Profile output records files, groups, bytes and rows scanned. If events were randomly ordered, every group's time range might span most of the day and no groups could be excluded. A transformed predicate such as formatting timestamp to text may also block pushdown. Compaction creates appropriately sized files under a new atomic table snapshot and the old snapshot remains available for rollback until retention expires.

Conclusion

Partitioning, clustering, metadata and predicate form cooperate; Parquet alone does not guarantee pruning.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Expose dictionary encoding and min/max row-group pruning, then compare the result with an idiomatic PyArrow Parquet scan (Use It requires `pyarrow`).

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def dictionary_encode(values):
    dictionary=[]; index={} ; codes=[]
    for value in values:
        if value not in index:
            index[value]=len(dictionary); dictionary.append(value)
        codes.append(index[value])
    return dictionary,codes

def groups(rows,size):
    out=[]
    for start in range(0,len(rows),size):
        chunk=rows[start:start+size]
        out.append({'rows':chunk,'min_ts':min(r['ts'] for r in chunk),'max_ts':max(r['ts'] for r in chunk)})
    return out

def scan(groups_,lo,hi):
    selected=[g for g in groups_ if not (g['max_ts']<lo or g['min_ts']>hi)]
    return [r for g in selected for r in g['rows'] if lo<=r['ts']<=hi],len(selected)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
rows=[{'ts':i,'region':['EU','EU','US'][i%3],'amount':float(i)} for i in range(12)]
rows.sort(key=lambda r:r['ts'])
dictionary,codes=dictionary_encode([r['region'] for r in rows])
row_groups=groups(rows,4)
result,selected=scan(row_groups,5,6)
try:
    import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.parquet as pq, tempfile
except ImportError:
    pa=pq=None
if pa is not None:
    path=tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.parquet',delete=False).name
    pq.write_table(pa.Table.from_pylist(rows),path,row_group_size=4)
    arrow_rows=pq.read_table(path,columns=['ts','amount'],filters=[('ts','>=',5),('ts','<=',6)]).to_pylist()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Profile target-engine files, row groups, projected columns and bytes; compact under atomic snapshots, validate schemas/control totals across readers, monitor tiny files and pruning, and retain a trusted snapshot for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert dictionary==['EU','US']
assert [dictionary[code] for code in codes]==[r['region'] for r in rows]
assert [r['ts'] for r in result]==[5,6]
assert selected==1 and selected < len(row_groups)
if pa is not None:
    assert arrow_rows==[{'ts':5,'amount':5.0},{'ts':6,'amount':6.0}]

Common mistakes

  • Parquet automatically makes every query fast.

    Benefits depend on projection, filter translation, layout, statistics, file sizes, engine implementation, cache and query shape.

  • Predicate pushdown means no irrelevant data was read.

    The filter may be pushed but metadata may be too broad to skip blocks; inspect groups, rows and bytes scanned.

  • Replacing files in a directory is an atomic table update.

    Parquet supplies file representation, not multi-file transaction metadata; use an atomic publication/table layer.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a row group?

    A horizontal batch of rows containing one contiguous column chunk per leaf column; it is commonly a scan/parallelism and statistics unit.

  • Why does sorting help pruning?

    It narrows per-group min/max ranges for the sort key, letting a range predicate prove more groups cannot match.

  • Why are tiny files harmful?

    They multiply listing/footer requests and scheduling tasks, reduce sequential I/O and compression, and make planning dominate useful scan work.

Production / system-design connection

Benchmark real projections and predicates, profile files/groups/bytes/rows, and tune file/row-group layout from evidence. Enforce logical types, timestamp/decimal semantics and cross-engine compatibility; compact tiny files transactionally; monitor compression, pruning, requests, corruption and backlog. Use a snapshot/table layer for atomic publication, evolution, deletes and rollback, propagate encryption/access policy, and retain files according to time-travel and privacy rules.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    State the Parquet physical hierarchy.

    Show solution

    A file contains row groups; each row group has one column chunk per leaf column; each column chunk contains encoded and compressed pages.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Queries filter by event day and select four of eighty columns. Which layouts help?

    Show solution

    Partition/table metadata by an appropriate day transform, project only four columns, and cluster row groups by common selective fields if measurements justify it.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A timestamp filter is pushed but scans all row groups. Give likely causes.

    Show solution

    Random order produced broad ranges, statistics are absent/truncated, a cast changed comparison semantics, or each group genuinely overlaps the requested interval.

4.7

Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse

highverified
Roles: de, ds, da

Topic overview

A data warehouse, data lake and lakehouse are architectural patterns assembled from storage, metadata, transaction, governance and compute capabilities—not quality rankings. A warehouse offers managed relational tables, SQL optimization, transactions and governance with controlled storage and strong workload integration. A data lake places diverse data in scalable object storage with open files and multiple compute engines, gaining flexibility while requiring explicit metadata, quality and publication discipline. A lakehouse adds a transactional metadata/table layer over directly accessible open files to provide snapshots, atomic updates, schema and partition evolution, time travel and improved optimization. This chapter separates file format from table format, catalog, engine and semantic model; compares coupling, latency, interoperability, cost and operational burden; and explains why “one copy” does not mean one consistent interpretation. You will learn to select an architecture from workloads and ownership, design bronze/raw through curated publication without turning layers into dumping grounds, and manage small files, compaction, concurrent writes and rollback. A worked multi-engine platform uses immutable object storage plus snapshot metadata and reconciled marts. The goal is to evaluate concrete guarantees and failure behavior instead of choosing a fashionable label or assuming a lakehouse automatically replaces every operational and analytical system.

Prerequisites

  • oltp-olap
  • parquet-columnar
  • star-schema

Learning objectives

  • Compare warehouse, lake and lakehouse patterns across storage access, metadata, transactions, governance, workload support and operational ownership.
  • Explain how an open table format turns immutable files into atomic snapshots with evolution, pruning, concurrent commit and rollback.
  • Design a governed multi-workload analytical platform with explicit publication, reconciliation, security, cost, reliability and exit strategy.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A warehouse integrates managed relational storage, SQL compute, transactions, optimization and governance for analytical workloads. A data lake stores varied data in scalable object storage and open formats for many engines, but bare files lack atomic table updates and consistent metadata. A lakehouse adds a transactional metadata/table layer over open files, providing snapshots, schema and partition evolution, time travel and data skipping while retaining direct multi-engine access. The right choice depends on workload, latency, governance, interoperability, skills and total operating cost. Evaluate concrete guarantees—especially commits, deletes, concurrency, catalog consistency and rollback—not the architecture label.

What you must know

  • Architecture is a capability bundle
  • Files are not tables
  • Snapshots make publication atomic
  • Open access trades against centralized control
  • One storage copy can still have many semantics

Why this matters

Raw object storage is cheap and flexible but can become an unowned swamp of incompatible files. A warehouse can deliver excellent governance and SQL performance but may be costly or restrictive for direct ML and unstructured workloads. Lakehouse designs address multi-engine access and table reliability, yet bring metadata, compaction, compatibility and operational responsibilities. Migration decisions affect years of data and platform investment, so teams need a capability and failure analysis rather than a vendor slogan.

Intuition

A lake is a shared depot of durable packages. Parquet describes how one package is packed. A catalog says what datasets exist. A table format maintains a signed manifest of which packages form version 42 and atomically points readers to that manifest. Compute engines open the packages and run queries. A warehouse bundles many of these responsibilities behind one managed counter; a lakehouse exposes more components and direct access, which can increase flexibility and coordination work.

Compare capabilities, not labels

A warehouse traditionally provides relational tables, SQL, statistics, cost-based optimization, concurrency and workload management, transactions, role-based access, backup and managed operations. Storage may be proprietary or open, and modern warehouses can query external files. Strengths include integrated behavior and predictable governance; trade-offs can include data movement, compute/storage pricing, limited direct library access, vendor coupling and less natural handling of arbitrary binary data.

A lake uses filesystem or object-store primitives and open file formats. Multiple engines can read the same durable data, and raw structured, semi-structured and unstructured inputs coexist. Storage/compute separation supports independent scaling. But a directory listing is not a table transaction, and different writers can create schema drift, partial batches and incompatible partition conventions. Catalog, security, discovery, quality, lifecycle and performance must be supplied. Cheap storage does not mean cheap queries or operations.

A lakehouse retains direct-access files while adding a metadata layer that defines atomic table snapshots and management features. The original lakehouse paper highlights transactions, versioning, auditing, indexing/caching and query optimization over open storage. Systems differ: supported engines, isolation, delete models, streaming, catalog protocol and optimization are not interchangeable. Warehouses also adopted open-format access, while lakehouse platforms added managed SQL services, so examine APIs and guarantees rather than drawing a rigid product boundary.

Files, manifests, snapshots, and commits

Data files such as Parquet are commonly immutable. A table snapshot references a complete logical set of data and delete files through manifests or equivalent metadata. Readers resolve one snapshot and see a consistent version without discovering state from an object listing. A writer creates new files and metadata, validates assumptions, then atomically changes the table's current metadata pointer through a catalog operation. If another writer commits first, optimistic concurrency checks decide whether the operation can be safely retried or must fail.

This indirection enables append, overwrite, delete, compaction, schema and partition evolution, time travel and rollback without mutating files in place. Stable field identifiers can make rename safer than name-only matching. Hidden partition transforms let queries filter logical columns without exposing physical directory columns. Metadata statistics and manifests prune files before Parquet row-group pruning. A catalog provides table identity, namespaces, pointer updates, locking/coordination and access integration; its availability and correctness are part of table reliability.

Atomicity is usually table-scoped, not automatically multi-table. A fact and dimension commit can expose different cutoffs unless a higher-level publication pointer or compatible transaction mechanism coordinates them. Snapshot isolation does not guarantee application invariants under every concurrent write; examine conflict detection for append, overwrite, merge and compaction. Time travel is limited by metadata/file retention and is not a substitute for backup or privacy-compliant deletion.

Raw, refined, and published data products

Layer names such as bronze, silver and gold are useful only when each boundary has a contract. A raw/landing layer preserves source evidence, ingestion metadata and replayability with minimal irreversible transformation. It still needs ownership, encryption, schema capture, retention and quarantine; “raw” is not permission to store unrestricted sensitive data forever. A refined layer deduplicates, validates, standardizes types and identities, and applies reusable domain logic. Published marts or features define business grain, semantics, service levels and access for consumers.

Each transition should be idempotent and record source cutoff, code version and output snapshot. Promotion should expose only complete snapshots. Reconciliation follows data through layers: input/output counts, control totals, rejected records and deletion handling. Streaming and batch paths must converge on the same table semantics or declare differences. A medallion diagram does not solve late events, source corrections, mutable dimensions or cross-table consistency.

“One copy of data” is an aspiration, not semantic reality. Different snapshots, materialized views, feature windows, caches and masked projections exist for valid reasons. Direct file access can bypass row policies or semantic definitions if governance is enforced only through one SQL engine. Use catalog-level authorization and storage controls, supported engine integrations, audited access and purpose-specific views. Publish authoritative products while allowing sandbox exploration over appropriately governed inputs.

Performance, reliability, cost, and exit

Object stores favor large sequential objects, while distributed writers can create many tiny files. Small files increase listing/metadata, planning, request and task overhead. Compaction rewrites them into better layouts but consumes compute and creates concurrent-commit conflicts; perform it through the table protocol and expire unreferenced files only after snapshot retention. Partitioning and clustering should follow measured filters and volume. Monitor files per snapshot/partition, size distribution, manifest growth, pruning, scan bytes, spill, compaction backlog and metadata latency.

Separate workloads with compute pools, quotas, priorities and cost attribution. Cache and materialize hot paths, but track invalidation and staleness. Test engine interoperability for data types, deletes, schema evolution and snapshot features before claiming openness. Upgrade table-format and catalog versions deliberately. Back up catalog metadata or support reconstruction according to the chosen system; data files without valid metadata may be difficult to interpret. Run disaster exercises for catalog loss, accidental overwrite and regional outage.

Security requires identity propagation, least privilege at catalog and storage, encryption, row/column controls, audit, residency, retention and deletion across snapshots. Cost models include storage requests, egress, metadata services, compaction, idle compute, duplicated caches, people and incident complexity. An exit strategy records open formats, export paths, contract/lineage metadata and performance dependencies. Choose the simplest capability bundle that meets current and plausible workloads, and revisit with measured evidence.

Math / formal view

Let snapshot S_k reference metadata M_k and a set of immutable data/delete files F_k. A reader is snapshot-consistent when all planning and reads resolve from one S_k. A commit proposes S_{k+1}=T(S_k,Δ) and atomically swaps the catalog pointer only if validation against the current snapshot succeeds. File creation before pointer swap is not publication; orphan cleanup must respect concurrent writers and retained snapshots.

Shared analytical storage for BI and ML

Setup

A company needs governed SQL marts, Python feature generation, streaming updates and reproducible historical training over orders and events.

Committed source changes land as encrypted immutable files with source positions and schemas. An open table format publishes each landing batch through an atomic snapshot instead of directory listing. Refined tables deduplicate and standardize identities; a fact/dimension publication uses a shared release manifest so consumers see compatible cutoffs. SQL compute serves governed marts, while approved ML engines read the same snapshot through supported table APIs. Every output stores input snapshot IDs and code revision. Compaction rewrites small files as a validated table commit. Metrics track freshness, rejected events, source reconciliation, file sizes, pruning and engine cost. If a transformation is wrong, the publication pointer returns to the prior trusted release while the bad snapshot remains isolated for diagnosis. Privacy deletion creates supported delete/rewrite commits and later expires prohibited files under audited retention policy.

Conclusion

Open files enable multiple engines, while snapshot metadata, publication coordination and governance make the shared storage a reliable platform.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Model an immutable-file table snapshot, verify atomic pointer publication and rollback, and show why directory listing is not a consistent table view.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import json

class Table:
    def __init__(self):
        self.files={}; self.snapshots={0:[]}; self.current=0
    def stage(self,name,rows):
        self.files[name]=list(rows)
    def commit_append(self,base,new_files):
        if base!=self.current: raise RuntimeError('conflict')
        next_id=self.current+1
        self.snapshots[next_id]=self.snapshots[base]+list(new_files)
        self.current=next_id
        return next_id
    def read(self,snapshot=None):
        sid=self.current if snapshot is None else snapshot
        return [row for name in self.snapshots[sid] for row in self.files[name]]
    def rollback(self,snapshot):
        if snapshot not in self.snapshots: raise KeyError(snapshot)
        self.current=snapshot
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
table=Table()
table.stage('part-1',[{'id':1},{'id':2}])
s1=table.commit_append(0,['part-1'])
table.stage('part-2',[{'id':3}])
listed_before_commit=sorted(table.files)
s2=table.commit_append(s1,['part-2'])
manifest=json.dumps({'snapshot':s2,'files':table.snapshots[s2]},sort_keys=True)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use a real table format and catalog with atomic compare-and-swap, snapshot-aware compaction/cleanup, versioned input/output evidence, cross-engine tests, metadata recovery and audited rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert listed_before_commit==['part-1','part-2']
assert [r['id'] for r in table.read(s1)]==[1,2]
assert [r['id'] for r in table.read(s2)]==[1,2,3]
assert json.loads(manifest)['files']==['part-1','part-2']
try: table.commit_append(s1,['part-2'])
except RuntimeError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('stale commit must conflict')
table.rollback(s1)
assert [r['id'] for r in table.read()]==[1,2]

Common mistakes

  • A lakehouse is simply Parquet files in object storage.

    The defining management capabilities come from transactional metadata/catalog, snapshots, evolution and engine support around the files.

  • Open format guarantees every engine behaves identically.

    Readers differ in types, deletes, evolution, extensions and optimization; interoperability must be tested against the table protocol.

  • Time travel is a complete backup strategy.

    Retention or corruption can remove needed files/metadata, and the same administrative failure domain may affect history; define independent recovery.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does a table format add above Parquet?

    Atomic snapshots, file manifests, concurrent commit rules, schema/partition evolution, delete semantics, time travel and rollback metadata.

  • When is a warehouse still a strong choice?

    When managed SQL performance, integrated governance, predictable operations and team simplicity matter more than direct multi-engine file access.

  • What is the small-file problem?

    Many tiny objects make metadata requests, planning and task scheduling dominate useful I/O and reduce compression/throughput, requiring transactional compaction.

Production / system-design connection

Select architecture from concrete workload and guarantee requirements. Publish versioned atomic snapshots, record source/code versions, coordinate compatible multi-table releases, and reconcile every layer. Isolate compute, monitor metadata, file sizes, pruning, scan cost, compaction and freshness; test concurrent commits and cross-engine semantics. Enforce catalog/storage security and deletion, back up/recover metadata, retain rollback snapshots safely, and include operations, egress and exit costs in platform decisions.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What is the difference between a file format and a table format?

    Show solution

    A file format encodes values within individual files; a table format defines metadata, snapshots, commits, evolution and delete behavior across a logical collection of files.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Choose a starting architecture for a small SQL-only team with strict governance and no direct file consumers.

    Show solution

    A managed warehouse is often the simpler fit; verify cost, portability and recovery rather than adding a multi-engine lakehouse layer without a workload need.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Readers sometimes see both compacted files and their originals. What failed?

    Show solution

    They discovered files through listing or compaction bypassed atomic table metadata. Readers must resolve one snapshot and cleanup must follow retention/concurrency rules.

CHAPTER 05

∑ Math Foundations

Linear algebra, calculus, numerical thinking and optimization foundations.

8 lessons · 8 deep-complete · 16 visuals
Study order. Learn the interview answer first. Then make sure you can explain every key point without notes. Use the deep sections to understand trade-offs, failure modes, and production implications.
5.1

Vectors, Matrices & Dot Products

very highverified
Roles: all, as

Topic overview

Vectors and matrices are representations of linear relationships, not just rectangular containers of numbers. A vector can encode coordinates, features, parameters, probabilities or a direction; a matrix can encode a linear map, a collection of observations, a graph or a change of basis. This chapter builds the subject from shape and orientation through vector addition, scaling, inner and outer products, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication, transpose, identity, inverse, rank, column space, null space and affine bias. You will learn to read every multiplication as both a shape contract and a composition of transformations, distinguish elementwise multiplication from contraction, and explain why solving a linear system is preferable to explicitly forming an inverse. A worked batch prediction traces indices and dimensions from features to outputs. The implementation material exposes multiplication with loops, then uses NumPy while checking shapes and invariants. Production guidance covers dtype, broadcasting, memory layout, batching, sparse structure, conditioning, thread oversubscription, serialization and privacy. The goal is to make shape reasoning and geometric meaning automatic enough that later topics—least squares, gradients, attention, embeddings and neural networks—feel like precise extensions rather than new notation to memorize.

Learning objectives

  • Interpret vectors and matrices simultaneously as arrays, coordinate representations, collections of examples and linear transformations.
  • Derive shapes and index formulas for dot, outer, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products and reject invalid broadcasting.
  • Use rank, column space and null space to reason about solvability, identifiability and information loss in real systems.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A vector is an ordered coordinate representation; a matrix often represents a linear map or a batch of vectors. If A has shape m×n and x has shape n, then Ax has shape m and each output is a row of A dotted with x. If B is n×p, AB is m×p and composes B followed by A. The dot product measures aligned magnitude and defines geometry; the outer product creates a rank-one matrix. Rank counts independent directions preserved by a map, the column space contains possible outputs, and the null space contains inputs mapped to zero. Track orientation and shapes explicitly, distinguish `@` from elementwise `*`, and solve systems rather than computing inverses explicitly.

What you must know

  • Shape is part of meaning
  • Matrix multiplication composes maps
  • Dot and outer products differ
  • Rank counts independent directions
  • Solve systems; avoid explicit inverse

Why this matters

Most ML bugs involving linear algebra are not advanced-theorem failures. They are silent transposes, unintended broadcasting, inconsistent batch conventions, dtype overflow, or a model trying to estimate directions the data does not identify. Linear algebra supplies a compact language for feature transformations, regression, embeddings, convolutions, attention and optimization. Understanding what a product means lets you validate tensor code, choose stable algorithms and explain when data has lost information.

Intuition

A matrix is a machine whose columns show where basis directions go. Feeding vector x forms a weighted sum of those columns, with weights from x. Matrix multiplication connects machines: B transforms the input, then A transforms B's output. A dataset matrix uses a different but compatible story—rows are examples and columns are features—so multiplying by a parameter vector takes one dot product per example. Always state which convention you use.

Vectors, matrices, orientation, and shape

A vector in R^n is an ordered n-tuple once a basis is chosen. Geometrically it can represent a displacement; in data work it may represent one example's features, one embedding, or model parameters. A matrix A∈R^{m×n} has m rows and n columns. Its meaning comes from the domain, codomain and chosen bases, not only values. A column-vector convention treats A as a map R^n→R^m. A tabular dataset often stores N examples as rows X∈R^{N×d}; then predictions Xw use the same rule with one output per row.

Addition requires equal shape and combines corresponding coordinates. Scalar multiplication stretches or reverses a vector. Transpose exchanges axes: if A is m×n, A^T is n×m. For real vectors, a row x^T and column y can form the scalar x^T y, while xy^T is an outer product matrix. In code, a one-dimensional array may have shape `(n,)` rather than explicit `(n,1)`, so transpose can appear to do nothing. Add axes deliberately when orientation matters.

Shapes function like types. Before computing, label every axis: batch, feature, output, time, head or class. A valid numerical shape can still be semantically wrong—for example, broadcasting a per-class bias across the feature axis when dimensions happen to match. Name axes in comments/tests and include small asymmetric cases that expose swaps.

Products as contractions and transformations

The inner or dot product x^T y=Σ_i x_i y_i returns a scalar. It is bilinear and, in Euclidean coordinates, connects algebra to length and angle. An outer product xy^T has entries x_i y_j and rank at most one. Elementwise or Hadamard multiplication x⊙y preserves shape. These operations answer different questions; overloaded library functions and broadcasting make the distinction important.

For A∈R^{m×n} and x∈R^n, y=Ax has y_i=Σ_j A_{ij}x_j. Each output is a row-vector dot product, and simultaneously y is a linear combination of A's columns. For A∈R^{m×n} and B∈R^{n×p}, C=AB has C_{ik}=Σ_j A_{ij}B_{jk}. The shared dimension n is contracted and the outer dimensions m,p remain. Composition order matters: AB means apply B first, then A under column-vector convention; generally AB≠BA.

Associativity permits `(AB)x=A(Bx)`, but computational cost and intermediate memory differ. If x is a vector, applying B then A can be much cheaper than forming AB. Distributivity supports batching and decomposition. Matrix multiplication is not elementwise and cannot be justified by “matching total element counts.” Write index notation for one output when a tensor contraction is unclear.

Column space, null space, rank, and solvability

The column space of A is the set of all Ax: every output reachable by combining columns. The null space is the set of x with Ax=0: input directions erased by the transformation. Rank is the dimension of the column space and equals the number of independent rows. By rank-nullity for A:R^n→R^m, rank(A)+nullity(A)=n. A rank-deficient design matrix contains redundant or unobserved feature directions, so different parameter vectors can produce the same predictions.

The system Ax=b has an exact solution only when b lies in the column space. If columns are independent and m≥n, a solution is unique when it exists. If the null space is nontrivial, adding any null vector to a solution produces another. Overdetermined inconsistent systems lead to least squares; underdetermined systems need a criterion such as minimum norm or regularization. Rank in floating point is threshold-dependent because tiny singular values may represent noise rather than meaningful directions.

The identity I leaves vectors unchanged. An inverse A^{-1} exists only for a square full-rank matrix and reverses the map. In numerical work, compute `solve(A,b)` rather than `inv(A)@b`: factorization-based solves are typically more stable and efficient. Rectangular or singular problems use least squares or pseudoinverse concepts, with conditioning and regularization considered separately.

Implementation, batching, and production checks

Dense multiplication cost for m×n times n×p is roughly proportional to mnp scalar multiply-adds, but optimized BLAS libraries use cache blocking, vector instructions, multiple cores and accelerators. Memory layout and contiguous access affect throughput. Sparse matrices store only nonzeros and can reduce work dramatically when sparsity patterns and operations are supported; converting to dense may destroy that benefit. Batch dimensions let libraries execute many products efficiently, but broadcasting rules must match intended semantics.

Dtype affects range, precision, memory and hardware. Integer multiplication can overflow; low-precision floating point may need higher-precision accumulation or loss scaling. Validate finiteness, shapes, units and expected norm/range before and after critical transforms. Compare a small case with a trusted implementation, test identity and associativity within tolerance, and use relative as well as absolute tolerance. Exact equality is inappropriate after most floating-point operations.

In production, record feature order and preprocessing with the model; a mathematically valid matrix applied to reordered columns is wrong. Bound input sizes to prevent memory denial of service, control BLAS/thread pools to avoid oversubscription, batch under latency limits, and monitor NaN/Inf, shape failures and output drift. Quantization, sparse kernels and accelerator changes require accuracy regression. Embeddings and matrices can contain sensitive information, so apply access control and retention policy to artifacts and logs.

Math / formal view

For A∈R^{m×n}, B∈R^{n×p}, (AB)_{ik}=Σ_{j=1}^n A_{ij}B_{jk}. For x∈R^n, Ax=Σ_j x_j a_j where a_j are A's columns. The fundamental subspaces include Col(A)⊆R^m and Null(A)⊆R^n, with rank(A)+dim Null(A)=n. A linear map satisfies T(αx+βy)=αT(x)+βT(y); an affine map Ax+b adds a translation and is not linear unless b=0.

Batch linear prediction with explicit axes

Setup

Three examples have four features and a model produces two outputs plus a bias.

Let X have shape 3×4, with rows as examples. Let W have shape 4×2, whose columns parameterize the two outputs, and b have shape 2. Then Z=XW+b has shape 3×2. In indices, Z_{ik}=Σ_{j=1}^4 X_{ij}W_{jk}+b_k. The feature dimension is contracted; batch and output dimensions remain. Broadcasting b across rows is intended because b_k is output-specific. Tests use 3,4,2 rather than equal dimensions so an accidental transpose fails. Verify `Z[i,k]` by a manual dot product, check zero X produces repeated b, and store the feature-name order with W. If X has dependent columns, multiple W values may yield the same predictions even though the product is defined.

Conclusion

Shape derivation tells both the code operation and the semantic axes that must be preserved.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement matrix multiplication from its index definition, then verify shape, manual entries, identity, associativity and NumPy agreement.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def matmul(a,b):
    if not a or not b or len(a[0])!=len(b): raise ValueError('shape mismatch')
    if any(len(row)!=len(a[0]) for row in a) or any(len(row)!=len(b[0]) for row in b): raise ValueError('ragged')
    return [[sum(a[i][k]*b[k][j] for k in range(len(b))) for j in range(len(b[0]))] for i in range(len(a))]

def transpose(a):
    return [list(col) for col in zip(*a)]
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
A=[[1.,2.,3.],[4.,5.,6.]]
B=[[2.,0.],[1.,1.],[0.,3.]]
manual=matmul(A,B)
np_result=np.asarray(A)@np.asarray(B)
I=np.eye(2)
C=np.array([[1.,2.],[0.,1.]])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use named axis contracts, trusted BLAS/LAPACK routines, dtype and finiteness checks, thread/batch limits, versioned feature order and numerical regression before deploying matrix-heavy paths.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert manual==[[4.0,11.0],[13.0,23.0]]
assert np.allclose(manual,np_result)
assert np_result.shape==(2,2)
assert np_result[1,0]==sum(A[1][k]*B[k][0] for k in range(3))
assert np.allclose(I@np_result,np_result)
assert np.allclose((np_result@C)@I,np_result@(C@I))
try: matmul([[1,2]],[[1,2]])
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('invalid contraction must fail')

Common mistakes

  • If NumPy broadcasts, the operation must be mathematically intended.

    Broadcast compatibility checks sizes, not semantic axes; label axes and test asymmetric shapes.

  • Matrix multiplication is elementwise multiplication.

    Matrix multiplication contracts an inner dimension and composes transformations; elementwise multiplication preserves shape.

  • Compute an inverse whenever solving Ax=b.

    Use a factorization-based solve; inverses are usually slower, less stable and unavailable for rectangular/rank-deficient systems.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does matrix rank mean?

    The number of independent output directions, equivalently the dimension of the column space and row space.

  • Why is matrix multiplication not commutative?

    It composes maps in order; changing order changes the intermediate space and transformation and may not even be shape-valid.

  • What is the difference between linear and affine?

    A linear map is Ax and preserves zero and linear combinations; an affine map Ax+b adds a translation and maps zero to b.

Production / system-design connection

Persist axis meaning, feature order, dtype and preprocessing with every artifact. Validate shapes, finiteness, ranges, rank/conditioning when relevant and small trusted cases. Use optimized solve/decomposition routines, control threads and batch sizes, preserve sparsity, and test low-precision or accelerator changes against accuracy tolerances. Monitor shape errors, NaN/Inf, latency, memory and output drift; restrict access to sensitive feature and embedding matrices.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    If A is 5×3 and B is 3×7, what is the shape of AB and which dimension is contracted?

    Show solution

    AB is 5×7; the shared dimension of size 3 is summed over.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Interpret Xw when X is N×d and w is d.

    Show solution

    It produces N scalar predictions, one dot product between each example row and the feature-parameter vector.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Two different parameter vectors make identical predictions for every training row. What linear-algebra property explains this?

    Show solution

    Their difference lies in the null space of the design matrix; the matrix is rank-deficient in that parameter direction.

5.2

Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & SVD

highverified
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as

Topic overview

Eigenvectors identify directions preserved by a square linear transformation up to scale; singular value decomposition (SVD) gives an orthonormal input/output basis and nonnegative gains for any rectangular matrix. This chapter distinguishes eigendecomposition from SVD, derives their geometry, and connects them through `AᵀA` and `AAᵀ`. You will learn when a real matrix may lack a complete real eigenbasis, why symmetric matrices behave especially well, how singular values reveal rank and conditioning, and how truncated SVD yields the best low-rank approximation under standard norms. The chapter connects these ideas to principal component analysis, latent semantic structure, image compression, pseudoinverse and iterative power methods while separating centered covariance PCA from an uncentered matrix factorization. A worked 2×2 example verifies reconstruction and rank-one error. The lab implements power iteration and uses NumPy SVD with sign-invariant checks. Production guidance covers scaling, missing data, randomized algorithms, component stability, sign/rotation ambiguity, reconstruction versus downstream utility, privacy, resource cost and rollback. The aim is to make decompositions tools for understanding which directions a system amplifies, suppresses or cannot identify—not mysterious functions that merely return three arrays.

Prerequisites

  • vectors-matrices
  • projections-least-squares

Learning objectives

  • Explain eigenvectors/eigenvalues and singular vectors/values geometrically and state when each decomposition applies.
  • Use singular values to reason about rank, conditioning, pseudoinverse, energy and optimal low-rank approximation.
  • Apply PCA or truncated SVD without leakage, centering mistakes or invalid interpretations of unstable components.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

An eigenvector v of square A satisfies Av=λv, so its direction is preserved and scaled by eigenvalue λ. General matrices may have complex eigenvalues or lack a full eigenbasis; real symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenvectors and real eigenvalues. Any m×n matrix has an SVD `A=UΣVᵀ`: V gives orthonormal input directions, Σ nonnegative gains, and U the corresponding output directions. Singular values expose rank and conditioning, and keeping the top k terms gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius and spectral norm. PCA is SVD/eigendecomposition applied to centered data/covariance, with preprocessing fitted on training data.

What you must know

  • Eigenvectors preserve direction
  • SVD works for rectangular matrices
  • Singular values quantify gain
  • Truncation is optimal for reconstruction norms
  • PCA requires centering and leakage control

Why this matters

Decompositions power dimensionality reduction, compression, latent factors, spectral clustering, covariance analysis, stable least squares and condition diagnostics. Misuse is common: calling singular vectors eigenvectors, performing PCA without centering, fitting components before splitting, treating sign flips as model drift, or assuming high explained variance guarantees predictive value. First-principles geometry explains the outputs and their limitations.

Intuition

A general matrix maps the unit sphere in its input space to an ellipsoid in its output space. Right singular vectors are orthogonal input directions along the ellipsoid's axes; singular values are their stretch factors; left singular vectors point along the resulting output axes. Eigenvectors instead ask for directions that remain on their own line inside the same square input/output space.

Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and symmetric structure

For square A, a nonzero vector v is an eigenvector if Av=λv. Scaling v gives the same direction, so normalization is conventional. Eigenvalues satisfy `det(A−λI)=0`. Repeated eigenvalues can have one or multiple independent eigenvectors. A matrix is diagonalizable when it has a basis of eigenvectors, giving `A=VΛV^{-1}` and making powers easy: `A^t=VΛ^tV^{-1}`. Not every matrix is diagonalizable, and real matrices can have complex eigenpairs.

Real symmetric matrices are special: the spectral theorem gives real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, `A=QΛQ^T`. Positive semidefinite matrices have nonnegative eigenvalues and define nonnegative quadratic forms. Covariance and Gram matrices have this structure, enabling stable geometric interpretation. For a Markov transition convention, a dominant eigenvector can describe stationary behavior under appropriate conditions; network spectral methods depend on which Laplacian/adjacency normalization is used.

Eigenvalue magnitude often governs repeated linear dynamics, but non-normal matrices can show transient amplification not predicted by eigenvalues alone. Eigenvector conditioning matters. Production conclusions should not reduce a general dynamical system to “largest eigenvalue wins” without checking diagonalizability, normalization and the actual operator.

Singular value decomposition and fundamental subspaces

For A∈R^{m×n}, SVD is `A=UΣV^T`. In a reduced SVD of rank r, U has r orthonormal columns in R^m, V has r orthonormal columns in R^n, and diagonal Σ contains singular values `σ1≥…≥σr>0`. Applying A first expresses x in the right-singular basis V, scales components by σ, and expresses the result in U. Null-space right singular directions have zero gain.

The right singular vectors are eigenvectors of `A^TA` with eigenvalues σ²; left singular vectors are eigenvectors of `AA^T`. This connection avoids conflating dimensions: A's singular vectors live in different spaces when A is rectangular. Rank equals the number of nonzero singular values in exact arithmetic. The spectral norm is σ1, the Frobenius norm squared is the sum of σ_i², and full-rank condition number is σ1/σmin. Tiny values amplify noise in inverse problems.

The pseudoinverse `A^+=VΣ^+U^T` reverses nonzero directions and zeroes the null space. A tolerance determines which values count as numerical zero. Scaling features changes singular values, components and condition, so compare only under a fixed representation.

Low-rank approximation and PCA

Writing SVD as `A=Σ_i σ_i u_i v_i^T` expresses A as rank-one components. The Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem says truncating after k components gives a best rank-k approximation under spectral and Frobenius norms. The squared Frobenius reconstruction error is `Σ_{i>k}σ_i²`. This is an optimal statement for those matrix norms, not necessarily for classification accuracy, fairness, interpretability or perceptual quality.

Principal component analysis centers data matrix X by the training mean. Right singular vectors of centered X are principal feature directions; scores are XV, and covariance eigenvalues are proportional to σ² depending on the covariance denominator. Explained variance ratio reports reconstruction variance, not supervised usefulness. Standardizing features changes PCA from covariance geometry toward correlation geometry and should follow unit/goal reasoning. Sparse/truncated SVD on term-document matrices is often applied without centering because centering destroys sparsity; call the method accurately.

Fit centering, scaling and components only on training data. Transform validation/test with those fitted parameters. Choose k using reconstruction, downstream validation, latency/storage and slice behavior. Component signs are arbitrary, and nearly equal singular values allow rotations within a subspace; compare subspaces or reconstructed outputs rather than raw columns alone.

Algorithms and production operation

Dense full SVD is expensive for very large matrices. If only top components are needed, Lanczos/Krylov or randomized SVD methods use matrix-vector products and subspace iteration. Power iteration repeatedly normalizes Av to approach a dominant eigenvector when spectral separation and initialization conditions are favorable; convergence slows when leading magnitudes are close and can miss components orthogonal to initialization. Sparse and linear-operator interfaces avoid materializing huge matrices.

Validate reconstruction `A≈UΣV^T`, orthonormality `U^TU≈I`, `V^TV≈I`, sorted nonnegative values and expected residual. Use relative tolerances tied to dtype and norm. Compare randomized results across seeds by subspace angles or reconstruction, not signs. Monitor iteration convergence and fallback on nonconvergence. Mixed precision can distort small singular values, while oversubscribed BLAS threads can hurt latency.

Version row/feature definition, centering, scaling, missing-value treatment, k, solver, seed and tolerance. Monitor input scale/covariance drift, explained/reconstruction error, downstream metrics, component/subspace stability, latency and memory. Decompositions may encode sensitive population structure; restrict artifacts and evaluate subgroup effects. Keep a prior transform plus compatible downstream model/index for rollback, since changing the basis invalidates stored coordinates.

Math / formal view

Eigenpair: Av=λv for square A and v≠0. SVD: A=UΣV^T with orthonormal U,V and σ_i≥0. Then A^TA v_i=σ_i²v_i and AA^T u_i=σ_i²u_i. Rank-r A has r positive singular values. The truncated A_k=Σ_{i=1}^kσ_i u_i v_i^T minimizes ||A−B||_2 and ||A−B||_F over rank(B)≤k, with ||A−A_k||_F²=Σ_{i>k}σ_i².

Diagonal stretch and rank-one approximation

Setup

Let A=diag(3,1), a transformation that stretches the first coordinate three times and preserves the second.

Its eigenvectors and singular vectors are the coordinate axes. Eigenvalues are 3 and 1; singular values are also 3 and 1 because A is symmetric positive. Full SVD reconstructs A exactly. The best rank-one approximation keeps `3 e1 e1^T`, producing diag(3,0). Its spectral error is 1 and squared Frobenius error is 1, equal to the discarded singular value contributions. If the second axis contained crucial rare-class information, optimal reconstruction error would not guarantee optimal classification. A sign flip of e1 in both left/right vectors represents the same component.

Conclusion

Singular values quantify directional gain and reconstruction loss, but the downstream task decides whether a discarded direction matters.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement dominant-eigenvector power iteration, then verify SVD reconstruction, orthogonality, sign-invariant eigen behavior and optimal rank-one error.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def power_iteration(a,start,steps=100):
    v=list(map(float,start))
    for _ in range(steps):
        w=[sum(row[j]*v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in a]
        norm=math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in w))
        if norm==0: raise ValueError('zero iterate')
        v=[x/norm for x in w]
    av=[sum(row[j]*v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in a]
    value=sum(v[i]*av[i] for i in range(len(v)))
    return value,v
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
A=np.array([[3.,0.],[0.,1.]])
value,vector=power_iteration(A.tolist(),[1.,1.])
U,s,Vt=np.linalg.svd(A,full_matrices=False)
rank1=s[0]*np.outer(U[:,0],Vt[0])
reconstruction=(U*s)@Vt
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use stable library/randomized decompositions, training-only preprocessing, convergence and reconstruction checks, versioned basis metadata, downstream slice evaluation, drift monitoring and compatible rollback artifacts.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(value-3.0)<1e-10
assert abs(abs(vector[0])-1.0)<1e-8
assert np.allclose(reconstruction,A)
assert np.allclose(U.T@U,np.eye(2)) and np.allclose(Vt@Vt.T,np.eye(2))
assert np.allclose(s,[3.,1.])
assert np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(A-rank1,2),s[1])
assert np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(A-rank1,'fro')**2,sum(s[1:]**2))

Common mistakes

  • Every square matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

    Real symmetric matrices do; general matrices may be non-normal, defective or have complex eigenpairs.

  • PCA on all data before splitting is harmless preprocessing.

    The mean and components learn validation/test distribution, causing leakage; fit only on training data.

  • Component sign changes indicate a different solution.

    Singular/eigenvectors are sign-ambiguous, and repeated/near-equal values permit basis rotations; compare subspaces/reconstruction.

Likely follow-ups

  • How are eigenvalues and singular values related?

    Singular values of A are square roots of eigenvalues of positive-semidefinite A^TA; they are nonnegative and apply to rectangular A.

  • What does a tiny singular value imply?

    The map nearly erases that input direction, so inversion/coefficients can amplify noise and the problem is ill-conditioned.

  • What does truncated SVD optimize?

    Matrix reconstruction error among rank-k approximations under spectral and Frobenius norms, not every downstream objective.

Production / system-design connection

Fit centering/scaling and decomposition on training data only; version representation, k, solver, seed and tolerances. Validate orthogonality, reconstruction, convergence, rank/condition and downstream metrics across slices. Use sparse/randomized operators for scale with exact-subset regression, control dtype/threads and monitor covariance/subspace drift. Protect sensitive components and roll back the transform with all dependent coordinates/models.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Where do left and right singular vectors live for an m×n matrix?

    Show solution

    Left singular vectors live in the m-dimensional output space; right singular vectors live in the n-dimensional input space.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Why use truncated SVD for a sparse term-document matrix rather than centered PCA?

    Show solution

    Centering can destroy sparsity; uncentered truncated SVD preserves sparse computation, though its components are not covariance PCA.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Two runs have flipped component signs but identical reconstruction. Is that a failure?

    Show solution

    No. Signs are arbitrary when paired consistently. Compare reconstruction or subspace, not raw sign.
