5.3

Derivatives, Gradients & Chain Rule

very highverified
Roles: all, as

Topic overview

A derivative is the coefficient of the best local linear approximation, not merely a symbolic slope rule. For a scalar function of one variable it measures first-order change; for a scalar function of many variables the gradient collects partial derivatives and points in the direction of steepest increase under Euclidean geometry. For vector-valued functions the local linear map is a Jacobian. This chapter develops limits, differentials, directional derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients and the multivariable chain rule, then shows how computation graphs organize reverse-mode backpropagation. You will learn to track shapes and evaluation points, distinguish a derivative from a finite difference, handle broadcasting and shared parameters, and recognize nondifferentiable or saturated regions. A worked two-layer scalar graph traces forward values and reverse sensitivities. The lab implements central differences and a tiny dual-number forward derivative, then checks an analytic chain-rule result. Production guidance covers gradient checks, autodiff modes, nondeterminism, precision, exploding/vanishing gradients, custom operations, monitoring and secure artifact handling. The goal is to see differentiation as propagation of local sensitivity through a composed system, which makes both mathematical derivations and debugging modern ML code much more reliable.

Prerequisites

  • vectors-matrices

Learning objectives

  • Interpret derivatives, differentials, directional derivatives and gradients as local linear approximations with explicit assumptions and shapes.
  • Apply scalar and multivariable chain rules through a computation graph and explain forward versus reverse accumulation.
  • Validate and operate automatic differentiation using analytic invariants, finite-difference checks, precision controls and failure diagnostics.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The derivative is the linear map that best approximates a function near a point. In one dimension, `f(x+h)=f(x)+f'(x)h+o(h)`. For scalar `f:R^n→R`, the differential is `df=∇f(x)^T dx`; the directional derivative along unit u is `∇f·u`, so the Euclidean gradient points toward steepest local increase. For compositions, derivatives multiply in the chain rule. Reverse-mode autodiff propagates a scalar output sensitivity backward through local Jacobian-transpose products, making it efficient for many parameters and one loss. Track tensor shapes, evaluate derivatives at forward-pass values, and verify custom or risky gradients against finite differences on small cases.

What you must know

  • Derivative is a local linear map
  • Gradient represents the differential under an inner product
  • Chain rule composes sensitivities
  • Reverse mode uses vector-Jacobian products
  • Finite differences validate but do not replace derivatives

Why this matters

Training neural networks, fitting models, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty propagation and numerical optimization all depend on derivatives. A wrong gradient can still produce decreasing loss for a while, while a correct formula can fail numerically because activations saturate or precision underflows. Memorizing derivative tables is insufficient when tensors are batched, parameters are reused and operations broadcast. The local-linear and computation-graph views give one consistent framework for derivation, implementation and debugging.

Intuition

Zoom in on a smooth curve until it resembles a line. In many dimensions, zoom in until a nonlinear function resembles a plane or linear map. The gradient is the arrow encoding how a scalar surface tilts. A computation graph is a network of small zoomed-in maps; the chain rule connects them. Reverse mode starts from “one unit of loss” and asks every upstream value how much it contributed.

Derivatives and local linear approximation

For scalar f, the derivative at x is the limit `lim_{h→0}(f(x+h)−f(x))/h` when it exists. More informatively, `f(x+h)=f(x)+f'(x)h+r(h)` where `r(h)/|h|→0`. The derivative is local: it does not say a large step follows the tangent, nor that a stationary point is a minimum. Differentiability implies continuity but not the reverse; `|x|` is continuous and nondifferentiable at zero.

A differential writes the same first-order change as `df=f'(x)dx`. Higher-order terms determine approximation error. Taylor expansion, when assumptions hold, adds curvature: `f(x+h)≈f(x)+f'(x)h+½f''(x)h²`. Units help catch mistakes: if x is seconds and f is meters, f' is meters per second. Scaling coordinates changes numeric derivative components.

Finite differences approximate a derivative. Forward difference has truncation error proportional to h; central difference is often more accurate for the same scale. Making h arbitrarily small is not always better because floating-point subtraction cancels and roundoff dominates. Complex-step differentiation avoids subtraction for analytic code paths, while symbolic and automatic differentiation apply exact chain rules to represented operations but still use finite-precision arithmetic.

Partial, directional, and gradient derivatives

For f:R^n→R, the partial derivative changes one coordinate while holding others fixed. Differentiability requires a single linear approximation `f(x+h)=f(x)+L(h)+o(||h||)`, stronger than existence of all partials. Under the standard Euclidean inner product, the linear functional L can be represented by gradient vector ∇f so `L(h)=∇f^T h`. The derivative is fundamentally the linear functional; the gradient representation depends on the chosen inner product/coordinates.

The directional derivative along u is `D_u f=∇f^T u` for differentiable f. For unit Euclidean u, Cauchy–Schwarz shows the maximum is `||∇f||`, attained along the gradient. The negative gradient is steepest descent only for that geometry. Feature scaling or a preconditioner changes what equal-size movement means, which motivates natural gradient and second-order/preconditioned methods.

For a batch loss that is a mean, gradients scale differently than for a sum. Broadcasting creates reductions in backward passes: if a bias is shared across examples, its gradient sums contributions along the broadcast batch axis. A reused parameter receives the sum of sensitivities from every path. Shape checks should name parameter and output axes rather than accepting a gradient that merely has a broadcastable size.

Chain rule and computation graphs

For scalar composition y=f(g(x)), `dy/dx=f'(g(x))g'(x)`. In multiple dimensions, local linear maps compose. If g:R^n→R^m and f:R^m→R^p, the Jacobian of f∘g is `J_f(g(x))J_g(x)` under a column-Jacobian convention. Order follows map composition and shapes expose mistakes. For a scalar loss, reverse mode avoids materializing full Jacobians by propagating vector-Jacobian products.

A computation graph stores forward intermediate values. Reverse accumulation assigns the output loss adjoint 1 and traverses nodes backward. At multiplication z=ab, contributions are `bar_a += bar_z b` and `bar_b += bar_z a`, evaluated with forward values. At addition, the upstream sensitivity copies to both inputs. Contributions add when paths merge. Stop-gradient/detach intentionally removes a path and must be reviewed because it changes the objective's derivative.

Forward mode propagates a tangent/Jacobian-vector product with the forward computation and is efficient for few inputs/directions and many outputs. Reverse mode is efficient for one/few scalar outputs and many inputs, which matches training. Mixed forward/reverse techniques compute Hessian-vector products without a full Hessian. Memory/checkpointing trade recomputation for stored activations. In-place mutations can invalidate saved forward values or autodiff version checks.

Gradient validation and production failure modes

Validate derivatives on small deterministic inputs using central differences and several random directions: compare `∇f^T v` to `(f(x+hv)−f(x−hv))/(2h)`. Directional checks scale to many parameters and catch global errors, while coordinate checks localize. Use double precision for checks, choose h relative to scale, avoid nondifferentiable boundaries and compare relative error when magnitudes are meaningful. Also test analytic invariants: symmetry, conservation, zero gradients for unused inputs and known simple cases.

Exploding gradients arise from products of large Jacobian gains; vanishing gradients from gains below one, saturation or long chains. Monitor gradient norms by layer, parameter/update ratio, NaN/Inf, activation saturation and loss-scale overflows. Gradient clipping changes the update and should be measured, not used to hide a broken model. Normalization, residual paths, initialization and architecture address causes.

Custom kernels and fused operations need verified backward definitions, dtype/device coverage and higher-order behavior when required. Nondeterministic parallel reductions can create small differences; define tolerances and reproducibility scope. Bound input graphs and batch sizes, protect training samples captured in traces, and avoid logging raw gradients that may leak data. Store framework, compiler, hardware, precision and code versions with the model; rollback includes optimizer state and preprocessing, not only weights.

Math / formal view

Differentiability at x means there exists a linear map Df(x) such that `||f(x+h)−f(x)−Df(x)h||/||h||→0`. For scalar f under Euclidean coordinates, Df(x)h=∇f(x)^T h. If h=f∘g, `Dh(x)=Df(g(x))Dg(x)`. Reverse mode computes cotangent propagation `bar_x=J_g(x)^T bar_y` without explicitly forming J when local vector-Jacobian products are available.

Reverse a small computation graph

Setup

Let a=wx, z=a+b and loss L=z², with x=3, w=2 and b=1.

Forward: a=6, z=7, L=49. Reverse begins with `bar_L=1`. For squaring, `bar_z=2z=14`. Addition gives `bar_a=14` and `bar_b=14`. Multiplication a=wx gives `bar_w=bar_a*x=42` and `bar_x=bar_a*w=28`. Direct expansion `(wx+b)²` yields `dL/dw=2(wx+b)x=42`, confirming the graph. If w were used on two branches, its adjoints would add. A central difference around w=2 should agree within tolerance but degrades if the step is too small.

Conclusion

Backpropagation is the chain rule plus accumulation over every path, evaluated using saved forward values.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement a dual-number forward derivative and central-difference gradient check, then verify a chained analytic derivative.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
class Dual:
    def __init__(self,value,tangent=0.0): self.value=float(value); self.tangent=float(tangent)
    def __add__(self,other):
        other=other if isinstance(other,Dual) else Dual(other)
        return Dual(self.value+other.value,self.tangent+other.tangent)
    __radd__=__add__
    def __mul__(self,other):
        other=other if isinstance(other,Dual) else Dual(other)
        return Dual(self.value*other.value,self.tangent*other.value+self.value*other.tangent)
    __rmul__=__mul__

def central_diff(f,x,h=1e-6): return (f(x+h)-f(x-h))/(2*h)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
def graph(w,x=3.0,b=1.0):
    z=w*x+b
    return z*z
w=Dual(2.0,1.0)
loss=graph(w)
analytic=2*(2*3+1)*3
numeric=central_diff(lambda value: graph(value),2.0)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use framework autodiff for real models, keep double-precision directional checks for custom operations, monitor gradient/update norms and nonfinite values, and version optimizer plus model state for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert loss.value==49.0
assert loss.tangent==analytic==42
assert abs(numeric-analytic)<1e-8
for step in (1e-3,1e-4,1e-5):
    assert abs(central_diff(lambda value: graph(value),2.0,step)-analytic)<1e-6
unused=Dual(5.0,1.0)
assert (Dual(2.0,0.0)*unused).tangent==2.0

Common mistakes

  • The gradient always points toward the nearest global optimum.

    It gives steepest local increase under a chosen geometry; nonconvex surfaces and finite steps can behave differently.

  • Choose an extremely tiny finite-difference step.

    Truncation falls initially, then cancellation/roundoff grows; choose scale-aware steps and use double precision.

  • A broadcast bias gradient is copied from one example.

    Because the parameter is shared, reverse mode sums contributions over every broadcast axis/path.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is reverse mode efficient for neural networks?

    A scalar loss has one output but millions of parameters; one reverse sweep obtains sensitivities for all parameters.

  • What is a directional derivative?

    The first-order rate along direction u; for differentiable scalar f it is ∇f^Tu.

  • What does detach/stop-gradient do?

    It treats a value as constant for differentiation, removing chain-rule paths and therefore changing the computed objective gradient.

Production / system-design connection

Track tensor axes and reduction conventions, verify custom/high-risk gradients with analytic and directional finite-difference checks, and test dtype/device variants. Monitor gradient and update norms, NaN/Inf, saturation and clipping rates; use stable architectures and precision controls. Version framework/compiler/hardware, preprocessing, optimizer and model state, bound graph/batch resources, protect gradient traces and maintain compatible rollback checkpoints.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What is the differential of scalar f:R^n→R under Euclidean coordinates?

    Show solution

    `df=∇f(x)^T dx`, the first-order scalar change for perturbation dx.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Differentiate L=(wx+b)^2 with respect to w.

    Show solution

    Let z=wx+b. By chain rule `dL/dw=2z·x=2(wx+b)x`.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A bias gradient is too small by batch size. What reduction mismatch is likely?

    Show solution

    The implementation averaged where the objective summed, or failed to sum adjoints across the broadcast batch dimension.

5.4

Gradient Descent & Learning Rate

very highverified
Roles: all, as

Topic overview

Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters opposite the gradient to reduce a differentiable objective, but its behavior is governed by local curvature, scaling, noise and step-size policy. This chapter derives descent from first-order approximation and the descent lemma, analyzes a quadratic through Hessian eigenvalues, and explains why learning rates that are too large oscillate or diverge while tiny rates stall along flat directions. You will learn full-batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradients; momentum and preconditioning; learning-rate warmup, decay and line search; stopping criteria; saddle points; and the difference between optimization loss, validation metric and business objective. A worked anisotropic quadratic makes conditioning and zig-zagging concrete. The lab implements gradient descent with backtracking and verifies monotonic decrease, gradient accuracy and convergence. Production guidance covers reproducibility, checkpoint/optimizer state, gradient accumulation, mixed precision, clipping, distributed reductions, cost, monitoring, rollback and safe failure. The objective is not to memorize optimizer names but to reason about the update as a dynamical system whose scale and noise must match the model, data and operational budget.

Prerequisites

  • derivatives-gradients
  • norms-distances

Learning objectives

  • Derive gradient-descent updates from local approximation and analyze learning-rate stability on smooth quadratics.
  • Distinguish batch, stochastic, momentum and preconditioned updates and choose schedules/stopping rules from measurable behavior.
  • Operate training with reproducible checkpoints, numerical safeguards, validation separation, cost controls and rollback.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Gradient descent updates `θ_{t+1}=θ_t−η_t∇f(θ_t)`. The negative gradient is steepest local descent in Euclidean geometry, while the learning rate decides how far the local approximation is trusted. For an L-smooth objective, a step below roughly `2/L` gives stable descent in the quadratic case; on a positive-definite quadratic, convergence speed depends on condition number. Mini-batch SGD uses noisy unbiased or approximately unbiased gradients for scale and sometimes useful noise. Momentum averages directions; preconditioning rescales coordinates. Monitor loss, gradient/update norms, validation metrics and numerical health, and checkpoint weights, optimizer, scheduler, random/data state together.

What you must know

  • Direction and step size are separate
  • Curvature sets stability scale
  • Conditioning sets speed disparity
  • SGD introduces gradient noise
  • Checkpoint the whole training state

Why this matters

A correct gradient does not guarantee useful training. Poor feature scaling creates narrow valleys; a fixed learning rate that is safe for steep curvature barely moves in flat directions; mixed precision can underflow; a validation metric can worsen while training loss falls. Optimizer choices also change compute, communication and reproducibility. Understanding the base dynamics lets engineers diagnose training instead of changing optimizers blindly.

Intuition

The gradient is a downhill arrow drawn from the tangent plane. The learning rate is stride length. On a round bowl, repeated steps head directly to the bottom. In a narrow tilted valley, the steep wall gradient causes side-to-side motion while progress along the valley is slow. Rescaling, momentum or curvature-aware preconditioning makes the landscape easier to traverse.

From local model to iterative descent

For differentiable f, `f(θ+Δ)≈f(θ)+∇f(θ)^TΔ`. Among Euclidean steps of fixed small norm, choosing Δ opposite the gradient gives the largest predicted decrease. Gradient descent sets Δ=−η∇f. This is a local argument; finite steps also see curvature. If f has an L-Lipschitz gradient, the descent lemma bounds `f(θ−ηg)≤f(θ)−η(1−Lη/2)||g||²`, so η<2/L gives a decrease for nonzero g under the bound.

A stationary point has zero gradient but may be a local minimum, maximum or saddle. Convex differentiable objectives make every local minimum global; strongly convex objectives give uniqueness and rates. Neural-network objectives are nonconvex, so theory is more limited, yet gradient and curvature diagnostics remain useful. Parameter symmetries create flat directions and multiple equivalent minima.

Scaling changes dynamics. If one coordinate's curvature is a thousand times another, the largest stable scalar step is set by the steep direction. Standardizing inputs, normalization and reparameterization can improve conditioning. The negative gradient is steepest only under Euclidean norm; preconditioning chooses a different geometry by multiplying the gradient with a positive-definite scale matrix.

Quadratics, eigenvalues, and learning-rate stability

For `f(θ)=½θ^THθ−b^Tθ` with symmetric positive-definite H, the error from optimum evolves as `e_{t+1}=(I−ηH)e_t`. In H's eigenbasis, each component multiplies by `1−ηλ_i`. Stability requires magnitude below one for all eigenvalues, so `0<η<2/λmax`. Components with small eigenvalues shrink slowly when a single η must accommodate λmax. Condition number κ=λmax/λmin describes this spread.

If η approaches the upper stability boundary, steep directions oscillate; above it they diverge. A very small η decreases smoothly but wastes iterations. Exact line search on a quadratic selects the best step along the current gradient but can still zig-zag under poor conditioning. Backtracking line search starts from a candidate step and shrinks until a sufficient-decrease condition holds, useful for deterministic smooth problems but expensive when each evaluation is costly or noisy.

Learning-rate schedules address different phases. Warmup limits unstable early updates when activations/optimizer statistics are uncalibrated. Decay reduces noise and refines late training. Cosine, step and polynomial schedules are policies, not universal laws. Report schedule relative to optimizer steps, effective batch size and gradient accumulation; changing any of these can change the useful rate.

Stochastic gradients, momentum, and adaptive scaling

Full-batch gradients use every example and can be prohibitively expensive. SGD samples one example; mini-batch SGD averages a subset and exploits hardware. When sampling and weighting match the objective, the mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimator, with variance decreasing as batch size grows under assumptions. Correlated batches, class reweighting, hard-negative mining and distributed sharding change the estimator and must be documented.

Momentum maintains a velocity that averages directions, dampening oscillation and accelerating persistent components. Exact formulas differ across classical, Nesterov and framework conventions, so compare implementations carefully. Adaptive methods estimate coordinatewise first/second moments and rescale updates; they can train poorly scaled models effectively but do not remove the need for a learning-rate schedule, epsilon choice, weight-decay semantics or generalization evaluation. Decoupled weight decay differs from adding L2 penalty under adaptive scaling.

Gradient clipping by norm prevents individual updates from exceeding a threshold and is important for some recurrent/large models, but frequent clipping signals instability or scale mismatch. Gradient accumulation emulates a larger batch only when loss scaling, normalization, randomness and optimizer stepping are handled consistently. Distributed all-reduce must specify sum versus mean; a world-size mistake changes the effective learning rate.

Stopping, monitoring, and production training

Stop based on a combination of budget, gradient/update magnitude, training progress and validation behavior. Tiny loss change can mean convergence, an overly small rate, saturation or numeric underflow. A small gradient can indicate a minimum, saddle or dead activation. Early stopping selects a checkpoint using validation data and therefore is part of model selection; retain an untouched final test set. Training loss, validation task metric and business/constraint metrics are distinct.

Log objective components, learning rate, batch/effective batch, gradient norm, update norm, parameter norm, clipping fraction, nonfinite counts, throughput, memory and validation slices. Detect divergence quickly, skip or fail safely on nonfinite gradients according to policy, and cap retries/cost. Mixed precision uses scaled losses and higher-precision accumulation where needed; track scale overflows. Reproducibility records code, data snapshot/order, seed, initialization, libraries, hardware and distributed topology, while acknowledging nondeterministic kernels.

Checkpoint atomically and include weights, optimizer moments, scheduler, scaler, step, random generators and data-sampler position. Validate a checkpoint before promotion. Resume tests should match an uninterrupted short run within defined tolerance. Security includes untrusted training data, artifact integrity and access to gradients/checkpoints. Deploy through evaluation and canary gates, monitor post-deployment outcomes and keep a prior compatible model/preprocessing bundle for rollback.

Math / formal view

Update: θ_{t+1}=θ_t−η_tg_t. For exact gradient on quadratic f(θ)=½θ^THθ−b^Tθ with H≻0, error e_{t+1}=(I−ηH)e_t; convergence requires spectral radius max_i|1−ηλ_i|<1. With 0<η<2/λmax this holds. For L-smooth f, `f(θ−η∇f)≤f(θ)−η(1−Lη/2)||∇f||²`.

An anisotropic quadratic

Setup

Minimize f(x,y)=½(100x²+y²) from (1,1).

Gradient is (100x,y) and Hessian eigenvalues are 100 and 1, so condition number is 100. With η=0.01, x becomes zero in one ideal step while y multiplies by 0.99 and needs hundreds of steps. With η=0.019, x multiplies by −0.9 and oscillates while y slowly shrinks. At η=0.021, x multiplies by −1.1 and diverges because the step exceeds 2/100. Rescaling x or preconditioning by approximately diag(1/100,1) makes both directions comparable. Backtracking detects a stable step without knowing λmax, while a stochastic objective would make its sufficient-decrease tests noisy.

Conclusion

The steepest curvature determines stability and the flattest direction determines slow progress for a scalar learning rate.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement gradient descent with Armijo backtracking for a quadratic and verify gradient correctness, monotonic descent and convergence.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def objective(v):
    x,y=v; return 0.5*(100*x*x+y*y)

def gradient(v):
    x,y=v; return [100*x,y]

def step_with_backtracking(v,start=1.0,c=1e-4):
    g=gradient(v); eta=start; current=objective(v); norm2=sum(value*value for value in g)
    while objective([v[i]-eta*g[i] for i in range(2)]) > current-c*eta*norm2:
        eta*=0.5
        if eta<1e-12: raise RuntimeError('line search failed')
    return [v[i]-eta*g[i] for i in range(2)],eta
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
v=[1.0,1.0]; history=[objective(v)]; rates=[]
for _ in range(800):
    v,eta=step_with_backtracking(v); history.append(objective(v)); rates.append(eta)

def central(i,h=1e-6):
    plus=list(v); minus=list(v); plus[i]+=h; minus[i]-=h
    return (objective(plus)-objective(minus))/(2*h)

Common mistakes

  • If loss decreases, the learning rate is optimal.

    It may be stable but far too small; inspect convergence speed, update norms and validation behavior.

  • Changing batch size leaves optimizer behavior unchanged.

    It changes gradient variance, number of steps, normalization and often the useful schedule/rate.

  • Saving model weights is enough to resume training.

    Optimizer moments, scheduler, scaler, RNG and sampler/data position are part of the dynamical state.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why can gradient descent zig-zag?

    In ill-conditioned valleys the gradient points strongly across steep walls, so a safe scalar step oscillates while moving slowly along flat directions.

  • What does momentum do?

    It accumulates a velocity from past gradients, smoothing alternating directions and accelerating persistent ones.

  • Why separate training loss and validation metric?

    The optimizer directly reduces the training objective; generalization and business utility are evaluated on held-out data and may move differently.

Production / system-design connection

Version data/order, objective, batch/effective batch, optimizer equations, schedule, precision and distributed reduction. Monitor loss components, validation slices, learning/update/gradient/parameter norms, clipping, nonfinite values, throughput and cost. Atomically checkpoint full training state, test resume equivalence, bound failure/retry budgets, validate before promotion and keep compatible model plus preprocessing for rollback.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What is the stable constant-step interval for a positive-definite quadratic with largest eigenvalue L?

    Show solution

    `0<η<2/L`; smaller restrictions may be used for monotonicity or conservative guarantees.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    How can scaling help a narrow quadratic valley?

    Show solution

    Rescale/precondition coordinates so curvature eigenvalues are more similar, permitting comparable progress in all directions.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Training resumes with a sudden loss spike although weights loaded correctly. What state may be missing?

    Show solution

    Optimizer moments, scheduler step, loss scaler, RNG or data-sampler position may not have been restored.

5.5

Norms, Distances & Similarity

highverified
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as

Topic overview

Norms measure vector or matrix magnitude; metrics measure distance between objects; similarity functions rank resemblance but may not satisfy metric axioms. Those choices encode geometry and can change nearest neighbors, clustering, regularization, robustness and retrieval quality. This chapter develops L1, L2, L∞ and general Lp norms, weighted and Mahalanobis distance, cosine similarity, Hamming distance and key matrix norms. You will learn the norm and metric axioms, the role of scaling and covariance, why cosine discards magnitude, how high-dimensional distance concentration changes intuition, and why comparing raw mixed-unit features is usually meaningless. A worked retrieval example contrasts Euclidean and cosine rankings before and after normalization. The lab implements core measures, checks symmetry, triangle inequality examples and library agreement, and rejects zero-vector cosine. Production guidance covers preprocessing/versioning, approximate nearest-neighbor index compatibility, floating-point clipping, missing values, privacy, distribution drift and monitoring of neighbor stability. The goal is to make “distance” a modeled assumption tied to invariances and decision cost, not a default call chosen after features have already defined an accidental geometry.

Prerequisites

  • vectors-matrices

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish norms, metrics and similarities and verify the properties each downstream algorithm assumes.
  • Choose Lp, cosine, weighted or Mahalanobis geometry from feature units, invariances, covariance and task cost.
  • Operate distance-based systems with stable preprocessing, index-metric consistency, drift checks and meaningful retrieval evaluation.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A norm measures magnitude and must be nonnegative, definite, homogeneous and satisfy the triangle inequality. A metric measures pairwise distance and must be nonnegative, identity-preserving, symmetric and satisfy the triangle inequality. L1 sums absolute coordinates, L2 is Euclidean length, and L∞ takes the largest absolute coordinate. Cosine similarity uses angle and ignores positive scale after normalization; cosine distance conventions are not always metrics. Feature scaling defines the geometry, while Mahalanobis distance accounts for covariance through a positive semidefinite precision matrix. Choose the measure from desired invariances and costs, then keep preprocessing and ANN index configuration consistent.

What you must know

  • Geometry is a modeling choice
  • Scaling changes nearest neighbors
  • Cosine ignores positive magnitude
  • Mahalanobis uses covariance structure
  • Index and evaluation metric must agree

Why this matters

K-nearest neighbors, clustering, anomaly detection, recommenders and embedding search are only as meaningful as their geometry. Age measured in years and income in cents make unscaled Euclidean distance mostly income. Cosine can call a tiny and huge vector identical in direction even when magnitude carries confidence or activity. Correlated features can be counted twice. A mathematically valid metric may also misalign with false-positive and false-negative costs. Production retrieval requires the metric, preprocessing, index and evaluation to be one versioned system.

Intuition

A norm draws a unit ball around the origin. L2 draws a circle, L1 a diamond and L∞ a square in two dimensions. Those shapes decide which deviations cost equally and which points are near. Scaling an axis stretches the map before measuring. Cosine looks only at direction from the origin, while Mahalanobis first reshapes correlated, differently scaled data into a standardized space.

Norm and metric foundations

A norm ||x|| on a vector space is nonnegative, equals zero only at zero, is absolutely homogeneous `||αx||=|α| ||x||`, and obeys `||x+y||≤||x||+||y||`. It induces a metric d(x,y)=||x−y||. A metric instead starts with pairwise axioms: nonnegativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry and triangle inequality. A similarity may be larger for closer items but need satisfy none of these; algorithms relying on triangle-inequality pruning can fail or lose guarantees with a nonmetric score.

For p≥1, `||x||_p=(Σ|x_i|^p)^{1/p}`. L1 tolerates a few large coordinate differences differently and produces diamond-shaped balls; L2 is rotation-invariant Euclidean length; L∞ is the maximum absolute difference and enforces a worst-coordinate view. The expression with p<1 encourages sparsity-like behavior but is not a norm because the triangle inequality fails. L0 is informal notation for nonzero count, not a norm.

Weighted norms encode coordinate importance and units. Positive weights in weighted Euclidean distance correspond to scaling axes. Weights should derive from measurement scale or task cost, not be tuned against a leaked test set. Standardization by training statistics can prevent a large-unit feature from dominating, but it does not make every feature semantically comparable.

Angle, correlation, and covariance-aware distance

Cosine similarity is `(x·y)/(||x||_2||y||_2)` for nonzero vectors. It measures angle and is invariant to positive rescaling. If vectors are L2-normalized, squared Euclidean distance and cosine similarity are monotonically related: `||x−y||²=2−2cos(x,y)`. This equivalence explains why an index for normalized inner product can serve cosine ranking, but only when normalization is actually applied. Define behavior for zero vectors rather than returning an unexplained NaN. Floating error can push a computed cosine slightly outside [-1,1], so clip before inverse cosine.

Centered cosine becomes correlation-like and removes coordinate means, which changes the object being compared. Dot product preserves both norm and alignment and may favor high-magnitude items. Decide whether magnitude represents popularity, confidence, exposure or an unwanted nuisance. Retrieval evaluation should reveal this rather than relying on intuition alone.

Mahalanobis distance is `sqrt((x−y)^T Σ^{-1}(x−y))`, where Σ is a covariance estimate or another positive semidefinite scale matrix. It downweights high-variance directions and accounts for correlations; equivalently, it is Euclidean distance after whitening. Singular or poorly estimated covariance requires regularization, diagonal approximation, shrinkage or a learned low-rank transform. Estimate it on training data only and monitor drift.

High-dimensional geometry and alternative domains

As dimension grows, points can become sparse relative to volume and distances may concentrate: nearest and farthest distances become less separated under some distributions. Irrelevant noisy dimensions accumulate in L2, while a handful of extreme coordinates can dominate L∞. This does not mean all high-dimensional distance is useless; learned embeddings exploit low-dimensional structure, normalization and task supervision. It means raw dimensionality and distribution must be measured.

Inspect neighbor-distance ratios, recall, hubness (a few points appearing in many neighbor lists), cluster stability and performance across slices. Dimensionality reduction or feature selection can improve signal but may erase minority structure. Approximate nearest-neighbor algorithms trade exact recall for speed and support different metrics. Index build metric, query preprocessing and reranking metric must match or be explicitly staged.

Other domains need other distances. Hamming counts unequal positions for fixed-length categorical/binary strings. Jaccard compares set intersection to union. Edit distance models insertions, deletions and substitutions. Dynamic time warping aligns sequences at nonlinear time but can match implausible paths without constraints. Geodesic distance is needed on the sphere; treating latitude/longitude as planar coordinates causes distortion. Choose a domain-valid representation before choosing an efficient index.

Evaluation and production geometry

Version the full transform: field selection, missing-value policy, categorical encoding, centering/scaling, embedding model, normalization and metric. Fit learned statistics only on training/reference data. The same raw item processed by two versions may land in incompatible coordinate systems, so rebuild or dual-index migrations. Validate finite values and dimension; reject or explicitly route zero vectors; enforce bounded query sizes.

Offline evaluation uses labeled relevance, recall@k, precision@k, ranking metrics and task-specific costs, plus ANN recall against an exact subset. Compare simple baselines and inspect qualitative neighbors. Segment by language, geography, item popularity and sensitive cohorts because one global metric can hide failures. Online metrics must separate retrieval quality from later ranking and user feedback loops.

Monitor embedding/norm distributions, zero and missing rates, nearest-distance distribution, hubness, index freshness, ANN recall samples, latency and memory. Drift may require recalibration or re-embedding. Do not log raw sensitive vectors casually; embeddings can leak membership or attributes. Apply access control, deletion and retention across indices and backups. Have rollback to a prior compatible embedding-index-metric bundle, not only old application code.

Math / formal view

For p≥1, ||x||_p=(Σ_i|x_i|^p)^{1/p}. A norm-induced distance d_p(x,y)=||x−y||_p is a metric. Cosine similarity is s(x,y)=x^Ty/(||x||_2||y||_2) for nonzero x,y. Mahalanobis squared distance is d_M²=(x−y)^TM(x−y), where M is positive semidefinite; if M=L^TL, this equals ||L(x−y)||_2².

Magnitude versus direction in retrieval

Setup

A query q=(1,1) compares document A=(10,10) and B=(1,0).

Cosine gives A similarity 1 because it points in exactly q's direction, while B has similarity 1/√2. Raw Euclidean distance makes B much closer: `||q−B||=1`, whereas `||q−A||=√162`. Neither result is a contradiction. If vector magnitude reflects document length and should be ignored, L2-normalize query and documents and use cosine or equivalent Euclidean distance on normalized vectors. If magnitude represents calibrated confidence or activity that should matter, discarding it is wrong. Evaluate relevance labels and inspect norm correlations. Store the chosen normalization with the index and reject zero vectors.

Conclusion

The two measures answer different invariance questions; task evidence decides which geometry is useful.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement L1, L2, L∞ and cosine, then verify metric properties, normalized equivalence and NumPy agreement.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def lp(x,y,p):
    if len(x)!=len(y): raise ValueError('shape mismatch')
    delta=[abs(a-b) for a,b in zip(x,y)]
    if p==math.inf: return max(delta,default=0.0)
    if p<1: raise ValueError('p must be at least 1')
    return sum(value**p for value in delta)**(1/p)

def cosine(x,y):
    dot=sum(a*b for a,b in zip(x,y)); nx=math.sqrt(sum(a*a for a in x)); ny=math.sqrt(sum(b*b for b in y))
    if nx==0 or ny==0: raise ValueError('zero vector')
    return max(-1.0,min(1.0,dot/(nx*ny)))
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
x=np.array([1.,2.,-1.]); y=np.array([3.,0.,2.]); z=np.array([0.,1.,1.])
manual={'l1':lp(x,y,1),'l2':lp(x,y,2),'linf':lp(x,y,math.inf),'cosine':cosine(x,y)}
library={'l1':np.linalg.norm(x-y,1),'l2':np.linalg.norm(x-y,2),'linf':np.linalg.norm(x-y,np.inf),'cosine':float(x@y/(np.linalg.norm(x)*np.linalg.norm(y)))}
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert all(math.isclose(manual[k],library[k]) for k in manual)
assert math.isclose(lp(x,y,2),lp(y,x,2))
assert lp(x,z,2)<=lp(x,y,2)+lp(y,z,2)+1e-12

assert math.isclose(np.linalg.norm(xn-yn)**2,2-2*cosine(xn,yn),rel_tol=1e-12)
try: cosine([0.,0.],[1.,0.])
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('zero cosine must be defined explicitly')

Common mistakes

  • Standardize features using the entire dataset before evaluation.

    That leaks validation/test distribution; fit transform statistics on training data and version them.

  • Cosine similarity and dot product are always interchangeable.

    Only after consistent normalization; raw dot product also depends on vector norms.

  • Any distance-like score is a metric.

    Check identity, symmetry and triangle inequality before relying on metric-index guarantees.

Likely follow-ups

  • When are cosine and Euclidean rankings equivalent?

    For L2-normalized vectors, squared Euclidean distance is `2−2cosine`, so one decreases exactly as the other increases.

  • What problem does Mahalanobis distance address?

    Different scales and correlated directions; it measures Euclidean distance after a covariance-aware linear transformation.

  • Why can distance degrade in high dimensions?

    Noise accumulates, volume is sparse and nearest/farthest distances may concentrate; learned structure and evaluation are needed.

Production / system-design connection

Version features, learned scaling, embedding model, normalization, metric and ANN configuration as one artifact. Validate dimension, finiteness, missing/zero behavior and index compatibility; evaluate exact and approximate retrieval on representative labels and slices. Monitor norms, neighbor distances, hubness, recall, freshness, latency and drift. Protect and delete sensitive vectors across indexes/backups, bound requests and keep a prior compatible bundle for rollback.

5.6

Orthogonality, Projections & Least Squares

highverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

Orthogonal projection chooses the point in a subspace closest to a target, and least squares uses that geometry to fit inconsistent linear systems. Given a design matrix A and observations b, the fitted vector A x̂ is the projection of b onto A's column space, so the residual is orthogonal to every column. This chapter derives normal equations, explains why QR and singular value decomposition are safer computational routes, and connects rank, pseudoinverse, minimum-norm solutions, regularization, leverage and residual diagnostics. You will learn to construct projection onto a vector or orthonormal basis, distinguish coefficient uncertainty from predictive error, include intercepts and categorical encodings correctly, and identify when collinearity or ill-conditioning makes coefficients unstable even though predictions look reasonable. A worked line fit checks residual orthogonality by hand and with NumPy. Production guidance covers train/test separation, scaling, solver choice, dtype, robust alternatives, monitoring, privacy, artifact versioning and rollback. The objective is to connect the geometric statement “closest point in a subspace” to practical regression code and to know where ordinary least squares assumptions stop supporting statistical conclusions.

Prerequisites

  • vectors-matrices
  • norms-distances

Learning objectives

  • Derive projection and least-squares optimality from residual orthogonality and the geometry of column space.
  • Choose QR, SVD, pseudoinverse or regularization instead of relying blindly on normal equations or explicit inverse.
  • Validate fits using rank, conditioning, residual structure, leakage-safe evaluation and production monitoring.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Least squares chooses x̂ minimizing `||Ax−b||²`. At the optimum the residual r=b−Ax̂ is orthogonal to the column space, giving `AᵀA x̂=Aᵀb`. The fitted values are the projection of b onto Col(A). Normal equations are useful for derivation but square the condition number; production solvers use QR or SVD. If A is rank-deficient, coefficients are not unique and the pseudoinverse returns a minimum-norm solution. Always include the intended intercept, inspect rank and conditioning, evaluate out of sample, and remember that unbiasedness or confidence intervals require assumptions beyond numerical minimization.

What you must know

  • Fitted values lie in column space
  • Residual is orthogonal to features
  • Normal equations are a derivation
  • QR/SVD are safer solvers
  • Rank deficiency breaks coefficient uniqueness

Why this matters

Linear regression, calibration, embeddings, filters and many optimization steps reduce to projection or least squares. The formula can produce numbers even when columns are duplicated, scales differ by orders of magnitude or data leaks future information. Understanding geometry reveals why coefficients become unstable, why residual checks matter and why computing an inverse is the wrong implementation. It also separates the deterministic approximation problem from statistical claims about noise and causality.

Intuition

The columns of A span a flat surface of predictions that the model can express. Observation b usually lies off that surface. Least squares drops a perpendicular from b to the surface; the landing point is A x̂ and the leftover arrow is the residual. Coefficients describe how to combine columns to reach the landing point. If columns point in redundant directions, the landing point can be unique while the coordinate recipe is not.

Projection onto vectors and subspaces

For nonzero vector a, the projection of b onto span(a) is `a(a^Tb)/(a^Ta)`. The coefficient is the aligned component measured relative to a's squared length. The residual `b−proj_a b` is orthogonal to a. If Q has orthonormal columns spanning a subspace, projection is `QQ^T b`, and P=QQ^T is symmetric and idempotent: `P^T=P`, `P²=P`. The complementary projector I−P maps onto the orthogonal complement.

For a general full-column-rank A, the projection matrix can be written `A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T`, but this expression is primarily conceptual. Forming it is unnecessary and often expensive; solving for coefficients or using an orthonormal factor is better. If columns are not independent, the inverse does not exist even though the subspace and its projection remain well defined. SVD/pseudoinverse supplies the orthogonal projector onto the column space.

Projection depends on the inner product. Weighted least squares changes geometry so some residuals count more, commonly using inverse-variance weights under a noise model. Generalized least squares handles correlated errors through a covariance-aware metric. Weights must reflect the intended objective and be included consistently in evaluation; arbitrary large weights can create numerical and fairness problems.

Least squares and the normal equations

Define `f(x)=||Ax−b||²=(Ax−b)^T(Ax−b)`. Its gradient is `2A^T(Ax−b)`. Setting it to zero yields `A^TA x=A^Tb`, equivalent to residual orthogonality `A^T(b−Ax)=0`. When A has independent columns, `A^TA` is positive definite and the minimizer is unique. With dependent columns, there are multiple coefficient minimizers but all share the same fitted projection.

An intercept corresponds to a column of ones. Omitting it forces the fitted hyperplane through the origin and changes residual-mean and interpretation. Centering features and target can separate intercept computation, but preprocessing must be fitted on training data and replayed identically. Categorical one-hot encoding plus an intercept creates exact dependence if every category column is retained; drop a reference level or use a solver/regularization with an explicit identification convention.

Least squares minimizes vertical squared residuals in the modeled target coordinate. It is sensitive to outliers because squaring grows rapidly. It does not minimize perpendicular distance to both feature and target measurement errors, and it does not by itself produce causal effects. Statistical inference adds assumptions about error mean, variance, independence or distribution and data collection.

QR, SVD, pseudoinverse, and regularization

Solving normal equations by forming `A^TA` is numerically risky because its condition number is approximately the square of A's condition number. QR factorization writes A=QR with Q orthonormal and R triangular; solve `Rx=Q^Tb` without squaring conditioning. Householder QR is a standard stable dense method. SVD writes A=UΣV^T and exposes singular directions, rank, condition number and minimum-norm solutions. It costs more but is robust for rank deficiency and diagnostics.

The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse `A^+=VΣ^+U^T` reciprocates nonzero singular values under a tolerance and returns the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution among least-squares minimizers. Tiny singular values amplify noise, so numerical rank depends on scale and tolerance. Do not interpret the library default as domain truth.

Ridge regression minimizes `||Ax−b||²+λ||x||²`, leading to `(A^TA+λI)x=A^Tb` (usually excluding the intercept from penalty). It shrinks unstable directions and guarantees a unique solution for λ>0 but introduces bias. Choose λ using validation without leakage. Feature scaling changes the effective ridge penalty, so preprocessing and penalty are one model. Lasso uses L1 penalty and changes the solver/geometry.

Diagnostics, evaluation, and operation

Verify solver status, shape, rank, singular values/condition estimate, finite coefficients and residual orthogonality within tolerance. Compare predictions from two stable solvers on a small fixture. Inspect residuals versus fitted values, time, groups and important features for nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity, autocorrelation and bias. High leverage observations have unusual feature geometry and can influence the fit; large residual and leverage together deserve investigation, not automatic deletion.

Split evaluation according to deployment: chronological for future prediction, grouped for new entities, spatial for new regions. Fit scaling, imputation and encoding only on training folds. Compare to intercept/mean and simple domain baselines. Report prediction error and uncertainty separately from coefficient p-values. Robust regression, transformed targets, generalized linear models or nonlinear features may better match data and outcome.

In production, version column order, units, encoder, scaler, solver, regularization and training cutoff. Validate incoming schema/range/missingness, monitor prediction and residual drift when labels arrive, and alert on rank/conditioning changes. Bound matrix sizes and resource use, avoid logging sensitive raw rows, and audit protected-group performance. Keep training data lineage and a prior artifact for rollback. Refit only through the same tested pipeline; a mathematically equivalent feature reorder is not operationally equivalent without metadata.

Math / formal view

For A∈R^{m×n}, b∈R^m, minimize f(x)=||Ax−b||_2². Since ∇f=2A^T(Ax−b), optimality gives A^Tr=0 for r=b−Ax̂. If A has full column rank, x̂=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb conceptually. With SVD A=UΣV^T, x̂=A^+b=VΣ^+U^Tb is the minimum-norm least-squares solution. The fitted projector is P=AA^+.

Fit a line and verify orthogonality

Setup

Fit y≈β0+β1x for x=(0,1,2) and y=(1,2,2).

The design matrix has rows `(1,x_i)`. Solving gives β0=7/6 and β1=1/2, so fitted values are `(7/6,5/3,13/6)`. Residuals `b−Aβ` are `(-1/6,1/3,-1/6)`. Their sum is zero, showing orthogonality to the intercept column; their dot product with x is also zero, showing orthogonality to the slope column. The data vector is decomposed into fitted projection plus residual. Use `lstsq`/QR rather than explicitly inverting A^TA. With only one x value or a duplicated feature column, coefficients would not be uniquely identified.

Conclusion

Residual orthogonality is both the derivation and a powerful implementation check.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Project by solving least squares and verify the normal-equation, orthogonality, minimum-error and NumPy invariants.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def solve_two_by_two(a,b,c,d,u,v):
    det=a*d-b*c
    if abs(det)<1e-12: raise ValueError('singular')
    return ((u*d-b*v)/det,(a*v-u*c)/det)

def least_squares_line(xs,ys):
    n=len(xs); sx=sum(xs); sxx=sum(x*x for x in xs); sy=sum(ys); sxy=sum(x*y for x,y in zip(xs,ys))
    return solve_two_by_two(n,sx,sx,sxx,sy,sxy)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
xs=np.array([0.,1.,2.]); y=np.array([1.,2.,2.])
beta=np.array(least_squares_line(xs,y))
A=np.column_stack([np.ones_like(xs),xs])
library,residuals,rank,singular=np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)
fitted=A@beta; residual=y-fitted

Use target-library QR/SVD least squares with rank/condition telemetry, leakage-safe preprocessing and evaluation, versioned features/artifacts, drift monitoring and a prior reproducible model for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions

assert np.allclose(beta,library)

for delta in ([.01,0.],[0.,.01],[-.01,.02]):
    assert np.linalg.norm(A@(beta+delta)-y)>=np.linalg.norm(residual)-1e-12

Common mistakes

  • Use `(A.T@A)^{-1}@A.T@b` in production.

    Normal equations explain geometry but square conditioning; use `lstsq`, QR or SVD without an explicit inverse.

  • A low training residual proves a useful model.

    Evaluate under deployment-like splits and inspect residual structure, leakage, baseline improvement and stability.

  • Rank-deficient coefficients have a unique interpretation.

    Many coefficient vectors yield the same projection; pseudoinverse selects one convention and regularization changes the objective.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is the residual orthogonal to every feature column?

    Any component along the column space could be added to the fitted vector to reduce squared distance, so at the closest point none remains.

  • Why prefer QR to normal equations?

    It solves through an orthonormal/triangular factorization without forming A^TA and avoids squaring the condition number.

  • What does the pseudoinverse return?

    A least-squares solution, specifically the minimum-Euclidean-norm one when coefficients are not unique.

Production / system-design connection

Use `lstsq`/QR/SVD with explicit rank and tolerance diagnostics; never form an inverse for solving. Version features, preprocessing, solver, penalty and cutoff. Use leakage-safe splits, baselines and residual/slice diagnostics, validate schema/finiteness/conditioning, monitor feature and residual drift, protect training data and keep a reproducible prior artifact for rollback.

    Show solution

  2. Exercise 2 · application

5.7

Jacobians, Hessians & Second-order Thinking

mediumverified
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as

Topic overview

The Jacobian is the matrix representation of a vector-valued function's local linear map; the Hessian records second derivatives of a scalar function and describes local curvature. These objects clarify tensor shapes, sensitivity, inverse problems, uncertainty propagation and optimization, but full materialization is often unnecessary or impossible at ML scale. This chapter derives Jacobian-vector products (JVPs), vector-Jacobian products (VJPs), Hessian-vector products, quadratic Taylor models, curvature eigenvalues and positive-definiteness tests. You will learn to distinguish output-by-input conventions, interpret mixed partial symmetry under regularity assumptions, identify minima, maxima and saddles, and explain why Newton's method can fail when curvature is indefinite or the linear solve is unstable. A worked two-input/two-output map and scalar objective checks all shapes. The lab compares analytic Jacobian/Hessian values to finite differences and validates directional products. Production guidance covers autodiff mode choice, Gauss-Newton and Fisher approximations, damping, conjugate gradients, conditioning, precision, custom operations, monitoring and rollback. The objective is to use derivative operators and products as practical tools instead of treating giant derivative matrices as objects that must always be formed.

Prerequisites

  • derivatives-gradients
  • eigen-svd

Learning objectives

  • Derive Jacobian, JVP, VJP, Hessian and Hessian-vector shapes and interpret them as local sensitivity operators.
  • Use Hessian eigenstructure and quadratic models to classify stationary points and reason about conditioning and Newton-like steps.
  • Choose exact products or structured approximations with numerical checks, damping, scalable solves and production monitoring.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

For f:R^n→R^m, the Jacobian J has entries `J_ij=∂f_i/∂x_j` under the output-by-input convention and maps a small input change to `df≈J dx`. A JVP computes Jv; a VJP computes uᵀJ and is what reverse mode uses. For scalar f, the Hessian H has `H_ij=∂²f/∂x_i∂x_j` and gives the quadratic term `½dxᵀHdx`. At a stationary point, positive-definite H indicates a strict local minimum, negative definite a maximum, and mixed eigenvalue signs a saddle. Full matrices are usually avoided; autodiff computes products, while Newton/Gauss-Newton methods solve damped systems with conditioning and validation checks.

What you must know

  • Jacobian maps input perturbations to output perturbations
  • JVP and VJP avoid full matrices
  • Hessian encodes local curvature
  • Eigenvalue signs classify stationary geometry
  • Newton steps require safe solves and damping

Why this matters

Modern models have millions of inputs or parameters, so a full derivative matrix is too large. Yet products with that matrix power backpropagation, influence approximations, sensitivity analysis and second-order optimization. Shape confusion, wrong transpose conventions and indefinite curvature lead to subtle errors. Operator thinking makes the useful computations explicit and exposes when a second-order promise depends on smoothness, local validity and numerical conditioning.

Intuition

The Jacobian is a tiny local machine: feed it a small direction and it predicts how every output moves. The Hessian describes how the gradient machine itself changes. Around a point, the Hessian turns a flat tangent plane into a bowl, dome or saddle. In large systems, you rarely print the machine; you ask it targeted questions such as ‘what happens along this vector?’

Jacobians, JVPs, and VJPs

For f:R^n→R^m, differentiability gives `f(x+h)=f(x)+J_f(x)h+o(||h||)`. With output-by-input convention, J is m×n and row i is the gradient transpose of output f_i. A JVP `Jv` is the directional rate of all outputs along input direction v and can be computed by forward-mode autodiff without forming J. A VJP `u^TJ` combines output sensitivities into input sensitivities and is computed by reverse mode.

Shape reasoning decides mode efficiency. If n is small and m huge, columns/JVPs are cheap; if a scalar loss m=1 depends on huge n, one reverse VJP obtains the gradient. A full Jacobian needs roughly min(n,m) sweeps plus storage and should be requested only when genuinely needed. Batches introduce a block structure: many examples are independent, but asking a framework for a Jacobian of the whole batch can materialize zeros and huge dimensions. Use per-example APIs or vectorization deliberately.

Jacobians propagate uncertainty locally: covariance approximately maps as `JΣJ^T`, assuming linearization is adequate. Singular values reveal local amplification and insensitive/null directions. Inverse problems become unstable when small singular values make inputs poorly identifiable. Normalize units before comparing sensitivities across coordinates.

Hessians and local curvature

For twice-differentiable scalar f:R^n→R, H=∇²f has entries of second partial derivatives. Under continuity of mixed partials near the point, H is symmetric. Taylor's quadratic model is `f(x+p)≈f(x)+g^Tp+½p^THp`. Directional curvature along unit v is `v^THv`; Hessian eigenvectors give principal curvature directions and eigenvalues their curvature.

At a stationary point g=0, positive-definite H implies a strict local minimum, negative definite a maximum, and both positive/negative eigenvalues a saddle. Positive semidefinite alone can be inconclusive because higher-order terms matter; a zero Hessian does not prove a minimum. Away from stationary points, curvature classification does not replace the nonzero first-order slope. Nonsmooth objectives may not have a classical Hessian at kinks.

Condition number among positive eigenvalues affects optimization. Very large eigenvalues set small stable first-order steps; tiny ones create flat directions. Negative curvature can provide an escape direction from a saddle but makes an undamped Newton system aim in a non-descent direction. Hessian trace, diagonal and top eigenvalues are useful summaries but cannot fully describe a complex landscape.

Newton, Gauss-Newton, and structured approximations

Newton's method minimizes the quadratic model by solving `Hp=−g` and setting x←x+p. Near a well-behaved minimum it can converge rapidly. Globally, the quadratic model may be poor, H may be singular/indefinite and a full factorization may be unaffordable. Line search or trust regions constrain the step; damping solves `(H+λI)p=−g` to improve definiteness and conditioning. Never compute H^{-1} explicitly—solve the linear system.

Hessian-vector products can be obtained by differentiating a gradient-vector product (or forward-over-reverse), enabling conjugate-gradient solves and eigenvalue estimates with memory proportional to vectors. Conjugate gradient assumes a symmetric positive-definite operator for its standard form; damping or alternative Krylov solvers may be needed. Preconditioning approximates curvature cheaply to reduce iterations.

For nonlinear least squares, Gauss-Newton uses `J^TJ` and omits residual-weighted second derivative terms; it is positive semidefinite and accurate near small residuals. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping. Fisher information and empirical Fisher appear in probabilistic/natural-gradient contexts but are not generally identical to the Hessian. Diagonal, block-diagonal and low-rank approximations trade fidelity for cost and must be evaluated on the actual objective.

Validation and production operation

Check a JVP against directional finite differences of f, a VJP against dot-product identity `u^T(Jv)=(u^TJ)v`, and an HVP against finite differences of gradients. For smooth scalar code, check Hessian symmetry within tolerance. Use double precision and scale-aware steps on small deterministic cases; avoid branch boundaries. Validate shape conventions with asymmetric n and m. Custom differentiation rules require tests for batched, broadcast, dtype/device and zero-size edge cases.

At scale, instrument product latency, linear-solver residual, iteration count, damping/trust radius, predicted versus actual objective decrease, nonfinite values and curvature estimates. Fail safely when solves do not converge or the step is not descent. Cache/reuse products only when parameters and data match; stale curvature can be harmful. Distributed products must use consistent reductions and deterministic tolerance policy.

Version the exact objective, regularization, data batch/snapshot, parameter order, autodiff/compiler framework, damping and solver settings. Curvature calculations may expose training data through influence or gradient information, so restrict outputs and logs. Bound product requests to prevent resource exhaustion. Compare second-order cost against first-order baselines and downstream benefit. Checkpoint all optimizer/preconditioner state and retain a simpler fallback/previous model for rollback.

Math / formal view

For f:R^n→R^m, J_f(x)∈R^{m×n} satisfies f(x+h)=f(x)+Jh+o(||h||). A JVP is Jv and VJP is u^TJ. For scalar φ, H=∇²φ and `φ(x+p)=φ(x)+g^Tp+½p^THp+o(||p||²)`. HVP is Hv. Newton solves Hp=−g; damped Newton solves (H+λI)p=−g.

Two-output map and scalar curvature

Setup

Let f(x,y)=(x²y, sin x+y) and φ(x,y)=½(x²+4y²).

The Jacobian is `[[2xy,x²],[cos x,1]]`. At (1,2), J=`[[4,1],[cos1,1]]`. For v=(1,−1), Jv=`(3,cos1−1)`, predicting the first-order output change. The scalar φ has gradient `(x,4y)` and constant Hessian diag(1,4). Its positive eigenvalues show a strict convex bowl; the y direction has four times the curvature. Newton solves H p=−g and reaches the origin in one exact quadratic step. A finite-difference JVP and HVP should agree, while computing a full Hessian would be unnecessary if only H v were needed.

Conclusion

The Jacobian handles output sensitivity; the Hessian handles scalar-objective curvature, and products expose both economically.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement central-difference Jacobian and Hessian checks, then verify JVP, VJP, symmetry and analytic curvature.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def vector_f(v):
    x,y=v; return [x*x*y,math.sin(x)+y]

def scalar_f(v):
    x,y=v; return 0.5*(x*x+4*y*y)

def jacobian_fd(f,x,h=1e-6):
    base=f(x); J=[[0.0]*len(x) for _ in base]
    for j in range(len(x)):
        plus=list(x); minus=list(x); plus[j]+=h; minus[j]-=h
        fp,fm=f(plus),f(minus)
        for i in range(len(base)): J[i][j]=(fp[i]-fm[i])/(2*h)
    return J

def gradient_fd(f,x,h=1e-5):
    out=[]
    for j in range(len(x)):
        plus=list(x); minus=list(x); plus[j]+=h; minus[j]-=h
        out.append((f(plus)-f(minus))/(2*h))
    return out
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
x=np.array([1.,2.]); J=np.array(jacobian_fd(vector_f,x.tolist()))
J_true=np.array([[4.,1.],[math.cos(1.),1.]])
H=np.array(jacobian_fd(lambda z: gradient_fd(scalar_f,z),x.tolist(),h=1e-4))
H_true=np.diag([1.,4.]); v=np.array([1.,-1.]); u=np.array([2.,3.])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use framework derivative products for large models, keep dot-product/finite checks for custom operators, damp and monitor iterative solves, secure derivative traces and checkpoint compatible optimizer/model state for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert np.allclose(J,J_true,atol=1e-8)
assert np.allclose(J@v,[3.,math.cos(1.)-1.],atol=1e-8)
assert np.isclose(u@(J@v),(u@J)@v)
assert np.allclose(H,H_true,atol=1e-5)
assert np.allclose(H,H.T,atol=1e-8)
assert np.all(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)>0)
grad=np.array([x[0],4*x[1]]); step=np.linalg.solve(H_true,-grad)
assert np.allclose(x+step,[0.,0.])

Common mistakes

  • A Jacobian has the same orientation in every source/library.

    Conventions differ; state output-by-input or its transpose and derive product shapes explicitly.

  • A positive semidefinite Hessian always proves a strict minimum.

    Zero-curvature directions require higher-order analysis; strict positive definiteness is a sufficient second-order condition.

  • Newton's method means multiply by an inverse Hessian.

    Solve a possibly damped system and globalize with line search/trust region; never form the inverse explicitly.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the difference between a JVP and VJP?

    JVP maps an input direction to output change; VJP maps output sensitivities backward to input sensitivities.

  • How can you compute Hv without H?

    Differentiate the scalar/vector product of the gradient with v using mixed autodiff modes, obtaining a Hessian-vector product.

  • Why add damping to Newton?

    It improves conditioning, can make the system positive definite and limits trust in an inaccurate local quadratic model.

Production / system-design connection

Prefer JVP/VJP/HVP operators to full matrices; validate dot-product, finite-difference and symmetry invariants on small cases. Use damped solves/trust or line search, monitor solver residual, iterations, curvature, actual versus predicted decrease, nonfinite values and cost. Version objective/data/order/framework/solver state, restrict sensitive derivative products, bound resources and retain a tested first-order or previous-model rollback path.

Exercises

    Show solution

    3×5; it maps a 5-vector input perturbation to a 3-vector output perturbation.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    How do you test a VJP implementation without forming J?

    Show solution

    Check `uᵀ(Jv)=(uᵀJ)v` using independently computed JVP and VJP for random u,v.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A Newton step increases loss at a saddle. Why?

    Show solution

    The Hessian is indefinite and the unconstrained quadratic solution need not be a descent direction; use damping/trust-region/line search or negative-curvature handling.
