5.8

Numerical Stability: log-sum-exp, overflow & conditioning

highverified
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as

Topic overview

Numerical stability asks whether an algorithm produces an accurate result in finite-precision arithmetic; conditioning asks whether the underlying problem itself is sensitive to small input changes. This chapter develops floating-point representation, unit roundoff, overflow, underflow, subnormals, cancellation and non-associativity, then derives stable log-sum-exp, softmax, log-probability, variance, norm and linear-system practices. You will learn to distinguish forward from backward error, use condition numbers, avoid explicit inverses and normal equations, choose dtypes and tolerances, and detect when no algorithm can recover information absent from ill-conditioned data. A worked extreme-logit example shows why subtracting the maximum preserves softmax exactly in real arithmetic while preventing overflow. The lab implements stable log-sum-exp/softmax and compensated summation with invariants against high-precision references. Production guidance covers mixed precision, loss scaling, deterministic reductions, NaN/Inf policy, telemetry, cross-hardware regression, adversarial inputs, resource limits and rollback. The goal is to make numerical behavior part of algorithm design and system observability rather than a late response to a mysterious NaN.

Prerequisites

  • vectors-matrices
  • eigen-svd
  • derivatives-gradients

Learning objectives

  • Explain floating-point rounding, range limits, cancellation and non-associativity and predict common failure modes.
  • Separate problem conditioning from algorithm stability using forward/backward error and condition-number reasoning.
  • Implement and operate stable transformations, reductions and linear solves with dtype-aware tests, telemetry and safe failure policy.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Floating point represents a finite set of values with limited precision and exponent range, so operations round, addition is non-associative, large exponentials overflow, tiny values underflow and subtracting nearly equal numbers loses significant digits. Stable algorithms reformulate without changing the mathematical result: log-sum-exp subtracts the maximum, softmax shares that shift, probabilities multiply in log space, and linear systems use factorization-based solves rather than inverses or normal equations. Conditioning is sensitivity of the problem; stability is behavior of the algorithm. Use condition estimates, scale-aware tolerances, higher-precision accumulation where needed, nonfinite monitoring and adversarial numerical tests across hardware.

What you must know

  • Finite precision changes algebraic behavior
  • Conditioning belongs to the problem
  • Stability belongs to the algorithm
  • Shift/scaling avoids range failure
  • Solve and factorize; do not invert

Why this matters

A model can be mathematically correct and still produce NaNs, zero probabilities, negative variances or wildly unstable coefficients. These failures vary by dtype, batch order, compiler and accelerator, making them hard to reproduce. Numerical issues also create security and reliability risks when extreme untrusted inputs exhaust retries or bypass checks through NaN comparisons. Stable formulations and observability prevent entire classes of incidents.

Intuition

Floating point is scientific notation with a fixed number of significant digits and bounded exponent. It can represent very large and very small scales, but not every real number. Adding a grain of sand to a mountain may round back to the mountain; subtracting two nearly equal mountains can leave a difference with few trustworthy digits. Stable algorithms move the calculation into a safe scale before doing sensitive work.

Floating-point model and error mechanisms

A normalized binary floating-point number has sign, significand and exponent. Rounding maps each real result to a nearby representable value, often modeled as `fl(a op b)=(a op b)(1+δ)` for ordinary-range results with |δ| bounded near unit roundoff. This model excludes overflow, underflow and some subnormal cases. Machine epsilon is commonly the gap from 1 to the next value and differs by dtype; terminology varies, so inspect library `finfo`.

Overflow produces infinity or raises depending on operation/policy. Underflow rounds tiny magnitudes toward zero; subnormals extend range with reduced relative precision and may have hardware performance behavior. Invalid operations create NaN. Comparisons with NaN are false except inequality, so naive range checks can be bypassed unless finiteness is checked first. Signed zero can affect reciprocals and branch behavior.

Floating addition is not associative: `(a+b)+c` can differ from `a+(b+c)`. Parallel reductions therefore vary with tree/order. Adding small values to a huge accumulator can lose them; pairwise or compensated summation reduces error. Catastrophic cancellation occurs when subtracting nearby approximations, exposing their rounding error. Algebraically equivalent formulas may have drastically different numerical quality.

Stable exponentials, probabilities, and statistics

For values x_i, `log Σ exp(x_i)` overflows when any x is large. Let m=max x. Then `logsumexp(x)=m+log Σ exp(x_i−m)`, mathematically identical because the common factor exp(m) is extracted. Every shifted exponent is at most one, preventing positive overflow. If all inputs are −∞, handle the special case explicitly. Softmax uses the same shift; its probabilities are invariant to adding a constant to all logits.

Multiply many probabilities in log space: sums of log-probabilities avoid underflow and turn products into additions. Use `log1p(x)` for log(1+x) near zero and `expm1(x)` for exp(x)−1; direct forms lose small differences. Stable logistic/softplus formulas branch or use logaddexp to avoid exp overflow. Clamp probabilities only with a documented objective effect; arbitrary epsilon can bias loss and hide invalid logits.

The textbook one-pass variance `E[x²]−E[x]²` cancels when variance is small relative to mean. Two-pass centered computation or Welford's recurrence is safer. Euclidean norm can overflow when squaring huge values and underflow for tiny ones; scaled sum-of-squares algorithms avoid both. Centering and scaling can help algorithms but must not leak evaluation data.

Conditioning, forward error, and stable linear algebra

Conditioning measures sensitivity of the exact problem: how much output can change under a small relative input change. For solving Ax=b, condition number in a compatible norm is `κ(A)=||A||||A^{-1}||` when invertible. A large κ means some input direction is nearly erased, so measurement/rounding error can be greatly amplified. No stable algorithm can recover digits the problem does not contain. Rescaling can improve numeric representation but does not always remove intrinsic identifiability.

Forward error compares computed output with the exact desired output. Backward error asks whether the computed output is exact for a nearby input. A backward-stable solver can still have large forward error on an ill-conditioned problem, roughly amplified by κ. Residual `||b−A x̂||` alone can be small while x̂ is inaccurate when A is ill-conditioned; report scaled residual and condition estimates.

Use LU/Cholesky/QR/SVD solves appropriate to structure rather than explicit inverse. Forming A^TA squares the condition number. Symmetric positive-definite systems benefit from Cholesky after verifying assumptions; adding jitter changes the problem and must be justified/monitored. Singular values expose weak directions, and regularization trades bias for stability. Pivoting, equilibration and iterative refinement can improve solves, but target-library behavior and precision matter.

Testing and operating numerical reliability

Test numerical code across scales: zeros, subnormals where relevant, maximum finite values, mixed signs, near equality, repeated values, singular/nearly singular matrices, all −∞ logits and NaNs/Infs. Compare to higher precision or a trusted stable implementation on small cases. Assert invariants such as softmax nonnegativity and sum, log-sum-exp bounds, symmetry, monotonicity and solve residual. Use relative plus absolute tolerance based on scale, dtype, algorithm and condition—not a universal decimal count.

Mixed precision stores/executes parts in lower precision for speed, with higher-precision accumulation, master weights or dynamic loss scaling. Monitor overflows, skipped steps and scaler value. Quantization adds calibration and saturation error. Compiler fast-math flags may reassociate or weaken IEEE semantics; test the built artifact on deployment hardware. Cross-device bitwise equality may be unrealistic, but defined accuracy envelopes and deterministic modes are possible.

In production, check finiteness before comparisons, bound magnitudes and input sizes, classify numeric failures separately, and avoid retry loops that repeat deterministic NaNs. Log rates and safe summaries rather than sensitive values. Monitor nonfinite tensors, clipping/saturation, condition estimates, solver residual/iterations and output distribution. Canary new kernels/dtypes, retain a stable fallback and roll back code plus model/optimizer state. Treat adversarial extreme inputs and malformed arrays as security cases with bounded CPU/memory.

Math / formal view

For ordinary rounded operations, `fl(z)=z(1+δ)` with |δ| on the order of unit roundoff u, subject to range caveats. A problem y=f(x) has relative condition approximately `κ=lim_{ε→0} sup_{||Δx||≤ε||x||} (||Δy||/||y||)/ε`. For invertible A, κ(A)=||A||||A^{-1}||. Stable log-sum-exp: `L=m+log Σ_i exp(x_i−m)`, m=max_i x_i.

Softmax of extreme logits

Setup

Compute softmax for logits (1000, 999, 998).

Direct exp(1000) overflows in ordinary floating point, so dividing exponentials yields invalid values. Subtract m=1000 to get shifted logits (0,−1,−2). Exponentials are approximately (1,0.3679,0.1353), all representable, and normalization yields roughly (0.6652,0.2447,0.0900). Adding or subtracting a common constant leaves exact softmax unchanged because numerator and denominator share the factor. `logsumexp` is `1000+log(1+e^{-1}+e^{-2})`. Verify probabilities are finite, nonnegative and sum to one. For all −∞ logits, the usual max shift gives undefined −∞−(−∞), so the calling contract must define an error or masked result.

Conclusion

A mathematically invariant shift moves exponentials into a safe numeric range without changing the distribution.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement stable log-sum-exp, softmax and compensated summation, then verify extreme-value invariants and high-precision agreement.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def logsumexp(values):
    if not values: return -math.inf
    m=max(values)
    if m==math.inf: return math.inf
    if m==-math.inf: return -math.inf
    return m+math.log(sum(math.exp(x-m) for x in values))

def softmax(values):
    lse=logsumexp(values)
    if not math.isfinite(lse): raise ValueError('softmax requires a finite normalizer')
    return [math.exp(x-lse) for x in values]

def kahan_sum(values):
    total=0.0; correction=0.0
    for value in values:
        adjusted=value-correction; new=total+adjusted
        correction=(new-total)-adjusted; total=new
    return total
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from decimal import Decimal,getcontext
values=[1000.0,999.0,998.0]
probs=softmax(values); lse=logsumexp(values)
getcontext().prec=50
reference=float(Decimal(1000)+(Decimal(1)+Decimal(-1).exp()+Decimal(-2).exp()).ln())
sequence=[1e16,1.0,-1e16]
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use tested SciPy/framework primitives and stable solvers, maintain extreme-scale regression suites per dtype/hardware, monitor nonfinite/condition/residual signals, bound adversarial inputs and retain a stable numerical fallback for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert all(math.isfinite(p) and p>=0 for p in probs)
assert math.isclose(sum(probs),1.0,rel_tol=1e-14,abs_tol=1e-14)
assert math.isclose(lse,reference,rel_tol=1e-14)
shifted=softmax([x-12345 for x in values])
assert all(math.isclose(a,b,rel_tol=1e-12) for a,b in zip(probs,shifted))
assert sum(sequence)==0.0
assert kahan_sum([1e16,-1e16,1.0])==1.0
assert logsumexp([-math.inf,-math.inf])==-math.inf
try: softmax([-math.inf,-math.inf])
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('undefined normalizer must fail explicitly')

Common mistakes

  • Machine epsilon is the tolerance for every comparison.

    Tolerance depends on dtype, scale, operation count, conditioning and the invariant being checked; use relative and absolute components.

  • A small linear-system residual proves accurate coefficients.

    Ill-conditioning can allow small backward/residual error but large forward solution error; inspect κ and weak singular directions.

  • Clipping NaNs or probabilities fixes the numerical issue.

    It may hide invalid inputs/overflow and change the objective; use stable formulas and explicit failure semantics.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the difference between conditioning and stability?

    Conditioning is sensitivity of the exact problem to inputs; stability is how much extra error the algorithm introduces in finite precision.

  • Why subtract the maximum in softmax?

    Softmax is shift-invariant, and the shift makes all exponent arguments nonpositive, preventing positive exponential overflow.

  • Why avoid normal equations numerically?

    A^TA squares the condition number and loses accuracy in weak directions; QR or SVD is safer.

Production / system-design connection

Adopt stable primitives for log/probability/statistics and factorization-based solves; test adversarial scales against high-precision/trusted references and dtype-aware invariants. Check finiteness before comparisons, monitor nonfinite/saturation/condition/residual/scaler signals, bound resources and deterministic retries, canary compiler/hardware/dtype changes and keep stable fallback plus full-state rollback artifacts.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Why is floating-point addition non-associative?

    Show solution

    Each intermediate is rounded to a finite representable value, and different grouping creates different intermediates and lost low-order terms.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Rewrite `log(exp(a)+exp(b))` stably.

    Show solution

    Let m=max(a,b); compute `m+log(exp(a−m)+exp(b−m))`, with explicit handling if both are −∞.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A solver has tiny residual but coefficients vary enormously under tiny perturbations. What is happening?

    Show solution

    The problem is ill-conditioned; small input/rounding changes are amplified in weak singular directions despite backward-stable solving.

🎲 Probability

Random variables, distributions, expectation, conditioning and probabilistic reasoning.

8 lessons · 8 deep-complete · 16 visuals

6.1

Conditional Probability & Bayes Rule

very highverified
Roles: ds, mle, aie, as

Topic overview

Probability is a mathematical language for uncertain outcomes under a stated model. Events are subsets of a sample space; probability assigns them coherent weights. Conditional probability restricts attention to cases where evidence occurred, the multiplication rule connects joint and conditional events, and Bayes' rule reverses a condition by combining likelihood with a base rate. This chapter develops complements, unions, intersections, inclusion–exclusion, odds, partitions, diagnostic testing and repeated evidence while separating mathematical probability from causal claims and poorly calibrated subjective confidence. You will learn to define the population and experiment before calculating, avoid confusing `P(A|B)` with `P(B|A)`, and recognize when selection or model misspecification invalidates a posterior. A worked medical-screening example uses a natural-frequency table to make false positives and prevalence visible. The lab enumerates a finite population and verifies Bayes through counts and formulas. Production guidance covers prevalence drift, calibration, threshold decisions, uncertain labels, monitoring, privacy, adversarial likelihood inputs and rollback. The objective is to make every probability statement answer four questions: probability of what event, under which population/model, conditional on what information, and for which decision.

Learning objectives

  • Represent uncertain experiments with sample spaces and events and apply probability axioms, complements, unions, intersections and inclusion–exclusion.
  • Derive conditional probability, multiplication, total probability and Bayes' rule and solve base-rate-sensitive problems with natural frequencies.
  • Translate probabilistic outputs into monitored decisions while distinguishing calibration, causation, selection, model uncertainty and cost.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Conditional probability is `P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B)` for `P(B)>0`; it restricts the population to cases where B occurred. The multiplication rule is `P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B)`. Bayes' rule reverses the condition: `P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)`, where the denominator can be expanded across mutually exclusive hypotheses. The prior/base rate matters: a highly sensitive test can have low positive predictive value when the condition is rare. Define events and population explicitly, use counts to sanity-check, and remember Bayes updates beliefs within the assumed likelihood and prior—it does not prove causality or model correctness.

What you must know

  • Name the experiment and events
  • Conditioning changes the reference population
  • Joint equals conditional times marginal
  • Bayes combines likelihood and base rate
  • Posterior quality depends on model and data

Why this matters

Risk scores, fraud alerts, medical tests, spam filters and model confidence all require conditional reasoning. Teams often report sensitivity as if it were the probability a flagged case is truly positive, ignore prevalence changes, or treat an observational association as causal. These errors affect people and budgets. A disciplined event model and natural-frequency check make the assumptions and false-positive burden visible before deployment.

Intuition

Imagine a table of all possible cases. Conditioning on B covers every row outside B and renormalizes the rows that remain. Bayes' rule does not create information; it reads the same intersection from the opposite direction. Natural frequencies—such as 10 true cases and 990 noncases—often make the arithmetic clearer than percentages because the numerator and denominator populations stay visible.

Sample spaces, events, and probability rules

A sample space Ω lists possible outcomes at the resolution relevant to the question. An event A is a subset of outcomes. A probability measure satisfies nonnegativity, P(Ω)=1 and additivity over disjoint events. From these follow P(A^c)=1−P(A), monotonicity and inclusion–exclusion `P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)`. For a finite equally likely space, probability is favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes, but equal likelihood is an assumption—not a universal counting rule.

Define the experiment and population. “The probability of rain” needs location, time window, threshold, information set and forecast model. A customer churn probability is conditional on feature availability, observation policy and a prediction horizon. Changing the sample space can change probability even when event wording is similar. Impossible under the model does not always mean physically impossible; probability-zero events in continuous models can still be possible exact outcomes.

Mutually exclusive means events cannot occur together, `P(A∩B)=0`. It does not mean independent; if one occurs, the other becomes impossible. Exhaustive events cover Ω. A partition is mutually exclusive and exhaustive and lets complicated probabilities be computed by splitting across cases. Venn intuition helps for small event sets, while algebra prevents double counting.

Conditioning, multiplication, and Bayes

Conditional probability `P(A|B)` divides the mass of the intersection by P(B), making B the new universe. The multiplication rule follows directly. The chain rule extends: `P(A,B,C)=P(A)P(B|A)P(C|A,B)` for a chosen order. Conditioning can increase, decrease or leave a probability unchanged. Independence is the special case where learning B does not change A.

Bayes' rule combines prior P(H) and likelihood P(E|H) into posterior P(H|E). With hypotheses H_i forming a partition, `P(E)=Σ_i P(E|H_i)P(H_i)`. Posterior odds equal prior odds times a likelihood ratio, which is often convenient for sequential evidence. Evidence items cannot be multiplied as independent likelihoods unless conditional independence under hypotheses is justified.

A prior may represent population prevalence, previous data or explicit belief. The likelihood is a model for evidence given the hypothesis. Bayes is an identity once these are specified, but a precise posterior can still be wrong if prevalence drifts, labels are biased, evidence selection is ignored or likelihoods are misspecified. Sensitivity analysis over plausible priors/likelihoods shows robustness.

Diagnostics, scores, and decisions

For a binary test, sensitivity is P(test+|condition) and specificity is P(test−|no condition). Positive predictive value is P(condition|test+) and depends strongly on prevalence. Negative predictive value has the analogous base-rate dependence. A threshold changes sensitivity and specificity; no threshold is universally optimal without false-positive/negative costs, capacity and fairness constraints.

A classifier score may be a ranking score rather than a calibrated probability. Calibration asks whether cases assigned probability p occur about p fraction of the time under the deployment distribution. Evaluate reliability by bins or proper scoring rules with uncertainty and important slices. Calibration can drift when base rates or conditional feature distributions change. Selective labels—only investigated alerts get outcomes—bias estimates of precision and likelihoods. Random audits or designed follow-up may be necessary.

Decision theory combines posterior uncertainty with actions and losses. The action minimizing expected loss can differ from the most probable class. Human review, abstention and resource constraints create more than two actions. Probability does not choose values or policy; it makes consequences under a model explicit. Report uncertainty and sensitivity rather than a naked percentage.

Production assumptions and failure behavior

Version the event definition, population, horizon, prior/prevalence estimate, evidence transformation, likelihood/calibration model and threshold/cost policy. Prevent training-serving skew in evidence. Monitor base rate, sensitivity/specificity where labels are available, calibration, alert volume, review capacity, outcome delay and slice disparities. Correct evaluation for sampling/audit design.

Handle missing evidence as its own modeled state; do not silently treat it as negative. Validate probabilities are finite and in [0,1], use log odds for extreme repeated updates and cap resource use for evidence lists. Adversaries may manipulate evidence or prevalence, so monitor feature integrity and feedback loops. Protect sensitive health/fraud attributes and posterior logs.

When assumptions fail, safe behavior may be abstention, conservative routing, wider uncertainty or reverting to a simpler rule. Keep an older calibrated model and threshold bundle for rollback. Recalibration alone cannot repair a broken ranking or changed event definition. Document which claims are associative/predictive rather than causal, and require stronger design before interventions are justified.

Math / formal view

A probability measure P on Ω satisfies P(A)≥0, P(Ω)=1 and countable additivity for disjoint events. For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). Thus P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B) and `P(H_i|E)=P(E|H_i)P(H_i)/Σ_jP(E|H_j)P(H_j)` for a hypothesis partition.

Rare-disease screening with natural frequencies

Setup

Prevalence is 1%, sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. What does a positive result mean?

Imagine 10,000 people. About 100 have the condition; 90 test positive. About 9,900 do not; 5% or 495 test positive falsely. Total positives are 585, so `P(condition|positive)=90/585≈15.4%`, not 90%. Bayes formula gives the same numerator `0.9×0.01` and denominator `0.9×0.01+0.05×0.99`. If prevalence in the tested population differs from 1%, predictive value changes. Repeated tests require a model of dependence; multiplying sensitivities as if independent can be badly wrong.

Conclusion

High sensitivity does not imply high positive predictive value when false positives act on a much larger base population.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute diagnostic Bayes probabilities from natural frequencies and verify formula/count agreement, normalization and prevalence sensitivity.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def diagnostic(prevalence,sensitivity,specificity,population=100000):
    if not all(0<=x<=1 for x in (prevalence,sensitivity,specificity)): raise ValueError('probability')
    cases=population*prevalence; noncases=population-cases
    tp=cases*sensitivity; fn=cases-tp; fp=noncases*(1-specificity); tn=noncases-fp
    positive=tp+fp
    return {'tp':tp,'fp':fp,'fn':fn,'tn':tn,'ppv':tp/positive if positive else float('nan')}

def bayes(prior,likelihood,false_positive):
    denominator=likelihood*prior+false_positive*(1-prior)
    return likelihood*prior/denominator
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
counts=diagnostic(.01,.90,.95,10000)
posterior=bayes(.01,.90,.05)
low_base=bayes(.001,.90,.05)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use audited prevalence and outcome sampling, stable calibrated probabilities, explicit cost/capacity thresholds, slice monitoring, sensitive-data controls and a versioned model-threshold rollback bundle.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert counts=={'tp':90.0,'fp':495.0,'fn':10.0,'tn':9405.0,'ppv':90/585}
assert abs(counts['ppv']-posterior)<1e-15
assert sum(counts[k] for k in ('tp','fp','fn','tn'))==10000
assert 0<=posterior<=1 and low_base<posterior
assert bayes(.01,1.0,0.0)==1.0
try: diagnostic(1.1,.9,.9)
except ValueError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('invalid probabilities must fail')

Common mistakes

  • Confuse P(A|B) with P(B|A).

    They have the same intersection numerator but different denominators; Bayes includes the base rate needed to reverse them.

  • Mutually exclusive events are independent.

    For positive-probability exclusive events, observing one makes the other impossible, so they are dependent.

  • A posterior probability proves a causal hypothesis.

    It updates within a specified model and evidence process; causal claims require causal assumptions/design.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does prevalence affect precision?

    False positives come from the noncase population; when that population is much larger, even a small false-positive rate can dominate positives.

  • What is a likelihood ratio?

    The probability of evidence under one hypothesis divided by its probability under another; it multiplies prior odds into posterior odds.

  • When can sequential evidence updates multiply?

    Using conditional likelihoods; simple multiplication requires appropriate conditional independence given each hypothesis.

Production / system-design connection

Version the event/population/horizon, base-rate source, likelihood/calibration, evidence policy and decision costs. Monitor prevalence, calibration, diagnostic rates, volume/capacity and slices with label-delay and selection corrections. Validate finite bounded probabilities, use stable log odds, secure sensitive evidence, support abstention on invalid/drifted inputs and roll back the calibrated model-threshold bundle when assumptions fail.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    State Bayes' rule for events A and B.

    Show solution

    `P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)` when P(B)>0.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    A fraud test has 80% sensitivity, 99% specificity and 0.1% prevalence. Estimate precision.

    Show solution

    `0.8×0.001/(0.8×0.001+0.01×0.999)≈0.074`, about 7.4%.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Precision falls after expansion to a lower-risk market although sensitivity/specificity are stable. Why?

    Show solution

    The fraud/condition base rate decreased, so false positives comprise a larger share of alerts.

6.2

Common Probability Distributions

highverified
Roles: ds, mle, as

Topic overview

A probability distribution describes how mass or density is assigned to a random variable under a model. Choosing a distribution means choosing support, parameter interpretation, tail behavior, dependence assumptions and a data-generating story—not matching a familiar bell-shaped plot. This chapter distinguishes probability mass functions, density functions, cumulative distribution functions and quantiles, then develops Bernoulli, Binomial, Categorical, Poisson, Geometric, Uniform, Normal, Exponential, Gamma, Beta and related approximations. You will learn when probabilities come from mass versus density, how location/scale/rate parameterizations differ across libraries, why the Normal can be a poor model for counts or heavy tails, and how memorylessness and support constraints encode assumptions. A worked support-ticket example contrasts Binomial and Poisson models and checks the rare-event approximation. The lab implements a Binomial PMF and verifies moments and sampling against NumPy/SciPy. Production guidance covers truncation, censoring, mixtures, zero inflation, parameter estimation, posterior predictive/model checks, numerical log probabilities, version drift and safe simulation. The objective is to choose and validate a distribution from the mechanism and decision consequences rather than from convenience.

Prerequisites

  • probability-basics

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish PMF, PDF, CDF, survival function and quantile and use each correctly for discrete and continuous variables.
  • Select common distributions from support and generative assumptions and translate parameterizations across formulas and libraries.
  • Validate probabilistic models with moments, tail/quantile checks, simulation, calibration and production drift/failure monitoring.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A discrete distribution assigns probability mass `p(x)=P(X=x)` that sums to one. A continuous distribution has density f whose integral over a region is probability; `P(X=x)=0` at any exact point for a continuous variable even when density is positive. The CDF `F(x)=P(X≤x)` works for both. Choose a family from support and mechanism: Bernoulli for one binary trial, Binomial for a fixed number of conditionally independent equal-probability trials, Poisson for event counts under a rate model, Exponential for memoryless waiting time, Normal for additive symmetric variation, and Beta for a probability parameter. Verify parameter conventions, tails and data assumptions rather than relying on shape alone.

What you must know

  • Support comes before family
  • Density is not point probability
  • Parameters encode a generative story
  • Tail behavior drives risk
  • Library conventions must be verified

Why this matters

Likelihoods, simulations, anomaly thresholds, forecasts and uncertainty intervals all depend on a distribution. An inappropriate family can assign impossible negative counts, understate tail risk, or produce confident alerts because overdispersion and zero inflation were ignored. Rate versus scale mistakes can change results by orders of magnitude. Distribution knowledge is therefore both modeling and software-interface knowledge.

Intuition

A distribution is a rule for spreading one unit of probability over possible values. Discrete rules place coins on outcomes; continuous rules spread paint whose area, not height at a point, is probability. Parameters move, stretch or reshape the pattern. A good family describes how variation could arise and which extremes remain plausible.

Mass, density, CDF, and quantiles

For discrete X, a PMF p(x) is nonnegative and sums to one. For continuous X, a PDF f(x) is nonnegative and integrates to one; probability over [a,b] is the integral. Density can exceed one when concentrated on a narrow interval because it is probability per unit, not probability. Point probability is zero for a purely continuous variable. Mixed distributions can contain both atoms and density.

The CDF `F(x)=P(X≤x)` is nondecreasing, right-continuous and approaches zero/one at extremes. It handles all distribution types. The survival function `1−F(x)` is often computed directly for numerical accuracy in upper tails. The quantile function is a generalized inverse and maps a probability level to a threshold; conventions at jumps and sample quantiles vary.

Expectation and variance summarize but do not determine most distributions. Equal mean/variance can hide skew, multimodality or different tails. Visual checks should compare CDF/quantiles and tail exceedances, not only histograms. Empirical data are affected by censoring, truncation, measurement rounding and selection, which must be incorporated in the observation model.

Discrete distribution families

Bernoulli(p) models one indicator with P(X=1)=p. Binomial(n,p) counts successes in n trials when trial count is fixed, success probability is common and trials are conditionally independent. Its mean is np and variance np(1−p). Heterogeneous probabilities yield a Poisson-binomial distribution, while dependence can inflate or reduce variance. Categorical generalizes one trial to K outcomes; Multinomial counts categories over fixed n.

Poisson(λ) models a nonnegative event count with mean and variance λ under a homogeneous independent-increment process interpretation. It is a useful approximation to Binomial for large n, small p with np fixed. Real counts often show overdispersion, clustering, seasonality, exposure differences or excess zeros; Negative Binomial, hierarchical, zero-inflated or point-process models may be more appropriate. Include exposure/observation time in the rate.

Geometric models trials until first success and is memoryless in the discrete setting, but conventions count failures before success or trials including success. State support. Hypergeometric models successes sampled without replacement from a finite population, unlike Binomial's independent/effectively-with-replacement trials. These distinctions follow the data-generating mechanism.

Continuous distribution families

Uniform(a,b) assigns constant density on a bounded interval. Normal(μ,σ²) models symmetric unbounded variation and arises in additive approximations, but negative values and light tails can be implausible for positive skewed quantities. Standard deviation σ is not variance. Multivariate Normal adds covariance and elliptical contours; zero covariance implies independence only under special families such as a jointly Gaussian model.

Exponential(rate λ) models nonnegative waiting time with constant hazard and memorylessness, mean 1/λ. Libraries may use `scale=1/λ`; confusing rate and scale is common. Gamma generalizes positive waiting/amount variability with shape and rate/scale conventions. Weibull permits increasing/decreasing hazard. Lognormal arises when a logarithm is Normal and produces positive right-skewed values with heavier tail than Normal.

Beta(α,β) lives on [0,1] and flexibly models probabilities/proportions; it is conjugate to Bernoulli/Binomial likelihoods under a standard Bayesian model. Dirichlet generalizes to probability vectors. Student t resembles Normal centrally but has heavier tails controlled by degrees of freedom and supports robust likelihoods. A family name alone is insufficient: state support, parameterization and whether parameters describe population, latent heterogeneity or observation noise.

Fitting, checking, and operating distributions

Estimate parameters by maximum likelihood, method of moments, Bayesian posterior or robust procedures according to the goal. Account for truncation/censoring and selection in the likelihood. Comparing fitted curves on training data is insufficient; use held-out log score, probability integral transform/rank checks, quantile coverage, tail exceedance, posterior predictive simulation and domain consequences. Mixtures can capture subpopulations but introduce identifiability and local-optimum issues.

Use log PMF/PDF for small probabilities and stable tail functions (`sf`, `logsf`) rather than subtracting a CDF near one. Verify library parameter order and `loc`/`scale` semantics with a known moment or quantile. Random samples require a controlled Generator for reproducibility; statistical PRNGs are not cryptographic. Parallel streams must be spawned correctly rather than seeded identically.

Version family, support transformations, parameter convention, fitted parameters, training cutoff and library. Monitor outcome support violations, mean/variance/quantiles/tails, zero rate, calibration and log-score drift across slices. Define fallback when fit is invalid or tail thresholds become unstable. Protect sensitive simulated/fitted data, bound sampling sizes and keep a prior validated model for rollback.

Math / formal view

Discrete PMF p(x)≥0 with Σ_xp(x)=1. Continuous PDF f(x)≥0 with ∫f=1 and `P(a≤X≤b)=∫_a^b f(x)dx`. CDF F(x)=P(X≤x). Examples: Binomial PMF `C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^{n−k}`; Poisson `e^{−λ}λ^k/k!`; Normal density `(σ√(2π))^{-1}exp(−(x−μ)^2/(2σ²))`.

Model daily support-ticket counts

Setup

One thousand customers independently open a ticket with probability 0.002 per day.

The exact count is Binomial(n=1000,p=0.002), with mean 2 and variance 1.996. A Poisson(λ=np=2) approximation is close because n is large and p small. `P(0)` is `(0.998)^1000≈0.1351` exactly and `e^{-2}≈0.1353` under Poisson. If customers influence each other during outages or risk differs greatly, independence/equal-p fail and observed variance likely exceeds two. Add exposure and outage covariates or use a hierarchical/Negative Binomial model. Verify tail probabilities against operational staffing costs, not only the mean.

Conclusion

The approximation follows a rare independent-event mechanism; overdispersion is evidence that the mechanism needs revision.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement the Binomial PMF, verify normalization and moments, and compare generated samples with NumPy and SciPy references.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def binomial_pmf(k,n,p):
    if not (isinstance(k,int) and isinstance(n,int) and 0<=k<=n and 0<=p<=1): return 0.0
    return math.comb(n,k)*(p**k)*((1-p)**(n-k))

def moments(values,probs):
    mean=sum(x*p for x,p in zip(values,probs))
    variance=sum((x-mean)**2*p for x,p in zip(values,probs))
    return mean,variance
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import binom
n=20; p=.1; values=list(range(n+1)); probs=[binomial_pmf(k,n,p) for k in values]
mean,variance=moments(values,probs)
rng=np.random.default_rng(20260821); samples=rng.binomial(n,p,size=100000)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use verified SciPy distribution/log-tail APIs and independent NumPy Generator streams, version parameter conventions and seeds, monitor tail/dispersion/support drift and keep a validated fallback model.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert math.isclose(sum(probs),1.0,rel_tol=1e-12)
assert math.isclose(mean,n*p,rel_tol=1e-12)
assert math.isclose(variance,n*p*(1-p),rel_tol=1e-12)
assert np.allclose(probs,binom.pmf(values,n,p))
assert abs(samples.mean()-n*p)<.02
assert abs(samples.var()-n*p*(1-p))<.04
assert all(0<=x<=n for x in samples)

Common mistakes

  • Treat a PDF value as P(X=x).

    For a continuous distribution, point probability is zero; integrate density over an interval.

  • Use a Normal model for any symmetric-looking sample.

    Check support, tails, censoring, mixtures and mechanism; a small histogram is weak evidence.

  • Pass a rate as a library's scale parameter.

    Confirm documentation; Exponential/Gamma scale is commonly reciprocal of rate.

Likely follow-ups

  • When is Poisson a Binomial approximation?

    For large n, small p and λ=np held moderate, under approximately independent equal-probability trials.

  • What does memoryless mean?

    The remaining waiting distribution is unchanged by time already waited; Exponential and Geometric have this property.

  • Why use a survival function directly?

    Computing `1−CDF` near one can lose precision; a direct tail implementation is numerically stable.

Production / system-design connection

Version support, family, observation process, parameter convention, fit data and library. Test moments/quantiles/log probabilities against known cases, use stable log/tail APIs, controlled noncryptographic RNG streams and bounded sampling. Monitor support, quantile/tail/zero/dispersion and score drift by slice, define fallback for invalid fits and retain a prior validated distribution model for rollback.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What is the difference between PMF and PDF?

    Show solution

    A PMF assigns point probabilities that sum; a PDF assigns density whose integral over a region is probability.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    Which distribution models successes in draws without replacement?

    Show solution

    Hypergeometric, given a finite population with a fixed number of successes.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Poisson fitted counts have variance far above their mean. What might be missing?

    Show solution

    Heterogeneous rates, clustering/dependence, seasonality, exposure differences or zero inflation; consider covariates/hierarchical or Negative Binomial structure.

  • scipy-stats

    Documents current distribution PMF/PDF/CDF/SF/log and fitting/sampling interfaces.

    Provides current Generator-based distribution sampling, state, seed and parallel-stream guidance.

6.3

Expectation, Variance & Covariance

very highverified
Roles: ds, mle, as

Topic overview

Expectation is a probability-weighted average of a random variable; variance measures expected squared deviation from its mean; covariance measures linear co-movement. These are properties of a specified distribution, not guarantees about one observation. This chapter develops linearity of expectation, indicator variables, transformations, variance identities, covariance matrices, correlation, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds, conditional moments and laws of total expectation/variance. You will learn why expectations add without independence while variances require covariance terms, why zero covariance does not generally imply independence, and how scaling and nonlinear transformations change moments. A worked portfolio/system-load example derives aggregate variance under dependence. The lab computes exact weighted moments, merges online summaries and compares them with NumPy. Production guidance covers population versus sample denominators, weighted data, missingness, streaming algorithms, numeric cancellation, nonstationarity, tail risk, covariance regularization, privacy and rollback. The objective is to use moments as compact but limited summaries, understand precisely which algebra they support, and avoid turning correlation or an average into a causal or distributional claim.

Prerequisites

  • probability-basics

Learning objectives

  • Compute expectations of functions and exploit linearity and indicator variables without requiring independence.
  • Derive variance/covariance rules for sums and affine transformations and interpret covariance matrices geometrically.
  • Estimate and operate moments with correct denominators, weights, stable streaming algorithms, drift/tail checks and explicit limits.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Expectation is `E[X]=Σx p(x)` or `∫x f(x)dx` when it exists, and linearity gives `E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c` without independence. Variance is `Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]=E[X²]−μ²`. For sums, `Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)`; covariance vanishes for independent finite-variance variables, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence. Correlation standardizes covariance to [−1,1] when variances are positive and measures linear association, not causation. In data, distinguish population from sample estimators, use stable online/two-pass algorithms and inspect tails and drift beyond mean/variance.

What you must know

  • Linearity of expectation needs no independence
  • Variance of sums includes covariance
  • Correlation is standardized linear association
  • Moments may not exist or characterize a distribution
  • Stable estimation needs denominator and weight semantics

Why this matters

Expected cost, model loss, traffic, portfolio risk, ensemble error and sample-size calculations all use moments. Common mistakes—adding standard deviations, omitting covariance, using ddof inconsistently, calculating variance by subtracting huge nearly equal values, or reading correlation causally—can materially distort decisions. Moment algebra is powerful precisely because it states what can and cannot be simplified.

Intuition

Expectation is the balance point of a probability distribution. Variance is its average squared spread around that point. Covariance asks whether two variables tend to deviate from their means in the same direction. When combining uncertain quantities, aligned deviations reinforce risk; opposing deviations cancel; independent deviations add only in variance, not standard deviation.

Expectation, transformations, and indicators

For discrete X, `E[g(X)]=Σ_x g(x)p(x)`; for continuous X, integrate `g(x)f(x)`. You do not need the distribution of g(X) to compute its expectation this way. Expectation may be infinite or undefined for heavy-tailed variables, so algebra requiring finite moments needs assumptions. `E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b`, and linearity extends to sums regardless of dependence.

Indicator I_A equals one when event A occurs, zero otherwise, so `E[I_A]=P(A)`. Counts can be written as sums of indicators, making expected counts the sum of individual probabilities even when events depend. For example, expected number of collisions or occupied bins may be easy while the full count distribution is hard. Independence becomes relevant for products: if X,Y independent and integrable, E[XY]=E[X]E[Y], but the converse is not generally true.

Expectation of a nonlinear function is not generally the function of the expectation. Jensen's inequality says `g(E[X])≤E[g(X)]` for convex g, explaining why variability raises expected convex cost. Ratios, logs and thresholds need full distribution information or approximations; substituting means can bias decisions.

Variance, covariance, and correlation

Variance `E[(X−μ)²]` is nonnegative and has squared units. The identity `E[X²]−E[X]²` is algebraically useful but can be numerically unstable in finite precision. Scaling gives `Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X)`. Standard deviation returns original units but does not add for sums.

Covariance `E[(X−μ_X)(Y−μ_Y)] = E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]`. Thus `Var(Σ_iX_i)=Σ_iVar(X_i)+2Σ_{i<j}Cov(X_i,X_j)`. Independence implies zero covariance for finite moments, but dependent symmetric/nonlinear relationships can have zero covariance. Correlation divides by standard deviations and lies in [−1,1] by Cauchy–Schwarz; it is undefined for constant variables and invariant to positive affine scaling.

A covariance matrix Σ has entries Cov(X_i,X_j), is symmetric positive semidefinite, and gives variance of any linear combination a^TX as `a^TΣa`. Near-singular covariance reflects redundant directions or insufficient data and destabilizes inverses. Sample covariance in high dimensions often needs shrinkage or structured assumptions. Correlation matrices remove units but do not solve confounding or nonlinear dependence.

Conditional moments and decomposition

Conditional expectation `E[X|Y]` is itself a random variable/function of Y and is the best mean-squared predictor among functions of Y under suitable conditions. The tower property says `E[E[X|Y]]=E[X]`. The law of total variance splits `Var(X)=E[Var(X|Y)]+Var(E[X|Y])`: average within-group uncertainty plus variation of group means.

This decomposition explains hierarchical data and mixture variance. Overall variance can be large even if every group is tight because means differ; conversely groups can be noisy around a common mean. Aggregating correlations can produce Simpson-like reversals because group composition changes. Report within/between components and the conditioning variables.

For vector X, the law generalizes to covariance: total covariance equals expected conditional covariance plus covariance of conditional means. Uncertainty propagation through linear maps A is `Cov(AX+b)=AΣA^T`. For nonlinear maps, a Jacobian approximation can be used locally, but tail/nonlinearity may require simulation. Conditional moments are descriptive unless the conditioning/intervention distinction is justified causally.

Estimating and operating moments

Population variance divides by population mass. The common unbiased sample variance for IID observations divides the sum of squared deviations by n−1 after estimating the mean; maximum-likelihood Normal variance uses n. Weighted data require clarity: frequency weights, probability weights and inverse-probability weights have different effective sample-size and denominator formulas. Library `ddof` defaults differ.

Use two-pass centered variance or Welford's recurrence rather than one-pass `mean(x²)−mean(x)²` for large offsets. Parallel/streaming summaries can merge count, mean and centered sum of squares exactly up to rounding. Missing-value deletion changes the target population when missingness is informative. Time dependence makes an IID standard error invalid; moments may drift and autocorrelation reduces effective information.

Monitor count/weight, mean, variance, quantiles/tails, covariance conditioning and slice/time changes. Robust summaries complement moments when outliers/heavy tails dominate. Cap or quarantine invalid values according to domain policy, not silently. Covariance and means can reveal sensitive attributes; restrict release and use privacy techniques when appropriate. Version window, filters, weights, units and algorithm; keep previous aggregates/checkpoints for rollback and recompute from source when invariants fail.

Math / formal view

E[g(X)]=Σg(x)p(x) or ∫g(x)f(x)dx. `Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]`; `Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−μ_X)(Y−μ_Y)]`. `Var(a^TX)=a^TΣa`. Total expectation: `E[X]=E[E[X|Y]]`. Total variance: `Var(X)=E[Var(X|Y)]+Var(E[X|Y])`.

Variance of combined service load

Setup

Services A and B each have mean load 100, standard deviation 10 and correlation 0.8. What is total-load uncertainty?

Each variance is 100 and covariance is `0.8×10×10=80`. Expected total is 200 by linearity regardless of dependence. Total variance is `100+100+2×80=360`, so standard deviation is about 18.97—not 20 (adding standard deviations) and not 14.14 (assuming independence). If correlation were −0.8, variance would be 40. Correlation may change during incidents, so a historical estimate can understate joint tail load. Capacity planning should inspect conditional/tail scenarios, not only Normal mean ± standard deviation.

Conclusion

Dependence controls diversification or reinforcement; covariance terms are not optional.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute exact weighted moments and stable mergeable sample summaries, then verify covariance and total-variance identities against NumPy.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def weighted_moments(values,probs):
    if abs(sum(probs)-1)>1e-12: raise ValueError('weights must sum to one')
    mean=sum(x*p for x,p in zip(values,probs))
    variance=sum((x-mean)**2*p for x,p in zip(values,probs))
    return mean,variance

def summary(values):
    n=0; mean=0.0; m2=0.0
    for x in values:
        n+=1; delta=x-mean; mean+=delta/n; m2+=delta*(x-mean)
    return n,mean,m2

def merge(a,b):
    n1,m1,s1=a; n2,m2,s2=b
    if n1==0:return b
    if n2==0:return a
    d=m2-m1; n=n1+n2
    return n,m1+d*n2/n,s1+s2+d*d*n1*n2/n
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
values=[1.,2.,4.]; probs=[.2,.3,.5]; exact=weighted_moments(values,probs)
data=np.array([1e9+1,1e9+2,1e9+4,1e9+8],dtype=float)
combined=merge(summary(data[:2]),summary(data[2:]))
x=np.array([1.,2.,3.]); y=np.array([2.,4.,8.])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Use stable mergeable summaries with explicit weights/ddof/window, compare streaming against batch fixtures, monitor tails and covariance conditioning, secure aggregates and retain replayable source plus checkpoints for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert np.allclose(exact,[2.8,1.56])
assert combined[0]==len(data) and np.isclose(combined[1],data.mean())
assert np.isclose(combined[2]/combined[0],data.var())
cov=np.cov(x,y,ddof=0)[0,1]
assert np.isclose(np.var(x+y),np.var(x)+np.var(y)+2*cov)
groups={0:[0.,2.],1:[8.,10.]}; all_values=np.array(groups[0]+groups[1])
within=np.mean([np.var(v) for v in groups.values()]); between=np.var([np.mean(v) for v in groups.values()])
assert np.isclose(all_values.var(),within+between)

Common mistakes

  • Linearity of expectation requires independence.

    Expectations of sums always add when defined; independence is used for products and variance simplifications.

  • Zero correlation means independence.

    It only rules out linear covariance; nonlinear dependence can remain unless special joint-family assumptions hold.

  • Use `E[X²]−E[X]²` directly on huge-offset data.

    Subtraction can catastrophically cancel; use centered two-pass or Welford algorithms.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is covariance matrix positive semidefinite?

    For any a, `a^TΣa=Var(a^TX)≥0`.

  • What does total variance separate?

    Average variance within conditioning groups and variance between their conditional means.

  • When does E[g(X)]=g(E[X])?

    Generally for affine g; nonlinear equality requires special circumstances. Jensen gives an inequality for convex/concave g.

Production / system-design connection

Define population/window, units, filters, weights and ddof; use stable mergeable moment algorithms and validate against batch references. Monitor count/effective weight, means, variances, quantiles/tails, covariance conditioning and slice/time dependence. Treat missing/outlier policy explicitly, restrict sensitive aggregates, retain source lineage and checkpointed summaries, and roll back/recompute when invariants or drift thresholds fail.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    Write variance of X+Y.

    Show solution

    `Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)`.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    If X_i are dependent indicators, what is E[ΣX_i]?

    Show solution

    `ΣP(X_i=1)`; dependence is irrelevant for the expectation.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    Variance becomes slightly negative in code. What likely happened?

    Show solution

    Catastrophic cancellation in `mean(x²)−mean(x)²` and rounding; use a stable centered algorithm and clamp only tiny roundoff after diagnosis.

6.4

Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem

highverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

The law of large numbers (LLN) explains convergence of sample averages to an expectation; the central limit theorem (CLT) explains why a properly centered and scaled sum often has an approximately Normal distribution. They answer different questions and require assumptions that real data can violate. This chapter develops weak/strong LLN intuition, standard error, IID CLT, finite variance, rate/quality of approximation, continuity correction and the delta method. It then examines dependence, clustering, heavy tails, rare events, bounded and non-identical variables, bootstrap connections and why “n>30” is not a theorem. You will learn to separate population size from effective sample size, distinguish the distribution of data from the sampling distribution of a statistic, and choose cluster/time-aware uncertainty. A worked conversion-rate example calculates standard error and diagnoses user-level dependence. The lab simulates Bernoulli/exponential sample means across n and verifies `1/√n` scaling and approximate coverage. Production guidance covers sampling frames, sequential looks, drift, label delay, random streams, monitoring, privacy and rollback. The objective is to use asymptotics as checked approximations, not automatic permission to attach a Normal interval to any large table.

Prerequisites

  • expectation-variance
  • distributions
  • independence

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish LLN convergence from CLT distributional approximation and state the assumptions/normalization for each.
  • Compute standard errors for means/proportions and diagnose dependence, heavy tails, skew, rare events and effective sample size.
  • Validate and operate asymptotic uncertainty using simulation/resampling, design-aware estimators, monitoring and safe reporting.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The LLN says a sample average converges to the population expectation under conditions; it explains consistency. The IID finite-variance CLT says `√n(Ȳ−μ)/σ` converges in distribution to standard Normal; it explains approximate sampling uncertainty and `SE(Ȳ)=σ/√n`. It does not say the raw data become Normal. Approximation quality depends on skew, tails, rarity and dependence, not a universal n threshold. Clustered/time-correlated data have smaller effective sample size and need cluster-robust, block or model-based methods. Verify with design-aware simulation/bootstrap and use the estimated standard error appropriate to the sampling process.

What you must know

  • LLN is convergence of averages
  • CLT is scaled sampling distribution
  • Standard error shrinks as 1/√n under IID
  • Data need not be Normal
  • Dependence changes effective sample size

Why this matters

Confidence intervals, experiment readouts, monitoring thresholds and Monte Carlo error often rely on asymptotics. Treating millions of events as independent when they come from thousands of users creates tiny false standard errors. Heavy tails can make variance unstable, and rare-event proportions can have poor Normal intervals. Understanding what converges and under which sampling design prevents false precision.

Intuition

The LLN says repeated independent-ish measurements average away noise and settle near the balance point. The CLT zooms into the shrinking error around that point by multiplying it by √n; the shape of that scaled error often approaches a bell curve. Without the zoom, the average collapses to a point, so the two laws describe consistency and uncertainty at different scales.

Law of large numbers and consistency

For IID variables with finite expectation μ, the weak LLN says the sample mean converges in probability to μ: for any ε>0, probability of an error larger than ε goes to zero. Strong LLN gives almost-sure convergence under conditions. Neither supplies a finite-sample confidence level by itself. Convergence can be slow for heavy-tailed/skewed data, and an average of biased or selected samples converges to the wrong population expectation.

Variance of an IID sample mean is σ²/n when finite, which supports Chebyshev bounds and explains noise reduction. Dependence adds covariance terms; positive correlation can keep variance much larger. Identical distribution is not always required—there are LLNs for non-identical and dependent sequences—but assumptions must match the design. Nonstationary data may converge to a moving or mixture target with little decision value.

Consistency of an estimator means convergence to the target as information grows. More rows created by duplicating events do not add information. Population target, sampling frame, weighting and observation process must be defined before invoking the LLN.

CLT, standardization, and intervals

For IID finite-variance X_i, the classical CLT states `(ΣX_i−nμ)/(σ√n)=√n(Ȳ−μ)/σ` converges in distribution to N(0,1). Thus the sampling distribution of Ȳ is approximately Normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n for sufficiently suitable n. Replacing σ by a consistent estimate yields common large-sample intervals; small Normal-population samples lead to t distributions when variance is estimated.

The approximation concerns repeated samples of the statistic, not the empirical distribution of observations. A skewed Exponential population can have approximately Normal sample means. Berry–Esseen-type results show error depends on third absolute moment and √n under conditions, explaining why tail/skew matter. A continuity correction can improve Normal approximation to lattice/discrete counts.

For Bernoulli p, mean is p and variance p(1−p), but Wald intervals can fail near 0/1 or with few expected successes/failures. Wilson, exact or Bayesian methods may be better. The delta method linearizes smooth transformations g(Ȳ), giving approximate variance `(g'(μ))²σ²/n`; it fails near nonsmooth points or singular derivatives.

Dependence, clustering, and heavy tails

Repeated events within a user, classroom, hospital or time block are correlated. If clusters are independent but observations within cluster are not, treat clusters as sampling units and use cluster-robust estimators or aggregate/cluster bootstrap. Time series require long-run variance including autocovariances and may use HAC, block bootstrap or explicit models. Effective sample size can be far below row count.

Heavy-tailed distributions may have finite mean but enormous/infinite variance, slowing LLN and invalidating the classical finite-variance CLT. Stable-law limits can replace Normal scaling. Outliers are then expected under the model, not necessarily data errors. Robust estimators such as trimmed means or median-of-means target related quantities/offer different guarantees and should be chosen explicitly.

Sampling without replacement from a finite population introduces dependence and finite-population corrections. Survey weights, unequal probabilities and stratification change variance. Adaptive experiments and sequential monitoring create dependence between stopping and estimates; always-valid methods or pre-specified sequential designs are needed rather than repeated fixed-horizon intervals.

Validate and operate asymptotic approximations

Simulate from a plausible data-generating/design model and examine standardized statistic histograms, quantiles and interval coverage at actual n. Bootstrap resamples according to independent units, not rows by default. Compare analytic standard errors with cluster/block/bootstrap estimates and inspect sensitivity to influential units. Coverage on synthetic IID data validates implementation, not real-world assumptions.

Version target population, unit, estimator, window, weights, clustering/time rule, standard-error method and stopping policy. Monitor cluster counts/sizes, autocorrelation, tail metrics, effective sample size, label delay and composition drift. Report numerator/denominator and uncertainty together. Avoid displaying false precision or treating overlapping intervals as a complete hypothesis test.

Use reproducible independent random streams for simulation, bound resample cost and protect row/unit data. If diagnostics show poor approximation, use design-based exact/randomization methods, robust/bootstrap alternatives, larger independent sample or abstain. Keep prior metric/uncertainty implementation for rollback and backtest new methods on archived windows without peeking into active decisions.

Math / formal view

LLN: `Ȳ_n→μ` in probability (or almost surely under stronger form/conditions). IID CLT with finite variance σ²>0: `√n(Ȳ_n−μ)/σ ⇒ N(0,1)`. Hence `SE(Ȳ)=σ/√n` under IID. For dependent observations, `Var(Ȳ)=n^{-2}[ΣVar(X_i)+2Σ_{i<j}Cov(X_i,X_j)]`, not generally σ²/n.

Conversion rate with repeated users

Setup

A table has 100,000 sessions and 5% conversion, but only 10,000 users with correlated sessions.

Treating sessions IID gives approximate SE `sqrt(.05×.95/100000)=0.000689`, a very tight interval. If outcomes cluster by user, session count overstates independent information. Aggregate to user-level outcomes for the target or compute a user-cluster robust/bootstrap SE; the effective sample size might be closer to 10,000 and SE roughly three times larger, depending on cluster structure. The LLN/CLT can still apply over independent users, not sessions. If product mix or conversion propensity drifts during the window, even user independence/stationarity needs review.

Conclusion

The unit of independence, not row count, determines information and valid standard error.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate non-Normal sample means, verify `1/sqrt(n)` standard-error scaling and approximate CLT interval coverage with reproducible streams.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def mean(values): return sum(values)/len(values)

def interval(sample,z=1.96):
    m=mean(sample); variance=sum((x-m)**2 for x in sample)/(len(sample)-1); se=math.sqrt(variance/len(sample))
    return m-z*se,m+z*se
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(20260821); reps=20000
means_25=rng.exponential(1.0,size=(reps,25)).mean(axis=1)
means_100=rng.exponential(1.0,size=(reps,100)).mean(axis=1)
# independent coverage experiment
samples=rng.exponential(1.0,size=(5000,100))
covered=np.mean([lo<=1.0<=hi for lo,hi in (interval(row) for row in samples)])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Simulate the actual clustered/time sampling design, use design-aware SE/bootstrap, version units/windows/stopping, monitor effective size/dependence/tails and retain a prior uncertainty pipeline for rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(means_25.mean()-1)<.01 and abs(means_100.mean()-1)<.01
ratio=means_25.std(ddof=1)/means_100.std(ddof=1)
assert abs(ratio-2)<.08
standardized=np.sqrt(100)*(means_100-1.0)
assert abs(standardized.mean())<.03 and abs(standardized.std(ddof=1)-1)<.03
assert .935<covered<.96
# Raw exponential data stay skewed even when means are closer to Normal.
raw=rng.exponential(1.0,size=100000)
assert np.quantile(raw,.9)>2.2

Common mistakes

  • The CLT says observed data become Normal.

    It concerns the centered/scaled sampling distribution of sums/means under assumptions.

  • n≥30 guarantees a good Normal approximation.

    Required n depends on skew, tails, rarity, dependence and statistic; validate coverage/quantiles.

  • Every database row is an independent sample.

    Rows often cluster by entity/time/source; variance must reflect the independent sampling unit.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do LLN and CLT differ?

    LLN gives convergence of averages to the mean; CLT characterizes the √n-scaled error distribution.

  • What is standard error?

    The standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution under the specified design/model.

  • Why does dependence matter?

    Covariance terms change variance of the sum/mean, often reducing effective sample size far below row count.

Production / system-design connection

Define target, independent unit, sampling/weighting, window and stopping rule. Use cluster/time/design-aware standard errors, validate with unit-aware simulation/bootstrap and monitor tail, autocorrelation, cluster/effective-size and drift signals. Report uncertainty without false precision, bound secure random resampling and roll back or abstain when assumptions/coverage fail.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · recall

    What quantity converges to Normal in the IID CLT?

    Show solution

    The centered and scaled mean `√n(Ȳ−μ)/σ` (or equivalent standardized sum), not raw observations.

  2. Exercise 2 · application

    If IID sample size quadruples, how does mean SE change?

    Show solution

    It halves, because SE scales as 1/√n.

  3. Exercise 3 · diagnosis

    A million events yield unstable daily estimates because they come from 500 devices. What failed?

    Show solution

    Independence is at device/cluster level, so row-based SE is drastically understated; use cluster-aware analysis.
