7.2

Hypothesis Testing & p-values

very highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Hypothesis testing is a calibrated procedure for measuring how incompatible observed data are with a specified null model, not a machine for assigning truth probabilities to hypotheses. This chapter connects the scientific question, estimand, null and alternative, test statistic, reference distribution, p-value, decision rule, Type I error, Type II error, power, effect size, and confidence interval. It contrasts Fisher-style evidence with Neyman–Pearson decision rules without pretending that one p-value settles a scientific or product decision. You will learn how sidedness, optional stopping, model assumptions, randomization, and multiple testing alter validity; why “fail to reject” is not “accept”; and why a tiny p-value may accompany a negligible effect in a huge dataset. The worked example separates statistical evidence from launch utility. The lab implements a one-sample randomization test and verifies its tail count against SciPy. Production guidance covers preregistration, metric governance, sequential monitoring, audit trails, privacy, and reporting estimates with uncertainty rather than threshold badges.

Prerequisites

  • sampling-distributions
  • confidence-intervals

Learning objectives

  • Translate a domain question into an estimand, explicit null/alternative, statistic, and valid reference distribution.
  • Interpret p-values, Type I/II errors, and power without common probability reversals.
  • Choose sidedness and stopping rules before observing results and diagnose assumption violations.
  • Report effect estimates, intervals, practical thresholds, and multiplicity context alongside test results.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A p-value is the probability, assuming the null model and test assumptions, of obtaining a statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability the null is true, not the false-positive probability of this result, and not effect size. A complete test specifies the estimand, null and alternative, statistic, reference distribution, sidedness, alpha, and stopping rule before looking. Then report the estimate and interval, check assumptions and multiplicity, and interpret the result against practical costs.

What you must know

  • The null is a complete enough data-generating claim to calibrate a statistic
  • p-values are conditional tail areas, not posterior probabilities
  • Alpha controls a procedure's Type I error under valid use
  • Power depends on a specific alternative
  • Evidence, effect magnitude, and action utility are distinct

Why this matters

Tests influence experiments, model comparisons, quality monitoring, medical evidence, and policy. Misinterpretation can ship useless features, suppress real harm, or manufacture discoveries by trying many analyses. A p-value can be numerically correct while answering the wrong question because the unit, outcome, subgroup, or null was chosen after inspection. Conversely, rigidly banning tests discards a useful calibration tool. Interviews focus on p-values because they expose conditional-probability reasoning and experimental discipline. The practical skill is to design a procedure whose error behavior matches the decision, then communicate what the result does and does not establish. The ASA explicitly warns against basing conclusions only on a threshold and against treating significance as effect importance. That principle belongs in analytics systems, not only academic papers.

Intuition

Assume a card shuffler is fair and choose a score that grows when the observed sequence looks suspicious. Run the fair shuffler many times and see how often its score is at least as extreme. That frequency is a simulation picture of the p-value. A rare score says the data and the fair-shuffler model are in tension; it does not identify which assumption failed or calculate the probability of cheating. Alpha is a rule chosen before play that limits false alarms when the model holds. Power asks how often the rule detects a particular kind and size of cheating. If you inspect many scores and report only the strangest, the original calibration no longer applies. The same logic governs product tests: define the metric and analysis before observing treatment labels, respect assignment, and separate evidence from business value.

From question to calibrated statistic

Start with the target population and estimand, such as the intention-to-treat difference in 14-day retention. State H0 and a scientifically meaningful alternative. Choose a statistic sensitive to that alternative. Derive or simulate its distribution under H0 while preserving the design. Define one- or two-sided extremeness and alpha before inspecting results. A two-sided test spends error in both directions; a one-sided test is justified only when the opposite direction would not trigger a claim and was excluded in advance. Nuisance parameters may be estimated, conditioned out, or handled through asymptotics. Every choice affects calibration.

p-values, alpha, and the two error types

The p-value P_H0(T at least as extreme as t_obs) conditions on H0. It does not provide P(H0|data), which would require prior odds and likelihoods. Alpha is the maximum or nominal probability of rejection under H0 for a fixed procedure. A Type I error rejects a true null. A Type II error fails to reject under a specified alternative; beta and power 1-beta depend on effect size, variance, design, and sample size. A p-value above alpha does not prove H0, because the study may be underpowered or the statistic insensitive. The observed p-value is not the achieved Type I error rate or the probability the decision is wrong.

Assumptions, optional stopping, and researcher degrees of freedom

A t test relies on independence and a reference model or approximation; a randomization test relies on assignment and a sharp or otherwise specified null; a permutation test relies on exchangeability for the chosen shuffle. Repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon p-value and stopping below 0.05 inflates false positives. Trying transformations, exclusions, subgroups, outcomes, and covariates until one passes does the same. Pre-specification, held-out confirmation, sequential tests, alpha-spending, or always-valid evidence processes restore calibration for their settings. Log every analysis attempt, not only the successful query. Model diagnostics matter because a small p-value may reflect outliers, dependence, or misspecification rather than the intended alternative.

Evidence is not effect size or utility

With enough independent observations, a negligible deviation can yield a tiny p-value; with few observations, a valuable effect can remain uncertain. Report the estimate and interval against minimum worthwhile benefit and maximum acceptable harm. Decision theory adds costs, opportunity, reversibility, and prior information. Equivalence and noninferiority tests answer targeted absence-of-material-difference questions; ordinary failure to reject does not. Multiple outcomes require a defined family and error criterion. Replication and external validity matter after internal calibration. A test is one input to a decision record, not an automatic launch switch.

Exact, conservative, and asymptotic validity

A level claim can be exact for every finite sample under a design, conservative because discreteness prevents using all alpha, or asymptotic as sample size grows. The label p-value does not reveal which. Small cell counts, boundary parameters, weak identification, or estimated nuisance quantities can make an asymptotic reference inaccurate. Exact conditioning may protect size but lose power or target a narrower null. Parametric bootstrap and permutation calibration can improve finite-sample behavior when their models are credible. Before deployment, simulate the complete procedure at several null parameter settings, not only one convenient point. The maximum false-rejection rate across relevant nulls is the operating characteristic that a composite-null level claim must control.

Math / formal view

For statistic T and observed t, an upper-tail p-value is P_H0(T>=t); a two-sided definition must specify how both tails are ordered. A level-alpha test has sup over theta in H0 of P_theta(reject)<=alpha. At alternative theta1, power is P_theta1(reject)=1-beta(theta1). For a normal mean with known sigma, Z=(Xbar-mu0)/(sigma/sqrt(n)); reject a two-sided H0 at level alpha when |Z|>z_(1-alpha/2). The matching interval excludes mu0 exactly when the test rejects. These probabilities describe repeated procedure behavior.

A precise but economically negligible lift

Separate incompatibility with an exact-zero null from the magnitude and value of the estimated effect. Then audit stopping and multiplicity before using the nominal p-value.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build an exact sign-flip randomization test, compare its tail count with SciPy, and verify null calibration by construction.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import itertools

def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def sign_flip_pvalue(differences):
    observed = abs(mean(differences))
    stats = []
    for signs in itertools.product((-1, 1), repeat=len(differences)):
        stats.append(abs(mean([s*x for s,x in zip(signs,differences)])))
    return sum(t >= observed-1e-12 for t in stats)/len(stats), stats

diffs = [1.2, 0.5, 0.9, -0.1, 1.4, 0.7, 0.3, 1.0]
p_value, null_stats = sign_flip_pvalue(diffs)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import permutation_test
result = permutation_test((np.asarray(diffs),), lambda x: np.mean(x), permutation_type='samples', alternative='two-sided', n_resamples=np.inf)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Prespecify the statistic and exchangeability/randomization mechanism, log every analysis, use sequentially valid monitoring, and report effect estimates and intervals with the p-value.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert len(null_stats) == 2**len(diffs)
assert 0.0 <= p_value <= 1.0
assert abs(p_value-result.pvalue) < 1e-12
assert sign_flip_pvalue([1.0,-1.0,2.0,-2.0])[0] == 1.0

Common mistakes

  • Saying p=0.03 means a 97% probability the alternative is true.
  • Treating p>=0.05 as evidence of equality or no effect.
  • Choosing a one-sided test after seeing the effect direction.
  • Ignoring repeated peeking, multiple metrics, subgroup search, or model-selection attempts.
  • Reporting significance without effect size, interval, assumptions, or practical threshold.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the difference between alpha and a p-value?

    Alpha is a prechosen operating threshold for a procedure's Type I error. The p-value is a data-dependent tail area under H0. Comparing them implements a rule, but they are not the same probability.

  • Does p=0.001 prove the alternative?

    No. It indicates strong incompatibility with the specified null model for the chosen statistic, assuming the design and analysis are valid. It does not rule out bias, misspecification, multiplicity, or data errors.

  • How should continuous experiment monitoring be handled?

    Use a prespecified group-sequential design, alpha-spending rule, confidence sequence, or other always-valid method. Fixed-horizon tests repeatedly inspected without adjustment lose their nominal error control.

Production / system-design connection

Create an experiment or inference specification before data access: owner, population, unit, estimand, hypotheses, sidedness, primary and guardrail metrics, exclusions, covariance adjustment, alpha, power target, stopping rule, and multiplicity family. Validate sample-ratio balance, exposure logging, missing outcomes, cluster dependence, novelty effects, and implementation integrity. Store all attempted analyses and immutable code/data versions. Dashboards should display estimates, intervals, practical thresholds, and sequential status; avoid binary green labels. Restrict small-cell data and secure sensitive subgroup results. Monitor repeated-test false-alert rates with simulations. If analysis code changes after results, label it exploratory and obtain fresh confirmation. Rollback decisions should consider guardrail harm and reversibility, while preserving the original audit trail. A centralized metric registry prevents silent redefinition across teams.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Define a p-value in one conditional-probability sentence.

    Show solution

    It is the probability, under the specified null model and assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    A test returns p=0.20 with 20% power for the effect of interest. Can you conclude no effect?

    Show solution

    No. The procedure frequently fails to reject when that effect exists. Report the interval and acknowledge that the data are weakly informative; consider a better-powered study.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why is choosing one-sidedness after seeing the sign invalid?

    Show solution

    It uses the data twice and changes the tail rule to favor the observation, so the claimed Type I error calibration no longer matches the procedure actually used.

    Provides authoritative principles for interpreting and reporting p-values without threshold misuse.

  • stanford-stats200

    Provides formal test construction, error rates, power, and likelihood-based inference foundations.

  • scipy-stats

    Documents current exact, permutation, and Monte Carlo testing interfaces used in the lab.

    Authoritative principles on p-value interpretation, transparency, effect magnitude, and avoiding threshold-only conclusions.

  • STATS 200: Introduction to Statistical InferenceStanford University · Primary university course · Intermediate → Advanced

    Rigorous inference: hypothesis tests, MLE, confidence intervals, bootstrap, Bayesian analysis, multiple testing, regression and proportional hazards.

  • NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical MethodsNational Institute of Standards and Technology · Official statistical handbook · Foundation → Advanced

    Authoritative applied coverage of confidence intervals, tests, ANOVA, chi-square methods, diagnostics, and experimental analysis.

  • SciPy Statistical FunctionsSciPy · Official documentation · Intermediate

7.3

MLE vs MAP

highverified
Roles: ds, mle, da, as

Topic overview

Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameter values that make the observed data most likely under a specified statistical model. Maximum a posteriori estimation multiplies that likelihood by a prior density and chooses the posterior mode. This chapter carefully distinguishes probability of data given parameters from a probability distribution over parameters, derives log-likelihood objectives for Bernoulli and Gaussian models, connects Gaussian and Laplace priors to common regularizers, and explains why MAP remains a point estimate rather than full Bayesian inference. You will learn how identifiability, constraints, reparameterization, boundary solutions, weak data, and misspecified likelihoods affect both methods; why maximizing a density is coordinate-sensitive; and why optimization convergence does not prove statistical validity. The worked example derives smoothed Bernoulli estimates and contrasts MLE, MAP, and posterior mean. The lab implements them from first principles and verifies against an analytic Beta–Binomial result. Production guidance covers numerical stability, calibration, prior governance, reproducibility, monitoring, and rollback when data or likelihood assumptions shift.

Prerequisites

  • distributions
  • expectation-variance

Learning objectives

  • Write likelihood and log-likelihood objectives without reversing their conditioning.
  • Derive MLE and MAP estimates for simple models and connect priors to regularization penalties.
  • Distinguish MAP, posterior mean, posterior predictive inference, and full posterior uncertainty.
  • Diagnose identifiability, numerical, boundary, prior, and misspecification failures in estimation.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

MLE maximizes p(data|theta), treating the observed data as fixed and theta as the optimization variable. MAP maximizes p(data|theta)p(theta), equivalently log likelihood plus log prior. A zero-mean Gaussian prior often yields an L2 penalty and a Laplace prior an L1 penalty, with scaling determined by noise and prior parameters. Both return point estimates; MAP is not full Bayesian inference and is not invariant to arbitrary reparameterization. Validate the model, identifiability, optimization, and predictive calibration separately.

What you must know

  • Likelihood is a function of parameters, not a normalized parameter probability
  • Logs turn products into stable sums
  • MAP adds prior information and can regularize weak data
  • Point estimation discards posterior shape
  • A converged optimizer can fit a wrong or unidentified model

Why this matters

MLE connects probability assumptions to losses used throughout statistics and machine learning. Squared error follows from Gaussian observation noise; cross-entropy follows from Bernoulli or categorical likelihoods. MAP explains one source of regularization and makes prior commitments explicit. Without this foundation, practitioners treat losses as arbitrary functions and misread penalties as universally equivalent priors. In interviews, likelihood questions test conditional reasoning and optimization. In production, a misspecified likelihood can yield poor tail probabilities or calibration even when predictive ranking looks good. A prior chosen for numerical convenience may dominate low-volume segments. Conversely, unregularized MLE can diverge under complete separation or overfit sparse categories. Estimation is therefore both a mathematical objective and an engineering contract about data generation.

Intuition

Suppose a coin produced eight heads and two tails. MLE asks: which head probability would make this exact outcome pattern most plausible? The answer is 0.8. MAP adds a prior belief, perhaps that extreme probabilities are uncommon, then finds the peak after combining evidence and prior. With little data, the prior moves the estimate; with abundant regular data, the likelihood usually dominates. The posterior mean averages parameter values under the posterior, while MAP selects only its highest point, so they need not match. In a multimodal posterior the MAP may describe one narrow peak while ignoring substantial mass elsewhere. In high-dimensional models, a penalty can stabilize the optimizer, but it also encodes geometry and scale. Standardizing features changes what an isotropic coefficient prior means.

Likelihood, log-likelihood, and sufficient information

For independent observations, L(theta)=product_i p(x_i|theta). Maximizing log L=sum_i log p(x_i|theta) gives the same optimizer because log is monotone, while avoiding underflow and exposing additive contributions. The score is the gradient of log likelihood; observed or expected information describes curvature and often determines asymptotic uncertainty. Sufficient statistics compress the sample without losing likelihood information about theta for a model—for a Bernoulli sample, the head count is sufficient. Likelihood compares parameter values conditional on the observed data; it is not P(theta|x). Likelihood ratios are invariant to parameter-independent constants, but absolute densities require careful units and support.

MLE behavior: invariance, consistency, and failure modes

Under regularity, identifiability, and correct specification, MLEs are often consistent and asymptotically normal with covariance related to inverse Fisher information. The MLE is invariant under one-to-one transformations: if eta=g(theta), eta_hat=g(theta_hat). Finite-sample bias can remain. Nonidentifiability creates ridges or multiple equivalent optima. Mixture likelihoods can be singular; logistic MLE can diverge under separation; variance estimates can hit boundaries. Local optimization may find a poor mode. Under misspecification, the MLE targets the closest model in a Kullback–Leibler sense rather than truth, and model-based standard errors may be wrong. Sandwich uncertainty and diagnostics may be needed.

MAP, priors, and regularization scaling

MAP maximizes log L(theta)+log pi(theta). A Gaussian N(0,tau squared) prior contributes -||theta|| squared/(2 tau squared); Gaussian observation variance also scales the data term, so the resulting ridge coefficient is not simply 'the prior' without conventions. An independent Laplace prior contributes an L1 penalty and may produce zeros at a posterior mode. Priors can encode signs, monotonicity, plausible scales, or hierarchical sharing more meaningfully than generic shrinkage. Hyperparameters must be chosen without outcome leakage and documented. MAP is sensitive to parameterization because a density transforms with a Jacobian; posterior probabilities are invariant when transformed correctly, but the location of a density mode need not be.

A point is not a posterior or a predictive distribution

MAP discards posterior width, correlation, skewness, and multimodality. Posterior mean minimizes squared-error loss for the parameter; posterior median minimizes absolute error; MAP has a local density interpretation. A posterior predictive distribution integrates p(y_new|theta) over posterior uncertainty, whereas plugging in theta_MAP ignores that uncertainty. In sparse or safety-critical settings the difference matters for tail risk and abstention. Laplace approximation, variational inference, MCMC, bootstrap, and profile likelihood capture different uncertainty approximations. Choose an estimator and uncertainty method based on the decision loss, not because one optimizer is convenient.

Curvature, profile likelihood, and uncertainty

At a regular interior optimum, negative Hessian curvature of the log likelihood approximates observed information; its inverse gives an asymptotic covariance estimate. Flat directions signal weak identification and large uncertainty even when optimization reports convergence. Profile likelihood fixes a parameter of interest, reoptimizes nuisance parameters, and uses likelihood-ratio contours that can capture asymmetry better than a Wald interval. Bayesian posterior curvature adds prior information and a Laplace approximation, but can miss skewness or other modes. Compare Hessian eigenvalues, profile traces, bootstrap variation, and predictive calibration. An optimizer tolerance measures numerical stationarity, not inferential precision. Save enough diagnostics to distinguish a sharp data-supported optimum from one created mainly by constraints or priors.

Math / formal view

For Bernoulli data with k successes in n trials, log L(p)=k log p+(n-k)log(1-p), whose MLE is k/n for 0<k<n. With Beta(a,b) prior, the posterior is Beta(a+k,b+n-k). For a+k>1 and b+n-k>1, MAP=(a+k-1)/(a+b+n-2), while posterior mean=(a+k)/(a+b+n). For Gaussian linear regression y=Xw+epsilon, epsilon~N(0,sigma^2 I), plus w~N(0,tau^2 I), negative log posterior is ||y-Xw||^2/(2sigma^2)+||w||^2/(2tau^2)+constant, so MAP is ridge with lambda=sigma^2/tau^2 under an unnormalized squared-error convention.

Sparse conversion with a Beta prior

Derive MLE, posterior, MAP, and posterior predictive mean for the same two observations. The comparison makes clear what each point estimate retains and discards.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Derive Bernoulli MLE, Beta-prior MAP, and posterior mean, then verify each analytic formula on sparse data.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def bernoulli_mle(k, n):
    if not 0 <= k <= n or n <= 0: raise ValueError('invalid counts')
    return k/n

def beta_posterior(k, n, a, b):
    return a+k, b+n-k

def beta_map(alpha, beta):
    if alpha <= 1 or beta <= 1: raise ValueError('interior MAP formula requires shapes > 1')
    return (alpha-1)/(alpha+beta-2)

k,n,a,b = 1,2,2.0,8.0
alpha,beta = beta_posterior(k,n,a,b)
mle = bernoulli_mle(k,n)
map_est = beta_map(alpha,beta)
post_mean = alpha/(alpha+beta)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import beta as beta_dist
grid = np.linspace(1e-5, 1-1e-5, 200000)
numeric_map = grid[np.argmax(beta_dist.logpdf(grid, alpha, beta))]
scipy_mean = beta_dist.mean(alpha, beta)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version likelihood, parameterization, feature scale, priors, objective normalization, optimizer diagnostics, and predictive calibration; never deploy a point estimate without failure and uncertainty handling.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert mle == 0.5
assert abs(map_est-0.2) < 1e-12
assert abs(post_mean-0.25) < 1e-12
assert abs(numeric_map-map_est) < 1e-4
assert abs(scipy_mean-post_mean) < 1e-12

Common mistakes

  • Calling L(theta;x) a probability distribution over theta without a prior and normalization.
  • Saying MAP is full Bayesian inference or always equals the posterior mean.
  • Claiming L2 always means the same Gaussian prior without tracking objective scaling and feature units.
  • Trusting optimizer convergence without checking identifiability, boundaries, local modes, or misspecification.
  • Using an outcome-informed prior or regularization search on the final evaluation data.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why maximize log likelihood?

    Log is monotone, so the maximizer is unchanged; products become sums, gradients are simpler, and numerical underflow is reduced. Stable implementations still use log-sum-exp and distribution-specific log-probability functions.

  • When do MLE and MAP become similar?

    When regular, highly informative data make the likelihood sharply concentrated relative to a smooth positive prior near the optimum. This is not guaranteed with weak identification, boundaries, high dimension, or a prior that excludes the likelihood optimum.

  • Why is MAP not invariant to reparameterization?

    A posterior density acquires a Jacobian under transformation, and the highest density point can move beyond simply transforming the old mode. Posterior probabilities transform consistently, but density modes depend on coordinates.

Production / system-design connection

Define support, parameterization, likelihood, censoring/missingness assumptions, prior source, feature scaling, and hyperparameter-selection data. Use distribution log-probability functions, stable transforms, gradient checks, multiple initializations, and convergence diagnostics. Test analytic estimates on synthetic data with known parameters and on boundary cases. Monitor calibration, residuals, tail scores, parameter drift, condition numbers, prior-to-data influence, and optimizer failures. Persist software, seed, initialization, data snapshot, objective scaling, and convergence status. Protect sensitive priors and small-segment estimates. Set fallback estimates for sparse groups and abstain when identification is weak. Rollback must restore preprocessing and prior settings alongside parameters. For high-stakes decisions, propagate uncertainty through posterior predictive or validated frequentist procedures rather than treating a MAP point as certainty.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    For 7 successes in 10 Bernoulli trials, find the MLE.

    Show solution

    p_hat=7/10=0.7 by maximizing k log p+(n-k)log(1-p).

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    With Beta(2,2) prior and 7/10 data, find posterior mean and MAP.

    Show solution

    Posterior is Beta(9,5). Mean=9/14. MAP=(9-1)/(9+5-2)=8/12=2/3, since both shape parameters exceed one.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Explain why a Gaussian prior's ridge strength depends on scale.

    Show solution

    The penalty coefficient depends on prior variance, observation-noise variance, and the convention used for averaging or summing loss. Feature scaling changes coefficient units and therefore the meaning of an isotropic prior.

    Connects probabilistic assumptions, likelihood objectives, MAP estimation, and regularization in machine learning.

  • stanford-stats200

    Provides formal likelihood theory, estimator properties, and asymptotic inference context.

  • scipy-stats

    Documents the current Beta distribution implementation used to verify the analytic conjugate example.

    Canonical mathematical ML course covering supervised learning, unsupervised learning, learning theory and practical model reasoning.

  • STATS 200: Introduction to Statistical InferenceStanford University · Primary university course · Intermediate → Advanced

  • SciPy Statistical FunctionsSciPy · Official documentation · Intermediate

    Current probability-distribution, summary-statistic, sampling and statistical-function reference for verified library use.

7.4

Sampling Distributions & Standard Error

very highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic over repeated samples generated by the same population and sampling design. It is the bridge from observed data to uncertainty about an estimator. This chapter separates the population distribution, the empirical distribution of one sample, and the sampling distribution of an estimator; derives the standard error of a mean; explains why standard deviation and standard error answer different questions; and shows how dependence, unequal weights, clustering, and finite populations change the calculation. You will learn when a central-limit approximation is credible, why an unbiased estimator can still be too noisy to use, and why a low standard error cannot repair selection bias. The worked example and lab simulate repeated samples so that sampling variability is visible rather than merely asserted. Production guidance covers unit-of-analysis mistakes, correlated observations, design-aware uncertainty, reproducible simulation, and monitoring effective sample size. The goal is to make every later interval, test, and power calculation rest on a clear data-generating and sampling model.

Prerequisites

  • expectation-variance
  • clt

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish a population distribution, a sample distribution, and an estimator's sampling distribution.
  • Derive and interpret standard error for independent means and recognize when the square-root-n rule fails.
  • Diagnose how bias, dependence, weighting, clustering, and finite-population sampling affect uncertainty.
  • Estimate sampling uncertainty analytically or by simulation and verify the result against repeated samples.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A sampling distribution describes how a statistic would vary over repeated samples from the same data-generating process and design. Its standard deviation is the statistic's standard error. For an independent sample mean with finite variance, SE is sigma divided by square root n, estimated by s divided by square root n. That is different from the standard deviation of individual observations. The formula changes under clustering, time dependence, unequal weights, or finite-population sampling, and a small SE says nothing about selection bias.

What you must know

  • Random data make estimators random before sampling
  • Standard error measures estimator variability, not raw spread
  • Independence and design determine effective information
  • Bias and variance are separate failure modes
  • Simulation can audit analytic uncertainty formulas

Why this matters

Every confidence interval, p-value, power calculation, and error bar assumes some sampling distribution. If that hidden layer is wrong, polished downstream inference is wrong. A common analytics mistake treats millions of events as millions of independent units even when only thousands of users generated them. The naive standard error then shrinks dramatically while the real information has barely changed. Another mistake reports a small standard error from a convenience sample and calls the estimate accurate, ignoring systematic coverage or nonresponse bias. Interviewers ask about standard error because the answer reveals whether a candidate understands repeated-sampling uncertainty, unit of analysis, and asymptotic approximation rather than memorizing a formula. In production, the sampling distribution is also the basis of alert thresholds and metric-change detection. It must reflect how data arrive, which units are randomized, and which sources of variation will recur.

Intuition

Imagine repeatedly drawing 100 orders from the same population and computing the mean order value. The histogram of all order values may be broad and skewed. Each sample has its own empirical histogram. The histogram of the thousands of sample means is a third object: it is narrower because positive and negative deviations partly cancel. Increasing sample size usually narrows that distribution, but duplicating the same customers' orders does not add the same information as observing new independent customers. Standard error is the width of that estimator histogram. Bias is the displacement of its center from the target. An estimator may be centered correctly but too noisy, or tightly concentrated around the wrong value. The central limit theorem often makes the center of the sampling distribution approximately normal even when observations are not normal, provided the required independence or weak-dependence and finite-variance conditions are credible. That approximation is a claim to diagnose, not a license to ignore heavy tails, rare events, or dependence.

Three distributions that must not be confused

The population distribution describes values for units in the target population or superpopulation. The empirical distribution gives probability 1/n to each observed value in one sample. A sampling distribution describes a statistic T(X1,...,Xn) across repeated samples. The first concerns units, the second summarizes observed units, and the third concerns an estimator. Their spreads have different meanings. Population standard deviation measures heterogeneity among units; standard error measures uncertainty in a statistic. A sample mean of 10,000 purchases can have a tiny SE while purchases themselves vary enormously. Conversely, a robust median may have a larger SE than the mean under a clean Gaussian model but behave better under contamination. Always name the random unit and the target statistic before writing a denominator.

Deriving the square-root-n rule

For independent identically distributed Xi with mean mu and variance sigma squared, Var(Xbar)=Var(sum Xi/n)=n sigma squared/n squared=sigma squared/n, so SE(Xbar)=sigma/sqrt(n). Replacing unknown sigma by sample s yields the estimated SE. The reduction is proportional to 1/sqrt(n): halving uncertainty requires roughly four times as many independent observations. The derivation depends on covariance terms being zero. With correlation, Var(Xbar) includes 2 times the sum of pairwise covariances divided by n squared. Positive within-user, household, device, school, or time correlation reduces effective sample size. Negative dependence can reduce variance. For sampling without replacement from a finite population, multiply by the finite-population correction sqrt((N-n)/(N-1)) when the design and target warrant it.

Bias, variance, consistency, and efficiency

The sampling distribution exposes estimator quality. Bias is E[T]-theta; variance is E[(T-E[T]) squared]; mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias. Unbiasedness alone is not optimal if a slightly biased estimator has much lower variance and lower MSE. Consistency asks whether the estimator converges to the target as information grows. Efficiency compares variances among estimators under a model. Robustness asks how sensitive the estimator is to contamination or model violations. These are properties of a procedure under specified conditions, not permanent labels. Sample variance with denominator n-1 is unbiased under iid sampling, but an unbiased formula does not fix an unrepresentative sample. Regularized estimators deliberately introduce bias to reduce variance. Report the target, loss, and operating conditions when comparing estimators.

Design-aware and dependence-aware uncertainty

Simple iid SE formulas fail for clustered samples, repeated measurements, time series, spatial data, survey weights, and adaptive collection. Cluster-robust or sandwich estimators aggregate score contributions at the independent cluster level. Block methods preserve local dependence in time or space. Survey estimators incorporate stratification, primary sampling units, unequal selection probabilities, and sometimes finite-population corrections. Unequal weights often lower effective sample size; one useful diagnostic is (sum w)^2/sum(w^2), though a complete design variance needs more than that scalar. When clusters are few, asymptotic cluster corrections can be unreliable. Validate analytic SEs against design-respecting simulation or resampling and avoid silently switching the unit from users to events.

Math / formal view

Let T=T(X1,...,Xn) estimate theta. Bias(T)=E[T]-theta, Var(T)=E[(T-E[T])^2], and MSE(T)=Var(T)+Bias(T)^2. For iid Xi with variance sigma^2, Var(Xbar)=sigma^2/n. If every distinct pair has correlation rho, Var(Xbar)=sigma^2[1+(n-1)rho]/n, giving the design effect 1+(n-1)rho. The effective independent sample size is approximately n divided by that design effect. A standardized statistic (T-theta)/SE(T) may approach a reference distribution, but only under the theorem's regularity conditions.

Order value with repeated customers

Start with the iid SE, identify customer as the independent cluster, calculate a design effect, and compare against customer-level bootstrap results. The example shows why row count is not information count and why uncertainty and representativeness require separate checks.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate a sampling distribution, verify the analytic SE, and show how cluster dependence invalidates a row-level iid calculation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math
import random

def repeated_means(population, n, repeats, seed=7):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [sum(rng.choices(population, k=n)) / n for _ in range(repeats)]

def sample_sd(xs):
    mean = sum(xs) / len(xs)
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in xs) / (len(xs) - 1))

population = [float(x) for x in range(1, 101)]
means = repeated_means(population, n=25, repeats=4000)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
array = np.asarray(population)
draws = rng.choice(array, size=(4000, 25), replace=True)
np_means = draws.mean(axis=1)
analytic_se = array.std(ddof=0) / np.sqrt(25)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Resample the independent business unit, preserve design weights and clusters, compare analytic and simulation estimates in CI, and version the metric grain with its uncertainty method.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
empirical_se = sample_sd(means)
assert abs(empirical_se - analytic_se) / analytic_se < 0.05
assert abs(np_means.std(ddof=1) - analytic_se) / analytic_se < 0.05
assert sample_sd(repeated_means(population, 100, 4000)) < empirical_se

Common mistakes

  • Dividing the raw standard deviation by square root of the number of rows when rows are not independent units.
  • Calling the sample's empirical histogram a sampling distribution.
  • Equating a small standard error with low total error while ignoring selection, measurement, or model bias.
  • Invoking the CLT without checking tail behavior, dependence, sample size, or whether the statistic is regular.
  • Using event-level bootstrap resampling when assignment and dependence operate at user or cluster level.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is standard error usually smaller than standard deviation?

    Standard deviation describes heterogeneity of individual values, while the mean averages deviations. Under iid sampling, averaging n observations divides variance by n and standard deviation by square root n. Dependence can substantially weaken that reduction.

  • Can an estimator have zero standard error and still be wrong?

    Yes. A constant estimator has zero variance but may be badly biased. More realistically, a huge nonrepresentative sample can yield a tiny estimated SE around a biased target. Precision and validity are different dimensions.

  • How would you estimate SE when no closed form is available?

    Use a design-respecting bootstrap, jackknife, influence-function or Monte Carlo simulation. The resampling unit and mechanism must mimic the source of repeated-sample variation; otherwise computation only produces precise nonsense.

Production / system-design connection

Define metric grain, estimand, independent unit, exposure window, and sampling design in the metric contract. Preserve cluster IDs and weights so uncertainty can be reproduced. Compare analytic and resampling SEs on stable reference datasets; large disagreement is a diagnostic. Monitor raw count, distinct independent units, weight concentration, cluster-size distribution, missingness, tail quantiles, and estimated design effect. Version variance code with the metric definition and log seeds for simulations. For streaming metrics, account for autocorrelation and delayed outcomes; do not emit iid error bars on every event. Apply privacy controls to small slices and avoid leaking individual records through debugging samples. When the design changes, invalidate historical uncertainty thresholds or recompute them. Rollback means restoring the estimator, variance method, and population definition together, not only reverting a dashboard query.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A sample has raw SD 12 and n=144 iid observations. Estimate the mean's SE and explain the unit.

    Show solution

    SE=12/sqrt(144)=1. It is the repeated-sample standard deviation of the sample mean, expressed in the original measurement unit, not the spread of individual observations.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Ten observations are exact duplicates of each of 100 independent units. Should n be 1,000 in the iid formula?

    Show solution

    No. Duplicate rows add no independent information. Aggregate or cluster by the 100 independent units; otherwise the naive SE is understated by treating copies as new evidence.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    An estimator has bias 2 and variance 9. Compute MSE.

    Show solution

    MSE=variance+bias squared=9+4=13. This demonstrates why variance alone is not total estimation error.

7.5

Bootstrap & Resampling

highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

The bootstrap estimates an estimator's sampling behavior by repeatedly sampling with replacement from the empirical distribution and recomputing the complete statistic. It is powerful because it can approximate standard errors, bias, and confidence intervals when analytic derivations are inconvenient, but it is not assumption-free. This chapter develops the plug-in principle, explains why replacement matters, distinguishes ordinary, paired, stratified, cluster, block, parametric, and residual bootstraps, and compares percentile, basic, normal, and bias-corrected accelerated intervals. You will learn when the empirical distribution is a reasonable stand-in for the population, why rare events and nonsmooth statistics cause instability, and why resampling rows breaks dependence. The worked example estimates a difference in medians while preserving treatment groups. The lab implements a bootstrap distribution from first principles, compares it with SciPy's current API, verifies reproducibility and interval behavior, and demonstrates the effect of sample size. Production guidance covers resampling grain, pipeline refitting, Monte Carlo error, seeds, compute budgets, privacy, and coverage audits.

Prerequisites

  • sampling-distributions
  • confidence-intervals

Learning objectives

  • Explain the empirical plug-in principle and why bootstrap resamples have the original sample size with replacement.
  • Choose a resampling scheme that preserves pairing, groups, clusters, time dependence, weights, and model-fitting steps.
  • Compare common bootstrap interval constructions and diagnose skewness, bias, discreteness, and boundary failure.
  • Implement reproducible bootstrap uncertainty and verify it against simulation or an official library.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The nonparametric bootstrap treats the empirical distribution as an estimate of the population: draw many size-n samples with replacement, recompute the entire estimator, and use the resulting distribution for standard errors or intervals. It works when the observed sample represents the repetition mechanism and the estimator is sufficiently regular. Resample the independent unit—pairs, users, clusters, or time blocks—not blindly rows. Bootstrap cannot repair selection bias, absent rare classes, or a fundamentally misspecified pipeline, and interval choice and Monte Carlo error must be reported.

What you must know

  • Resampling approximates repeated sampling from an estimated population
  • Replacement preserves iid draws from the empirical distribution
  • The estimator must be recomputed end to end
  • Dependence determines the resampling unit
  • Coverage must be checked rather than assumed

Why this matters

Modern metrics are often ratios, quantiles, ranking scores, or outputs of fitted pipelines whose standard errors are messy. The bootstrap turns a difficult derivation into a simulation procedure that exposes estimator variability. That convenience also encourages misuse. Row bootstrap on repeated user events invents independence; bootstrapping only final predictions ignores model-training variation; independently resampling paired outcomes destroys the pairing; and resampling a biased dataset reproduces its bias. Interviews ask for the algorithm, but a strong answer states the target repetition mechanism and failure cases. In production, a stochastic interval must also be reproducible, computationally bounded, and stable enough for decisions. The bootstrap is best understood as a model—the empirical distribution plus a resampling design—not as a magical guarantee.

Intuition

The observed sample is the only concrete glimpse of the population. Place equal probability mass on each observed independent unit, then pretend that discrete empirical distribution generated new studies. Sampling with replacement allows some units to appear multiple times and others not at all, producing the variation that sampling would create. Recompute the statistic for each pseudo-study. The spread of those values estimates standard error; their shape reveals skewness or instability. Without replacement, every size-n resample would merely reorder all observations and many statistics would not change. The approximation is strongest when the original sample captures the population features relevant to the statistic. If no failure event appears, the empirical distribution assigns it probability zero, so no bootstrap replicate can discover it. If dependence exists, the empirical units must be clusters or blocks rather than rows.

The plug-in distribution and algorithm

Given iid observations x1,...,xn, the empirical distribution F_n places mass 1/n on each xi. A bootstrap sample draws n times independently from F_n, which is equivalent to sampling observed rows with replacement. For each replicate b, compute theta_hat_b*=T(x_b*), including every preprocessing and fitting step that would vary in a new sample. The bootstrap standard error is the sample SD of replicate estimates. Estimated bias is mean(theta_hat*)-theta_hat. Thousands of replicates reduce Monte Carlo noise but do not fix statistical invalidity. Report the number of replicates, random generator, seed policy, and interval method.

Resampling must mirror the data design

Paired measurements are resampled as pairs. Two independently sampled groups are resampled within group when estimating a two-sample effect. Cluster bootstrap samples independent clusters and carries all their rows. Stratified bootstrap samples within design strata. Time-series block bootstrap samples contiguous blocks long enough to retain relevant dependence; moving, circular, and stationary variants differ. Parametric bootstrap simulates from a fitted model, trading empirical flexibility for model dependence. Regression residual bootstrap assumes a residual structure; case bootstrap resamples observations; wild bootstrap can handle heteroskedasticity. Survey replicate weights may be preferable to ad hoc row resampling. The unit and scheme follow from the estimand and design.

Bootstrap standard errors and interval choices

The normal interval uses theta_hat plus-or-minus a critical value times bootstrap SE and assumes approximate symmetry. The percentile interval takes quantiles of theta_hat*, which is intuitive but can inherit bias and transformation issues. The basic interval reflects percentile endpoints around theta_hat. Studentized intervals bootstrap a pivotal statistic and can improve accuracy at extra computational cost. BCa adjusts for median bias and acceleration related to estimator influence, and SciPy currently defaults to BCa. No method dominates every setting. Compare interval shape, replicate histogram, jackknife influence, and simulation coverage across plausible distributions. Transform bounded positive parameters when appropriate.

Where ordinary bootstrap breaks

Nonsmooth estimators, sample extremes, parameters on boundaries, very small samples, infinite-variance distributions, weak identification, and model selection can defeat ordinary bootstrap approximations. The sample maximum's empirical bootstrap cannot exceed the observed maximum. Rare classes absent from the sample remain absent. Some estimators require an m-out-of-n or subsampling approach. Cross-validation metrics need resampling that accounts for training and evaluation roles; leaking the same rows across stages biases uncertainty. A bootstrap distribution can look smooth and still target the wrong population. Audit against synthetic data with known truth, alternative resampling schemes, influence diagnostics, and domain shifts.

Bootstrapping learned pipelines and evaluation metrics

For a trained model's future performance, uncertainty can arise from training-sample variation, evaluation-sample variation, hyperparameter selection, and deployment population drift. Bootstrapping only a fixed test set conditions on the fitted model and estimates a narrower quantity. To capture training variation, each replicate must redo feature fitting, model training, tuning logic, threshold selection, and evaluation on an independent or appropriately out-of-bag sample. Naive reuse can leak observations and create optimistic metrics. Nested resampling is expensive, so state which randomness is included. For paired model comparisons, resample evaluation units jointly so both models face the same cases; the covariance substantially improves precision. Distribution shift remains outside an iid bootstrap unless explicitly simulated.

Math / formal view

For B bootstrap replicates theta_hat_1*,...,theta_hat_B*, bootstrap SE is sqrt(sum_b(theta_hat_b*-mean*)^2/(B-1)). A percentile (1-alpha) interval uses empirical quantiles alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2. A basic interval is [2 theta_hat-q_(1-alpha/2)*, 2 theta_hat-q_(alpha/2)*]. Monte Carlo uncertainty of estimated quantiles decreases with B but depends on density near the quantile. Statistical validity concerns n tending large; increasing B only approximates the conditional bootstrap distribution more precisely.

Difference in group medians

Resample within each independent group, recompute both medians, inspect the replicate distribution, and interpret its interval only after validating the unit and censoring rules.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build a bootstrap confidence interval for a median, compare with SciPy BCa output, and verify reproducibility and narrowing with more data.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import random
import statistics

def bootstrap_statistic(xs, statistic, repeats=5000, seed=17):
    rng = random.Random(seed); n=len(xs)
    return [statistic(rng.choices(xs,k=n)) for _ in range(repeats)]

def percentile_interval(values, level=0.95):
    ys=sorted(values); tail=(1-level)/2
    lo=ys[int(tail*(len(ys)-1))]; hi=ys[int((1-tail)*(len(ys)-1))]
    return lo,hi

x=[8,9,10,10,11,12,13,17,22,30,31,35]
replicates=bootstrap_statistic(x,statistics.median)
interval=percentile_interval(replicates)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import bootstrap
rng=np.random.default_rng(17)
result=bootstrap((np.asarray(x),),np.median,confidence_level=0.95,n_resamples=5000,method='BCa',rng=rng)
scipy_interval=(float(result.confidence_interval.low),float(result.confidence_interval.high))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Resample the independent unit and full pipeline, use deterministic independent RNG streams, track failed replicates and Monte Carlo error, and coverage-test the chosen interval method.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert bootstrap_statistic(x,statistics.median,100,17)==bootstrap_statistic(x,statistics.median,100,17)
assert interval[0] <= statistics.median(x) <= interval[1]
assert scipy_interval[0] < scipy_interval[1]
wide=percentile_interval(bootstrap_statistic(x*8,statistics.median,3000,19))
assert wide[1]-wide[0] <= interval[1]-interval[0]

Common mistakes

  • Resampling rows when users, devices, schools, or time blocks are the independent units.
  • Bootstrapping only the final metric while holding learned preprocessing or model parameters fixed.
  • Believing more bootstrap replicates compensate for a tiny or unrepresentative original sample.
  • Using a percentile interval without checking bias, skewness, boundaries, or empirical coverage.
  • Forgetting that paired observations and treatment strata must remain paired or stratified.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why sample with replacement?

    The empirical distribution generates independent draws with replacement. Without replacement, a size-n resample contains every observed unit exactly once, so permutation-invariant statistics such as the mean would not vary.

  • What does increasing B accomplish?

    It reduces Monte Carlo error in approximating the bootstrap distribution conditional on the observed data. It does not add information to the original sample or repair a statistically invalid bootstrap scheme.

  • When would you use a block bootstrap?

    When observations have local serial or spatial dependence and blocks can preserve the dependence relevant to the statistic. Block length is a modeling choice and should be checked by sensitivity analysis.

Production / system-design connection

Specify bootstrap target, independent resampling unit, strata or blocks, replicate count, interval method, full pipeline steps, RNG algorithm, and seed derivation in configuration. Parallelize with independent random streams and make results deterministic for the same artifact version. Monitor failed fits, degenerate replicates, class loss, interval width, quantile Monte Carlo error, cluster coverage, and runtime. Cache only when data and code hashes match. Avoid storing raw replicate samples when estimates suffice, especially for sensitive records. Validate coverage with simulated and historical replay cases, including rare outcomes. Set failure behavior: widen, fall back to an analytic conservative interval, or suppress the estimate rather than silently dropping failed replicates. Version and roll back the resampler with preprocessing and estimator code.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Why does a bootstrap sample of size n contain about 63% distinct observations on average for large n?

    Show solution

    Each observation is omitted with probability (1-1/n)^n, approaching e^-1. Thus the included fraction approaches 1-e^-1, about 0.632.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    How should 500 users with repeated sessions be bootstrapped for a user-level treatment effect?

    Show solution

    Sample users with replacement and carry all relevant sessions/outcomes for each sampled user. Row resampling would destroy within-user dependence.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    You increase B from 1,000 to 100,000 and the interval remains biased. Why?

    Show solution

    B controls simulation precision conditional on the sample. Bias from an invalid resampling model, estimator, or unrepresentative data is a statistical problem, not Monte Carlo noise.

7.6

Permutation & Randomization Tests

highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Permutation and randomization tests build a reference distribution by applying transformations that are valid under a null hypothesis—often reallocating treatment labels or swapping paired signs—and comparing the observed statistic with that distribution. Their strength is transparent design-based calibration with few distributional assumptions; their danger is the casual belief that any labels may be shuffled. This chapter distinguishes Fisher randomization inference from observational permutation tests, defines exchangeability, shows exact and Monte Carlo tail calculations, handles paired and blocked designs, and explains studentization, ties, two-sided definitions, and the plus-one correction for sampled permutations. You will learn how interference, clustering, covariate-adaptive assignment, unequal variances, and data-dependent statistic selection invalidate naive shuffles. The worked example uses a randomized conversion experiment with a difference-in-means statistic. The lab enumerates a small exact test, compares it with SciPy, and verifies symmetry and p-value bounds. Production guidance covers assignment reconstruction, reproducible RNG, batch computation, audit logs, precision, and sequential use.

Prerequisites

  • hypothesis-testing

Learning objectives

  • Identify the exact transformation group justified by random assignment or exchangeability under the null.
  • Construct exact and Monte Carlo permutation distributions for independent, paired, blocked, and clustered designs.
  • Choose and predefine a statistic and two-sided extremeness rule appropriate to the alternative.
  • Diagnose invalid shuffles caused by dependence, unequal assignment, interference, or post-selection.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A permutation test compares an observed statistic with values obtained by shuffling in a way justified under the null. In a randomized experiment, reassign labels according to the actual assignment mechanism; in observational data, a label shuffle additionally requires exchangeability. Preserve pairs, blocks, clusters, and treatment counts. Exact enumeration is possible for small designs; otherwise sample permutations and use a correction such as (b+1)/(B+1). The p-value is valid for the specified statistic, null, design, and extremeness rule—not because permutation is automatically nonparametric.

What you must know

  • Randomization mechanism can supply the null distribution
  • Exchangeability is a substantive assumption
  • Pairs, blocks, and clusters constrain valid transformations
  • The statistic determines sensitivity and two-sided ordering
  • Monte Carlo p-values have simulation uncertainty

Why this matters

Permutation tests make the source of calibration visible: if treatment truly had no effect, would relabeling assignments produce a statistic as large as observed? They are useful for custom metrics whose parametric null distribution is difficult. But shuffling can erase real structure. Permuting sessions across users, observations across time, or outcomes across unequal-variance groups can generate worlds the design never allowed. In randomized experiments, the assignment algorithm—not a generic shuffle—is authoritative. In observational comparisons, exchangeability is rarely guaranteed without conditioning or adjustment. Interviewers value these tests because the algorithm is simple but correct use requires deep design reasoning. In production, exactness also depends on reconstructing assignment and predefining the statistic, not merely calling a resampling API.

Intuition

Freeze every observed outcome and ask which treatment-label arrangements could have occurred under the assignment process if treatment changed none of them. Compute the chosen effect statistic for each allowed arrangement. The observed assignment is one member of that reference set. If its statistic lies in an extreme tail, the no-effect assignment model has difficulty explaining it. In a matched-pair experiment, only swapping labels within pairs is allowed; a global shuffle breaks the match. In a cluster-randomized experiment, whole cluster labels move together. For observational groups, the same picture requires the stronger claim that units were exchangeable under the null. A nonparametric test does not mean assumption-free—it relocates assumptions from a distribution family to invariance and design.

Randomization inference and the null being tested

Under Fisher's sharp null, every unit's outcome would be identical under every treatment, so all missing potential outcomes are known and outcomes can be held fixed while assignments vary. Recompute the statistic over assignments allowed by the experiment, respecting fixed treatment counts, blocks, unequal probabilities, or clusters. The resulting p-value is exact conditional on the observed outcomes and assignment design. A weak null such as zero average effect does not impute every missing potential outcome; an unstudentized randomization test may not be exact for it under heterogeneous effects. State whether the null is sharp, distributional equality, equal means, or conditional independence.

Exchangeability and constrained permutations

Exchangeability means the joint distribution is invariant to the permitted label permutations under H0. Independent identically distributed samples support broad permutations under a distribution-equality null. Paired data support within-pair swaps or sign flips. Blocked experiments permute within blocks. Repeated measures may require subject-level transformations. Time and spatial structures rarely permit arbitrary global shuffles; cyclic shifts or restricted permutations may be justified under specific stationarity claims. Covariate-adaptive randomization must be replayed faithfully. If the transformation destroys dependence or changes nuisance distributions, the reference distribution is wrong even if the code executes.

Statistic choice, exact tails, and Monte Carlo estimates

Choose a statistic before unblinding: mean difference for location, studentized difference for unequal variances, rank statistic for stochastic ordering, or a domain metric for practical sensitivity. Two-sided p-values can be based on absolute statistic, doubled smaller tail, or probability ordering; definitions differ for asymmetric discrete distributions. Exact p is the fraction of allowed transformations at least as extreme, typically including the observed arrangement. When B random permutations are sampled, (b+1)/(B+1) avoids zero and yields a valid conservative Monte Carlo estimate under standard sampling. Report B and simulation uncertainty; a p-value near a threshold may need more permutations.

Confounding, interference, and post-selection

Permutation does not create randomization in observational data. Confounding can make labels nonexchangeable even under no causal effect. Matching or conditioning can narrow the transformation set, but validity then depends on the adjustment and design. Interference means one unit's assignment changes another's outcome, violating usual potential-outcome structure. Missing outcomes and noncompliance complicate estimands. Selecting the largest statistic from many metrics and testing it with a single-metric permutation distribution is invalid; permute the whole selection procedure or adjust multiplicity. Sequentially rerunning permutation tests requires a sequential design. Computational expense is not the main risk—the wrong invariance claim is.

Inverting randomization tests for effect intervals

Randomization tests can produce more than a p-value. Under an additive constant-effect model, subtract a candidate effect from treated outcomes, test the resulting sharp null, and collect candidate effects not rejected; this inverts the test into a confidence set. The construction inherits the assignment-based calibration and may be asymmetric or discrete. It does not establish that treatment effects are truly constant, so interpret the interval for the model being inverted. Hodges–Lehmann-style estimates use the effect value that centers a rank or randomization statistic. In clustered or blocked experiments, inversion must replay the same restricted assignments at every candidate. This connection shows that design-based estimation and testing belong to one coherent procedure rather than isolated significance output.

Math / formal view

For transformation set G and statistic T, an exact upper-tail p-value is |{g in G:T(gX)>=T(X)}|/|G| when transformations are equally likely. With unequal assignment probabilities, weight assignments accordingly. For B randomly sampled transformations and b exceedances, p_hat=(b+1)/(B+1). Conditional Monte Carlo standard error is approximately sqrt(p_hat(1-p_hat)/(B+1)), useful as a precision diagnostic but not a substitute for design validity.

Twelve-store randomized promotion

Enumerate only assignments allowed by the actual randomization, compute the statistic for each, count the appropriate two-sided tail, and contrast complete randomization with paired assignment.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Enumerate an exact two-sample permutation test, verify its tail calculation against SciPy, and preserve fixed group sizes.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import itertools

def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def exact_difference_test(a,b):
    pooled=list(a)+list(b); n_a=len(a)
    observed=abs(mean(a)-mean(b)); stats=[]
    for idx in itertools.combinations(range(len(pooled)),n_a):
        chosen=set(idx)
        left=[x for i,x in enumerate(pooled) if i in chosen]
        right=[x for i,x in enumerate(pooled) if i not in chosen]
        stats.append(abs(mean(left)-mean(right)))
    p=sum(t >= observed-1e-12 for t in stats)/len(stats)
    return observed,p,stats
a=[8,9,11,12]; b=[3,4,6,7]
observed,p_value,null_stats=exact_difference_test(a,b)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import permutation_test
res=permutation_test((np.asarray(a),np.asarray(b)),lambda x,y: np.mean(x)-np.mean(y),permutation_type='independent',alternative='two-sided',n_resamples=np.inf)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Replay the original assignment mechanism with its blocks, clusters, counts, and probabilities; predefine statistic/tails and record Monte Carlo precision and seeds.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
import math
assert len(null_stats)==math.comb(len(a)+len(b),len(a))
assert 0 <= p_value <= 1
assert abs(p_value-res.pvalue) < 1e-12
assert exact_difference_test(a,a)[1] == 1.0

Common mistakes

  • Saying permutation tests make no assumptions.
  • Globally shuffling labels when randomization occurred within blocks, pairs, or clusters.
  • Using observational label permutation as if it proved a causal effect despite confounding.
  • Changing the statistic or one-sided direction after observing the result.
  • Reporting zero from finite random permutations instead of a corrected Monte Carlo estimate and its precision.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is exchangeability?

    It is invariance of the joint distribution under the permitted permutations under H0. It is weaker or stronger depending on the transformation set and is a substantive design/model condition, not a property produced by shuffling.

  • When is a permutation test exact?

    When the null makes outcomes invariant to transformations, the transformation probabilities match the actual design or symmetry, and the statistic and tail rule were fixed. Exact enumeration removes Monte Carlo error, not design error.

  • Why studentize a permutation statistic?

    Dividing by an estimated standard error can make the statistic closer to pivotal and improve behavior when nuisance variance differs, especially for testing equal means rather than identical distributions. Validity still depends on conditions.

Production / system-design connection

Persist the randomization configuration, eligibility set, blocks, clusters, assignment probabilities, exposure logs, statistic code, tail definition, number of permutations, and RNG seed. Reconstruct the exact design rather than inferring it from observed treatment counts. Batch vectorized computations but compare optimized code with exact small fixtures. Monitor assignment integrity, missing outcomes, interference indicators, failed metric calculations, Monte Carlo precision, and runtime. Store aggregate null statistics only when privacy permits; avoid retaining duplicated sensitive rows. Predefine how ties and NaNs are handled. Use more permutations or an exact method near action thresholds. Label exploratory metrics and confirm them on fresh data. Roll back both metric and transformation rules when experiment design changes.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A paired experiment has 8 pairs. How many exact within-pair label swaps exist?

    Show solution

    Each pair has two orientations, so 2^8=256 transformations, assuming every pair can be swapped independently.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    In 999 random permutations, 4 are at least as extreme. Give the plus-one estimate.

    Show solution

    (4+1)/(999+1)=0.005. It avoids claiming an impossible zero tail probability from finite Monte Carlo sampling.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why is a global shuffle invalid for cluster randomization?

    Show solution

    It assigns different treatments to rows within a cluster, creating assignments the experiment could never produce and breaking within-cluster dependence. Shuffle whole cluster labels according to the design.
