7.7

Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate

very highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Testing many hypotheses creates many opportunities for false discoveries. Multiplicity is not solved by interpreting each p-value in isolation; the analyst must define a family, choose an error criterion, and apply a procedure whose dependence assumptions and selection process match the problem. This chapter derives why unadjusted family-wise error grows, contrasts family-wise error rate with false discovery rate, explains Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini–Hochberg, and Benjamini–Yekutieli ideas, and distinguishes adjusted p-values from local false-discovery probabilities. You will learn how hierarchical testing, gatekeeping, preregistration, holdout confirmation, and selective inference control different risks; why correlated tests complicate guarantees; and why adding hypotheses after looking changes the family. The worked example applies BH to ten feature metrics and interprets the rejection threshold. The lab implements Holm and BH from scratch, verifies monotonic adjusted values against SciPy, and checks invariants. Production guidance covers metric-family governance, lineage, online testing, dashboards, reproducibility, and audit of all attempted analyses.

Prerequisites

  • hypothesis-testing

Learning objectives

  • Quantify how repeated testing inflates the chance and number of false positives.
  • Choose between FWER and FDR according to the cost and volume of false discoveries.
  • Implement Bonferroni/Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg procedures with valid ordering and monotonicity.
  • Define hypothesis families and diagnose dependence, selection, and reporting practices that invalidate nominal control.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

With m tests, individual alpha does not control the overall error. Bonferroni and Holm control the probability of at least one false rejection in a defined family; BH controls the expected false discovery proportion under its conditions and is usually more powerful when many discoveries are acceptable. For BH, sort p-values, find the largest k with p_(k)<=kq/m, and reject through k. Define the family before seeing results, account for dependence and selection, report adjusted values and effect sizes, and do not call FDR the probability each discovery is false.

What you must know

  • Multiplicity begins with a declared family
  • FWER controls any false rejection; FDR controls expected false proportion
  • Holm dominates simple Bonferroni while retaining strong FWER control
  • BH is a step-up rule with dependence conditions
  • Adjustment does not repair biased tests or post-selection

Why this matters

A dashboard with 100 metrics, a genomics screen with 20,000 genes, and an ML evaluation sliced across dozens of groups all create multiple chances to see small p-values. At m independent true nulls tested at 0.05, the chance of at least one false rejection is 1-0.95^m, about 99.4% for 100. The appropriate response depends on consequences. A safety investigation may demand strong FWER control; discovery screening may tolerate some false leads for greater power and use FDR with later confirmation. Interviews often ask Bonferroni versus BH, but operational maturity means defining which hypotheses belong together, how exploratory and confirmatory stages interact, and how dependent metrics affect guarantees. Hiding failed tests is a data-governance bug, not merely a statistical detail.

Intuition

Imagine fishing with many hooks. Even if no fish exist, enough hooks will snag debris that looks like a catch. FWER asks to keep the probability of any false catch in the basket below a limit. FDR allows a controlled expected fraction of false catches among everything declared, which is useful when a screening stage can tolerate follow-up work. Bonferroni gives each hook a tiny share alpha/m. Holm starts with the smallest p-value and relaxes thresholds as hypotheses are removed. BH draws an increasing line kq/m against sorted p-values and accepts the largest prefix beneath it. None of these methods knows whether a test was biased, chosen after inspection, or omitted from the count. The family and evidence pipeline must be honest.

How multiplicity accumulates

If m true-null tests are independent at per-test alpha, P(at least one false rejection)=1-(1-alpha)^m, bounded above by m alpha via the union bound. Dependence changes the exact value but not the need for a family-level procedure. Expected false rejections under valid marginal tests is m0 alpha. Multiple outcomes, time points, subgroups, transformations, models, and stopping looks all consume opportunities. A family is the collection over which a claim or decision is made. It may be all primary outcomes for one experiment, all model variants competing for launch, or all genes in a screen. Define it by scientific and decision context, not by which results look promising.

Bonferroni and Holm family-wise control

Bonferroni rejects p_i<=alpha/m and controls FWER under arbitrary dependence by the union bound, but can be conservative. Adjusted p-values are min(m p_i,1). Holm's step-down procedure sorts p_(1)<=...<=p_(m), compares p_(k) with alpha/(m-k+1), and stops at the first failure; it strongly controls FWER under broad conditions and is never less powerful than Bonferroni. Closed testing and gatekeeping can exploit logical structure. FWER suits high-cost false claims, final confirmatory analyses, and small families where any false launch is serious. It does not guarantee that every nonrejected hypothesis is true or control selection bias.

Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery control

For target q, BH sorts p-values and finds largest k with p_(k)<=kq/m, rejecting all p_(1)...p_(k). Under independent true-null p-values and certain positive dependence structures it controls FDR at or below q m0/m. The original paper introduced this less stringent criterion to gain power when controlling the proportion of false discoveries is appropriate. Benjamini–Yekutieli adds a harmonic-factor correction for arbitrary dependence and can be conservative. BH-adjusted p-values are monotone reverse cumulative minima of m p_(k)/k. FDR is an expectation over repeated studies; q=0.05 does not mean each reported discovery has 5% probability of being false.

Hierarchies, dependence, and selective reporting

Correlated outcomes can make standard assumptions uncertain; permutation-based max statistics, hierarchical FDR, knockoffs, or domain-specific methods may be appropriate. Testing parent hypotheses before children can conserve error and match scientific structure. Independent holdout confirmation separates exploration from validation when the selection process is complex. Online FDR methods address hypotheses arriving over time; rerunning batch BH on a growing dashboard does not automatically provide online guarantees. Data-dependent filtering is safe only under conditions such as independence from null p-values. Record every hypothesis, preprocessing variant, and stopping look. Adjustment applied after suppressing inconvenient tests is not control.

Discovery, confirmation, and replicability

Error control within one screen does not guarantee that discoveries replicate in a new population. Winner's curse makes selected effect estimates too large because selection favors positive noise. A two-stage design can use FDR for discovery, then independent confirmatory data with a stricter family-wise criterion. Split proportions should reflect discovery volume and follow-up cost. Shrinkage estimates can improve magnitude reporting but do not retroactively change the testing family. Track directional errors as well as false rejections when sign matters. For recurring products, measure empirical replication and calibration by p-value bins; systematic failure may reveal bias, dependence violations, or shifting populations. Publish the complete discovery and confirmation funnel so consumers do not equate an adjusted p-value with durable truth.

Math / formal view

Under independence, FWER=1-(1-alpha)^m when all m nulls are true. Bonferroni uses alpha/m. Holm compares ordered p_(k) to alpha/(m-k+1). BH at target q finds k*=max{k:p_(k)<=kq/m}; reject ranks <=k*. Adjusted BH values in sorted order are qtilde_(i)=min_{j>=i}(m p_(j)/j,1), then mapped back to original hypotheses. The reverse cumulative minimum is essential so adjusted values are nondecreasing with rank.

BH on ten preregistered metrics

Sort p-values, compare each with its rank-dependent line, select the largest passing rank, reject the prefix, and interpret FDR as a repeated-procedure expectation rather than per-result probability.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement Holm FWER and BH FDR adjusted p-values, verify monotonicity, and compare BH output with SciPy.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def adjust_bh(pvalues):
    m=len(pvalues); order=sorted(range(m),key=pvalues.__getitem__)
    raw=[m*pvalues[i]/rank for rank,i in enumerate(order,1)]
    monotone=[0.0]*m; running=1.0
    for pos in range(m-1,-1,-1):
        running=min(running,raw[pos],1.0); monotone[pos]=running
    out=[0.0]*m
    for pos,i in enumerate(order): out[i]=monotone[pos]
    return out

def adjust_holm(pvalues):
    m=len(pvalues); order=sorted(range(m),key=pvalues.__getitem__)
    out=[0.0]*m; running=0.0
    for rank,i in enumerate(order):
        running=max(running,min(1.0,(m-rank)*pvalues[i])); out[i]=running
    return out

p=[0.001,0.006,0.011,0.020,0.031,0.070,0.20,0.42,0.60,0.90]
bh=adjust_bh(p); holm=adjust_holm(p)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import false_discovery_control
scipy_bh=false_discovery_control(np.asarray(p),method='bh')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Centralize immutable hypothesis families, include every attempted test, version correction and dependence assumptions, and report adjusted evidence with estimates, intervals, and confirmation status.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert all(0 <= x <= 1 for x in bh+holm)
order=sorted(range(len(p)),key=p.__getitem__)
assert all(bh[order[i]] <= bh[order[i+1]] for i in range(len(p)-1))
assert all(holm[i] >= min(1.0,p[i]) for i in range(len(p)))
assert np.allclose(bh,scipy_bh)

Common mistakes

  • Adjusting only the significant p-values while omitting all tests attempted.
  • Saying FDR q is the probability that each discovery is false.
  • Applying BH without considering dependence assumptions or how the family was selected.
  • Using multiplicity correction as a substitute for valid individual tests, effect sizes, or replication.
  • Treating repeated dashboard updates as one fixed batch family without an online or sequential method.

Likely follow-ups

  • When prefer FWER over FDR?

    Prefer FWER when even one false claim is costly, such as a small confirmatory safety family. Prefer FDR for large screening settings where some false leads are acceptable and discoveries receive follow-up.

  • Why is Holm generally preferable to plain Bonferroni?

    Holm uses progressively less stringent denominators after ordering p-values, retains strong FWER control under broad dependence, and is never less powerful than the single-step Bonferroni rule.

  • Does BH work under correlated tests?

    It controls under independence and certain positive dependence conditions; arbitrary dependence needs additional justification or more conservative/structured methods. Correlation should be part of the method choice, not ignored.

Production / system-design connection

Maintain a hypothesis registry with family ID, owner, estimand, metric version, population, planned direction, decision, and every attempted analysis. Freeze batch families before unblinding or use a formally designed online procedure for incoming tests. Compute adjusted values centrally to prevent teams from omitting tests. Monitor family size, rejection count, p-value histogram, dependence structure, exploratory-to-confirmatory conversion, and replication rate. Store raw and adjusted p-values plus effect intervals; never overwrite raw evidence. Access-control sensitive subgroup findings and apply minimum-cell rules. Version the correction algorithm and sort/tie behavior. Test implementations with known fixtures and invariants. If a family definition or metric changes, create a new analysis version rather than silently recomputing history. Rollback should restore both decisions and their full multiplicity context.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Compute the chance of at least one false positive for 20 independent true nulls at alpha=0.05.

    Show solution

    1-0.95^20, approximately 0.642. This illustrates why per-test alpha is not family-wise control.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    For m=5 and q=0.10, what is the BH threshold at rank 3?

    Show solution

    kq/m=3*0.10/5=0.06. This rank passes if the third sorted p-value is at most 0.06.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why must BH adjusted p-values use a reverse cumulative minimum?

    Show solution

    Without it, adjusted values could decrease at later, larger raw p-values, violating the ordered rejection structure. The cumulative minimum enforces monotonicity across ranks.

7.8

Effect Size vs Statistical Significance

very highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Effect size describes the magnitude of a difference or association; statistical significance describes how incompatible data are with a null model relative to sampling uncertainty. They answer different questions. This chapter covers raw effects, relative effects, standardized mean differences, correlations, odds and risk ratios, number needed to treat, and model-performance changes. It explains why standardization aids comparison but can hide domain meaning, how small-sample bias corrections such as Hedges' g work, and why odds ratios are often misread as risk ratios. You will learn to define a smallest effect of practical interest, pair estimates with uncertainty, distinguish clinical or business importance from detectability, and avoid interpreting noisy subgroup effect sizes without shrinkage. The worked example compares an accurately estimated tiny conversion lift with a larger uncertain one. The lab implements Cohen's d and Hedges' g, verifies scale/translation invariance, and checks against the raw mean difference. Production guidance covers estimand contracts, metric units, heterogeneous effects, decision curves, monitoring, and communication.

Prerequisites

  • confidence-intervals
  • hypothesis-testing

Learning objectives

  • Select raw, relative, standardized, or probability-scale effect measures that match the decision and outcome type.
  • Explain why p-values depend on effect magnitude, noise, sample size, and design while effect size is not significance.
  • Compute standardized mean differences with appropriate pooled variance and small-sample correction.
  • Interpret effects against predefined practical thresholds and report uncertainty, baseline risk, and heterogeneity.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Effect size is the magnitude of the estimand—such as a 1.2 percentage-point lift, relative risk, mean difference, correlation, or standardized mean difference. A p-value combines magnitude with uncertainty and sample size, so a tiny effect can be significant in a huge sample and a useful effect nonsignificant in a small one. Report the effect in domain units first, its interval, baseline risk, and a predefined minimum worthwhile effect. Standardized measures aid comparison but depend on the chosen standard deviation and population.

What you must know

  • Magnitude and evidence are separate
  • Domain units usually lead communication
  • Relative measures require baseline risk
  • Standardized effects depend on reference variability
  • Practical thresholds should be set before results

Why this matters

Decisions care about outcomes, costs, and harms—not whether a test statistic crossed 1.96. Significance-only reporting encourages shipping negligible wins in high-volume data and discarding potentially valuable but uncertain effects in small studies. Standardized effects can compare different scales, but a 'small' d may be important for cheap population-wide interventions and a 'large' d may be irrelevant if the outcome is a proxy. Relative lifts sound dramatic when baseline rates are tiny; absolute differences reveal impact. Interviews test this distinction because it connects statistics with product judgment. Production dashboards should expose both magnitude and uncertainty, with thresholds determined by economics, safety, reversibility, and opportunity cost.

Intuition

Two archers can hit different distances from the bullseye. Effect size is the distance between their average hits. Statistical evidence also considers how scattered the arrows are and how many were fired. Ten thousand tightly grouped arrows can establish a one-millimeter difference; five scattered arrows cannot precisely establish a ten-centimeter difference. A standardized effect divides the distance by a spread measure, making it unitless, but that denominator belongs to a population and design. If one group becomes more heterogeneous, standardized effect changes even when the raw difference does not. For binary outcomes, moving from 1% to 2% is a one-point absolute increase and a 100% relative increase; both are true, but operational consequences depend on population volume and cost.

Raw, relative, and standardized measures

For continuous outcomes, mean or median differences are directly interpretable. Standardized mean difference d divides a mean difference by a within-group SD, often pooled under homoscedastic assumptions. Glass's delta uses a control SD when treatment changes variability. Hedges' g corrects small-sample upward bias in d. Correlation r measures linear association and r squared describes variance explained only under a specified setting. For binary outcomes, risk difference gives absolute change, risk ratio gives multiplicative change, and odds ratio compares odds. Odds ratios increasingly exceed risk ratios as outcomes become common. Number needed to treat is reciprocal absolute risk difference under conditions and can be unstable near zero.

How magnitude, noise, and n produce evidence

A test statistic is often effect estimate divided by standard error. Holding variance and design fixed, larger effects or larger independent samples produce stronger evidence. Thus p-value is not a magnitude measure. Confidence intervals reveal the range of effects compatible with the procedure. A significant effect can lie entirely below the minimum worthwhile effect. A nonsignificant interval may contain both zero and large benefit, signaling insufficient information rather than no effect. Equivalence tests can support that effects are confined within prespecified negligible bounds. Power planning should use a meaningful alternative, not an effect reverse-engineered from a desired sample size.

What standardization clarifies and hides

Dividing by SD makes an effect unitless and facilitates meta-analysis or comparison across instruments, but the chosen SD is influenced by measurement reliability, population heterogeneity, range restriction, and treatment effects on variance. Standardized values can differ across populations for the same raw effect. Conventional labels such as 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 are context-dependent heuristics, not laws. Report the raw effect alongside standardized effect, specify denominator and weighting, and avoid standardizing binary outcomes without a clear latent-scale model. Feature importance scores are not automatically causal effect sizes.

Heterogeneous effects and decision consequences

An average effect can hide benefit for some groups and harm for others. Subgroup estimates have larger uncertainty and multiplicity; use prespecified interactions, hierarchical shrinkage, and validation rather than ranking noisy slices. Decision value combines effect distribution with implementation cost, risk, capacity, fairness, and reversibility. A treatment policy may target units with positive expected net benefit, but observational heterogeneity can reflect confounding. Report distributional outcomes and guardrails when averages conceal tails. Sensitivity to missing data and estimand choices—intention-to-treat versus per-protocol, risk difference versus ratio—belongs in the decision record.

Intervals and transformations for effect measures

Effect estimators have sampling distributions that can be skewed, especially ratios and number-needed-to-treat near a zero risk difference. Construct intervals on a stable scale when appropriate: log risk ratio or log odds ratio, then exponentiate endpoints. A symmetric interval on the ratio scale can include impossible negative values. Standardized mean differences also have nontrivial small-sample uncertainty because the denominator is estimated. For paired or clustered designs, effect and standard error must use the matching covariance structure. When communicating transformed measures, show representative absolute consequences at realistic baselines. An interval for a relative effect does not imply a constant absolute effect across populations with different baseline risk. Sensitivity to scale is substantive, not merely formatting.

Math / formal view

For two independent groups, raw effect Delta=Xbar1-Xbar0. With equal-variance convention, pooled s_p=sqrt(((n1-1)s1^2+(n0-1)s0^2)/(n1+n0-2)), and Cohen's d=Delta/s_p. Hedges' g=J d with approximate J=1-3/(4(n1+n0)-9). For binary outcomes, risk difference=p1-p0, risk ratio=p1/p0, and odds ratio=[p1/(1-p1)]/[p0/(1-p0)]. The standard error of an effect, not the effect alone, determines a test statistic.

Precise tiny lift versus uncertain large lift

Compare both intervals with zero and with a prespecified business threshold, then add baseline volume and cost. Statistical ranking and decision ranking need not agree.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute Cohen's d and Hedges' g, verify translation/scale invariance, and keep the raw effect beside the standardized result.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def variance(xs):
    m=mean(xs); return sum((x-m)**2 for x in xs)/(len(xs)-1)
def standardized_effect(a,b):
    n1,n0=len(a),len(b); v1,v0=variance(a),variance(b)
    pooled=math.sqrt(((n1-1)*v1+(n0-1)*v0)/(n1+n0-2))
    d=(mean(a)-mean(b))/pooled
    correction=1-3/(4*(n1+n0)-9)
    return mean(a)-mean(b),d,correction*d
a=[14,15,13,17,16,18,15,16]; b=[10,12,11,13,9,14,12,11]
raw,d,g=standardized_effect(a,b)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
a_np=np.asarray(a,float); b_np=np.asarray(b,float)
pooled=np.sqrt(((a_np.size-1)*a_np.var(ddof=1)+(b_np.size-1)*b_np.var(ddof=1))/(a_np.size+b_np.size-2))
numpy_d=(a_np.mean()-b_np.mean())/pooled
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Publish domain-unit and standardized effects with intervals, baseline risk, denominator definition, practical thresholds, and slice-aware shrinkage; monitor population scale drift.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(d-numpy_d) < 1e-12
assert abs(g) < abs(d)
_,shifted_d,_=standardized_effect([x+100 for x in a],[x+100 for x in b])
_,scaled_d,_=standardized_effect([x*3 for x in a],[x*3 for x in b])
assert abs(shifted_d-d) < 1e-12
assert abs(scaled_d-d) < 1e-12
assert raw == mean(a)-mean(b)

Common mistakes

  • Calling a smaller p-value a larger effect.
  • Reporting only relative lift without baseline rate or absolute difference.
  • Using universal small/medium/large labels for standardized effects without domain context.
  • Comparing Cohen's d values computed with incompatible populations or variance denominators.
  • Ranking subgroup effects without uncertainty, multiplicity control, or shrinkage.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why can a tiny effect have a tiny p-value?

    Standard error shrinks with independent information. A tiny estimate many SEs from zero can be statistically incompatible with the null while remaining practically negligible.

  • When prefer raw over standardized effect?

    Use raw units when stakeholders understand them and decisions have costs in those units. Add standardized measures for cross-scale comparison, but disclose the denominator and report raw effects too.

  • Why can odds ratio exaggerate intuition for common outcomes?

    Odds and probabilities diverge as baseline risk grows. An odds ratio is not a risk ratio; translate it to absolute risks for representative baselines before communicating impact.

Production / system-design connection

Define estimand, unit, population, horizon, contrast, baseline, effect scale, variance method, and minimum worthwhile benefit/maximum acceptable harm in a metric registry. Show absolute and relative changes with intervals and sample design. Monitor baseline risk, outcome variance, denominator composition, attrition, effect heterogeneity, weight concentration, and decision sensitivity. Use shrinkage and minimum-cell rules for slices, and protect sensitive subgroup data. Validate effect calculations with synthetic fixtures and invariance tests. Keep statistical evidence separate from expected-value modeling but link them in decision records. Version thresholds so teams cannot move them after results. Roll back launches based on guardrail effects and uncertainty, not headline significance alone. Re-estimate when population variance or baseline rate drifts because standardized and relative effects may change meaning.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Conversion rises from 2% to 2.5%. Give absolute and relative effects.

    Show solution

    Absolute risk difference is 0.5 percentage points. Relative risk is 2.5/2=1.25, a 25% relative increase.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Means differ by 4 and pooled SD is 8. What is Cohen's d?

    Show solution

    d=4/8=0.5. Its importance depends on outcome, population, costs, and uncertainty—not a universal label.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    A 95% interval is [0.01,0.05] but minimum worthwhile effect is 0.10. What follows?

    Show solution

    The effect is statistically above zero under the procedure but the entire compatible range is below the predefined worthwhile threshold, arguing against action on benefit grounds.

7.9

ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups

mediumverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Analysis of variance tests whether group means exhibit more between-group variation than expected from within-group variation under a specified model. It avoids the uncontrolled multiplicity of running every pairwise t-test, but a significant omnibus F test says only that not all means are equal. This chapter derives the sums-of-squares decomposition and F ratio, explains degrees of freedom, effect sizes, diagnostics, planned contrasts, post-hoc comparisons, Welch ANOVA, nonparametric alternatives, and extensions to factorial and repeated-measures designs. You will learn why normality concerns residuals rather than raw outcomes, why independence is usually more important than mild normality, and why unequal variance with unbalanced groups can distort classical ANOVA. The worked example decomposes three campaign groups and follows the omnibus test with corrected comparisons. The lab computes one-way ANOVA from first principles, verifies decomposition and translation invariance, and compares with SciPy. Production guidance covers experimental units, contrast registries, assumptions, multiplicity, drift, and reporting estimates rather than only an F statistic.

Prerequisites

  • hypothesis-testing
  • effect-size

Learning objectives

  • Derive between-, within-, and total sums of squares and explain the F ratio as signal relative to noise.
  • Interpret an omnibus rejection without claiming every group differs from every other group.
  • Choose classical, Welch, robust, permutation, or rank-based alternatives according to design and residual behavior.
  • Plan contrasts and adjust post-hoc comparisons while reporting group estimates, intervals, and effect sizes.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

One-way ANOVA tests H0 that all group means are equal by comparing between-group mean square with within-group mean square. F=MS_between/MS_within, with k-1 and N-k degrees of freedom under the classical independent normal equal-variance model. A significant F says at least one mean differs; it does not identify which. Inspect residuals and design, use Welch ANOVA for unequal variances when appropriate, then apply prespecified contrasts or multiplicity-adjusted post-hoc tests and report effect sizes and intervals.

What you must know

  • ANOVA partitions variability around the grand mean
  • The F statistic compares explained with residual variation
  • Omnibus rejection does not identify pairs
  • Residual independence and variance structure matter
  • Contrasts and post-hoc tests need multiplicity discipline

Why this matters

Teams often compare several models, campaigns, regions, or treatments. Repeating unadjusted pairwise tests inflates false-positive risk and fragments one scientific question. ANOVA provides a coherent omnibus comparison and a framework for richer designs. Yet the label is frequently misused: analysts infer that all groups differ, ignore an unbalanced heteroskedastic design, or stop at p<0.05 without estimating meaningful contrasts. Interviews ask for between versus within variance because it reveals whether the candidate understands the geometry. In production, the experimental unit, assignment design, and planned contrasts determine validity. ANOVA is a linear model with categorical predictors, which connects it directly to regression, covariate adjustment, interactions, and robust standard errors.

Intuition

Place each observation around its group mean and each group mean around the grand mean. If group labels contain no mean signal, the movement of group means should be small relative to scatter within groups. ANOVA measures both on comparable per-degree-of-freedom scales. F near one means between-group variation resembles residual variation under the model; a large F is unusual when all means are equal. Large F could arise because one group differs while the rest match, because several move gradually, or because assumptions are broken. The omnibus statistic deliberately compresses these patterns, so follow-up contrasts recover the scientific question. A plot of group estimates and uncertainty often communicates more than the test table.

Partitioning total variability

Let ybar_j be group j mean, ybar the grand mean, and n_j group size. Total sum of squares SST=sum_ij(y_ij-ybar)^2. Between sum SSB=sum_j n_j(ybar_j-ybar)^2. Within sum SSW=sum_ij(y_ij-ybar_j)^2. The identity SST=SSB+SSW is geometric: fitted group deviations and residuals are orthogonal in least squares. Degrees of freedom are N-1 total, k-1 between, and N-k within. Mean squares divide each component by its df. F=MSB/MSW. Under H0 and classical assumptions, both estimate common variance but the numerator grows when group means differ.

What the classical F reference needs

Observations should be independent at the experimental-unit level. Residuals within groups are modeled normal with common variance for the exact small-sample F distribution. Moderate normal departures are often less damaging with adequate balanced samples than outliers, dependence, or severe variance imbalance. Diagnose residual versus fitted plots, group spreads, tails, leverage, missingness, and assignment integrity. Do not test normality mechanically and then choose a method solely from another p-value. In clustered or repeated data, use mixed models, generalized estimating equations, cluster-robust methods, or design-based randomization inference.

Welch, robust, rank, and permutation approaches

Welch ANOVA adjusts weighting and degrees of freedom when variances differ and can be preferable for heteroskedastic groups. Robust trimmed-mean methods reduce sensitivity to outliers. Kruskal–Wallis tests distributional/rank differences and is not simply 'ANOVA on medians'; interpretation depends on distribution shapes. Permutation ANOVA can calibrate a chosen statistic when assignment or exchangeability justifies shuffling, with restrictions for blocks and clusters. Transformations may stabilize variance but change the estimand. Choose the method from the data-generating and decision model, then report the effect scale it actually targets.

Contrasts, post-hoc tests, and effect size

An omnibus rejection licenses investigation under the planned error procedure; it does not show every pair differs. Planned orthogonal or scientifically motivated contrasts are more powerful and interpretable than all pairs. Tukey's method targets family-wise error for pairwise comparisons under its assumptions; Holm can adjust general contrast p-values. Games–Howell is useful for unequal variances. Report group means or marginal means, contrast estimates, intervals, and practical thresholds. Eta squared SSB/SST describes sample variance attributed to group but is biased upward; omega squared applies a correction. Interaction or trend contrasts may answer the real question better than pairwise lists.

Factorial ANOVA, interactions, and estimable contrasts

With two or more factors, main effects average over levels of other factors and can be misleading when interactions are present. An interaction asks whether one factor's effect changes across another factor. Inspect interaction plots and estimate simple effects or planned contrasts instead of interpreting a main-effect p-value in isolation. In unbalanced observational data, sums of squares labeled Type I, II, and III test different hypotheses and depend on coding; there is no universally correct type. Write the estimable contrast explicitly and use a model matrix that matches it. Random factors, repeated measures, and nested units require mixed or hierarchical models rather than treating every level as a fixed independent group. The design determines the error term and denominator degrees of freedom.

Math / formal view

SSB=sum_j n_j(ybar_j-ybar)^2, SSW=sum_j sum_i(y_ij-ybar_j)^2, SST=SSB+SSW. MSB=SSB/(k-1), MSW=SSW/(N-k), and F=MSB/MSW. Under H0 with iid normal errors of common variance, F follows F_(k-1,N-k). Eta squared=SSB/SST. A common omega-squared estimate is (SSB-(k-1)MSW)/(SST+MSW), truncated or interpreted cautiously when negative in samples.

Three campaigns with one separated group

Decompose total variability, compute F, then use a planned C-versus-average(A,B) contrast to show why an omnibus result and pairwise claims are different.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute one-way ANOVA from first principles, verify the sums-of-squares identity and translation invariance, and compare F with SciPy.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def mean(xs): return sum(xs)/len(xs)
def one_way_anova(groups):
    all_values=[x for g in groups for x in g]; grand=mean(all_values)
    ss_between=sum(len(g)*(mean(g)-grand)**2 for g in groups)
    ss_within=sum(sum((x-mean(g))**2 for x in g) for g in groups)
    ss_total=sum((x-grand)**2 for x in all_values)
    df_b=len(groups)-1; df_w=len(all_values)-len(groups)
    f=(ss_between/df_b)/(ss_within/df_w)
    return f,ss_between,ss_within,ss_total
groups=[[8,9,10,11],[9,10,11,12],[15,16,17,18]]
f,sb,sw,st=one_way_anova(groups)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import f_oneway
scipy_result=f_oneway(*groups)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Register units, factors, contrasts, variance model, and multiplicity; validate decomposition and assumptions, then publish domain-unit estimates and adjusted contrast intervals with the omnibus result.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(st-(sb+sw)) < 1e-12
assert abs(f-scipy_result.statistic) < 1e-12
shifted=[[x+100 for x in g] for g in groups]
assert abs(one_way_anova(shifted)[0]-f) < 1e-12
assert f > 1

Common mistakes

  • Concluding every pair differs after a significant omnibus F test.
  • Running all unadjusted pairwise t-tests instead of a planned family-level procedure.
  • Checking normality of pooled raw outcomes rather than residual structure and design.
  • Ignoring unequal variances, unbalanced groups, clustering, repeated measures, or outliers.
  • Reporting only p-values without group estimates, contrasts, intervals, or effect size.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why not just run pairwise t-tests?

    Unadjusted pairwise tests inflate family-wise error and answer fragmented questions. An omnibus model plus planned or adjusted contrasts provides coherent error control and often better power.

  • What does significant ANOVA tell you?

    It rejects the hypothesis that all modeled group means are equal. It does not identify which groups differ, guarantee practical importance, or prove assumptions.

  • When use Welch ANOVA?

    When independent groups have meaningfully unequal variances, especially with unequal sample sizes. It adjusts the reference calculation; still inspect outliers, independence, and the estimand.

Production / system-design connection

Register experimental unit, groups, allocation, factors, interactions, contrasts, primary outcomes, variance method, and multiplicity family before analysis. Validate group counts, randomization balance, missingness, residuals, influence, variance ratios, and cluster structure. Build reusable tests that verify SST=SSB+SSW and match reference libraries on fixtures. Monitor group composition and variance drift; historical thresholds may fail after population change. Report marginal/group means and contrast intervals in domain units with practical boundaries. Protect small-cell results and sensitive categories. Persist model matrix, coding, contrast weights, software versions, and excluded records. When assumptions fail, switch via a documented rule rather than shopping for significance. Rollback conclusions and downstream launch decisions if assignment or outcome instrumentation was faulty.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    ANOVA with k=4 groups and N=40 has what degrees of freedom?

    Show solution

    Between df=k-1=3, within df=N-k=36, and total df=N-1=39.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    If F is significant, may you claim group 1 differs from group 2?

    Show solution

    Not without a corresponding planned or multiplicity-adjusted contrast. The omnibus result only says not all group means are equal.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why can variance imbalance be especially harmful with unequal n?

    Show solution

    The pooled within variance weights groups in a way that may mismatch the sampling variance of mean differences, distorting the classical F reference; the direction depends on the pairing of variances and sizes.

7.10

Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data

mediumverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Chi-square methods compare observed categorical counts with counts expected under a null model. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether one categorical distribution matches specified probabilities; the independence or homogeneity test asks whether two categorical variables are associated or whether group distributions agree. This chapter derives Pearson's statistic from standardized cell residuals, explains degrees of freedom and expected-count calculation, connects the contingency-table test with likelihood-ratio and log-linear models, and distinguishes association from causation. You will learn why tests operate on counts rather than percentages, when asymptotic calibration is unreliable, how sparse tables and structural zeros require exact, Monte Carlo, or category-restructuring approaches, and why a significant table needs cell-level residuals and effect sizes such as Cramér's V. The worked example analyzes channel by conversion status and identifies which cells drive the result. The lab computes expected counts and Pearson's statistic from first principles, verifies marginal preservation and decomposition, and compares with SciPy. Production guidance covers category contracts, rare-level handling, weighting, multiplicity, privacy, and drift.

Prerequisites

  • hypothesis-testing
  • distributions

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish chi-square goodness-of-fit, independence, and homogeneity questions and formulate their null models.
  • Compute expected counts, Pearson cell contributions, the total statistic, and correct degrees of freedom.
  • Diagnose sparse counts, structural zeros, dependence, sampling weights, and post-hoc cell inspection.
  • Report residual patterns and association magnitude without interpreting association as causation.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Pearson's chi-square statistic sums (observed-expected)^2/expected across categorical cells. For an r-by-c independence table, expected count is row total times column total divided by grand total and df=(r-1)(c-1), assuming independent units and adequate asymptotic counts. A significant result says the variables are associated, not which cells differ or that one causes the other. Inspect standardized residuals, report an effect size such as Cramér's V, adjust post-hoc analyses, and use exact or Monte Carlo methods for sparse tables.

What you must know

  • Expected counts come from the null and fixed margins
  • Each cell contributes a squared standardized discrepancy
  • Degrees of freedom reflect marginal constraints
  • Sparse or dependent data break the usual reference
  • Association magnitude and cell pattern follow the omnibus test

Why this matters

Categorical questions appear everywhere: device by failure type, region by churn state, model by error category, or treatment by outcome. A contingency table is easy to create, which makes it easy to misuse. Analysts test percentages instead of counts, treat thousands of repeated events as independent, combine categories after seeing significance, or conclude causation from association. A single chi-square p-value also hides whether one rare cell or a broad pattern drives the result. Interviews ask expected-count formulas and assumptions, but production work additionally needs category lineage, stable denominators, privacy safeguards, and effect interpretation. Chi-square is best seen as a model comparison for counts rather than a ritual attached to a crosstab.

Intuition

Under independence, knowing the row should not change the column distribution. If 30% of all observations converted, each row is expected to have roughly 30% conversions, scaled to its row total. Compare every observed cell with that expected value. A discrepancy of 10 matters more when only 5 were expected than when 5,000 were expected, so Pearson divides squared discrepancy by expected count. The contributions add; cells with large contributions reveal where the table departs from the null. Because row and column totals constrain the table, only (r-1)(c-1) cell directions vary freely. As sample size grows, even tiny association can be highly significant, so pair the test with residuals and a magnitude measure.

Goodness of fit, independence, and homogeneity

Goodness of fit compares one observed count vector O_i with fully specified null probabilities p_i, so E_i=n p_i and typically df=k-1 minus parameters estimated from the same data. Independence uses one joint sample cross-classified by two variables and tests p_ij=p_i+ p_+j, estimating expected counts from both margins. Homogeneity compares category distributions across independently sampled populations; its table statistic can be identical but the design and verbal conclusion differ. A two-by-two treatment table may also be analyzed through risk difference, ratio, odds ratio, exact randomization, or regression. Choose based on estimand rather than defaulting to chi-square.

Expected counts, residuals, and degrees of freedom

For r-by-c independence, E_ij=(row_i total)(column_j total)/N. Pearson X^2=sum_ij (O_ij-E_ij)^2/E_ij. Raw Pearson residual is (O-E)/sqrt(E); adjusted standardized residuals account for estimated row and column proportions and are more comparable. The total decomposes into cell contributions, but examining many residuals after a significant omnibus test creates multiplicity and selection concerns. Degrees of freedom (r-1)(c-1) arise because fixed margins impose r+c-1 independent constraints on rc cells. For goodness of fit, estimating model parameters consumes additional df. Software conventions should be verified.

Sparse tables, zeros, and alternative calibration

The chi-square approximation can be poor when expected counts are small or the table is sparse. The familiar 'all expected at least five' is a conservative heuristic, not a universal theorem. Fisher's exact test conditions on margins for a two-by-two table and tests an odds-ratio null; larger exact tests can be expensive. Monte Carlo sampling from the correct null provides calibrated approximations. Combining rare categories is acceptable only when substantively defensible and preferably prespecified. A structural zero is impossible by design and should not be treated as a sampling zero. For ordered categories, a trend test can be more powerful than an unordered omnibus test. Penalized or hierarchical models help with many sparse levels.

Dependence, weights, effect size, and causality

Repeated observations from a user, clustered survey samples, and time dependence violate multinomial independence. Survey-weighted tables require design-based tests such as Rao–Scott adjustments, not simply feeding weighted noninteger counts to an ordinary test. A significant association may reflect confounding, selection, measurement, or reverse causality. Cramér's V=sqrt(X^2/(N min(r-1,c-1))) summarizes strength but remains sample/population dependent and does not convey direction; for two-by-two tables report risks and odds ratios with intervals. Visualize observed-minus-expected residuals and report absolute cell rates. Large N can make negligible associations significant.

Log-linear and regression connections

A contingency table can be modeled with Poisson log-linear terms. Independence corresponds to row and column main effects without their interaction; adding the interaction saturates a two-way table. Pearson X-squared and likelihood-ratio G-squared compare observed counts with the fitted independence model and become asymptotically equivalent. Logistic regression conditions on one margin and expresses a binary column outcome through row predictors, allowing covariate adjustment and interpretable odds ratios. These models extend beyond an omnibus table but add specification choices and sparse-cell risks. For multiway tables, marginal associations can reverse after stratification, echoing Simpson's paradox. Choose a model that preserves the sampling design and report adjusted and unadjusted patterns rather than treating one aggregated chi-square result as complete.

Math / formal view

For independence, E_ij=R_i C_j/N and X^2=sum_ij (O_ij-E_ij)^2/E_ij, approximately chi-square with (r-1)(c-1) df under H0 and regularity. The likelihood-ratio statistic G^2=2 sum O_ij log(O_ij/E_ij), treating zero terms as zero, has the same asymptotic reference. Cramér's V=sqrt(X^2/[N min(r-1,c-1)]). Pearson cell contributions are nonnegative and sum exactly to X^2, providing an audit trail from table to statistic.

Acquisition channel and conversion

Construct expected counts from margins, decompose Pearson's statistic by cell, inspect residual direction, and translate the association back to channel-specific rates without making a causal claim.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute a Pearson independence test from scratch, verify expected margins and cell decomposition, and compare with SciPy.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def chi_square_independence(table):
    rows=len(table); cols=len(table[0])
    row_totals=[sum(row) for row in table]
    col_totals=[sum(table[i][j] for i in range(rows)) for j in range(cols)]
    total=sum(row_totals)
    expected=[[row_totals[i]*col_totals[j]/total for j in range(cols)] for i in range(rows)]
    contributions=[[(table[i][j]-expected[i][j])**2/expected[i][j] for j in range(cols)] for i in range(rows)]
    statistic=sum(sum(row) for row in contributions)
    return statistic,expected,contributions,(rows-1)*(cols-1)
table=[[90,10],[160,40],[150,50]]
statistic,expected,contrib,df=chi_square_independence(table)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
result=chi2_contingency(np.asarray(table),correction=False)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version taxonomy and independent unit, retain counts and expected cells, diagnose sparse/clustered designs, protect rare categories, and publish residual patterns plus effect size with the omnibus result.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(statistic-result.statistic) < 1e-12
assert df == result.dof == 2
assert np.allclose(expected,result.expected_freq)
assert all(abs(sum(expected[i])-sum(table[i])) < 1e-12 for i in range(len(table)))
assert abs(sum(sum(row) for row in contrib)-statistic) < 1e-12

Common mistakes

  • Applying the formula to percentages rather than original counts and sample sizes.
  • Treating repeated rows from the same unit as independent categorical observations.
  • Using an asymptotic chi-square reference with sparse expected counts or structural zeros without diagnosis.
  • Concluding causation or claiming every category differs after an omnibus rejection.
  • Inspecting many cell residuals without adjustment and reporting only the most surprising one.

Likely follow-ups

  • How are expected counts computed for independence?

    Multiply the cell's row total by its column total and divide by grand total. This is the fitted count under the product of estimated marginal proportions.

  • What if expected counts are small?

    Inspect the whole table and design. Consider an exact or Monte Carlo test, substantively justified category pooling, or a sparse categorical model; do not rely mechanically on an asymptotic reference.

  • Does significant chi-square imply a strong relationship?

    No. Significance combines discrepancy with sample size. Report cell rates/residuals and an association measure such as Cramér's V, then judge practical importance.

Production / system-design connection

Version category definitions, ordering, unknown handling, observation unit, population window, and table construction. Validate that counts reconcile with source totals and expected margins. Monitor rare-level frequency, structural/sampling zeros, expected-count distribution, residual hotspots, Cramér's V, sample size, and cluster duplication. Apply design-aware methods for surveys and repeated units. Prespecify category pooling and post-hoc residual families. Enforce minimum cell sizes and disclosure controls for sensitive groups; avoid dashboards that expose rare identities. Keep raw counts alongside percentages and test metadata. Test implementations with known tables, transpose invariance, marginal preservation, and contribution sums. When taxonomy changes, do not compare old and new chi-square statistics without a mapping. Roll back downstream alerts if category instrumentation or deduplication failed.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A row total is 80, column total 50, and N=200. What is expected count under independence?

    Show solution

    E=80*50/200=20.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    What are df for a 3-by-4 independence table?

    Show solution

    (3-1)(4-1)=6, assuming no structural zeros or additional fitted constraints.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why can a huge chi-square test reject for an unimportant association?

    Show solution

    The statistic scales with N for a fixed discrepancy in proportions. With huge samples, tiny deviations become detectable; effect size and domain consequences must be reported.

7.11

Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size

very highverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Statistical power is the probability that a prespecified procedure rejects its null under a particular alternative. Sample-size planning connects that operating characteristic to a meaningful effect, variance, alpha, allocation, design, attrition, and decision horizon. This chapter derives normal-mean scaling, distinguishes minimum detectable effect from minimum worthwhile effect, explains one- versus two-sided tests, unequal allocation, clustering, multiple testing, sequential designs, and simulation-based power for complex estimators. You will learn why post-hoc observed power adds little beyond the p-value, why plugging optimistic variance or conversion assumptions understates required sample size, and why increasing rows does not overcome correlation or bias. The worked example plans a two-arm conversion experiment in absolute percentage points and inflates for attrition and design effect. The lab implements an approximate two-sample proportion calculation, verifies monotonic relationships, and compares a t-test case with statsmodels. Production guidance covers preregistered assumptions, traffic forecasts, guardrails, simulation, re-estimation without unblinding effects, monitoring, and stopping behavior.

Prerequisites

  • hypothesis-testing
  • effect-size
  • sampling-distributions

Learning objectives

  • Define power as a function of a specific alternative, procedure, design, and sample size.
  • Distinguish minimum detectable, minimum worthwhile, and observed effects in planning and interpretation.
  • Compute approximate sample sizes and adjust for allocation, clustering, attrition, multiplicity, and sequential monitoring.
  • Use simulation to validate analytic power for complex metrics and avoid post-hoc observed-power misuse.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Power is P(reject H0|a specified alternative is true), equal to 1-beta for a fixed design and test. Sample size grows with variance, stricter alpha, higher target power, and smaller effect—often approximately inverse-square in the detectable effect. Plan using the smallest effect worth acting on, realistic baseline/variance, independent unit, allocation, attrition, clustering, multiplicity, and stopping rule. MDE is what a design can reliably detect, not necessarily what matters. Do not use observed post-hoc power as new evidence; report the effect interval.

What you must know

  • Power is a curve over alternatives, not one universal number
  • Effect threshold and variance drive sample size
  • Independent information matters more than row count
  • Design corrections must be included before launch
  • Simulation audits formulas for real metrics and pipelines

Why this matters

Underpowered studies waste traffic and produce ambiguous intervals; overpowered studies may waste time detecting effects too small to matter. Product teams often choose 80% power by convention, back-solve an MDE from available traffic, then mistake detectability for value. Planning forces the decision threshold, baseline variability, unit, and analysis into the open. Interviews test how n changes with effect size and variance. Production planning must also incorporate cluster assignment, unequal traffic costs, guardrails, attrition, repeated looks, and ramp schedules. Because power is conditional on assumptions, a precise sample-size number should be accompanied by sensitivity analysis. Bias and instrumentation errors are not cured by large n.

Intuition

Picture null and alternative sampling distributions of an estimator. Alpha chooses a rejection boundary in the null tail. Power is the area of the alternative distribution beyond that boundary. Increasing independent sample size narrows both distributions, separating them in standard-error units. A larger true effect also separates their centers. Stricter alpha moves the boundary outward, reducing power unless n grows. More noise broadens distributions and requires more information. If users generate correlated events, adding events without users barely narrows the relevant estimator. An MDE is the alternative whose power reaches the target under the planned design. A minimum worthwhile effect comes from economics or safety. Good plans align them or explain the gap.

Alpha, beta, effect, and the power curve

For a one-sided normal test with known SE, choose a critical boundary so null rejection probability is alpha. Under alternative delta, power is the probability the shifted estimator crosses that boundary. At delta=0, power equals alpha for a simple boundary. As delta grows in the targeted direction, power rises. Two-sided tests allocate error to both tails and require more separation for the same directional effect. Power should be shown across a range including harm, zero, minimum worthwhile effect, and optimistic effect. Type S (wrong sign) and Type M (magnitude exaggeration conditional on significance) risks can be substantial in low-power studies.

Approximate scaling and planning inputs

For equal-size normal groups with common SD sigma and target raw difference delta, a common approximation per arm is n≈2 sigma^2(z_(1-alpha/2)+z_power)^2/delta^2. Halving delta quadruples n; doubling sigma quadruples n. Proportions require variance tied to baseline and alternative, and rare events may need exact or simulation methods. Unequal allocation increases total n for fixed precision unless one arm is cheaper or constrained. Use variance from representative historical data without leaking future treatment outcomes. Include uncertainty in baseline and variance through scenarios rather than one optimistic input.

Clustering, attrition, multiplicity, and sequential designs

For equal cluster size m and intraclass correlation rho, design effect is approximately 1+(m-1)rho; multiply simple-random sample size, then account for the number of independent clusters and small-cluster inference. Inflate for expected attrition by dividing by retained fraction, while addressing whether attrition is differential and biasing. Multiple primary comparisons may use adjusted alpha, increasing n. Covariate adjustment can reduce residual variance if planned and measured pre-treatment. Sequential or group-sequential designs have their own boundaries and expected sample sizes; do not mix a fixed-horizon calculation with continuous peeking. Ramp-up and delayed outcomes determine calendar duration.

Simulation-based power and what not to do

For ratios, quantiles, clustered assignment, CUPED, missing outcomes, complex models, or adaptive rules, simulate the full data-generating and analysis pipeline under many alternatives. Include assignment, preprocessing, estimator, exclusions, variance, stopping, and multiplicity. Verify Type I error at the null before trusting power. Post-hoc observed power computed by plugging the observed effect into the prospective formula is a monotone transformation of the test statistic and adds no independent information; use the confidence interval and sensitivity analysis. Re-estimating nuisance variance during a blinded design may be possible, but changing effect targets after seeing treatment differences compromises interpretation.

Planning for estimation precision instead of rejection

Some decisions need an interval narrow enough for action rather than a chosen rejection probability. Precision planning selects n so the expected or high-probability confidence-interval half-width falls below a tolerance. For a mean with known sigma, half-width is approximately z sigma/sqrt(n); proportions are widest near one-half. Precision criteria avoid framing an exact-zero null when the real question is how accurately an effect must be known. Assurance methods integrate power over uncertainty in nuisance parameters or prior beliefs, producing a probability that a future study meets its goal. Whatever criterion is used, simulate interval width and decision success across plausible baselines, variances, attrition, and effects. State whether n guarantees expected, median, or worst-case precision.

Math / formal view

For equal-size two-sample means with known common sigma and two-sided alpha, approximate per-arm n=2 sigma^2(z_(1-alpha/2)+z_(1-beta))^2/delta^2. Standardized effect d=delta/sigma gives n≈2(z_alpha+z_power)^2/d^2. Cluster design effect DE=1+(m-1)rho under equal cluster sizes. Attrition inflation is n_enroll=n_analyzable/(1-a). Exact formulas vary with test, finite df, baseline proportion, allocation, correction, and sequential boundary; official software conventions must be verified.

Conversion experiment with clustering and attrition

Start from a business-derived absolute lift, calculate simple-design n, multiply by design effect, divide by retention, then simulation-check the actual estimator and stopping rule.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute approximate two-proportion sample size, verify monotonic design relationships, and compare an independent t-test case with statsmodels.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math
from statistics import NormalDist

def n_per_arm_proportions(p0,p1,alpha=0.05,power=0.8):
    if not (0<p0<1 and 0<p1<1 and p0!=p1): raise ValueError('valid distinct probabilities required')
    z_alpha=NormalDist().inv_cdf(1-alpha/2)
    z_power=NormalDist().inv_cdf(power)
    pbar=(p0+p1)/2
    numerator=(z_alpha*math.sqrt(2*pbar*(1-pbar))+z_power*math.sqrt(p0*(1-p0)+p1*(1-p1)))**2
    return math.ceil(numerator/(p1-p0)**2)
n=n_per_arm_proportions(0.10,0.11)
n_smaller_effect=n_per_arm_proportions(0.10,0.105)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower
analysis=TTestIndPower()
t_n=analysis.solve_power(effect_size=0.30,alpha=0.05,power=0.80,ratio=1.0,alternative='two-sided')
t_power=analysis.power(effect_size=0.30,nobs1=t_n,alpha=0.05,ratio=1.0,alternative='two-sided')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version all design assumptions, calculate on independent units, include clustering/attrition/multiplicity/stopping, and simulation-check both null error and power before enrollment.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert n > 0
assert n_smaller_effect > n
assert n_per_arm_proportions(0.10,0.12) < n
assert abs(t_power-0.80) < 1e-6
design_effect=1+(5-1)*0.20
assert design_effect == 1.8

Common mistakes

  • Choosing MDE only from available traffic and presenting it as a minimum worthwhile effect.
  • Computing post-hoc observed power and treating it as evidence beyond the estimate and p-value.
  • Using row count instead of independent assignment units or ignoring cluster design effect.
  • Planning with optimistic variance, baseline, compliance, or attrition and no sensitivity analysis.
  • Using a fixed-horizon power calculation while continuously peeking or adjusting many primary metrics.

Likely follow-ups

  • What happens to n if the target effect is halved?

    Under common normal approximations, n scales as 1/delta squared, so halving the effect requires about four times the independent sample size, all else equal.

  • Is 80% power always correct?

    No. It is a convention. Choose power from the cost of missing a worthwhile effect, test cost, decision reversibility, available traffic, and error trade-offs; safety contexts may demand more.

  • Why avoid observed post-hoc power?

    Plugging the observed effect into the same test formula makes observed power largely a re-expression of the p-value and encourages circular conclusions. The confidence interval more directly shows uncertainty and compatible effects.

Production / system-design connection

Maintain a versioned design document with estimand, unit, baseline, variance source, worthwhile effect, alpha, power, sidedness, allocation, covariates, clusters, attrition, multiplicity, stopping rule, ramp, and outcome delay. Generate sensitivity tables over plausible inputs and simulation-check Type I error and power. Forecast eligible independent units—not events—and monitor enrollment, balance, attrition, cluster sizes, ICC, metric variance, and data latency without unblinding effect-driven changes. Predefine blinded nuisance re-estimation if needed. Secure treatment outcomes and subgroup plans. Store simulator code, RNG streams, software versions, and result summaries. If traffic or variance assumptions fail, extend or stop according to the protocol rather than moving targets. Roll back decisions if integrity checks invalidate the planned operating characteristics.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    If SD doubles while effect, alpha, and power stay fixed, how does approximate n change?

    Show solution

    n is proportional to sigma squared, so it increases by a factor of four.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    A cluster design has m=5 and rho=0.20. Compute equal-size design effect.

    Show solution

    DE=1+(5-1)*0.20=1.8. Multiply the simple-random information requirement by roughly 1.8, then ensure enough independent clusters.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    You need 10,000 analyzable units and expect 20% attrition. How many enroll?

    Show solution

    10,000/(1-0.20)=12,500. This inflation addresses quantity, not bias from differential attrition.

7.12

Sampling Design: Random, Stratified & Cluster Sampling

highverified
Roles: ds

Topic overview

Sampling design determines which population units can enter a dataset and with what probability. Simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, multistage, and unequal-probability samples trade cost, coverage, and precision differently; their weights and dependence structure must flow into estimation and uncertainty. This chapter defines target and frame populations, inclusion probabilities, base weights, stratification gains, cluster design effects, finite-population correction, probability-proportional-to-size sampling, and design-based versus model-based inference. You will learn why stratification and clustering are not opposites, how self-weighting designs can emerge across stages, why convenience and quota samples do not acquire probability-sample guarantees from large n, and how nonresponse adjustments and calibration alter both bias and variance. The worked example estimates a company-wide mean from disproportionate department strata. The lab implements a Horvitz–Thompson-style weighted mean, verifies recovery on a finite population, and demonstrates stratification variance reduction. Production guidance covers frame snapshots, inclusion-probability lineage, replicate variance, privacy, monitoring, and survey lifecycle controls.

Prerequisites

  • probability-basics
  • sampling-distributions
  • expectation-variance

Learning objectives

  • Map target population, sampling frame, unit, stages, strata, clusters, and inclusion probabilities before analysis.
  • Explain when stratification improves precision and when cluster sampling reduces cost while increasing variance.
  • Compute design-weighted estimates and understand finite-population and design-effect adjustments.
  • Diagnose coverage, unequal weighting, nonresponse, and variance-estimation failures in complex samples.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A probability sample gives each frame unit a known nonzero inclusion probability. Simple random sampling selects units directly; stratification samples within homogeneous subgroups to guarantee coverage and often improve precision; cluster sampling selects groups for cost efficiency but induces correlation and often increases variance; multistage designs combine them. Estimate population quantities with design weights, typically inverse inclusion probabilities, and compute design-aware variance using strata, clusters, finite-population corrections, or replicate weights. Large convenience samples do not have these guarantees.

What you must know

  • The frame is not automatically the target population
  • Known inclusion probabilities enable design-based weighting
  • Strata seek internal homogeneity; clusters are often internally heterogeneous but correlated
  • Weights affect point estimates and effective information
  • Variance must reflect every sampling stage

Why this matters

Inference quality begins before modeling. A perfectly computed confidence interval from a biased frame can be tightly wrong. Sampling designs balance travel, recruitment, rare-group coverage, and measurement cost. Data scientists encounter the same logic in annotation, evaluation sets, audits, telemetry subsampling, and human-feedback collection. Interviews ask stratified versus cluster sampling; a mature answer mentions inclusion probabilities, variance, and logistics. In production, samples are often joined to population totals, refreshed over time, or adjusted for nonresponse. Losing frame versions or weight lineage makes estimates irreproducible. Complex design is not a nuisance to drop in preprocessing—it defines the probability law supporting inference.

Intuition

To estimate a university-wide mean, simple random sampling draws students from one complete list. Stratification first separates undergraduates and graduates, then samples from both; this prevents a small but important group from disappearing and can reduce variance when groups differ but are internally consistent. Cluster sampling draws whole classes because visiting a few classrooms is cheap; students in the same class may be similar, so 100 clustered students carry less information than 100 spread across campus. Multistage sampling selects campuses, then classes, then students. If selection rates differ, each sampled unit represents a different number of population units, so inverse-probability weights reconstruct the target. The design saves cost at the price of more elaborate estimation.

Target, frame, and sampling units

The target population is the set about which the estimand speaks. The sampling frame is the operational list or mechanism from which units can be selected. Undercoverage excludes eligible target units; overcoverage includes ineligible or duplicate units. Define primary sampling units, later-stage units, eligibility dates, and frame version. An element may have multiple frame entries, changing inclusion probability. A probability sample requires known nonzero inclusion probability for every covered target unit; it does not guarantee zero nonresponse or measurement error. Coverage evaluation compares frame totals and distributions with authoritative benchmarks and investigates unreachable groups.

Simple, systematic, stratified, cluster, and multistage designs

Simple random sampling selects every size-n subset with equal probability. Systematic sampling chooses a random start and fixed interval; hidden periodicity in frame order can harm it. Stratified sampling partitions the frame and samples independently within strata, guaranteeing subgroup representation; proportional allocation can be self-weighting, while Neyman allocation assigns more sample to large, variable strata for precision. Cluster sampling selects groups and observes all or sampled elements inside them, reducing field cost but adding intracluster correlation. Multistage designs combine strata, PSUs, households, and people. Probability-proportional-to-size sampling can equalize later-stage weights when clusters vary greatly.

Inclusion probabilities, weights, and finite populations

Base weight w_i=1/pi_i represents how many population units sampled unit i stands for. Horvitz–Thompson totals sum y_i/pi_i; ratio or Hájek means divide weighted outcome by weighted count and trade small bias for stability. Adjust weights for nonresponse within cells or propensity models, then calibrate/rake to trusted margins. Trimming extreme weights reduces variance but can introduce bias. Effective sample size based on weight concentration is a diagnostic, not a complete variance estimator. When a large fraction of a finite population is sampled without replacement, the finite-population correction reduces variance. Preserve every adjustment factor, cap, and benchmark date.

Variance, design effects, and domain estimation

Strata usually reduce variance when internally homogeneous and all are represented; clusters often increase it because neighbors resemble one another. Taylor linearization, replication methods such as jackknife/BRR/bootstrap, or exact design formulas estimate variance. Replicate weights encode the agency's approved procedure and should be used as documented. Treating a complex survey as iid usually understates SE, as CDC guidance emphasizes. Domain estimates should retain the full sample and define subpopulation indicators so design variance includes correct PSUs/strata; physically filtering can lose variance information in some software. Small numbers of PSUs require special handling. Report unweighted n, weighted population size, design df, and effective precision.

Optimal allocation under cost and precision constraints

Proportional stratified allocation n_h proportional to N_h yields equal weights when within-stratum sampling fractions match. Neyman allocation n_h proportional to N_h S_h places more sample in large, variable strata to minimize variance for fixed n. With unequal per-unit costs, optimal allocation also discounts expensive strata by the square root of cost, subject to minimum subgroup requirements. Operational constraints and multiple estimands may override a single-variable optimum. Oversampling rare groups improves their domain precision but requires weights for population totals. Allocation values estimated from old data can drift; use conservative floors and sensitivity analysis. Record whether the design optimizes one primary estimand, balances several, or guarantees reporting standards, because the resulting sample is not universally optimal.

Math / formal view

For inclusion indicator I_i with P(I_i=1)=pi_i, Horvitz–Thompson total t_hat=sum_{i in s} y_i/pi_i is design-unbiased because E[I_i y_i/pi_i]=y_i. A Hájek mean is sum w_i y_i/sum w_i. For SRS without replacement, SE(mean)=sqrt((1-n/N) S^2/n) using an appropriate sample estimate. Equal-size cluster design effect is approximately 1+(m-1)rho. Weight-only Kish effective n is (sum w)^2/sum w^2, which omits stratification and clustering.

Disproportionate department stratification

Use inverse inclusion probabilities to recover the company population composition, then estimate uncertainty separately within strata with finite-population corrections.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute inverse-probability weighted estimates, verify a stratified finite-population mean, and show why the unweighted estimate is biased under disproportionate allocation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def weighted_mean(values,weights):
    if len(values)!=len(weights) or any(w<=0 for w in weights): raise ValueError('valid weights required')
    return sum(v*w for v,w in zip(values,weights))/sum(weights)

eng=[72.0]*90; support=[60.0]*50
values=eng+support
weights=[10.0]*len(eng)+[2.0]*len(support)
design_mean=weighted_mean(values,weights)
unweighted=sum(values)/len(values)
truth=(900*72+100*60)/1000
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
np_weighted=float(np.average(np.asarray(values),weights=np.asarray(weights)))
weight_effective_n=(sum(weights)**2)/sum(w*w for w in weights)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Preserve frame, stages, strata, clusters, inclusion probabilities, every weight adjustment, and replicate-variance method; publish weighted estimates with unweighted n and design diagnostics.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(design_mean-truth) < 1e-12
assert abs(np_weighted-design_mean) < 1e-12
assert abs(unweighted-truth) > 1.0
assert 0 < weight_effective_n <= len(values)
assert abs(sum(weights)-1000) < 1e-12

Common mistakes

  • Equating the sampling frame with the target population without coverage analysis.
  • Using unweighted estimates after disproportionate sampling or weight trimming without bias assessment.
  • Treating cluster members as independent and reporting iid standard errors.
  • Confusing stratification, which samples every stratum, with selecting a subset of clusters.
  • Believing a very large convenience or quota sample has probability-sample guarantees.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why can stratification reduce variance?

    If strata are internally homogeneous and differ in means, sampling within every stratum removes between-stratum composition fluctuation and allocates observations efficiently.

  • Why can clustering increase variance?

    Units within clusters often correlate, so additional members repeat similar information. The design saves collection cost but reduces effective sample size relative to dispersed independent units.

  • What is a sampling weight?

    A base weight is typically the inverse inclusion probability. Final weights may also include nonresponse adjustment, calibration, trimming, and other factors; their lineage and variance method must be retained.

Production / system-design connection

Snapshot target definition and every frame used for selection. Store unit IDs, stages, strata, PSUs, inclusion probabilities, base and adjustment weight factors, replicate weights, finite population sizes, eligibility rules, contact outcomes, and benchmark versions. Validate probability bounds, weight sums, duplicate frame links, selected counts, stratum coverage, and reconciliation to controls. Monitor weight concentration, design effect, response by stratum, frame churn, coverage gaps, PSU counts, and variance stability. Use privacy-preserving IDs and minimum domain sizes. Survey software and replicate-weight conventions should be verified against official documentation. Reproduce draws with secure seeded RNG where appropriate while preventing manipulation. If the frame or weights are corrupted, withdraw estimates and rebuild from the preserved snapshot rather than patching final tables. Rollback includes estimates, SEs, and published population totals.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A unit has inclusion probability 0.02. What is its base weight?

    Show solution

    1/0.02=50; it represents about 50 frame units before nonresponse or calibration adjustments.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Why does sampling 20 people in each of 50 clusters differ from sampling 1,000 people independently?

    Show solution

    Within-cluster correlation makes observations partially redundant. Variance depends on cluster sizes and ICC, so effective information can be much lower than 1,000 iid units.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    A sample takes 400 of N=1,000 units without replacement. What finite-population factor multiplies the iid SE approximately?

    Show solution

    sqrt((N-n)/(N-1))=sqrt(600/999), about 0.775, assuming SRS and a finite-population mean target.
