7.13

Selection, Coverage & Nonresponse Bias

very highverified
Roles: ds

Topic overview

Selection, coverage, and nonresponse bias arise when observed units differ systematically from the target population in ways related to the outcome or estimand. More rows reduce sampling variance but do not automatically reduce these biases; a massive opt-in dataset can be precisely wrong. This chapter decomposes total survey error, distinguishes target population, frame coverage, unit nonresponse, item nonresponse, attrition, and conditioning on selection, and explains why response rate alone does not determine bias. You will learn to draw selection diagrams, compare respondents with frame benchmarks, use inverse-probability weighting, calibration, imputation, follow-up samples, and sensitivity analysis, while stating the untestable assumptions each method needs. The worked example shows how differential response reverses an apparent support rate and how weighting helps only with observed adjustment variables. The lab simulates outcome-related response, quantifies bias, applies poststratification, and verifies when correction succeeds or fails. Production guidance covers contact paradata, consent, privacy, weight lineage, monitoring, bounded corrections, and transparent residual-uncertainty reporting.

Prerequisites

  • sampling-design
  • joint-marginal-conditional

Learning objectives

  • Separate undercoverage, overcoverage, unit nonresponse, item nonresponse, attrition, and measurement error in a total-error framework.
  • Explain why response rate and sample size alone do not identify nonresponse or selection bias.
  • Apply weighting, calibration, imputation, follow-up, and sensitivity methods with explicit exchangeability and positivity assumptions.
  • Design diagnostics and monitoring that compare observed samples with frames, benchmarks, and hard-to-reach follow-up data.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Selection bias occurs when inclusion depends on variables related to the outcome after conditioning on what the analysis uses. Coverage bias comes from the frame missing or duplicating target units; nonresponse bias comes when sampled respondents differ from nonrespondents on the estimand. Bias is not determined by response rate alone: it depends on response–outcome association. Weighting or imputation can correct differences explained by observed variables with overlap and valid models, but not unknown unmeasured selection without assumptions. Compare to frame benchmarks, model response, conduct targeted follow-up, and report sensitivity analyses.

What you must know

  • Large n attacks variance, not systematic selection
  • Response rate is a risk indicator, not a bias estimate
  • Adjustment needs outcome-relevant observed variables and positivity
  • Conditioning on a collider can create association
  • Residual selection uncertainty requires sensitivity and external evidence

Why this matters

Many data products observe only app users who consented, customers who answered, patients who remained, devices that connected, or labels that annotators could resolve. Modeling the observed rows as if they were a random population sample can dominate every later algorithmic choice. Interviews ask about survivorship and nonresponse because they test causal and survey reasoning. Production systems are especially vulnerable to feedback: a model changes who is shown an option, which changes who produces labels, which shapes the next model. Weighting can look scientific while extrapolating from near-zero-probability groups or calibrating only easy margins. Bias analysis requires operational data about the frame and contact process, not only the final table.

Intuition

Suppose satisfied and dissatisfied customers answer a survey at different rates. The respondent mean mixes two things: how common each group is and how likely each is to appear. A million responses do not reveal the silent group if its response probability is tiny. If response differences are fully explained by known age and region and every cell has respondents, weighting cells back to population shares can recover the target under a within-cell exchangeability assumption. If response also depends on unobserved satisfaction inside cells, weighting remains biased. Response rate can be low with little bias when response is unrelated to outcome, or high with serious bias when a small outcome-critical group is systematically absent.

Coverage, nonresponse, attrition, and measurement

Undercoverage occurs when target units have no frame representation; overcoverage includes ineligible or duplicate entries. Unit nonresponse means no usable record from a sampled unit; item nonresponse leaves specific variables missing. Attrition is longitudinal dropout and can depend on evolving outcomes. Measurement error can correlate with response and survive weighting. Processing errors, mode effects, and timing add further nonsampling error. Separate these mechanisms because remedies differ: improve the frame, deduplicate, redesign contacts, impute items, model censoring, validate instruments, or revise processing. A final complete-case dataset hides this lineage, so retain disposition codes and denominators.

Why response rate does not equal bias

For a mean, nonresponse bias can be expressed using response rate and the difference between respondent and nonrespondent means; the latter is usually unknown. A low rate increases concern but can have small bias if groups have similar outcomes. A high rate can hide large bias if the missing group is small but extreme. Compare respondents and nonrespondents on frame variables, early versus late responders, contact difficulty, administrative outcomes, and targeted follow-up. Census nonresponse-bias analyses combine multiple diagnostics rather than certify representativeness from one rate. Benchmark discrepancies can reflect both sample bias and benchmark mismatch, so document definitions and dates.

Weighting, calibration, imputation, and doubly robust ideas

If response is conditionally independent of Y given observed X and response probabilities are positive, inverse response weights can recover population moments. Estimate propensities using variables measured for respondents and nonrespondents, then stabilize or trim cautiously. Poststratification and raking align weighted margins with trusted population totals; they correct outcome bias only insofar as calibration variables explain it. Outcome imputation predicts missing Y under a missing-at-random model. Augmented inverse-probability estimators combine outcome and response models and may remain consistent if one is correct under conditions. Flexible models do not remove unmeasured-selection assumptions. Cross-fit complex nuisance models and audit overlap.

Colliders, feedback loops, and sensitivity

Conditioning on being observed can open a noncausal path when selection is influenced by both exposure and outcome or their causes—a collider mechanism. Case-only, hospitalized, approved-loan, and platform-active samples commonly induce such associations. Product ranking creates endogenous exposure and missing-not-at-random labels: items not shown cannot be clicked. Logging policies, randomized exploration, inverse propensity scoring, and off-policy evaluation can help under positivity and correct propensities. Sensitivity analysis varies unobserved respondent–nonrespondent outcome differences or selection odds and reports how conclusions change. Negative controls and external validation can reveal residual bias but cannot prove none remains.

Partial identification and bounds without ignorability

When conditional ignorability is not credible, point identification may be impossible. Bounds make the remaining uncertainty explicit. With a bounded outcome, worst-case bounds combine observed outcomes with extreme possible values for nonrespondents; they may be wide but honest. Monotone-response or bounded-difference assumptions narrow them and should be varied in sensitivity analysis. Pattern-mixture models specify how missing outcomes differ from predicted respondent outcomes; selection models specify response odds as a function of unobserved outcomes. Neither is testable from observed data alone. Report a tipping point: how large an unobserved selection difference must be to reverse the decision. This is more informative than presenting one heavily modeled adjustment as though the missing group had been observed.

Math / formal view

Population mean mu=E[Y]. Respondent mean is E[Y|S=1]. If response propensity pi(X)=P(S=1|X) is positive and Y is independent of S conditional on X, then E[S Y/pi(X)]=E[Y], motivating inverse-probability weighting. A normalized estimator is sum S_i w_i Y_i/sum S_i w_i. With overall response rate r, mean bias satisfies E[Y|S=1]-E[Y]=(1-r)(E[Y|S=1]-E[Y|S=0]); response rate alone is insufficient because the outcome gap is unknown.

Tier-dependent survey response

Calculate how selection changes group composition, recover the target with known-margin poststratification under conditional exchangeability, and state the within-tier assumption that remains unverified.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate outcome-related response, quantify respondent bias, apply poststratification, and verify exactly when observed-group adjustment recovers the population.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def weighted_mean(values,weights): return sum(v*w for v,w in zip(values,weights))/sum(weights)
# Deterministic expected-count population: 700 standard, 300 premium.
pop_values=[0.60]*700+[0.90]*300
groups=['standard']*700+['premium']*300
# 20% and 80% response, selected deterministically within identical cells.
respondent_values=[0.60]*140+[0.90]*240
respondent_groups=['standard']*140+['premium']*240
unweighted=sum(respondent_values)/len(respondent_values)
weights=[700/140 if g=='standard' else 300/240 for g in respondent_groups]
adjusted=weighted_mean(respondent_values,weights)
truth=sum(pop_values)/len(pop_values)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
np_adjusted=float(np.average(np.asarray(respondent_values),weights=np.asarray(weights)))
response_rate=len(respondent_values)/len(pop_values)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Preserve every selection denominator and contact outcome, calibrate only with defensible frame variables and overlap, monitor weights and benchmark gaps, and publish sensitivity to residual unmeasured selection.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(truth-0.69) < 1e-12
assert unweighted > truth
assert abs(adjusted-truth) < 1e-12
assert abs(np_adjusted-adjusted) < 1e-12
assert response_rate == 0.38
assert max(weights)/min(weights) == 4.0

Common mistakes

  • Claiming a large sample eliminates selection or nonresponse bias.
  • Using response rate as a direct estimate of bias without outcome information.
  • Weighting on variables measured only for respondents or with near-zero response overlap.
  • Calibrating to convenient margins and assuming all unmeasured selection is corrected.
  • Dropping missing or attrited units without preserving denominators, reasons, and time-varying selection.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a 90% response rate still be biased?

    Yes. If the missing 10% have outcomes very different from respondents, bias can be material. Rate measures quantity missing, not the respondent–nonrespondent outcome gap.

  • When does inverse response weighting work?

    When response propensities are correctly known/estimated, positive, and selection is ignorable for the outcome conditional on included covariates, with a representative frame and correct measurement.

  • How do you assess unmeasured selection?

    You cannot identify it from respondent data alone. Use targeted nonrespondent follow-up, administrative benchmarks, alternative frames, negative controls, longitudinal evidence, and quantitative sensitivity analyses.

Production / system-design connection

Retain target and frame definitions, selection and exposure probabilities, invitation/contact attempts, disposition reasons, timestamps, consent, device/mode, eligibility, item missingness, attrition events, and benchmark versions under strict privacy controls. Monitor response and coverage by outcome-relevant frame variables, weight concentration, propensity overlap, contact difficulty, benchmark gaps, attrition hazards, and downstream effect sensitivity. Cap or stabilize weights only under a documented bias–variance analysis. Test correction on simulations and historical cases with known outcomes. Use randomized exploration where policy-driven missing labels would otherwise destroy overlap. Do not expose small nonrespondent categories. Publish unweighted and weighted estimates, sample/frame counts, assumptions, and sensitivity ranges. If response instrumentation fails, preserve the incident, withdraw affected estimates, and rebuild weights from the last valid frame snapshot rather than silently imputing everything.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Response rate is 40%; respondent and nonrespondent means differ by 10. What is respondent-mean bias relative to population?

    Show solution

    Using bias=(1-r)(respondent mean-nonrespondent mean), bias=0.60*10=6 units.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Why can extreme inverse-probability weights be dangerous?

    Show solution

    They indicate poor overlap and make a few respondents represent many units, inflating variance and sensitivity to model error. Trimming trades variance for bias and must be disclosed.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    If weighting aligns age and region margins, is nonresponse bias eliminated?

    Show solution

    Only if selection is ignorable for the outcome conditional on those variables, positivity holds, benchmarks match the target, and models/measurement are valid. Unmeasured within-cell selection can remain.

🧮 Bayesian Statistics

6 lessons · 6 deep-complete · 12 visuals

8.1

Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior

highverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

Bayesian updating combines a prior distribution with a likelihood to produce a posterior distribution and then integrates that posterior to make predictions and decisions. The algebra is short, but responsible use requires clarity about what is conditioned on, how priors are chosen, which likelihood generated the data, and what uncertainty remains. This chapter develops Bayes' rule in odds and density form, separates prior predictive, posterior, posterior predictive, evidence, and likelihood, and explains sequential updating, exchangeability, sensitivity, and calibration. You will learn why the normalizing constant matters for model comparison but can be avoided by many samplers, why a posterior can be sharply wrong under misspecification, and how decision losses convert beliefs into actions. The worked example updates a Beta prior with conversion observations and computes the predictive chance of future successes. The lab implements a grid posterior from first principles, verifies it against the analytic Beta posterior, and checks normalization and sequential coherence. Production guidance covers prior governance, data lineage, numerical stability, monitoring, privacy, and rollback.

Prerequisites

  • probability-basics
  • joint-marginal-conditional
  • mle-map

Learning objectives

  • Apply Bayes' rule in probability, odds, and density form while keeping conditioning directions correct.
  • Distinguish prior, likelihood, evidence, posterior, and posterior predictive distributions.
  • Perform coherent sequential updates and diagnose when order, dependence, or data reuse breaks the calculation.
  • Evaluate prior sensitivity, model misspecification, predictive calibration, and decision consequences before deployment.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Bayesian updating is posterior proportional to likelihood times prior: p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/p(y). The prior encodes assumptions before the current data, the likelihood is the data model, the evidence normalizes, and the posterior represents uncertainty conditional on both. Prediction integrates p(y_new|theta) over the posterior. Independent data batches can be updated sequentially, but duplicated or dependent evidence cannot be multiplied as if independent. Always check prior predictive implications, posterior sensitivity, model fit, and decision loss.

What you must know

  • Bayes reverses conditioning through a generative model
  • The evidence normalizes and supports model comparison
  • Posterior uncertainty is conditional on model and prior
  • Prediction integrates rather than plugs in one parameter
  • Sequential updating requires correct conditional independence

Why this matters

Bayesian language appears in experimentation, forecasting, risk, personalization, anomaly detection, and ML. A candidate may recite Bayes' formula yet double-count evidence, use a prior fitted on the same data, or interpret a likelihood as a posterior. In production, posterior probability is attractive because it can answer decision-oriented questions such as P(lift exceeds a threshold), but that number is only as credible as the likelihood, prior, and selection process. Large samples can overwhelm weak priors under regular models, but they can also concentrate around a misspecified pseudo-truth. Bayesian updating therefore does not eliminate diagnostics or causal design. It supplies a coherent conditional calculus that must be embedded in a broader workflow.

Intuition

Start with a weighted set of plausible worlds. The prior assigns more weight to some parameter values than others. Ask how likely the observed data would be in each world; the likelihood reweights them. Normalize the new weights so they sum or integrate to one: that is the posterior. A diagnostic-test update works the same way in odds: prior odds multiplied by a likelihood ratio become posterior odds. Prediction then averages future outcomes over all surviving worlds, giving more weight to posterior-plausible parameters. A plug-in prediction at the posterior mean discards parameter uncertainty and can distort nonlinear risks. If the data were chosen because they looked extreme or reused from prior construction, the simple reweighting story omits the selection mechanism.

Prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior

The joint model factors as p(theta,y)=p(theta)p(y|theta). Conditioning on observed y gives p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/p(y), where p(y)=integral p(y|theta)p(theta)dtheta. The likelihood is a function of theta with y fixed and need not integrate to one over theta. The evidence is the prior predictive probability or density of the observed data and makes the posterior normalize. In continuous models, densities depend on units while probability over regions does not. Posterior odds between two hypotheses equal prior odds times their Bayes factor, which is a likelihood ratio after integrating nuisance parameters under each hypothesis.

Sequential updating and sufficient state

For conditionally independent batches y1 and y2 given theta, p(theta|y1,y2) is proportional to p(y2|theta)p(theta|y1); the posterior after batch one becomes the prior for batch two. The final result is order-invariant in exact arithmetic if the same joint model is used. Dependence, overlapping records, adaptive sampling, and changing populations require a joint likelihood that conditions on history. Saving only a posterior mean is insufficient for general updates because shape and covariance matter. Conjugate families can compress the posterior into hyperparameters; particle or posterior draws can approximate it otherwise. Version the data cutoff so evidence is never counted twice.

Posterior prediction and decisions

The posterior predictive distribution p(y_new|y)=integral p(y_new|theta)p(theta|y)dtheta includes outcome noise and parameter uncertainty. A posterior parameter interval is generally narrower than a predictive interval. Decisions require an action a and loss L(a,theta) or utility: choose the action minimizing posterior expected loss. Under squared loss, posterior mean is optimal for a scalar parameter; asymmetric business costs yield quantiles or custom rules. A launch rule may use expected net value plus a harm constraint such as P(effect<-delta|data)<epsilon. Utility parameters and thresholds should be decided before results rather than tuned to justify a preferred action.

Prior sensitivity, identifiability, and misspecification

Prior choice is part of the model, especially in sparse, weakly identified, hierarchical, and high-dimensional settings. Use prior predictive simulation to expose implausible outcomes, compare reasonable priors, and report how decisions change. An improper prior may yield an improper posterior or make evidence undefined. Posterior concentration does not prove the likelihood describes reality; omitted heterogeneity, selection, censoring, and dependence can create overconfidence. Check posterior predictive behavior, held-out calibration, residual structure, and alternative likelihoods. If prior and likelihood conflict strongly, investigate data quality and model assumptions rather than automatically trusting whichever is numerically sharper.

Normalization and computational forms

For small discrete or one-dimensional problems, enumerate a grid and normalize weights using log-sum-exp. Conjugacy gives analytic updates. Higher-dimensional models use quadrature, Laplace approximation, variational inference, sequential Monte Carlo, or MCMC. Algorithms that need only the posterior up to proportionality can omit p(y) during sampling, but model comparison and evidence calculations cannot. Numerical underflow occurs when multiplying many likelihood terms; sum log densities and subtract a maximum before exponentiating. Computation adds approximation error on top of statistical uncertainty, so diagnostics and reproducible seeds are part of inference.

Math / formal view

Bayes' rule is p(theta|y)=p(y|theta)p(theta)/integral p(y|u)p(u)du. In odds form, posterior odds H1:H0 equal prior odds times p(y|H1)/p(y|H0). For Beta(a,b) prior and k Bernoulli successes in n trials, posterior is Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Its mean is (a+k)/(a+b+n), and the next-trial predictive success probability is the same posterior mean. For m future Bernoulli trials, the predictive count is Beta–Binomial rather than Binomial at a fixed plug-in p.

Sequential Beta–Bernoulli conversion update

Update prior hyperparameters with successes and failures, compute posterior summaries and future predictive probability, then compare reasonable prior choices and verify that splitting the data into batches gives the same posterior.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build a grid posterior for a Bernoulli rate, verify it against the analytic Beta posterior, and test normalization and sequential coherence.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def normalize_log_weights(log_weights):
    peak=max(log_weights); weights=[math.exp(x-peak) for x in log_weights]
    total=sum(weights); return [w/total for w in weights]

def grid_update(grid, prior_weights, successes, failures):
    logs=[]
    for p,w in zip(grid,prior_weights):
        logs.append(math.log(w)+successes*math.log(p)+failures*math.log(1-p))
    return normalize_log_weights(logs)

grid=[(i+0.5)/1000 for i in range(1000)]
prior=[p**(2-1)*(1-p)**(8-1) for p in grid]
prior=[w/sum(prior) for w in prior]
posterior=grid_update(grid,prior,6,14)
grid_mean=sum(p*w for p,w in zip(grid,posterior))
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import beta
analytic_mean=beta.mean(8,22)
prob_above_025=beta.sf(0.25,8,22)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version priors, likelihood, data cutoff, and decision loss; deduplicate sequential evidence, run predictive/sensitivity checks, persist posterior diagnostics, and fail closed when model or computation checks break.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(sum(posterior)-1.0) < 1e-12
assert abs(grid_mean-analytic_mean) < 2e-4
first=grid_update(grid,prior,2,8)
sequential=grid_update(grid,first,4,6)
assert max(abs(a-b) for a,b in zip(posterior,sequential)) < 1e-12
assert 0 < prob_above_025 < 1

Common mistakes

  • Reversing p(data|theta) into p(theta|data) without a prior and evidence.
  • Multiplying likelihoods for duplicated, selected, or dependent evidence as if observations were conditionally independent.
  • Treating posterior probability as model-free certainty or as proof of causal effect.
  • Using a plug-in parameter for prediction while ignoring posterior uncertainty.
  • Choosing or tuning priors after seeing the final data without disclosing the reuse.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is the evidence often ignored in MCMC?

    For a fixed model and observed data it is constant in theta, so algorithms targeting relative posterior density can work with an unnormalized density. It is still required for normalized probabilities and Bayesian model comparison.

  • Does the prior always vanish with enough data?

    Under regular identifiable models a fixed positive prior often has diminishing local influence, but not under misspecification, weak identification, boundaries, growing dimension, or priors that exclude relevant values.

  • What is the difference between posterior and posterior predictive?

    The posterior is uncertainty about parameters conditional on data. The posterior predictive averages the future-data model over that parameter posterior, adding outcome variability to parameter uncertainty.

Production / system-design connection

Create a model card containing population, parameterization, likelihood, observation window, censoring and missingness rules, prior rationale, sensitivity alternatives, decision loss, and predictive target. Generate prior predictive samples in CI and reject obviously impossible scales. Compute in log space and test analytic fixtures. Persist data hash, code, package versions, RNG streams, posterior representation, and diagnostics. Monitor prior–posterior conflict, posterior drift, calibration, predictive residuals, effective sample size or approximation quality, and decision sensitivity. Protect small-segment posterior summaries and do not let priors leak sensitive historical rates. When new data overlap old batches, deduplicate before updating. Rollback must restore the previous posterior, prior version, likelihood, and evidence cutoff. If diagnostics fail, freeze or widen decisions rather than emitting overconfident probabilities.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A prior probability is 0.10 and evidence has likelihood ratio 4. What are posterior odds and probability?

    Show solution

    Prior odds are 0.1/0.9=1/9. Posterior odds are 4/9, so posterior probability is (4/9)/(1+4/9)=4/13≈0.3077.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Beta(3,7) prior observes 5 successes and 5 failures. What is the posterior?

    Show solution

    Beta(3+5,7+5)=Beta(8,12), with posterior mean 8/20=0.4.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why can splitting conditionally independent data into two updates be safe?

    Show solution

    Bayesian multiplication is associative: likelihood factors for both batches multiply the prior, so using the first posterior as the second prior yields the same normalized posterior when the joint model and evidence are unchanged.

8.2

Conjugate Priors

mediumverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

A conjugate prior produces a posterior in the same distribution family as the prior for a chosen likelihood. Conjugacy turns Bayesian updating into hyperparameter arithmetic, making it valuable for intuition, streaming updates, exact benchmarks, and low-latency systems. It does not make a prior objectively correct or every model realistic. This chapter derives Beta–Binomial/Bernoulli, Gamma–Poisson, and Normal–Normal updates, interprets pseudo-counts and precision weighting carefully, and explains posterior predictive distributions, exponential-family structure, improper limits, and when conjugacy becomes a modeling trap. You will learn how parameterization conventions change formulas, why sufficient statistics enable constant-memory updates, how prior strength differs from sample size under heterogeneous data, and when mixtures or hierarchical priors preserve flexibility. The worked examples cover conversion and event-rate estimation. The lab implements Beta–Binomial and Gamma–Poisson updates, checks batch-order invariance, and verifies moments against SciPy. Production guidance covers parameterization tests, numerical bounds, nonstationarity, prior versioning, predictive calibration, and analytic fallbacks.

Prerequisites

  • bayes-update
  • distributions

Learning objectives

  • Derive posterior hyperparameter updates for common conjugate likelihood–prior pairs.
  • Interpret hyperparameters through sufficient statistics without overclaiming literal prior sample size.
  • Compute posterior predictive distributions and distinguish them from plug-in likelihood predictions.
  • Recognize parameterization, support, misspecification, and nonstationarity cases where conjugacy should not drive model choice.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A prior is conjugate when the posterior stays in the same family after multiplying by a likelihood. Beta with Bernoulli/Binomial updates successes and failures; Gamma with Poisson updates shape by total counts and rate by exposure; Normal with known-variance Normal likelihood combines means by precision. Conjugacy gives exact, fast, sequential updates and useful test fixtures, but the likelihood and prior still need to fit the domain. Check rate-versus-scale conventions, predictive calibration, and whether drift or hierarchy requires a richer model.

What you must know

  • Conjugacy is algebraic closure under updating
  • Sufficient statistics compress the evidence
  • Hyperparameters depend on parameterization conventions
  • Predictive distributions integrate parameter uncertainty
  • Computational convenience never replaces model criticism

Why this matters

Conjugate models reveal the mechanics hidden inside general inference engines. A conversion posterior updates two counts; a Poisson-rate posterior updates count and exposure; a Gaussian posterior averages prior and sample information by precision. These formulas support real-time risk estimates and serve as golden tests for MCMC or variational systems. Misuse appears when teams call a prior 'ten observations' despite a mismatched population, confuse Gamma rate and scale, or force a single-rate Poisson model onto overdispersed counts solely to keep conjugacy. Interviewers test the updates, but engineers must also know what happens when traffic drifts, exposures differ, or groups share information. Exact inference in the wrong model is exactly wrong.

Intuition

Conjugate priors are containers designed to hold exactly the summaries that the likelihood adds. For coin flips, the likelihood contributes a power of p for each success and a power of 1-p for each failure; the Beta prior already has those powers, so exponents add. For Poisson counts, the likelihood contributes total count to the power of the rate and exposure to exponential decay; the Gamma prior has the same form. For a Gaussian mean, information is precision, inverse variance, so prior and data centers combine in proportion to their precision. The posterior distribution retains uncertainty; using only its mean would discard the remaining spread.

Beta–Bernoulli and Beta–Binomial

With p~Beta(a,b) and k successes in n Bernoulli trials, the likelihood kernel p^k(1-p)^(n-k) multiplies the prior p^(a-1)(1-p)^(b-1), yielding Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Posterior mean is (a+k)/(a+b+n), and interior mode is (a+k-1)/(a+b+n-2). Hyperparameters can be read as prior success/failure contributions, but this pseudo-count interpretation assumes exchangeability and compatible evidence. Jeffreys Beta(1/2,1/2), uniform Beta(1,1), and domain-informed priors behave differently near boundaries. A Beta–Binomial predictive distribution for future counts is overdispersed relative to a plug-in Binomial because it integrates uncertainty in p.

Gamma–Poisson for rates with exposure

Let counts y_i~Poisson(lambda t_i), where t_i is exposure, and lambda~Gamma(shape=a, rate=b). The likelihood kernel is lambda^(sum y_i) exp(-lambda sum t_i), so the posterior is Gamma(a+sum y_i,b+sum t_i) in shape–rate form. Shape–scale libraries instead use scale=1/rate; confusing them changes means and simulations. Posterior mean is (a+Y)/(b+T). The predictive count over future exposure t has a negative-binomial form after integrating lambda. If counts are more dispersed, zero-inflated, seasonally varying, or dependent, a single Poisson rate may be inadequate even though the update is exact.

Normal mean with known observation variance

For prior mu~N(m0,s0^2) and iid y_i~N(mu,sigma^2) with sigma known, posterior precision is 1/s0^2+n/sigma^2. Posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of m0 and ybar; posterior variance is the reciprocal precision. High-variance data contribute less information. Unknown variance leads to Normal–Inverse-Gamma or related conjugate families and Student-t predictives, with parameterization details. In multivariate Gaussian models, precision matrices add, but conditioning and positive-definiteness require care. Standardization changes the prior scale, so priors must be transformed with features.

Exponential families and sufficient statistics

Many likelihoods can be written h(y)exp(eta(theta)^T T(y)-A(theta)). Natural conjugate priors have a matching form whose hyperparameters accumulate T(y) and observation weight. This explains constant-memory sequential updates: retain sufficient totals instead of every row. It also clarifies limits—sufficiency is model-relative. Totals that preserve all information under an iid Bernoulli model lose ordering, covariates, drift, and dependence information. Keep raw or auditable aggregates when those assumptions may be revised. Distributed systems can merge additive sufficient statistics deterministically if data partitions are disjoint.

When convenience becomes a constraint

Real systems may need logistic regression, hierarchical varying rates, mixture components, censoring, measurement error, or nonstationary state models without simple closed forms. Approximate conjugate tricks can hide important dependence. Mixtures of conjugate priors retain analytic component updates and provide more flexible shapes, but component weights must update too. Empirical Bayes estimates hyperparameters from data and should not be described as a fixed external prior. Conjugate posteriors make excellent unit-test or fallback models; compare their predictions with richer models rather than forcing every question into them. Prior and posterior predictive checks remain mandatory.

Math / formal view

Beta–Binomial: p|y~Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Gamma–Poisson in shape–rate form: lambda|y~Gamma(a+sum y_i,b+sum t_i). Normal–Normal: s_n^2=1/(1/s0^2+n/sigma^2) and m_n=s_n^2(m0/s0^2+n ybar/sigma^2). These updates are associative through sufficient statistics. Predictive distributions integrate parameters: Beta–Binomial, negative binomial for Gamma–Poisson, and Normal with variance sigma^2+s_n^2 for a future Gaussian observation with known sigma.

Incident rate with unequal exposure

Aggregate total incidents and machine-time, update Gamma shape and rate, compute the posterior mean and predictive distribution, and test the result against the library's documented parameter convention.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement Beta–Bernoulli and Gamma–Poisson conjugate updates, verify batch-order invariance, and compare posterior moments with SciPy.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def beta_update(a,b,successes,failures):
    return a+successes,b+failures
def gamma_poisson_update(shape,rate,total_count,total_exposure):
    return shape+total_count,rate+total_exposure

a_post,b_post=beta_update(4,6,9,11)
shape_post,rate_post=gamma_poisson_update(3,5,7,20)
beta_mean=a_post/(a_post+b_post)
rate_mean=shape_post/rate_post
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import beta,gamma
scipy_beta_mean=beta.mean(a_post,b_post)
scipy_rate_mean=gamma.mean(shape_post,scale=1/rate_post)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Test parameter conventions, retain idempotent sufficient-statistic lineage and data cutoffs, monitor predictive dispersion and drift, and keep analytic updates as versioned model artifacts rather than naked counters.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert (a_post,b_post)==(13,17)
assert abs(beta_mean-scipy_beta_mean) < 1e-12
assert abs(rate_mean-0.4) < 1e-12
assert abs(rate_mean-scipy_rate_mean) < 1e-12
first=beta_update(4,6,4,6)
second=beta_update(*first,5,5)
assert second==(a_post,b_post)

Common mistakes

  • Treating conjugacy as evidence that the likelihood or prior is appropriate.
  • Confusing Gamma rate and scale or Normal variance and standard-deviation arguments.
  • Reading prior hyperparameters as literal sample counts without exchangeability or source justification.
  • Using a fixed-rate plug-in predictive distribution instead of integrating posterior uncertainty.
  • Discarding raw time, group, or covariate information needed to detect drift and heterogeneity.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why are conjugate updates easy to stream?

    The posterior is summarized by fixed-size hyperparameters updated by additive sufficient statistics. Disjoint batches can merge their counts/exposures, provided the likelihood assumptions and data lineage remain valid.

  • What is the predictive distribution for Beta–Bernoulli?

    The next Bernoulli success probability is the posterior mean. A batch future count follows Beta–Binomial, which includes extra variance from uncertainty in p.

  • When should you leave conjugacy?

    When relevant heterogeneity, covariates, dependence, censoring, mixture structure, drift, or a scientifically appropriate likelihood cannot be represented by the conjugate model.

Production / system-design connection

Define distribution parameterization explicitly in code and tests: shape/rate versus shape/scale, variance versus SD, exposure units, and support. Maintain sufficient-statistic lineage with unique event IDs and batch cutoffs so updates are idempotent. Reconcile distributed aggregates with source totals. Monitor posterior mean and spread, predictive calibration, dispersion, zero frequency, exposure mix, group heterogeneity, prior influence, and drift. Keep a richer holdout or residual view because sufficient statistics cannot reveal every model violation. Version priors and reset/discount rules; stationary conjugate accumulation can become dangerously overconfident under changing regimes. Protect small-group rates. Provide a validated analytic fallback when a heavier inference service fails, but label its assumptions. Rollback restores hyperparameters and the exact evidence watermark, not only a displayed mean.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Beta(4,6) prior sees 9 successes and 11 failures. Give posterior.

    Show solution

    Beta(13,17), with posterior mean 13/30.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Gamma(shape=3,rate=5) prior sees 7 events over exposure 20. Give posterior mean.

    Show solution

    Posterior Gamma(10,25), mean shape/rate=10/25=0.4 events per exposure unit.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why is future Gaussian predictive variance sigma squared plus posterior variance of mu?

    Show solution

    A future observation equals uncertain mean plus independent observation noise; total variance adds E[noise variance]=sigma^2 and Var(posterior mean parameter)=s_n^2.

8.3

Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals

highverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals can have similar numerical endpoints while making different probability statements. A credible interval contains a specified posterior probability under a prior and likelihood. A confidence interval is generated by a procedure with stated repeated-sample coverage under a sampling model. This chapter builds both from the same binomial example, compares equal-tailed and highest-density credible sets, explains parameter transformations, nuisance parameters, posterior predictive intervals, and the circumstances in which Bayesian and frequentist intervals approximately agree. You will learn why neither framework is assumption-free, why optional stopping and selection require framework-specific care, how prior sensitivity affects sparse-data credible intervals, and why a 95% posterior interval is not automatically calibrated across repeated real datasets. The worked example contrasts a Beta posterior interval with Wilson confidence coverage. The lab computes equal-tailed posterior intervals, simulates frequentist coverage, and verifies transformation behavior. Production guidance covers naming, metadata, calibration, priors, sequential policies, decision thresholds, privacy, and communication.

Prerequisites

  • bayes-update
  • confidence-intervals
  • conjugate-priors

Learning objectives

  • State the probability interpretation of credible and confidence intervals without mixing frameworks.
  • Construct equal-tailed and highest-density credible sets and contrast them with score or likelihood-based confidence intervals.
  • Distinguish parameter uncertainty from posterior predictive uncertainty and transform intervals coherently.
  • Evaluate prior sensitivity, frequentist coverage, calibration, selection, and stopping for deployed interval procedures.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A 95% credible interval has 95% posterior probability for the parameter conditional on the model, prior, and observed data. A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. The observed frequentist interval does not assign 95% probability to the parameter. Credible intervals may be equal-tailed or highest-density and depend on priors; confidence constructions differ too. Report the framework, estimand, method, assumptions, and practical thresholds, and evaluate both posterior sensitivity and repeated-sample calibration when useful.

What you must know

  • Credible probability is conditional on model, prior, and data
  • Confidence is a property of a repeated-sampling procedure
  • Equal-tailed and highest-density sets answer different geometric summaries
  • Prediction includes observation noise beyond parameter uncertainty
  • Numerical similarity does not erase interpretive differences

Why this matters

Teams increasingly mix Bayesian experiments with frequentist dashboards. If every interval is labeled '95%' without a framework, readers may treat coverage as posterior probability or interpret a credible interval as model-free calibration. Both errors create false certainty. Bayesian intervals answer natural questions such as P(effect>threshold|data), while confidence procedures offer operating guarantees under repetitions. Each depends on assumptions: priors and likelihoods for the former, sampling design and construction for the latter. Interviews emphasize the semantic difference; production systems also need consistent stopping, multiplicity, and calibration. The most useful practice is not framework tribalism but exact language, decision-aligned quantities, and diagnostics appropriate to the procedure.

Intuition

For one observed dataset, a Bayesian posterior is a probability distribution over possible parameter values. Mark off a region containing 95% of its mass: that is a credible set. For a frequentist procedure, imagine generating many datasets from one fixed parameter and drawing an interval each time; about 95% of those random intervals should cover the fixed value. One picture holds data fixed and varies the parameter under a posterior; the other varies data while the parameter stays fixed. Their endpoints may converge in regular large samples because the likelihood becomes approximately normal and a weak prior contributes little locally. Near boundaries, with sparse data or informative priors, they can differ substantially.

Two probability spaces

For posterior distribution p(theta|y), a credible set C(y) satisfies integral over C p(theta|y)dtheta=0.95. Probability conditions on observed y and the entire Bayesian model. A confidence procedure C(Y) satisfies P_theta(theta in C(Y))≈0.95 under repetitions Y~p_theta, ideally across relevant theta. Once y is observed, frequentist C(y) either contains theta or not. A confidence distribution is not automatically a Bayesian posterior. Likewise, a credible interval need not have nominal frequentist coverage, though some priors and regular asymptotic settings produce matching behavior. State what is random in the claim.

Equal-tailed, highest-density, and one-sided credible sets

An equal-tailed 95% interval cuts 2.5% posterior probability from each tail and transforms naturally under monotone transformations by transforming endpoints. A highest posterior density set contains points with density above a threshold and often minimizes length in one dimension, but it depends on parameterization and can be disconnected for multimodal posteriors. A single interval spanning a low-density valley can mislead; show the full posterior or disjoint regions. One-sided credible bounds may match risk questions better. The posterior probability above a business threshold is often more actionable than whether zero lies in a central interval, provided the decision model was prespecified.

Confidence constructions and coverage

Wald intervals use estimate plus-or-minus critical SE and can fail near boundaries or under skewness. Score/Wilson, likelihood-ratio/profile, exact, bootstrap, and randomization intervals have different finite-sample coverage and length. Exact discrete intervals may overcover. Coverage can be marginal rather than conditional in relevant subgroups. Repeated peeking, selecting a winner, or choosing the method after inspection changes operating characteristics unless accounted for. A confidence interval that excludes zero corresponds to a matching two-sided test, but equivalence needs an interval entirely inside prespecified negligible-effect bounds.

Prediction, transformations, and nuisance uncertainty

A parameter interval for a mean is not a prediction interval for a future outcome. Bayesian prediction integrates the likelihood over the joint posterior, including correlations among nuisance parameters. Frequentist prediction combines parameter-estimation and future-noise uncertainty through a procedure. For a monotone transform such as odds to probability, transform posterior draws or equal-tailed endpoints; highest-density regions may not transform into highest-density regions. For nonlinear functions or ratios, propagate joint uncertainty rather than transforming marginal intervals separately. Report the original and decision scale when stakeholders reason in absolute risk but modeling occurs in log odds.

Bayesian calibration and frequentist sensitivity

Bayesian simulation-based calibration can test whether an inference algorithm recovers prior-generated parameter ranks when data are generated from the model. Posterior predictive checks test data fit, not coverage directly. Repeated-sampling simulations can measure a Bayesian interval's coverage across fixed parameter values and a confidence interval's coverage under design variations. Prior sensitivity should examine posterior decisions under plausible alternatives; confidence sensitivity should examine nuisance, design, and robust-variance choices. Neither one diagnostic proves real-world validity when the data-generating process is outside all simulated models. Use external validation and decision loss as additional evidence.

Intervals, thresholds, and posterior decisions

A central interval is not always the best decision summary. If harm below h and benefit above b have different consequences, report posterior probabilities for both regions and expected utility, not only mass around the median. Frequentist decisions can similarly use one-sided bounds, equivalence intervals, or confidence sets inverted from decision-relevant tests. Predefine thresholds independently of observed endpoints. When several actions compete, a joint posterior or simultaneous confidence construction may be required; marginal intervals can understate the chance that at least one decision is wrong. Preserve the full draw-level or covariance information needed to evaluate new thresholds, but treat post hoc threshold search as exploratory. Interval presentation should support, not replace, a documented loss model.

Math / formal view

For posterior CDF F(theta|y), an equal-tailed 1-alpha credible interval is [F^{-1}(alpha/2),F^{-1}(1-alpha/2)]. A highest-density set has {theta:p(theta|y)>=c} with c chosen to contain 1-alpha mass. A confidence procedure satisfies P_theta(theta in C(Y))>= or approximately 1-alpha. For Beta(a+k,b+n-k), posterior quantiles give a credible interval. A Wilson binomial interval instead inverts a score test and targets repeated-sample coverage without a prior.

Three conversions in ten trials

Compute a Beta posterior interval and a Wilson confidence interval, say each interpretation precisely, vary the prior, and use simulation to inspect repeated-sample coverage without declaring one endpoint universally correct.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute a Beta credible interval, simulate its fixed-parameter coverage, and compare with a Wilson confidence interval.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math

def wilson_interval(k,n,z=1.959963984540054):
    p=k/n; denom=1+z*z/n
    center=(p+z*z/(2*n))/denom
    half=z*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n+z*z/(4*n*n))/denom
    return center-half,center+half

k,n=3,10
wilson=wilson_interval(k,n)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import beta
credible=tuple(beta.ppf([0.025,0.975],4,8))
rng=np.random.default_rng(23)
true_p=0.30
counts=rng.binomial(n,true_p,size=20000)
credible_intervals=np.asarray([beta.ppf([0.025,0.975],1+c,1+n-c) for c in counts])
coverage=np.mean((credible_intervals[:,0] <= true_p) & (true_p <= credible_intervals[:,1]))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Label interval framework and construction, version priors/design/stopping, coverage- and sensitivity-test decision-critical endpoints, and keep parameter, predictive, and practical-threshold uncertainty distinct in the UI.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert 0 < credible[0] < credible[1] < 1
assert 0 < wilson[0] < wilson[1] < 1
assert 0.90 < coverage < 0.99
logit_bounds=[math.log(x/(1-x)) for x in credible]
assert logit_bounds[0] < logit_bounds[1]

Common mistakes

  • Saying an observed frequentist interval contains the fixed parameter with 95% probability.
  • Presenting a credible interval without the prior, likelihood, and conditioning data.
  • Treating any interval excluding zero as evidence of practical importance.
  • Confusing a parameter interval with a future-outcome prediction interval.
  • Using a highest-density interval as if it were invariant to nonlinear reparameterization.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a credible interval have 95% frequentist coverage?

    It can under particular priors, models, and parameter values or asymptotically, but posterior probability does not automatically guarantee repeated-sample coverage. Measure or derive coverage for the intended regime.

  • Why might equal-tailed and highest-density intervals differ?

    Skewed or multimodal posteriors distribute density unevenly. Equal-tailed intervals balance tail probabilities; highest-density sets prioritize local density and may be shorter or disconnected.

  • Which interval should a dashboard show?

    Use the framework actually implemented and decision question. Label it clearly, include method and assumptions, show practical thresholds, and avoid mixing posterior probability language with confidence coverage.

Production / system-design connection

Require interval metadata: framework, estimand, population, unit, construction, confidence/credible level, sidedness, prior version, likelihood, variance method, stopping rule, multiplicity family, and data window. Render posterior probability statements only from an actual posterior. Run prior sensitivity and predictive checks for Bayesian intervals; run coverage simulations across fixed parameter and design scenarios for decision-critical procedures. Monitor interval width, boundary behavior, posterior drift, calibration, cluster structure, and small-cell instability. Preserve posterior draws or sufficient summaries needed to transform decisions correctly. Apply privacy thresholds. If a sequential policy changes, create a new interval version. Roll back displayed endpoints, labels, and decision status together when data or model integrity fails. Never let UI copy rewrite a confidence statement into a probability claim.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    State a 95% credible interval interpretation.

    Show solution

    Conditional on the specified prior, likelihood, and observed data, the posterior probability that the parameter lies in the reported set is 0.95.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    State a 95% confidence interval interpretation.

    Show solution

    Across repetitions of the specified sampling and interval procedure, about 95% of intervals contain the fixed true parameter under the assumptions.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why is a posterior parameter interval narrower than a posterior predictive interval in many models?

    Show solution

    Prediction adds irreducible future outcome variability to uncertainty about parameters, whereas the parameter interval summarizes only posterior parameter uncertainty.

8.4

MCMC & Posterior Sampling

mediumverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

Markov chain Monte Carlo approximates posterior expectations by constructing dependent draws whose stationary distribution is the target posterior. The central promise is asymptotic, while every real analysis uses finite chains that can fail to explore relevant modes or geometry. This chapter develops Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs sampling, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and the No-U-Turn Sampler; distinguishes warmup from retained sampling; and explains detailed balance, autocorrelation, effective sample size, Monte Carlo standard error, rank-normalized split R-hat, divergences, treedepth, energy diagnostics, and multimodality. You will learn why acceptance rate alone is not convergence, why thinning usually discards information, how centered versus noncentered parameterizations change hierarchical geometry, and how to validate an implementation against conjugate truth and simulation-based calibration. The worked example samples a one-dimensional Beta posterior, then contrasts its easy geometry with a funnel. The lab builds random-walk Metropolis, compares posterior moments with SciPy, and checks multiple-chain mixing. Production guidance covers deterministic seeds, chain parallelism, diagnostics gates, compute budgets, artifact storage, privacy, and safe failure behavior.

Prerequisites

  • bayes-update
  • conjugate-priors
  • numerical-stability

Learning objectives

  • Explain how a Markov transition kernel can leave a posterior invariant and why retained draws are dependent.
  • Implement Metropolis–Hastings and relate proposal scale to exploration, acceptance, and autocorrelation.
  • Interpret R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, Monte Carlo SE, divergences, treedepth, and trace diagnostics jointly.
  • Diagnose multimodality, funnels, constraints, initialization, and parameterization failures before using posterior summaries.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

MCMC constructs a Markov chain with the posterior as its stationary distribution, then estimates posterior expectations from retained dependent draws. Metropolis–Hastings accepts a proposal with the target-density and proposal-ratio correction; HMC uses gradients to propose distant moves and NUTS adapts trajectory length. Run multiple dispersed chains, separate warmup, and check rank-normalized split R-hat, bulk and tail ESS, Monte Carlo SE, trace plots, divergences, treedepth, and model-specific calibration. A high acceptance rate or long chain alone does not prove convergence, and thinning rarely fixes autocorrelation.

What you must know

  • Stationarity does not guarantee finite-chain exploration
  • Dependent draws reduce effective information
  • Multiple diagnostics target different failures
  • Geometry and parameterization dominate sampler performance
  • Computation must be validated against known and simulated truth

Why this matters

Most realistic Bayesian models lack closed-form posteriors. MCMC makes full posterior inference possible, but it also creates a second layer of uncertainty: the chain may not represent the target well. A model can produce plausible-looking histograms while one chain remains trapped in a mode, tail ESS is tiny, or HMC divergences avoid an important region. Interviews ask Metropolis acceptance and burn-in; advanced practice requires diagnostics and geometry. Production systems must turn those diagnostics into hard quality gates rather than warnings lost in logs. More iterations can reduce Monte Carlo error after mixing, but they do not repair a nonidentified model, disconnected modes, or systematically missed curvature.

Intuition

Imagine exploring a landscape whose height is posterior density. Random-walk Metropolis proposes a nearby step and always accepts uphill moves, while sometimes accepting downhill moves so it does not freeze at a local peak. Tiny steps accept often but crawl; huge steps reject often and repeat the same state. HMC adds momentum and follows gradients, traveling across smooth valleys with fewer random walks. Warmup tunes step size, mass matrix, and sometimes proposal scales; those adaptive draws are not ordinary samples. Even after warmup, neighboring states remain correlated. Effective sample size asks how many independent draws would provide comparable precision. Multiple chains started apart reveal whether explorers agree on the same terrain.

Metropolis–Hastings and invariance

From current theta, propose theta'~q(theta'|theta). Accept with probability min(1, pi(theta')q(theta|theta')/[pi(theta)q(theta'|theta)]); otherwise retain theta. This correction establishes detailed balance for many kernels, implying pi is invariant. Symmetric random-walk proposals cancel q. Work in log density to prevent underflow. Rejections are valid repeated draws and must remain in the chain. Proposal tuning changes efficiency, not target, if adaptation stops or follows valid adaptive rules. Irreducibility and aperiodicity matter: a proposal that cannot cross a support gap never discovers the other mode regardless of iterations.

Gibbs, HMC, and NUTS

Gibbs sampling draws each block from its full conditional and accepts automatically; strong posterior correlations can still make coordinate updates slow. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo augments parameters with momentum, simulates approximate Hamiltonian dynamics using leapfrog integration, and corrects integration error with Metropolis acceptance. A mass matrix rescales geometry. NUTS expands trajectories until a no-U-turn condition and adapts step size during warmup. Gradients enable distant proposals, but discontinuities, boundaries, heavy tails, and funnels challenge HMC. Divergences flag trajectories where numerical integration cannot follow curvature and often indicate biased exploration, not harmless noise to suppress blindly.

R-hat, ESS, MCSE, and visual diagnostics

Rank-normalized split R-hat compares between- and within-chain behavior after splitting chains and transforming ranks; values near one are necessary but not sufficient. Bulk ESS assesses central-location estimation and tail ESS assesses quantiles/tails. ESS incorporates autocorrelation and can differ by parameter and function. Monte Carlo SE estimates numerical uncertainty in a posterior summary, distinct from posterior SD. Trace plots should look stationary and overlapping; rank plots expose chain-specific distribution differences; autocorrelation plots show persistence. For HMC, inspect divergence count/location, maximum treedepth, energy behavior, and acceptance adaptation. Check transformed quantities and decisions, not only raw parameters.

Funnels, correlations, modes, and reparameterization

Hierarchical scale parameters create funnel geometry: when group-scale is small, latent effects occupy a narrow neck; when large, they spread widely. Centered parameterization can be efficient with strongly informed groups but poor with weak data. Noncentering writes effects as population mean plus scale times standard-normal latent variables, often easing weak-data geometry. Highly correlated parameters need mass-matrix adaptation or reparameterization. Label switching in mixtures yields symmetric modes; identifiability constraints or permutation-invariant summaries may be needed. Disconnected modes cannot be diagnosed solely by local HMC statistics if every chain initializes in one mode. Use prior predictive insight, dispersed starts, alternative algorithms, and tempered methods when relevant.

Warmup, initialization, and validation

Warmup removes initialization influence and adapts sampler settings; discarding an arbitrary fraction without checking mixing is not a proof. Initialize multiple chains over plausible dispersed regions, but avoid pathological invalid values. Validate code on prior-only simulation, conjugate models, and simulated datasets where parameters are known. Simulation-based calibration tests rank uniformity across repeated prior-generated datasets and can detect inference implementation bias. Compare independent software or analytic results on small cases. Thinning usually increases Monte Carlo error for a fixed computation and is justified mainly for storage or expensive downstream calculations. If diagnostics fail, revise model or computation before interpreting posterior output.

Math / formal view

For stationary scalar chain f_t with autocorrelations rho_k, asymptotic variance of the sample mean is Var_pi(f)/N times tau, where tau=1+2 sum_{k>=1}rho_k is integrated autocorrelation time; ESS=N/tau. MCSE(mean) is approximately posterior SD/sqrt(ESS). Metropolis–Hastings acceptance is alpha=min(1, exp(log pi(theta')-log pi(theta)+log q(theta|theta')-log q(theta'|theta))). Detailed balance pi(theta)K(theta,theta')=pi(theta')K(theta',theta) is sufficient, not necessary, for invariance.

Metropolis on a known Beta posterior

Use a conjugate target as a golden test, vary proposal scale, retain rejected states, compare all chains with analytic moments, and distinguish acceptance rate from effective exploration.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build random-walk Metropolis for a Beta target, verify moments and multiple-chain agreement, and quantify acceptance versus autocorrelation.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import math
import random

def log_beta_kernel(p,a,b):
    if not 0 < p < 1: return float('-inf')
    return (a-1)*math.log(p)+(b-1)*math.log1p(-p)
def metropolis(start,a,b,steps,proposal_sd,seed):
    rng=random.Random(seed); x=start; out=[]; accepted=0
    logp=log_beta_kernel(x,a,b)
    for _ in range(steps):
        candidate=x+rng.gauss(0,proposal_sd)
        logc=log_beta_kernel(candidate,a,b)
        if math.log(rng.random()) < min(0.0,logc-logp):
            x,logp=candidate,logc; accepted+=1
        out.append(x)
    return out,accepted/steps
chains=[metropolis(s,8,22,30000,0.08,seed) for s,seed in [(0.05,1),(0.2,2),(0.6,3),(0.9,4)]]
retained=[draws[5000:] for draws,_ in chains]
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import beta
combined=np.concatenate([np.asarray(c) for c in retained])
analytic_mean=beta.mean(8,22)
analytic_q=beta.ppf([0.025,0.975],8,22)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Run independent dispersed chains with immutable configs, gate every posterior on modern convergence/ESS/HMC diagnostics and analytic or simulated fixtures, and withhold output rather than suppressing failures.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(combined.mean()-analytic_mean) < 0.01
assert np.allclose(np.quantile(combined,[0.025,0.975]),analytic_q,atol=0.02)
chain_means=[np.mean(c) for c in retained]
assert max(chain_means)-min(chain_means) < 0.02
assert all(0.15 < rate < 0.85 for _,rate in chains)
assert all(len(c)==25000 for c in retained)

Common mistakes

  • Treating high acceptance, one smooth trace, or many iterations as proof of convergence.
  • Dropping rejected states or adapting proposals forever without a valid adaptive scheme.
  • Using thinning as a cure for poor mixing instead of improving geometry or running longer valid chains.
  • Ignoring divergences, tail ESS, treedepth, or diagnostic failures in derived decision quantities.
  • Running all chains from nearly identical starts and declaring agreement despite missed modes.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why retain repeated states after rejection?

    The self-transition is part of the Markov kernel that preserves the target. Removing rejections changes empirical weights and biases the sample toward accepted moves.

  • What is the difference between posterior SD and MCSE?

    Posterior SD is substantive uncertainty about the parameter under the model. MCSE is numerical uncertainty in an estimated posterior summary caused by a finite correlated simulation.

  • Why does noncentering help hierarchical models?

    With weak group data it separates standard latent effects from population scale, reducing funnel curvature and posterior dependence. With strongly informed groups, centered forms can sometimes be more efficient.

Production / system-design connection

Run at least multiple independent chains with deterministic, independent RNG streams and versioned initializations. Separate adaptation from retained draws. Define quality gates for R-hat, bulk/tail ESS relative to required summary precision, MCSE, divergences, treedepth saturation, energy diagnostics, failed transitions, and model-specific invariants. Store compact posterior draws or reproducible summaries with data/code hashes, sampler configuration, package/compiler/hardware versions, and diagnostics. Limit raw posterior access when draws reveal sensitive small-group values. Benchmark runtime and cap resources, but never silently return partial chains as valid. Retry only with a documented diagnostic hypothesis; otherwise fall back to a simpler validated model or withhold the decision. Rollback restores model, parameterization, sampler, prior, and posterior artifact together. Monitor predictive calibration after deployment because perfect MCMC cannot rescue a wrong model.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A chain has N=10,000 and integrated autocorrelation time 20. Approximate ESS.

    Show solution

    ESS=N/tau=10,000/20=500 independent-equivalent draws.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Posterior SD is 2 and ESS is 400. Approximate MCSE of the mean.

    Show solution

    2/sqrt(400)=0.1. This is simulation error in the posterior mean estimate, not posterior uncertainty of 2.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why can four chains with R-hat near one still miss a mode?

    Show solution

    If all initialize in and remain within the same mode, they can agree locally. Use dispersed starts, model knowledge, alternative methods, and predictive/sensitivity checks to search for disconnected regions.

8.5

Hierarchical / Multilevel Models

highverified
Roles: ds, as

Topic overview

Hierarchical Bayesian models represent related groups with group-specific parameters drawn from a population distribution whose hyperparameters are learned from all groups. The result is partial pooling: noisy groups shrink more toward the population pattern, while well-observed groups retain more local information. This chapter contrasts no pooling, complete pooling, and partial pooling; derives Normal–Normal shrinkage; explains exchangeability, hyperpriors, varying intercepts and slopes, cross-level interactions, centered and noncentered parameterizations, new-group prediction, and the distinction between population-level variation and residual noise. You will learn why shrinkage reduces winner's curse and multiple-comparison noise, when it can erase real subgroup structure, how weakly identified group scales create funnels, and why groups with few levels need careful priors. The worked example estimates conversion rates across stores with unequal traffic. The lab implements analytic partial pooling for known variances, verifies limiting cases, and expresses the equivalent PyMC model. Production guidance covers group taxonomy, cold start, fairness, drift, diagnostics, posterior storage, privacy, and rollback.

Prerequisites

  • bayes-update
  • conjugate-priors
  • mcmc

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish complete, no, and partial pooling and connect each to assumptions about group variation.
  • Derive shrinkage weights from within-group uncertainty and between-group variance.
  • Specify varying-intercept and varying-slope models with defensible exchangeability and hyperpriors.
  • Diagnose funnel geometry, sparse groups, taxonomy drift, overshrinkage, and new-group predictive behavior.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A hierarchical model assumes group parameters come from a shared population distribution, then learns both group effects and population hyperparameters. It partially pools: a group estimate is pulled toward the population mean in proportion to its uncertainty, so small noisy groups shrink more than large precise groups. This improves average estimation and handles multiplicity, but relies on exchangeability and a credible group distribution. Check hyperpriors, centered versus noncentered geometry, outliers, group count, fairness, and prediction for new groups.

What you must know

  • Partial pooling learns relatedness instead of choosing all-or-nothing pooling
  • Shrinkage strength follows relative within- and between-group precision
  • Exchangeability is a modeling claim
  • Hyperpriors regularize weakly identified group variation
  • New-group prediction integrates the population distribution

Why this matters

Products estimate metrics for stores, countries, sellers, models, cohorts, and annotators. Separate estimates make tiny groups look extreme by noise; one pooled estimate hides genuine heterogeneity. Hierarchical models offer a middle ground and reduce the need for ad hoc minimum-count thresholds. Interviews test partial pooling, while production requires more: groups change taxonomy, rare groups may be safety-critical, and automatic shrinkage toward a dominant population can hide inequity or local failure. A hierarchical posterior is not merely smoothing; it represents a generative assumption about how group effects relate. That assumption needs predictive checks and domain review.

Intuition

Imagine each store reports a conversion estimate with an error bar. A store with 20 visits has a wide bar, so the company-wide pattern should influence its estimate strongly. A store with 200,000 visits has a narrow bar and moves little. The population spread controls how similar stores are believed to be. If the learned between-store variance is near zero, pooling is strong; if stores genuinely vary greatly, shrinkage weakens. Unlike a fixed global penalty, the model propagates uncertainty about the population mean and spread. For a brand-new store, prediction starts from that population distribution rather than an arbitrary zero or a noisy nearest neighbor.

Complete, no, and partial pooling

Complete pooling sets every theta_j equal, assuming no group heterogeneity. No pooling estimates each independently, discarding cross-group information and amplifying noise and winner's curse. Partial pooling places a population distribution on theta_j. In a Normal model with group estimate ybar_j variance s_j^2 and prior theta_j~N(mu,tau^2), conditional posterior mean is w_j ybar_j+(1-w_j)mu with w_j=tau^2/(tau^2+s_j^2). Large measurement uncertainty means smaller w and stronger shrinkage. Mu and tau are themselves uncertain in a full hierarchy, so actual shrinkage integrates over their posterior.

Exchangeability and structured populations

Exchangeability says group labels carry no predictive information beyond modeled covariates before observing group outcomes: permuting labels leaves the prior joint distribution unchanged. Stores in different countries, sizes, or product tiers may not be exchangeable under one distribution. Add group-level predictors, nested structures, correlated varying effects, mixtures, or separate populations when justified. Exchangeability is not identicality; individual theta_j may differ. A heavy-tailed population distribution can protect genuine outliers from excessive shrinkage. Post hoc splitting after seeing outcomes risks overfitting and should be validated.

Varying intercepts, slopes, and correlations

A varying-intercept model lets baseline outcomes differ by group. Varying slopes let treatment or feature effects differ, enabling partial pooling of heterogeneous effects. A multivariate population distribution can correlate intercepts and slopes, but correlation matrices and scales need regularizing priors. Cross-level interactions explain systematic heterogeneity through group covariates. Center predictors so intercepts have meaningful scales and priors. Random-slope models need enough within-group treatment variation; a slope is not identified in a group with one exposure level merely because a hierarchy exists. Causal interpretation still requires valid treatment design.

Hyperpriors, few groups, and sampler geometry

With few groups, data weakly identify tau; a diffuse prior on group SD can put excessive mass on implausible heterogeneity or create computation problems. Use domain-scaled half-normal, half-t, or other defensible priors and sensitivity analysis. The centered parameterization theta_j~N(mu,tau) forms a funnel near tau=0 when group data are weak. Noncentering theta_j=mu+tau z_j, z_j~N(0,1), often improves geometry. Strongly informed groups may favor centering; mixed parameterizations can help. Inspect divergences, tail ESS, and posterior concentration of tau rather than trusting default sampling.

New groups, outliers, and fairness

Prediction for an unseen group draws a new theta from the posterior population distribution, which is wider than uncertainty for the average mu. Existing small groups borrow strength, but shrinkage can mask rare-group harms by pulling them toward the majority. Report raw data, partially pooled estimates, intervals, and shrinkage weights. Evaluate coverage and error by group size and protected attributes. If groups are policy-relevant rather than exchangeable random levels, fixed effects or structured priors may be more appropriate. Outlier handling should be modeled, not implemented by deleting groups whose posterior predictive checks fail.

Identifiability and information at each level

A hierarchy cannot manufacture information absent from every level. The population mean is informed by the number and precision of groups; the population variance needs multiple groups with distinguishable effects; group slopes need within-group predictor variation. Confounding between residual noise, group variance, and measurement error can yield broad or prior-dominated posteriors. Plot prior-to-posterior movement for hyperparameters and perform simulated-data recovery over realistic group counts and imbalance. If a group-level predictor is constant within higher-level clusters, its effect may be confounded with cluster variation. Report which parameters are data identified, partially pooled, or principally regularized by priors. A stable sampler around a prior-dominated posterior is computational success, not evidence that the desired contrast was learned.

Math / formal view

For y_j|theta_j~N(theta_j,s_j^2) and theta_j|mu,tau~N(mu,tau^2) with mu,tau fixed, posterior variance v_j=(1/s_j^2+1/tau^2)^{-1} and mean m_j=v_j(y_j/s_j^2+mu/tau^2)=w_j y_j+(1-w_j)mu, where w_j=tau^2/(tau^2+s_j^2). As s_j^2→0, w_j→1 (local data dominate); as s_j^2→infinity, w_j→0 (population dominates). Prediction for a new group integrates mu and tau uncertainty as well as theta_new variation.

Unequal-information store effects

Compute shrinkage weights from each store's standard error and the population spread, compare raw and pooled effects, then audit whether exchangeability and fairness justify borrowing strength.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement Normal hierarchical shrinkage with known hyperparameters, verify limiting behavior, and express the equivalent PyMC model.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def normal_partial_pool(observed,se,mu,tau):
    local_var=se*se; group_var=tau*tau
    posterior_var=1/(1/local_var+1/group_var)
    posterior_mean=posterior_var*(observed/local_var+mu/group_var)
    weight=group_var/(group_var+local_var)
    return posterior_mean,posterior_var,weight

observed=[0.50,0.20,-0.40]; ses=[0.50,0.10,0.60]
results=[normal_partial_pool(y,se,0.10,0.20) for y,se in zip(observed,ses)]
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import numpy as np
pooled=np.asarray([r[0] for r in results])
weights=np.asarray([r[2] for r in results])

# with pm.Model():
#   mu=pm.Normal('mu',0,1); tau=pm.HalfNormal('tau',0.5)
#   z=pm.Normal('z',0,1,shape=3); theta=mu+tau*z
