14.2

Randomized Experiment Design

very highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Randomized experiment design determines what causal question a test can answer before any statistical model is fit. This chapter develops experimental units, treatment versions, eligibility, potential outcomes, assignment mechanisms, complete and Bernoulli randomization, blocking and stratification, cluster and switchback designs, factorial experiments, unequal allocation, covariate balance, noncompliance, attrition, spillovers, exposure, power, preregistration, and analysis plans. You will learn to align randomization with the interference and delivery structure, separate design-stage balance from post-hoc adjustment, preserve intention-to-treat analysis, and avoid conditioning on variables affected by treatment. A worked marketplace example compares buyer-level, market-level, and time-block assignment under seller competition. The lab implements deterministic blocked randomization, checks allocation and balance invariants, and estimates a known treatment effect over repeated simulations. Production guidance covers assignment services, salts, mutual exclusion, ramps, identity changes, logging, privacy, monitoring, incident response, and rollback. A good design makes a simple estimator credible; no amount of downstream modeling can reconstruct counterfactual evidence destroyed by a flawed assignment or measurement process.

Prerequisites

  • ab-testing
  • sampling-design
  • causal-inference

Learning objectives

  • Choose an experimental unit and assignment mechanism that match treatment delivery, interference, carryover, and the target estimand.
  • Use blocking, clustering, factorial structure, and unequal allocation with correct analysis and power implications.
  • Specify intention-to-treat, exposure, attrition, noncompliance, and missing-outcome handling before observing effects.
  • Implement reproducible blocked assignment and verify determinism, allocation, covariate balance, and estimator behavior.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

I start with the causal estimand and target population, then choose the unit at which treatment can be assigned without unacceptable spillover or carryover. I define eligibility before randomization, stable assignment, treatment versions, primary outcomes, guardrails, duration, and exclusions. I use blocking on strong pre-treatment predictors to improve balance and precision, cluster randomization when units interact, and switchbacks when treatment operates at a shared time-varying system level. Analysis follows the assignment mechanism and preserves ITT. I predeclare power, multiplicity, stopping, missingness, and noncompliance handling, then validate assignment and exposure before reading effects.

What you must know

  • Design begins with estimand and interference structure
  • Randomization unit and analysis unit must remain aligned
  • Blocking can improve precision using pre-treatment information
  • Cluster and switchback designs trade bias control for effective sample size
  • ITT, missingness, and treatment versions must be specified before outcomes

Why this matters

Randomization is not a button labeled fifty-fifty. A messaging feature may spill across friends, a pricing change may shift marketplace equilibrium, and a ranking algorithm may operate on a shared inventory pool. Randomizing individuals in those systems can estimate a diluted or biased contrast. Conversely, clustering too coarsely can leave too few independent units for useful power. Design choices determine identification and uncertainty; analysis cannot repair missing control worlds after launch. Interviews test whether candidates recognize the experimental unit, potential interference, and post-treatment selection. In production, robust assignment and exposure infrastructure is as important as the estimator.

Intuition

An experiment deliberately creates comparable counterfactual worlds. The assignment coin determines which potential outcome is revealed for each unit. Blocking first groups similar units using pre-treatment information, then flips coins within groups so an unlucky imbalance on a strong predictor is less likely. Cluster randomization flips one coin for a connected group to keep spillovers mostly within treatment worlds, but members of a cluster do not provide independent replicas. Switchbacks assign a shared system by time block, balancing time patterns while requiring washout for carryover. Every efficiency gain or operational convenience changes what counts as independent evidence.

From causal question to experimental unit

Define potential outcomes under explicit treatment versions and a target contrast: ITT among all assigned eligible units, per-protocol effect, direct effect, or total equilibrium effect are not interchangeable. Choose the unit whose assignment can be implemented stably and whose outcomes are approximately unaffected by other units' assignments under the design. Users, devices, households, stores, geographic markets, graph clusters, or time blocks may be appropriate. If identities merge or treatment crosses units, document contamination. The unit of analysis should respect assignment dependence; millions of events from one randomized market do not create millions of independent experimental units.

Complete, Bernoulli, blocked, and unequal assignment

Bernoulli randomization assigns each unit independently with a fixed probability, producing random arm sizes. Complete randomization fixes arm counts and samples an assignment uniformly. Blocked randomization fixes or controls allocation within prespecified strata defined by pre-treatment variables, often improving balance and variance. Pair matching is an extreme block design. Unequal allocation can reduce exposure to risky treatment, satisfy capacity, or optimize precision under unequal variances and costs. Assignment probabilities must be known and positive for every target unit. Deterministic hashing is operationally stable only if the identifier, namespace, salt, traffic ramp, and modulo logic are versioned and collision behavior is understood.

Clusters, switchbacks, and factorial experiments

Cluster randomization assigns groups to reduce within-group interference or match delivery. Effective sample size depends on cluster count, size imbalance, and intracluster correlation; analysis uses cluster-level or cluster-robust methods. Switchbacks randomize a shared service or market across time blocks, requiring blocks long enough for treatment delivery yet short enough for replication, with washout for carryover and blocking by time-of-day or day-of-week. Factorial designs randomize multiple factors to estimate main effects and interactions efficiently, but interactions require power and compatible treatments. Mutual-exclusion layers prevent incompatible experiments from contaminating each other but reduce available traffic.

Noncompliance, attrition, exposure, and post-treatment bias

ITT compares assigned arms and remains protected by randomization even when delivery is imperfect. Conditioning on actual exposure, engagement, survival, or another treatment consequence can open selection bias. Record assignment, eligibility, delivery, exposure, and outcomes as distinct events. One-sided or two-sided noncompliance may support instrumental-variable estimands under exclusion, monotonicity, and other assumptions, but not by simply dropping noncompliers. Differential attrition or missing outcomes can bias ITT if missingness depends on treatment and potential outcome; predefine bounds, sensitivity analyses, or measurement recovery. Freeze treatment versions or model planned versions because changing implementation mid-test creates an ambiguous treatment.

Power, diagnostics, and prespecified analysis

Power the number of independent assignment units using baseline variance, design effect, MDE, allocation, expected attrition, and planned estimator. Prespecify primary and guardrail metrics, transformations, windows, covariate adjustment, subgroup hypotheses, multiplicity, stopping, and decision thresholds. After assignment, check counts, invariants, treatment delivery, and covariate balance as diagnostics; do not repeatedly rerandomize until outcome-correlated balance looks favorable unless the rerandomization rule was part of the design. Analyze according to the actual randomization, including block or cluster indicators and weights. Preserve every protocol deviation and report sensitivity rather than selecting the most favorable specification.

Math / formal view

With units i and assignment Z_i, potential outcomes Y_i(1),Y_i(0), the finite-sample average treatment effect is tau=N^{-1}sum_i[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)]. Under complete randomization, difference in arm means is unbiased for tau. In blocks b, combine block effects tau_hat_b with target weights N_b/N. For equal-size clusters with intracluster correlation rho and mean size m, the approximate design effect is 1+(m-1)rho; unequal sizes usually worsen it. Factorial main effects average contrasts across levels of other randomized factors.

Choosing a design for a two-sided marketplace

Map buyer-seller spillovers, compare individual, market-cluster, and switchback assignments, then choose the design whose estimand and carryover assumptions match the policy decision.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement reproducible blocked assignment, verify allocation and pre-treatment balance, and confirm difference-in-means behavior across repeated randomized assignments.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import hashlib,random
def score(namespace,unit):
    digest=hashlib.sha256(f'{namespace}:{unit}'.encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest[:8],'big')
def blocked_assign(rows,namespace):
    by_block={}
    for row in rows:by_block.setdefault(row['block'],[]).append(row)
    assignment={}
    for block,members in by_block.items():
        ordered=sorted(members,key=lambda r:score(namespace,r['id']))
        for i,row in enumerate(ordered):assignment[row['id']]=i%2
    return assignment
rows=[{'id':i,'block':'high' if i%3==0 else 'low','baseline':10+(i%3)*4} for i in range(120)]
assignment=blocked_assign(rows,'exp-v1')
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(rows); df['treatment']=df['id'].map(assignment)
block_counts=df.groupby(['block','treatment']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
balance=df.groupby('treatment')['baseline'].mean()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version the unit key, namespace, salt, eligibility, block map and allocation; preserve first assignment; monitor within-block counts and contamination; and use kill switches that stop treatment without deleting the randomized evidence.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert assignment==blocked_assign(rows,'exp-v1')
assert assignment!=blocked_assign(rows,'exp-v2')
assert (block_counts.max(axis=1)-block_counts.min(axis=1)).max()<=1
assert abs(balance[1]-balance[0])<0.5
rng=random.Random(7); estimates=[]
for rep in range(500):
    a=blocked_assign(rows,f'rep-{rep}')
    outcomes={r['id']:r['baseline']+2*a[r['id']]+rng.gauss(0,1) for r in rows}
    mt=sum(outcomes[i] for i,z in a.items() if z)/sum(a.values())
    mc=sum(outcomes[i] for i,z in a.items() if not z)/(len(a)-sum(a.values()))
    estimates.append(mt-mc)
assert abs(sum(estimates)/len(estimates)-2)<0.08

Common mistakes

  • Choosing the smallest convenient randomization unit

    Convenience can create interference or carryover; align assignment with treatment delivery and the causal estimand.

  • Counting events as independent units

    Inference follows assignment; repeated outcomes within randomized users or clusters are correlated.

  • Dropping users who were not exposed

    Exposure is post-assignment and may select on treatment effects; preserve ITT and analyze compliance only with explicit assumptions.

  • Blocking on a post-treatment variable

    Blocks must be determined before assignment from unaffected information.

Likely follow-ups

  • When should you cluster-randomize?

    When treatment or outcomes spill substantially within groups, delivery occurs at group level, or contamination makes individual assignment misaligned with the target effect.

  • Why block randomization?

    It guarantees controlled allocation within prespecified pre-treatment strata and can reduce variance when block variables predict outcomes.

  • What is a switchback experiment?

    A shared unit such as a market or service alternates variants across randomized time blocks; analysis must account for time, carryover, and block-level independence.

Production / system-design connection

Run assignment through a reviewed service with immutable experiment namespace, salt, eligibility version, unit key, allocation, ramp state, mutual-exclusion layer, block or cluster map, and treatment version. Make retries idempotent and preserve the first assignment. Log delivery and exposure independently. Validate counts within blocks, cross-experiment conflicts, identity churn, cluster leakage, and invariant outcomes. Ramps and kill switches change traffic only through recorded protocol events. Restrict identifiers and sensitive stratification fields. Reproduce assignments offline from snapshots and test A/A behavior. On incident, stop serving treatment while retaining assignments and outcome collection where safe; rollback configuration, treatment artifact, and analysis plan together without rewriting historical membership.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Why can cluster randomization reduce power?

    Show solution

    Members within a cluster are correlated, so information grows mainly with independent clusters rather than raw member count; imbalance and intracluster correlation inflate variance.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Can you block on last month's usage?

    Show solution

    Yes if measured before treatment, available for every eligible unit, and block construction is fixed before assignment.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    A user is assigned treatment but never loads the page. Include in ITT?

    Show solution

    Yes. ITT compares assignment policies and preserves randomization; a separate compliance estimand needs additional assumptions.

14.3

Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM)

highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) occurs when observed experiment allocation counts differ implausibly from the proportions specified by the randomization design. It is one of the highest-value trust diagnostics in online experimentation because many assignment, eligibility, exposure, identity, and logging defects first appear as unexpected arm counts. This chapter derives the multinomial chi-square check, explains its assumptions and scale sensitivity, distinguishes assignment-level from triggered-analysis SRM, and builds a root-cause taxonomy across randomization, delivery, telemetry, filtering, bots, joins, and time. You will learn why SRM is a symptom rather than a correction target, why balanced outcomes cannot rescue a failed trust check, how to localize onset and affected slices, and when unequal counts are expected by design. A worked redirect bug shows how treatment-dependent loss reverses an apparent effect. The lab implements the SRM statistic and p-value, compares it with SciPy, and diagnoses a time-slice failure using invariants. Production guidance covers continuous alerting, multiple looks, minimum counts, ownership, forensic snapshots, restart criteria, and rollback. The rule is simple: do not interpret treatment effects until the mismatch is understood and the causal sample is trustworthy.

Prerequisites

  • experiment-design
  • chi-square
  • missingness-mechanisms

Learning objectives

  • Compute an SRM goodness-of-fit statistic for arbitrary planned allocation proportions and interpret it as a trust diagnostic.
  • Separate valid random allocation fluctuation from assignment, delivery, exposure, logging, filtering, identity, and join failures.
  • Localize an SRM by event stage, time, platform, geography, eligibility, and identifier without outcome-driven fishing.
  • Define automated alert, investigation, restart, and evidence-preservation procedures for an experimentation platform.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

SRM means the observed variant counts are inconsistent with the planned allocation beyond ordinary random fluctuation. I test assignment-unit counts against expected proportions, usually with a chi-square goodness-of-fit check, before looking at effects. A very small p-value is a smoke alarm, not an effect adjustment: I investigate assignment, eligibility, exposure delivery, missing telemetry, identity changes, redirects, filters, joins, bots, and time of onset. I also distinguish all-assigned SRM from triggered-population SRM. Until the root cause is explained and shown not to bias the estimand, I quarantine the result and normally fix and restart the experiment.

What you must know

  • SRM tests allocation integrity, not treatment impact
  • Expected counts come from the actual design and ramp history
  • Assignment, exposure, and analysis populations need separate checks
  • The chi-square p-value detects a symptom but not its cause
  • A failed SRM gate blocks causal interpretation until diagnosed

Why this matters

A missing telemetry event can occur more often in one variant precisely because that variant crashes, redirects, or changes the code path. An analysis then drops affected units and turns harm into an apparent win. Duplicate identifiers, stale assignment cookies, inconsistent eligibility, or faulty joins can cause the same symptom. Because treatment effects are often small, even modest selective loss can dominate the signal. Microsoft's SRM taxonomy describes the diagnostic as analogous to fever: easy to detect, diverse in cause, and dangerous to ignore. Interviews ask SRM because it reveals whether a candidate trusts the experimental data-generating process before running inference.

Intuition

If a fair assignment service sends half of a large eligible population to each arm, arm counts wobble around fifty-fifty by chance. A difference of a few users is ordinary; a difference of thousands is not. The SRM statistic scales each squared deviation by its expected count, then asks how surprising the total would be under the design. But the alarm cannot tell whether the randomizer, treatment delivery, event logging, identity resolution, or analysis filter caused the loss. Build a chain of counts from eligible to assigned to delivered to exposed to measured, and find the first stage where arms diverge.

Expected counts and the goodness-of-fit test

For K variants with observed counts O_k, planned shares pi_k summing to one, and total N, expected counts are E_k=N*pi_k. Pearson's statistic is sum_k (O_k-E_k)^2/E_k and is approximately chi-square with K-1 degrees of freedom under independent assignment and sufficiently large expected counts. Use the assignment unit, not events or sessions, unless that is truly the randomized unit. Compute expectations from the allocation schedule when ramps changed over time. Tiny p-values are common for meaningful defects at scale, but fixed universal thresholds and repeated monitoring require an alerting design. Exact multinomial methods can handle small counts.

Assigned, exposed, triggered, and analyzed populations

Run SRM first on all eligible assigned units from the authoritative assignment log. Then reconcile treatment delivery, exposure, outcome telemetry, and the final analysis population. A triggered analysis can legitimately change arm proportions only if triggering is pre-treatment or unaffected by assignment; treatment-dependent triggering is post-randomization selection. Counts of exposure events can differ because users generate repeated events, so deduplicate at the unit level. A test that passes at assignment but fails after a metric join points downstream. A test that fails at assignment points toward eligibility, randomizer, identity, namespace, or ramp logic.

Root-cause taxonomy

Assignment causes include incorrect weights, inconsistent hashing libraries, overlapping experiments, missing salts, nonsticky IDs, and variant-specific eligibility. Delivery causes include redirects, caching, fail-open behavior, platform version gating, and capacity rejection. Instrumentation causes include variant-specific event paths, crashes before logging, schema drift, blocked scripts, and late events. Analysis causes include inner joins, asymmetric bot rules, timezone windows, deduplication, post-treatment filters, and incompatible snapshots. Identity causes include cookie deletion, device switching, merging, duplicate IDs, and logged-out users. External causes include crawlers or campaigns routed differently. The correction follows the first broken stage, not the final count table.

Localizing onset and affected slices

Plot cumulative observed-minus-expected counts over assignment time and annotate ramps, releases, schema changes, outages, and redirects. Test coarse prespecified slices such as platform, app version, country, data center, eligibility path, and identifier type to locate concentration, while controlling alert multiplicity and avoiding outcome-driven selection. Reconstruct the same units through raw assignment, exposure, and outcome tables with left joins and reason-coded attrition. Compare treatment and control missingness at each stage. Validate a suspected root cause by reproducing it on affected records and showing that the divergence begins where predicted, not merely by finding a correlated slice.

Quarantine, repair, restart, and prevention

Do not reweight arm counts to the planned ratio and declare the bias solved; missing units may differ in outcomes. If the cause is fully known and independent of potential outcomes under a defensible estimand, a planned correction may be possible, but this is exceptional and documented. Usually stop or quarantine, fix the system, choose whether old evidence is unusable, and restart with a new experiment version. Preserve the broken run for platform learning. Add prevention through shared assignment libraries, immutable exposure contracts, left-join analyses, event parity tests, A/A tests, ramp gates, automated stage-wise reconciliation, and incident owners. A passed rerun does not retroactively validate contaminated data.

Math / formal view

Given planned probabilities pi_1,...,pi_K and N observed assignment units, E_k=N*pi_k and X^2=sum_k(O_k-E_k)^2/E_k. Under the null and regularity, X^2 is approximately chi-square_{K-1}; p=P(ChiSq>=X^2). For two 50/50 arms this is equivalent to checking a binomial count. Standardized cell residuals (O_k-E_k)/sqrt(E_k) show direction but are dependent. Repeated looks or many slice tests require an alert policy; a small p-value does not quantify outcome bias.

A downstream SRM that manufactures a conversion win

Compare assignment and analysis counts, identify treatment-dependent event loss at the first divergent stage, reject reweighting as a causal repair, and restart after instrumentation and crash fixes.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement a multinomial SRM check, compare it with SciPy, and localize a treatment-specific count loss across time slices.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
from math import exp
def srm_stat(observed,proportions):
    total=sum(observed); expected=[total*p for p in proportions]
    stat=sum((o-e)**2/e for o,e in zip(observed,expected))
    return stat,expected
# For two arms, chi-square survival is erfc(sqrt(x/2)).
from math import erfc,sqrt
def srm_two_arm(observed,proportions=(0.5,0.5)):
    stat,expected=srm_stat(observed,proportions)
    return stat,erfc(sqrt(stat/2)),expected
global_report=srm_two_arm([10000,9700])
slices={'before':[5000,5002],'after':[5000,4698]}
slice_reports={k:srm_two_arm(v) for k,v in slices.items()}
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import chisquare
scipy_result=chisquare([10000,9700],f_exp=global_report[2])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Run unique-unit SRM at every evidence stage against versioned ramp expectations, gate effect visibility on trust, alert with onset and slices, preserve forensic snapshots, and restart rather than reweight when selective loss is plausible.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
stat,pvalue,expected=global_report
assert abs(sum(expected)-19700)<1e-12
assert abs(stat-scipy_result.statistic)<1e-12
assert abs(pvalue-scipy_result.pvalue)<1e-12
assert slice_reports['before'][1]>0.5
assert slice_reports['after'][1]<1e-4
assert srm_two_arm([9000,1000],(0.9,0.1))[1]>0.99
assert pvalue<1e-6

Common mistakes

  • Checking event counts instead of randomized units

    Repeated activity differs by treatment; deduplicate the actual assignment unit for the allocation check.

  • Ignoring SRM because baseline covariates look balanced

    Observed balance cannot rule out selective loss on unmeasured potential outcomes or broken telemetry.

  • Reweighting to 50/50

    Count weights do not recover selectively missing outcomes; diagnose the generating defect first.

  • Testing only the final analysis table

    Reconcile eligible, assigned, delivered, exposed, measured, and analyzed stages to localize the break.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does unequal arm size always mean SRM?

    No. Compare observed counts with the planned allocation, including ramp changes and capacity rules. SRM is implausible deviation from design, not inequality itself.

  • Can an experiment with SRM still be analyzed?

    Only after the cause is fully understood and a defensible estimand and correction are established. The safe default is quarantine, fix, and restart.

  • Why can assignment SRM pass while analysis SRM fails?

    Treatment-dependent delivery, event loss, filtering, identity, or joins can selectively remove units after correct assignment.

Production / system-design connection

Compute stage-wise unique-unit counts from immutable eligible, assignment, delivery, exposure, metric, and analysis snapshots. Derive expected counts from versioned allocation and ramp history. Alert with minimum-count and repeated-monitoring logic; route to an owner with experiment, slice, onset, residual, and lineage evidence. Automatically hide treatment effects behind a trust gate when SRM fails. Retain raw IDs under strict access and privacy controls for forensic joins, then aggregate incident artifacts. Version fixes and restart under a new experiment identifier. Monitor assignment-library versions, identifier churn, event parity, late arrival, and join attrition. Rollback treatment serving on correlated reliability harm, but never delete the malformed run that exposed the defect.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A 90/10 design observes 9000 and 1000 users. Is unequal size an SRM?

    Show solution

    No; those counts exactly match the planned ratio. Test against 90/10, not 50/50.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Assignment counts pass but exposed counts fail. Where do you investigate?

    Show solution

    Treatment delivery, redirects, caching, failures before exposure logging, identity, and exposure-event parity before downstream metric logic.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why does a tiny SRM p-value not tell you effect bias magnitude?

    Show solution

    It measures incompatibility of counts with allocation, not which outcomes are missing or how selection changes the treatment contrast.

14.4

Variance Reduction & CUPED

mediumverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Controlled-experiment variance reduction uses pre-treatment information to make treatment-effect estimates more precise without changing the randomized causal contrast. CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) adjusts an outcome by a centered covariate measured before assignment, typically the same user metric in a historical window. This chapter derives the optimal linear coefficient, variance reduction factor, unbiasedness under randomization, cross-fitting and regression adjustment, missing pre-period data, triggered metrics, ratio metrics, multiple covariates, heterogeneity, and failure modes. You will learn why correlation determines precision gain, why post-treatment covariates create bias, why centering and a treatment interaction matter, and how to estimate gains on historical A/A-style data rather than selecting a favorable adjustment after seeing outcomes. A worked revenue experiment shows a large variance reduction with unchanged effect expectation. The lab implements CUPED from first principles, compares it with an OLS treatment coefficient, and verifies unbiased effect recovery plus reduced variance over repeated randomized trials. Production guidance covers cutoff enforcement, leakage checks, coefficient versioning, missingness, metric lineage, monitoring, fallback, and rollback. CUPED creates information by removing predictable noise; it cannot repair broken randomization or measurement.

Prerequisites

  • experiment-design
  • expectation-variance
  • linear-regression

Learning objectives

  • Derive the CUPED adjustment coefficient and variance reduction from covariance and correlation.
  • Choose covariates that are predictive, pre-treatment, consistently available, and unaffected by assignment or exposure.
  • Connect CUPED to regression adjustment, interactions, cross-fitting, and robust analysis for complex metrics.
  • Implement and validate an adjustment using unbiasedness, variance, leakage, missingness, and reproducibility checks.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

CUPED reduces experiment variance by subtracting the predictable part of an outcome from a pre-treatment covariate. With outcome Y and centered covariate X, define Y_adj=Y-theta(X-E[X]), where theta=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X). Because treatment is randomized and X is measured before treatment, arm means of X are equal in expectation, so the treatment contrast stays unbiased while residual variance falls; with an optimal single covariate the ideal reduction is rho squared. I freeze the pre-period cutoff, estimate theta without outcome-driven selection, handle missing X explicitly, preserve ITT, and verify the adjusted effect against the raw estimate and historical simulations.

What you must know

  • CUPED removes outcome variation predictable before treatment
  • Pre-treatment timing protects the causal contrast
  • Ideal single-covariate variance reduction is governed by squared correlation
  • Regression adjustment generalizes CUPED but needs design-aware specification
  • Precision gains never excuse SRM, leakage, or post-treatment selection

Why this matters

User-level revenue, sessions, and engagement are heterogeneous: a small group of naturally heavy users creates large variance even after randomization balances groups in expectation. Historical behavior predicts much of that variation but cannot be affected by today's treatment. Removing it can detect the same decision-relevant effect with fewer units or a narrower interval at the same sample size. The original CUPED paper demonstrated the value of pre-experiment data for online experiments. However, a covariate contaminated by treatment, a cutoff tied to exposure, or post-hoc selection among many adjustments can bias or overstate gains. Production implementations therefore treat temporal lineage and analysis governance as first-class requirements.

Intuition

Two randomized arms may contain slightly different numbers of naturally high-spending users by chance. If last month's spend predicts this month's spend, subtract each user's expected baseline tendency before comparing arms. The adjusted outcome asks whether a user did unusually well relative to their pre-treatment pattern. Centering preserves the overall scale, and randomization means neither arm should receive systematically different baseline adjustments. Stronger pre-to-post correlation removes more noise. A user with no history requires a prespecified representation; silently keeping only returning users changes the target population.

Control-variate derivation

Let X be a pre-treatment covariate with mean mu_X and define Y_cv=Y-theta(X-mu_X). Its expectation equals E[Y] for any fixed theta because the centered term has mean zero. Its variance is Var(Y)+theta^2 Var(X)-2 theta Cov(Y,X), minimized at theta*=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X) when Var(X)>0. Substitution gives Var(Y_cv)=Var(Y)(1-rho^2), where rho is correlation between X and Y. In an experiment, comparing adjusted arm means retains ITT because assignment is independent of pre-treatment X in expectation. Finite-sample estimates of theta add uncertainty, usually small at scale but still part of method validation.

Choosing and constructing covariates

Good covariates predict the outcome, are available before assignment for the target units, have stable semantics, and cannot be altered by treatment. The same metric in a comparable pre-period is common; multiple historical periods, geography, device, or model predictions can add signal. Freeze an absolute cutoff before any unit could receive treatment, not a user-relative window starting from exposure. Do not use post-treatment clicks, survival, session count, or eligibility consequences. Avoid selecting covariates solely because they maximize precision in the current treatment comparison. Evaluate expected gains on historical periods, A/A splits, or cross-validation and keep a versioned covariate contract.

Regression adjustment, interactions, and cross-fitting

CUPED with one linear control is equivalent to residualizing outcomes or including a centered covariate in a treatment regression under corresponding specification. With treatment effects heterogeneous by X, include treatment-by-covariate interactions or use a fully interacted estimator so adjustment does not impose a common slope across arms. Robust standard errors protect heteroskedasticity. Flexible machine-learning predictions can serve as control variates when trained without treatment-period leakage; cross-fitting separates prediction training from residual evaluation and supports modern covariate adjustment. The target remains the randomized marginal effect, not the regression coefficient's associational interpretation outside the design.

Missing history, new users, and nonlinear metrics

New users have no pre-period metric. Complete-case CUPED changes the estimand to returning users and can interact with eligibility. Instead predefine zero plus a missingness indicator, group-specific centering, or a prediction model that accepts available features, then verify balance and effect interpretation. Heavy tails may need winsorization defined independently of treatment and applied consistently. Ratio metrics require unit-level definitions, delta-method or influence-function adjustment, or numerator and denominator treatment that preserves the estimand; subtracting a covariate from an already aggregated ratio is generally invalid. Triggered analyses must ensure the trigger is pre-treatment or assignment-invariant.

Validating gains and guarding failure modes

Always compute raw and adjusted effects: material divergence beyond expected noise suggests leakage, imbalance, implementation error, or estimand change. On historical null periods, verify centered adjusted effects and interval calibration. Measure covariance, theta, raw and residual variance, empirical reduction, missingness, and gains by prespecified platform or cohort. Re-estimate or version theta when behavior drifts, but do not tune repeatedly on live treatment effects. CUPED does not fix differential logging, SRM, interference, or noncompliance. If the covariate pipeline is late or invalid, fall back to the prespecified unadjusted estimator rather than blocking safety decisions or imputing from treatment-period outcomes.

Math / formal view

For centered X_c=X-mu_X, Y_cuped=Y-theta X_c. E[Y_cuped]=E[Y]. The variance-minimizing theta*=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X), yielding Var(Y_cuped)=Var(Y)-Cov(Y,X)^2/Var(X)=Var(Y)(1-rho^2). Estimate the treatment effect as mean(Y_cuped|Z=1)-mean(Y_cuped|Z=0). In a sample, center X using a treatment-blind population mean and compute uncertainty for the adjusted outcome at the randomization unit, with robust or cluster-aware methods matching the design.

Reducing revenue noise without changing the target

Use a frozen historical revenue covariate, derive theta, retain new users with explicit missingness handling, compare raw and adjusted effects, and validate empirical variance reduction on historical splits.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement CUPED adjustment, compare it with regression adjustment, and verify effect unbiasedness plus variance reduction over repeated randomized experiments.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
def cuped(y,x):
    x=np.asarray(x,float); y=np.asarray(y,float)
    xc=x-x.mean(); theta=float(np.dot(xc,y-y.mean())/np.dot(xc,xc))
    return y-theta*xc,theta
rng=np.random.default_rng(7); n=4000
x=rng.normal(10,3,n); z=rng.integers(0,2,n)
y=5+0.8*x+1.5*z+rng.normal(0,2,n)
y_adj,theta=cuped(y,x)
def arm_effect(values,z): return values[z==1].mean()-values[z==0].mean()
raw_effect=arm_effect(y,z); adjusted_effect=arm_effect(y_adj,z)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import statsmodels.api as sm
design=sm.add_constant(np.column_stack([z,x-x.mean()]))
fit=sm.OLS(y,design).fit(cov_type='HC1')
regression_effect=float(fit.params[1])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Freeze covariate cutoff and missingness semantics, version theta/model, publish raw and adjusted estimates, monitor leakage and realized variance reduction, and fall back to the unadjusted ITT estimator if the covariate pipeline is invalid.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(theta-0.8)<0.05
assert abs(adjusted_effect-regression_effect)<1e-10
assert np.var(y_adj)<np.var(y)
assert abs(adjusted_effect-1.5)<0.12
raw=[]; adjusted=[]
for seed in range(200):
    local=np.random.default_rng(seed); zz=local.integers(0,2,n); yy=5+0.8*x+1.5*zz+local.normal(0,2,n); aa,_=cuped(yy,x)
    raw.append(arm_effect(yy,zz)); adjusted.append(arm_effect(aa,zz))
assert abs(np.mean(adjusted)-1.5)<0.03
assert np.var(adjusted)<0.6*np.var(raw)

Common mistakes

  • Using a covariate measured after assignment

    Treatment may change it, so subtraction can remove part of the effect or induce selection bias; enforce a pre-treatment cutoff.

  • Dropping users without history

    That changes the population and can bias a triggered analysis; handle missing history explicitly.

  • Expecting CUPED to fix a broken test

    It reduces random variance under a trustworthy design; it does not repair SRM, logging loss, or interference.

  • Selecting the best covariate after reading results

    Prevalidate and version adjustment choices to avoid analysis multiplicity and overstated gains.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does CUPED remain unbiased?

    The centered covariate has zero expected arm contrast under randomization and is unaffected by treatment, so subtracting a fixed multiple does not change the expected treatment difference.

  • How much variance can it remove?

    For the optimal single linear covariate, the ideal outcome variance reduction is rho squared; treatment-effect variance also depends on allocation and estimation details.

  • What if theta is estimated from the experiment?

    Treatment-blind pooled estimation is common and often asymptotically valid, but fully interacted regression, robust errors, and historical validation improve protection under heterogeneity and finite samples.

Production / system-design connection

Create a covariate contract with source, unit, historical window, absolute cutoff, transformation, missingness handling, and owner. Enforce that no input timestamp reaches the assignment or treatment period. Version theta or model artifacts and compute them treatment-blind. Persist raw and adjusted outcomes, effects, intervals, covariance, correlation, variance reduction, sample inclusion, and balance. Monitor cutoff violations, missing-history drift, feature availability, theta instability, residual variance, raw-adjusted divergence, and coverage on A/A traffic. Limit access to historical user behavior and minimize retention. If the adjustment pipeline fails, publish the valid raw estimator with wider uncertainty. Rollback the CUPED artifact without changing assignments, outcomes, or the prespecified causal target.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    If pre/post correlation is 0.6, what ideal variance fraction remains?

    Show solution

    1-rho^2=1-0.36=0.64, so ideal variance reduction is 36% and standard error scales by sqrt(0.64)=0.8.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Why center X?

    Show solution

    Centering keeps the adjusted outcome mean on the original scale and makes the control-variate expectation zero; arm contrasts would cancel a common constant, but centering clarifies interpretation and numerics.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Can treatment-period session count be a CUPED covariate?

    Show solution

    No if treatment can affect sessions. It is post-treatment and adjustment could remove the treatment pathway or create selection bias.

14.5

Sequential Testing, Peeking & Early Stopping

highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Sequential experimentation allows data-dependent monitoring or stopping while preserving a declared error guarantee. Repeatedly applying a fixed-horizon p-value whenever new data arrive does not do this: optional stopping selects unusually favorable noise and inflates false positives. This chapter develops fixed-horizon designs, group-sequential looks, alpha spending, sequential probability ratio tests, always-valid p-values, e-values, confidence sequences, futility, harm stopping, minimum run constraints, delayed outcomes, and decision-theoretic trade-offs. You will learn why stopping rules are part of the statistical procedure, how time-uniform intervals differ from ordinary intervals, how to choose between planned looks and continuous monitoring, and why operational kill switches should not be confused with efficacy claims. A worked product experiment contrasts naive peeking with an anytime-valid rule. The lab simulates false-positive inflation from fixed-horizon peeking and verifies control from a Bonferroni group-sequential design using SciPy. Production guidance covers dashboards, information time, alpha budgets, metric multiplicity, late data, restarts, safety escalation, audit logs, and rollback. Sequential methods provide flexibility only when the monitoring rule and evidence process are designed together.

Prerequisites

  • ab-testing
  • hypothesis-testing
  • confidence-intervals

Learning objectives

  • Explain mathematically and through simulation why optional stopping invalidates repeatedly viewed fixed-horizon p-values.
  • Choose and interpret fixed-horizon, group-sequential, alpha-spending, confidence-sequence, and e-value procedures.
  • Separate efficacy, futility, harm, operational, and business stopping rules with their distinct guarantees.
  • Implement and validate a planned-look design using family-wise error simulations and an immutable monitoring schedule.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A fixed-horizon test controls Type I error only for its planned sample and analysis. If I repeatedly peek and stop when p<0.05, I give noise multiple chances to cross the threshold and inflate false positives. Valid options include prespecified group-sequential looks with alpha spending, a sequential probability ratio test for specified alternatives, or anytime-valid p-values, e-values, and confidence sequences. I define the stopping rule, information times, minimum duration, primary metric, multiplicity, and delayed-outcome handling before launch. Safety kill switches can stop exposure immediately, but confirmatory efficacy claims still follow their declared evidence procedure.

What you must know

  • Optional stopping changes the sampling distribution
  • Monitoring schedule and stopping rule are part of the design
  • Group-sequential methods spend a finite error budget across planned looks
  • Confidence sequences provide simultaneous coverage over time
  • Safety stopping and efficacy inference answer different questions

Why this matters

Teams naturally watch experiments daily, want to stop losing variants early, and want to ship obvious wins without waiting. Traditional fixed-horizon reports tempt users to treat today's p-value as if no earlier looks occurred. Under a true null, enough looks make a threshold crossing increasingly likely. Valid sequential tools reconcile monitoring with error control, but their intervals are often wider early and their assumptions still depend on assignment, dependence, and metric construction. Interviews ask peeking because it exposes whether a candidate understands a procedure rather than a one-time formula. Experiment platforms must encode the rule so dashboards cannot silently change inferential meaning.

Intuition

A fixed-horizon threshold is like one finish-line photograph. Peeking takes many photographs and keeps the most flattering one. Even when treatment does nothing, a noisy estimate wanders and may briefly look significant. Alpha spending divides a finite false-positive budget across planned checkpoints; early evidence must be stronger because more opportunities remain. A confidence sequence is a sequence of intervals constructed so the true value is covered simultaneously at all times with high probability, allowing observation at an arbitrary stopping time. Flexibility is paid for through wider early boundaries, not obtained for free.

Why naive repeated testing fails

A p-value is calibrated under a null distribution and an analysis rule. At each independent or correlated look, the estimate has another opportunity to produce an extreme statistic. The probability of ever crossing 0.05 exceeds 5%, even though adjacent looks reuse data and are dependent. Stopping at a favorable crossing also biases the reported effect upward, known as the winner's curse. Continuing after an unfavorable result but stopping after a favorable one is asymmetric optional stopping. A final ordinary interval calculated at that selected time no longer has its nominal fixed-horizon coverage. Simulation under the complete pipeline is a powerful audit of the actual rule.

Planned looks and alpha spending

Group-sequential designs specify interim information times and efficacy boundaries so the probability of any false rejection stays at alpha. Bonferroni can allocate alpha/K across K looks and is simple but conservative. Pocock-like boundaries spend more evenly; O'Brien-Fleming-like boundaries demand very strong early evidence and approach conventional thresholds later. Alpha-spending functions allow looks at flexible information times while tracking cumulative budget. Information time should reflect precision, not merely calendar days, especially with uneven traffic or delayed outcomes. Correlated endpoints and multiple variants consume an additional multiplicity budget.

SPRT, e-values, and confidence sequences

Wald's sequential probability ratio test accumulates a likelihood ratio between specified simple hypotheses and stops at evidence boundaries. Always-valid p-values remain valid at any stopping time under their construction. An e-process is a nonnegative process with null expectation controlled over time; a large e-value supplies evidence, and Ville's inequality bounds the probability its running maximum crosses 1/alpha. Confidence sequences invert sequential tests to provide intervals with simultaneous coverage across time. Modern nonparametric confidence sequences handle means and treatment effects under stated boundedness or variance assumptions. These objects are not ordinary p-values or confidence intervals with a new label; use matched estimators and implementations.

Efficacy, futility, harm, and operational stopping

Efficacy stopping claims benefit under the confirmatory rule. Futility stops when the chance or value of reaching a useful conclusion is low; nonbinding futility can preserve some guarantees more easily than binding rules. Harm stopping may use asymmetric thresholds and multiple safety metrics because protecting users outweighs power. Operational kill switches respond to crashes, latency, security, or data corruption and need no permission from an efficacy test, but the stopped run may not support a causal product claim. Minimum runtime covers novelty, weekly cycles, and delayed outcomes. Maximum runtime prevents indefinite underpowered tests. Define whether restarts create new evidence or continue a valid sequence.

Information, delayed data, and platform validation

Assign each unit once and define when its outcome becomes observable. If recent units have incomplete windows, naive daily means compare arms with different maturity or repeatedly revise history. Use cohort-complete information sets, lag-aware estimators, or explicitly modeled delayed outcomes. Persist every look, sample, metric version, cumulative alpha or e-value, boundary, and action. Backtest and simulate null, alternative, heavy-tailed, clustered, missing, and late-event scenarios using the exact production code. Never let a dashboard toggle between fixed and sequential inference after seeing results. If assumptions fail, quarantine evidence and use safety behavior, not an improvised threshold.

Math / formal view

For K planned looks, Bonferroni rejects if any p_k<=alpha/K, guaranteeing family-wise error at most alpha without independence. An alpha-spending design chooses cumulative A(t)<=alpha and boundaries consistent with increments. A confidence sequence {C_t} satisfies P(theta in C_t for all t)>=1-alpha. An e-process E_t under H0 satisfies E[E_tau]<=1 for suitable stopping times; Ville gives P(sup_t E_t>=1/alpha)<=alpha. Exact formulas depend on metric, dependence, variance assumptions, and assignment design.

A tempting early p-value that does not cross the sequential boundary

Contrast naive repeated 0.05 testing with a finite alpha budget, preserve a separate harm switch, and use the final interval relative to a practical threshold.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate false-positive inflation from naive peeking and verify family-wise control from a planned Bonferroni group-sequential design.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
from math import erf,sqrt
def pvalue(x,y):
    n=len(x); effect=x.mean()-y.mean(); se=sqrt(x.var(ddof=1)/n+y.var(ddof=1)/n)
    z=effect/se; return 2*(1-0.5*(1+erf(abs(z)/sqrt(2))))
def simulate(rule,runs=3000,seed=7):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); rejected=0; looks=(40,80,120,160,200)
    for _ in range(runs):
        x=rng.normal(size=looks[-1]); y=rng.normal(size=looks[-1])
        if any(pvalue(x[:n],y[:n])<=rule(len(looks),i) for i,n in enumerate(looks,1)):rejected+=1
    return rejected/runs
naive=simulate(lambda k,i:0.05)
controlled=simulate(lambda k,i:0.05/k)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from scipy.stats import norm
bonferroni_z=float(norm.ppf(1-0.05/(2*5)))
fixed_z=float(norm.ppf(1-0.05/2))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Encode the monitoring method and information schedule immutably, record every look and remaining alpha/evidence, simulate production false positives, separate safety kills from efficacy claims, and restart rather than improvise after invalid data.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert naive>0.10
assert controlled<0.065
assert controlled>0
assert bonferroni_z>fixed_z
assert abs(simulate(lambda k,i:0.05,seed=7)-naive)<1e-12
assert 0<=naive<=1 and 0<=controlled<=1

Common mistakes

  • Peeking but claiming looks are highly correlated

    Correlation reduces but does not remove inflation; calibrate the entire planned or anytime-valid procedure.

  • Using an anytime-valid p-value with an ordinary interval

    Inference objects must be matched; use the corresponding confidence sequence for time-uniform interval claims.

  • Requiring statistical harm before stopping crashes

    Operational safety can stop exposure immediately; statistical evidence governs later causal interpretation, not user protection.

  • Restarting and combining p-values informally

    A restart changes assignment, treatment, or evidence history; define a new experiment or a valid continuation rule.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a confidence sequence?

    A sequence of intervals designed to cover the fixed parameter simultaneously over all times with probability at least 1-alpha, enabling valid inspection at a data-dependent time.

  • What is alpha spending?

    A rule allocating cumulative Type I error across information times, with boundaries calibrated so total false-rejection probability remains controlled.

  • Can you always stop an experiment for harm?

    Yes operationally when users are at risk. Whether the resulting data support a formal harm claim depends on the prespecified monitoring and multiplicity procedure.

Production / system-design connection

Store the inference mode, primary hypothesis, alternative or practical margin, maximum sample, minimum duration, information-time definition, planned looks, alpha-spending or e-process version, metric contracts, and delayed-outcome cutoff. The dashboard reads this immutable plan and cannot expose fixed-horizon significance at interim looks. Persist each look with data snapshot, counts, estimate, boundary, remaining budget, trust status, and action. Monitor SRM and invariants before sequential evidence. Simulate platform-wide false-positive behavior, including correlated metrics and overlapping tests. Safety alerts bypass efficacy gates but are audited. On invalid data or code, freeze claims, stop risky treatment, and restart under a new version; rollback must preserve the complete evidence path.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Why is p=0.03 at an interim look not automatically a win?

    Show solution

    Its meaning depends on the planned boundary or anytime-valid construction; an ordinary fixed-horizon threshold is invalid after optional monitoring.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    What is information time?

    Show solution

    The fraction of planned statistical information accumulated, often related to inverse variance, not necessarily the fraction of calendar duration.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why are early group-sequential boundaries often stricter?

    Show solution

    They reserve error budget for later looks and prevent weak early noise from triggering a high false-positive rate.

14.6

Metric Design: North Star, Driver & Guardrail Metrics

very highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Metric design translates a product objective into a measurable, sensitive, directionally trustworthy decision system. A North Star or Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC) should predict long-term value closely enough to guide short experiments, driver metrics explain mechanisms, and guardrails prevent unacceptable harm. This chapter develops metric contracts, populations, units, numerators, denominators, windows, attribution, directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, gaming, ratio estimands, heavy tails, missingness, delayed outcomes, composite scores, proxy risk, and metric lifecycle governance. You will learn why more activity is not always better, why per-user and per-event averages answer different questions, how denominator changes can reverse a result, and how to validate short-term proxies against long-term outcomes and known interventions. A worked recommendation-system scorecard separates engagement from satisfaction and ecosystem health. The lab builds a semantic metric contract and ratio-of-sums calculator, rejects grain and denominator errors, and verifies invariants against pandas. Production guidance covers lineage, versioning, backfills, dashboards, experiment inference, access control, alerts, deprecation, correction, and rollback. The goal is not one magical number; it is an auditable map from user and business value to decisions under uncertainty.

Prerequisites

  • experiment-design
  • groupby-pivot
  • causal-inference

Learning objectives

  • Define a metric through population, unit, event, numerator, denominator, window, attribution, direction, and missingness semantics.
  • Construct primary, driver, diagnostic, and guardrail metrics that map to a causal product theory rather than a dashboard inventory.
  • Evaluate directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, robustness, gaming risk, and long-term proxy quality.
  • Implement and test ratio metrics with grain, denominator, reconciliation, and versioning invariants.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

I start from the decision and long-term user/business objective, then create an OEC or primary metric whose direction is credibly aligned with that objective. I add driver metrics for the causal mechanism and guardrails for reliability, safety, fairness, cost, and ecosystem harm. Every metric has a contract: population, unit, numerator, denominator, time window, attribution, aggregation, missingness, direction, and version. I validate sensitivity on historical experiments and directionality against long-term outcomes and known bad changes. I avoid arbitrary composites and average-of-averages, report uncertainty, and treat metric changes like schema migrations because they alter historical and experimental meaning.

What you must know

  • Metrics operationalize values and assumptions
  • OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails serve different roles
  • Directionality and sensitivity must both be validated
  • Population, unit, denominator, and window define the estimand
  • Metric versions and lineage are part of scientific reproducibility

Why this matters

Teams optimize what dashboards reward. A click metric can encourage clickbait, time spent can reward confusion, short-term revenue can damage retention, and an average can improve by losing low-performing users. Even perfect randomization estimates the causal effect on the metric that was defined, not the value stakeholders intended. Research on online experimentation emphasizes directionality and sensitivity and documents recurring interpretation pitfalls. Interviews test whether a candidate can turn a vague goal into measurable components without laundering value judgments. In production, metrics are shared software artifacts whose bugs propagate to experiments, alerts, forecasts, and executive decisions.

Intuition

Think of a metric system as an instrument panel. The primary gauge answers whether the product is moving toward durable value. Driver gauges reveal how the change worked. Guardrails light up when the route creates unacceptable damage. A single speedometer cannot show overheating, fuel, or collision risk; a wall of gauges without a decision hierarchy is equally useless. Each gauge needs calibration: it should move when the underlying property changes, stay stable when nothing changes, and not reward a shortcut that violates the real objective. Its denominator decides who counts and can change the story as much as its numerator.

From objective to OEC, drivers, and guardrails

Write the long-term objective and stakeholder before choosing observables. The OEC combines or selects near-term measures believed to causally predict that objective and must have a clear preferred direction. Driver metrics correspond to mechanisms in a product theory: discoverability, activation, task success, or repeat value. Diagnostic metrics explain implementation and segments but do not automatically become claims. Guardrails encode noncompensable or constrained outcomes such as crashes, latency, complaints, fairness gaps, creator supply, privacy incidents, and cost. Draw edges between intervention, drivers, primary outcome, guardrails, and long-term value; mark assumptions and expected time lags. Avoid adding metrics simply because data exist.

The semantic metric contract

Specify metric name and version; target population and eligibility; analysis unit; observation and attribution windows; event sources and accepted versions; numerator and denominator; aggregation order; deduplication and identity; timezone; late-data policy; missingness; outlier treatment; direction; owner; and quality tests. A conversion rate among exposed users differs from ITT conversion among assigned eligible users. Sessions per active user conditions on activity and can improve if low-activity users disappear. Per-user mean, ratio of totals, mean of user ratios, and average of group averages are different estimands. Include sample rows and reconciliation identities so reviewers can test meaning without reading every query.

Directionality, sensitivity, validity, and reliability

Directionality asks whether an increase consistently represents improvement in the target objective. Validate with domain theory, known harmful and beneficial launches, long-term holdouts, and downstream outcomes. Sensitivity asks whether the metric detects decision-relevant changes with acceptable variance; estimate standard error, MDE, and experiment hit rate without favoring noisy false positives. Construct validity asks whether it measures the intended concept; criterion validity compares trusted outcomes. Reliability asks whether repeated equivalent measurement is stable. Robustness covers heavy tails, bots, missing data, seasonality, and implementation changes. An easy-to-move but weak proxy is dangerous; a perfect long-term outcome arriving too late may be unusable for iteration.

Ratios, transforms, and composite scores

For a ratio metric, state whether the estimand is total numerator divided by total denominator or average of unit-level ratios; they weight units differently. Denominator treatment effects can make relative movements hard to interpret. Use influence-function, delta-method, bootstrap, or unit-level analysis consistent with randomization. Winsorization and log transforms change the estimand and must be prespecified. Composite scores require direction alignment, scaling, weights, and missing-component rules; weights express value trade-offs, not statistical truth. A composite can hide a severe loss behind compensation, so preserve component reporting and keep true guardrails outside the compensating score.

Gaming, drift, and metric lifecycle

Goodhart's law warns that an optimized proxy can decouple from its target. Perform threat modeling: how could a feature increase the metric without helping users, exclude difficult cases, shift cost, or delay harm? Monitor component and population drift, metric correlation with long-term outcomes, missingness, event coverage, and conflicting movements. Use immutable versions for definition changes and dual-run old/new metrics through backfills and live experiments. Recompute historical series only under explicit version labels. Document known limitations and deprecation reasons. When a metric bug is found, identify affected experiments and decisions, publish corrections, and prevent silent dashboard rewrites.

Math / formal view

A ratio-of-sums estimand is R=sum_i A_i/sum_i B_i, while a mean-of-ratios is n^{-1}sum_i A_i/B_i; they are equal only in special cases. For experiment arms, Delta=R_T-R_C and uncertainty can use the influence value psi_i=(A_i-R B_i)/E[B] at the randomization unit. A composite S=sum_j w_j s_j requires defined scaling s_j and weights w_j. Sensitivity can be summarized by standard error or MDE, while directionality is a substantive claim requiring external or longitudinal validation.

Replacing raw engagement with a value-and-health scorecard

Trace the proxy's gaming path, define a directionally stronger primary outcome, separate drivers from diagnostics, and make ecosystem and reliability harms noncompensable guardrails.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Validate a semantic metric contract, compute a ratio of sums at user grain, and verify that aggregation, denominators, and pandas results reconcile.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
REQUIRED=['name','version','population','unit','numerator','denominator','window','direction','owner']
def validate_contract(contract):
    errors=[k for k in REQUIRED if not contract.get(k)]
    if contract.get('direction') not in ('up','down','target'):errors.append('direction')
    return errors
def ratio_of_sums(rows):
    ids=[r['unit_id'] for r in rows]
    if len(ids)!=len(set(ids)):raise ValueError('duplicate analysis unit')
    numerator=sum(r['numerator'] for r in rows); denominator=sum(r['denominator'] for r in rows)
    if denominator<=0:raise ValueError('nonpositive denominator')
    return numerator/denominator,numerator,denominator
contract={'name':'eligible_ctr','version':'v2','population':'assigned eligible users','unit':'user','numerator':'eligible clicks','denominator':'eligible impressions','window':'7 days','direction':'up','owner':'search'}
rows=[{'unit_id':1,'numerator':1,'denominator':2},{'unit_id':2,'numerator':1,'denominator':8},{'unit_id':3,'numerator':0,'denominator':5}]
metric,total_clicks,total_impressions=ratio_of_sums(rows)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(rows)
pandas_metric=df['numerator'].sum()/df['denominator'].sum()
mean_user_ratio=(df['numerator']/df['denominator']).mean()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version the complete metric contract and additive components, run grain/coverage/reconciliation tests, dual-run migrations, monitor proxy drift and guardrails, and freeze affected decisions when lineage or semantics fail.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert validate_contract(contract)==[]
assert total_clicks==2 and total_impressions==15
assert abs(metric-pandas_metric)<1e-12
assert abs(metric-mean_user_ratio)>0.05
bad=dict(contract); bad['denominator']=''; assert 'denominator' in validate_contract(bad)
try: ratio_of_sums(rows+[dict(rows[0])])
except ValueError as e: assert 'duplicate' in str(e)
else: raise AssertionError('duplicate grain not rejected')

Common mistakes

  • Choosing the easiest metric to move

    Sensitivity without directionality rewards proxy gaming; validate relationship to durable user and business value.

  • Averaging pre-aggregated rates

    Preserve numerators and denominators or define the intended unit weights; average-of-averages usually changes the estimand.

  • Making every metric a success criterion

    Use a hierarchy: primary/OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails with prespecified decision roles.

  • Silently changing a denominator

    Definition changes are versioned migrations and invalidate direct historical or experimental comparison unless dual-run and reconciled.

Likely follow-ups

  • What makes a good OEC?

    It is directionally aligned with long-term value, sensitive within experiment duration, computable and reliable, difficult to game, and paired with explicit guardrails.

  • Why can per-active-user metrics mislead?

    Treatment can change who becomes active, so conditioning on activity is post-treatment selection and denominator composition can drive the result.

  • Should guardrails be included in a composite?

    Usually severe noncompensable harms are clearer as constraints or decision gates; a composite can let primary gains conceal unacceptable damage.

Production / system-design connection

Store metrics in a governed semantic layer with source lineage, SQL or transformation version, population, unit, windows, numerator/denominator, attribution, missingness, direction, owner, tests, and access policy. Materialize additive components so totals reconcile across slices. Validate schema, uniqueness, coverage, lateness, denominator positivity, range, and invariant relationships. Dual-run definition changes and compare experiment decisions before migration. Monitor drift, sensitivity, correlation with long-term outcomes, guardrail breach rate, and metric gaming signals. Restrict sensitive user and fairness slices. On a bug, freeze affected decisions, identify every dashboard and experiment version, backfill under a new label, publish corrections, and roll back the semantic model without erasing historical definitions.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Why does average session duration sometimes rise after a bad change?

    Show solution

    If the change causes short-session users to leave, the remaining-session denominator selects longer sessions; the average can rise while total user value falls.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Give a ratio-of-sums example.

    Show solution

    Click-through rate as total clicks divided by total eligible impressions; preserve both components and define deduplication and attribution.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    How do you validate directionality?

    Show solution

    Use product theory, known interventions, long-term holdouts or downstream outcomes, component analysis, and attempts to find changes that game the proxy.

  • metric-development-kdd

    Provides peer-reviewed lessons for data-driven metric directionality and sensitivity development.
