14.7

Funnels & Conversion Analysis

highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Funnel analysis measures how eligible entities progress through a defined sequence of product states or events and where they fail, branch, repeat, or take too long. A funnel is not an objective map of user behavior: step definitions, order rules, identity, attribution, conversion window, denominator, and re-entry policy construct the result. This chapter develops strict and loose funnels, unique-user versus event conversion, closed versus open cohorts, step and cumulative rates, time-to-convert, competing paths, censoring, segmentation, instrumentation, causal limits, and experimental use. You will learn how repeated events and inner joins inflate conversion, why recent entrants have incomplete opportunity, how to distinguish a product obstacle from selection, and when a state machine or journey analysis is better than a linear funnel. A worked checkout example exposes an identity and window bug. The lab implements a deterministic ordered unique-user funnel from raw events, compares it with pandas, and verifies monotonic counts, window rules, deduplication, and denominator reconciliation. Production guidance covers event contracts, late data, sessionization, privacy, monitoring, metric versions, and rollback. The goal is a reproducible behavioral estimand that guides hypotheses, not a decorative narrowing chart that implies causality.

Prerequisites

  • metric-design
  • groupby-pivot
  • eda-workflow

Learning objectives

  • Define funnel population, entity, step events, ordering, window, attribution, repetition, and denominator semantics precisely.
  • Compute cumulative and step conversion without double counting entities or granting unequal observation opportunity.
  • Diagnose instrumentation, identity, time, competing-path, and selection explanations for apparent drop-off.
  • Implement and verify an ordered funnel while preserving raw counts, transition times, and alternative paths.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A funnel is a versioned sequence estimand, not just counts by event name. I define the eligible entity and entry cohort, strict or loose order, conversion window, repeat and re-entry rules, identity resolution, and whether conversion is unique entities or event completions. I deduplicate at the chosen unit, require complete follow-up or handle censoring, and reconcile cumulative counts so they cannot increase. I segment only with pre-step attributes for causal interpretation, inspect time-to-transition and alternative paths, and use experiments to test proposed causes. Drop-off shows where progression stops under the definition; it does not prove why.

What you must know

  • Funnel definitions construct the population and path
  • Entity counts and event counts answer different questions
  • Conversion windows and maturity prevent unequal opportunity
  • Step drop-off is descriptive, not a causal explanation
  • Identity and event-contract quality dominate trustworthy funnel analysis

Why this matters

Onboarding, checkout, application, and activation flows are operationally sequential, so aggregate conversion can hide where a change occurred. But a user may skip steps, repeat them, switch devices, complete offline, or enter through another path. A dashboard can show a dramatic drop simply because one event was renamed or a recent cohort lacks time to convert. Funnel analysis is valuable when it turns a product theory into explicit state transitions and testable hypotheses. Interviews probe whether analysts define denominators and time correctly. In production, funnel metrics share instrumentation with experiments and can bias launch decisions if event loss differs by variant.

Intuition

Imagine following each eligible person with a timestamped event ledger. A strict funnel asks whether the ledger contains step A, then a later B, then a later C, all within a clock that starts at A. Count each person once at the furthest qualified step. The narrowing bars are just an aggregation of these state-machine traces. If the last cohort entered yesterday and conversion allows seven days, its apparent failure is administrative censoring. If B is missing because an app version stopped logging, that is measurement loss, not user abandonment. Examine both the accepted path and what users did instead.

Entity, entry, steps, order, and window

Name the entity: user, account, order, application, device, or session. Define eligibility and entry event with source and version. A strict funnel requires step order; a loose funnel may allow intervening events while preserving order; any-order completion answers a different question. Define whether timestamps may tie, whether one event can satisfy multiple steps, and whether all steps must share an order or item property. The conversion window begins at a stated event and uses event time with a timezone and late-data policy. Closed cohorts fix entry membership; open funnels can mix changing populations. Version every semantic choice.

Unique entities, repeats, and denominators

Unique-entity conversion counts each entity once, usually using the earliest eligible entry and earliest qualifying next step. Event-total funnels can count repeated completions and may exceed entry entities; label them explicitly. Step conversion N_k/N_{k-1} differs from cumulative conversion N_k/N_1, and their product reconciles when definitions align. Decide whether users can re-enter after failure or complete multiple journeys; then use a journey identifier rather than accidental event pairs. Preserve numerator and denominator for every transition. An inner join of completed steps drops nonconverters and can make conversion appear 100%; start from the entry population and left join forward.

Time to convert and observation maturity

Report transition-time distributions, not only means, because latency is often skewed and long tails determine the window. A fixed window classifies no completion by its end, but entities entering near the data cutoff have not had equal opportunity. Restrict to matured entrants, use cohort-age tables, or apply survival methods when time-to-event is the target and right censoring assumptions are defensible. Calendar shocks and app releases affect cohorts differently. Sessionization adds an inactivity threshold that can split or merge journeys; document it and test sensitivity. Late events can revise earlier funnels, so publish a data-completeness cutoff.

Drop-off, segmentation, and competing paths

A large drop identifies a transition worth investigation, not its cause. Inspect errors, latency, validation messages, alternate events, support contacts, and qualitative evidence. Segment by pre-entry attributes such as platform or acquisition channel, while recognizing composition and multiplicity. Segmenting on a later step selects converters and can reverse interpretation. Users may reach the same value through a different sequence, so path or state-transition analysis can reveal false drop-off. Compare step rates on common cohorts and complete windows; decompose an aggregate change into entry mix, within-segment transition changes, and logging coverage.

Causal tests and data-quality controls

Funnel patterns generate hypotheses such as a form field causing abandonment. Randomize the proposed change and estimate ITT effects on prespecified end conversion plus transition drivers and guardrails. Do not declare causal impact from users who happened to complete a step. In experiment funnels, denominator should normally begin with assigned eligible units or an assignment-invariant trigger; treatment-dependent exposure filters bias comparison. Test event schema, uniqueness, ordering, property consistency, assignment coverage, and arm-specific missingness. Maintain synthetic journeys and expected counts. When a step event changes, dual-log and reconcile before migrating the metric.

Math / formal view

Let E be entry entities and S_k the subset that satisfies ordered steps 1..k within window W. Cumulative conversion C_k=|S_k|/|E| and step conversion c_k=|S_k|/|S_{k-1}|, with C_k=product_{j=2..k}c_j when sets and denominators align. Drop-off at k is |S_{k-1}|-|S_k|. Time-to-step T_k=t_k-t_entry is censored at the data cutoff or window for incomplete entities. Compare arms at the randomization-unit level and retain additive counts for reconciliation.

An identity reset that turns failures into apparent success

Trace raw entity histories, detect cross-step identity loss, rebuild from entry with complete windows, and separate instrumentation repair from the randomized product fix.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build an ordered unique-user funnel from event histories, compare counts with pandas, and verify monotonicity, deduplication, and conversion-window semantics.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
from collections import defaultdict
steps=['cart','payment','purchase']
events=[('u1','cart',0),('u1','payment',2),('u1','purchase',5),('u1','purchase',6),('u2','cart',0),('u2','purchase',3),('u3','cart',0),('u3','payment',8),('u3','purchase',12),('u4','cart',0),('u4','payment',2)]
def ordered_funnel(events,steps,window):
    by_user=defaultdict(list)
    for user,event,t in events:by_user[user].append((t,event))
    counts=[0]*len(steps); reached={}
    for user,history in by_user.items():
        history.sort(); index=0; start=None
        for t,event in history:
            if index==0 and event==steps[0]:start=t; index=1; counts[0]+=1
            elif start is not None and t-start<=window and index<len(steps) and event==steps[index]:
                index+=1; counts[index-1]+=1
        reached[user]=index
    return counts,reached
counts,reached=ordered_funnel(events,steps,10)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(events,columns=['user','event','time'])
entry_users=set(df.loc[df.event=='cart','user'])
pandas_entry=len(entry_users)
unique_event_users=df.groupby('event')['user'].nunique().to_dict()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version entity, step, order, window and identity semantics; build from entry with complete opportunity; persist additive counts and transition times; monitor event parity and monotonicity; and freeze decisions when instrumentation breaks.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert counts==[4,3,1]
assert counts==sorted(counts,reverse=True)
assert pandas_entry==counts[0]
assert reached['u1']==3 and reached['u2']==1
assert unique_event_users['purchase']==3 and counts[2]==1
assert ordered_funnel(events,steps,20)[0]==[4,3,2]
assert counts[2]/counts[0]==0.25

Common mistakes

  • Counting events as users

    Repeated events can inflate downstream steps; deduplicate the defined entity or use explicit journey IDs.

  • Comparing immature recent cohorts

    Require the full conversion window or use censoring-aware time-to-event analysis.

  • Treating drop-off as a cause

    It locates an observed transition; errors, alternatives, selection, and experiments are needed to identify mechanisms.

  • Joining only users with every step

    That removes nonconverters from the denominator; begin with entry and left join later states.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a strict funnel?

    An entity must complete defined steps in order, typically within a conversion window; intervening events may or may not be allowed according to the contract.

  • Why can cumulative counts increase?

    They should not for a unique-entity strict funnel. An increase signals inconsistent populations, repeated-event counting, re-entry, identity, or query errors.

  • How do you compare funnel conversion in an A/B test?

    Use assigned eligible units or an assignment-invariant trigger as denominator, prespecify the end metric, and treat intermediate steps as drivers without post-treatment filtering.

Production / system-design connection

Govern every step event with owner, schema, version, entity key, event-time semantics, and property tests. Build funnels from immutable entry cohorts and left-joined histories, using a versioned identity graph and late-data cutoff. Persist step counts, cumulative and transition rates, time distributions, window maturity, missingness, and alternate-path counts. Monitor monotonicity, event coverage, ordering violations, identity-link rates, transition shifts, and platform/version slices. Protect journey data and suppress small cohorts. Dual-log renamed events and reconcile before cutover. On instrumentation failure, freeze funnel-based decisions, publish the affected interval, backfill only under explicit versions, and roll back the metric or product change without rewriting prior definitions.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Counts are 1000, 800, 600. What are step and cumulative final conversion?

    Show solution

    Step conversions are 80% then 75%; final cumulative conversion is 600/1000=60%, equal to 0.8*0.75.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Why can a 30-day window bias the newest cohort?

    Show solution

    Members have not all had 30 days of follow-up; restrict to mature entries or use censoring-aware methods.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    A user completes B before A. Do they convert?

    Show solution

    Only under an any-order definition. A strict ordered funnel excludes that sequence; the contract must decide.

14.8

Cohort Retention Analysis

highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Cohort retention analysis follows entities from a common starting event and measures whether they return to a value-defining behavior at comparable ages. It separates lifecycle decay from calendar-time shocks, but only when cohort assignment, activity, interval boundaries, identity, denominator, and observation maturity are defined consistently. This chapter develops acquisition and behavioral cohorts, exact-period, rolling, and bracket retention, survival-style retention, resurrection, churn, cohort-age matrices, censoring, composition, seasonality, segmentation, uncertainty, and experimental interpretation. You will learn why recent cohorts form an incomplete triangle, why retention can rise when low-value users never enter the denominator, how identity and late events reshape curves, and when Kaplan-Meier or hazard analysis is more appropriate. A worked subscription example separates acquisition-mix change from product improvement. The lab builds a monthly exact-period retention matrix from first activity and later events, compares with pandas, and verifies cohort size, maturity, identity uniqueness, and denominator invariants. Production guidance covers semantic models, incremental updates, backfills, privacy, monitoring, causal tests, and rollback. The goal is a lifecycle measurement system that reveals durable value, not a color grid interpreted without population or time context.

Prerequisites

  • funnels
  • groupby-pivot
  • censoring-survival

Learning objectives

  • Define cohort membership, start event, retained behavior, age interval, denominator, and resurrection semantics.
  • Compute exact, rolling, and survival-style retention while handling right censoring and incomplete recent cohorts.
  • Decompose retention changes into cohort composition, lifecycle, calendar time, instrumentation, and product mechanisms.
  • Implement and validate a cohort matrix with maturity and reconciliation checks.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Retention starts with a fixed cohort, usually entities sharing a first value event or acquisition period, and asks what fraction performs a defined return behavior at each age. I specify exact-period versus rolling retention, interval boundaries, identity, denominator, resurrection, and observation cutoff. Recent cohorts do not have mature later ages, so I leave those cells unavailable rather than zero. I compare cohorts at the same age, inspect calendar effects and acquisition mix, and use survival or hazard methods when time-to-churn and censoring matter. A better curve is descriptive until an experiment or causal design supports attribution.

What you must know

  • Cohort time and calendar time are separate axes
  • Retention depends on the value event and denominator contract
  • Recent cohort cells are censored, not zero
  • Exact, rolling, and survival retention answer different questions
  • Composition and identity changes can mimic product retention gains

Why this matters

Aggregate active-user rates mix new, mature, resurrected, and seasonal users. Growth can make activity look healthy while every cohort decays, and acquisition quality can make a product change appear to improve retention. Cohorts align users by lifecycle age so teams can see activation and durable return patterns. Yet a signup cohort may include people who never experienced value, while an activated cohort conditions on a behavior treatment can change. Interviews test whether analysts handle denominator and censoring. In production, retention drives lifetime-value models and experiment decisions, so semantic drift creates large downstream errors.

Intuition

Imagine giving every user two clocks. The calendar clock says March or April; the lifecycle clock says week zero, one, or two since first value. A cohort matrix places acquisition time on rows and lifecycle age on columns. Comparing down a column asks whether newer cohorts retain better at the same age. Reading across a row shows decay for one cohort. The lower-right cells do not exist yet because those users have not aged enough. Exact retention asks for activity in one interval; rolling retention asks whether activity occurs on or after that age; survival retention asks whether a defined churn event has not yet occurred.

Cohort and retained-behavior contract

Choose the entity and immutable cohort anchor: signup, first purchase, activation, contract start, or first exposure answer different questions. Define timezone and interval boundaries, and assign one first qualifying cohort unless repeat journeys are intentionally modeled. Define retained behavior as a value event, not any telemetry heartbeat. The denominator can be all acquired users, activated users, payers, or eligible accounts; each changes the estimand. State treatment of internal users, bots, merged identities, deleted accounts, pauses, and resurrected users. Store cohort membership separately from mutable user profiles so later property changes do not rewrite history.

Exact, rolling, bracket, and survival retention

Exact-period retention at age k counts cohort entities active during that interval divided by original cohort size. Rolling retention at k counts those active at k or any later observed interval and can be monotone by construction, but future activity means values revise as data mature. Bracket retention groups multiple periods to reduce noise. Unbounded return within a window answers yet another question. Churn may mean contract cancellation, no activity for a grace period, or absorbing death; noncontractual inactivity is not directly observed churn. Kaplan-Meier estimates survival under censoring assumptions when a well-defined event time exists. Label the definition in every chart.

Right censoring and the incomplete triangle

A cohort entering near the data cutoff cannot contribute an observed month-six outcome. Mark cells beyond maximum observable age as unavailable. Even an age-k cell needs complete event ingestion through the interval end, including late-arrival allowance. Treating unavailable as not retained systematically makes recent cohorts look worse. Restrict comparisons to mature cells, use survival estimators for time-to-event, or model censoring under explicit assumptions. Administrative censoring at a common cutoff differs from loss to follow-up that may depend on outcome. Preserve cohort sizes and at-risk counts because percentages without support invite unstable rankings.

Lifecycle, calendar, composition, and causality

A diagonal disturbance across cohorts often indicates a calendar outage or holiday; a horizontal row pattern can indicate a particular acquisition campaign; a vertical age effect suggests lifecycle behavior. Decompose changes by acquisition channel, country, platform, plan, and eligibility using pre-cohort attributes while protecting small cells and multiplicity. Simpson reversals arise when channel mix changes. Instrumentation releases can create false activity or loss. Correlation between an activation behavior and later retention reflects selection as well as mechanism. Use randomized interventions to test whether causing activation or onboarding changes retention, and measure ITT from assigned cohorts rather than only users who activated.

Uncertainty, forecasting, and metric operation

Attach binomial or cluster-aware uncertainty to cohort-age rates and avoid overreacting to tiny cohorts. For forecasting, evaluate on chronological cohort cutoffs so future activity never leaks into features or labels. Retention curves feed LTV only after revenue, margin, churn, and discount assumptions are stated; a flat early curve does not prove a permanent plateau. Incremental pipelines must update mature cells for late events without changing cohort anchors. Reconcile active sets to raw events, monitor cohort-size and identity-link shifts, and dual-run definition migrations. Preserve old versions when return-event or grace-period semantics change.

Math / formal view

For cohort c with fixed member set C_c and exact retained set A_{c,k} active in age interval k, R_{c,k}=|C_c intersection A_{c,k}|/|C_c|. Rolling retention R^roll_{c,k}=|C_c intersection union_{j>=k}A_{c,j}|/|C_c| and may revise until follow-up closes. An available cell requires cohort_end(c)+end(k)<=data_cutoff-lateness. Approximate independent-binomial SE is sqrt(R(1-R)/n_c), but repeated users, clusters, and weighted populations need design-aware uncertainty.

A retention improvement created by acquisition mix

Separate cohort age from calendar time, mark immature cells unavailable, stratify by pre-acquisition channel, standardize composition, and confirm onboarding causally with randomized assignment.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Build an exact monthly cohort-retention matrix, compare it with pandas, and verify cohort membership, maturity, uniqueness, and denominators.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
from collections import defaultdict
events=[('u1',0),('u1',1),('u1',2),('u2',0),('u2',2),('u3',1),('u3',2),('u4',1),('u5',2)]
def retention(events,cutoff):
    periods=defaultdict(set)
    for user,period in events:periods[user].add(period)
    cohort={u:min(ps) for u,ps in periods.items()}
    sizes=defaultdict(int); retained=defaultdict(int)
    for u,c in cohort.items():
        sizes[c]+=1
        for p in periods[u]:retained[(c,p-c)]+=1
    rates={(c,age):retained[(c,age)]/sizes[c] for c in sizes for age in range(cutoff-c+1)}
    return cohort,dict(sizes),rates
cohort,sizes,rates=retention(events,2)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(events,columns=['user','period']).drop_duplicates()
df['cohort']=df.groupby('user')['period'].transform('min')
df['age']=df['period']-df['cohort']
pandas_sizes=df.groupby('cohort')['user'].nunique().to_dict()
pandas_rates=(df.groupby(['cohort','age'])['user'].nunique()/df.groupby('cohort')['user'].nunique()).to_dict()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Persist immutable cohort membership and unique entity-period activity, mark future ages unavailable, reconcile additive counts, monitor identity and acquisition mix, version retention semantics, and freeze dependent decisions when instrumentation fails.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert cohort=={'u1':0,'u2':0,'u3':1,'u4':1,'u5':2}
assert sizes==pandas_sizes=={0:2,1:2,2:1}
assert rates==pandas_rates
assert rates[(0,1)]==0.5 and rates[(0,2)]==1.0
assert (1,2) not in rates and (2,1) not in rates
assert all(0<=v<=1 for v in rates.values())
assert all(rates[(c,0)]==1 for c in sizes)

Common mistakes

  • Filling unavailable future cells with zero

    They are right-censored because follow-up has not occurred; mark them unavailable and compare only mature ages.

  • Calling any return event retention

    Choose a behavior that represents product value and specify exact or rolling semantics.

  • Comparing aggregate active rates

    They mix cohort ages and acquisition volumes; align entities by lifecycle age.

  • Attributing activated-user retention to onboarding

    Activation is selected and may be treatment-affected; use ITT in a randomized design to estimate causal impact.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is rolling retention?

    The fraction of the original cohort active at or after a given age; it differs from activity within exactly that interval and can revise as future data arrive.

  • Why is the cohort table triangular?

    New cohorts have not existed long enough to reach later ages, so those cells lack observation opportunity.

  • When should you use survival analysis?

    When the target is time to a defined event and right-censored entities should contribute their observed at-risk time under defensible censoring assumptions.

Production / system-design connection

Materialize an immutable cohort-membership table and a deduplicated entity-period activity table with source and identity versions. Compute additive cohort sizes and retained counts before percentages. Enforce one cohort per entity, nonnegative age, unique entity-period rows, mature-cell cutoff, late-event policy, and raw-event reconciliation. Monitor cohort volume, event coverage, identity merges, acquisition mix, calendar anomalies, and unexpected revisions. Attach minimum-support and privacy suppression. Version exact/rolling, start and return events, intervals, grace periods, and resurrection rules. On a definition or instrumentation bug, freeze downstream LTV and experiment decisions, publish affected dates, recompute under a new version, and retain the old series for audit and rollback.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    A cohort has 100 users; 40 are active in month two. Exact retention?

    Show solution

    40%, provided all 100 had complete month-two observation and activity semantics are fixed.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Why can rolling month-two retention exceed exact month-two retention?

    Show solution

    It also counts cohort members who return after month two even if inactive during month two itself.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    How does a calendar outage appear in a cohort matrix?

    Show solution

    Often as a diagonal pattern because different cohorts encounter the same calendar period at different lifecycle ages.

14.9

Churn, Lifetime Value & Unit Economics

highverified
Roles: ds, da

Topic overview

Customer lifetime value (LTV or CLV) is the discounted expected contribution margin generated by a customer or cohort over a declared future horizon, while churn describes a contractual cancellation or a modeled loss of future activity. Both are forecasts with behavioral, accounting, censoring, and policy assumptions; neither is a timeless label stored on a user. This chapter develops contractual versus noncontractual settings, retention and hazard, right censoring, revenue versus margin, discounting, acquisition cost, payback, cohort versus individual prediction, BG/NBD-style customer-base models, survival models, calibration, chronological validation, treatment effects, uncertainty, and decision use. You will learn why last activity is not observed churn, why a constant-retention formula can be dangerously optimistic, how heterogeneity changes aggregate value, and why marketing intervention can invalidate passive forecasts. A worked subscription example separates gross revenue from incremental contribution value. The lab implements Kaplan-Meier survival and discounted cohort LTV from first principles, compares grouped calculations with pandas, and verifies censoring and monotonicity invariants. Production guidance covers label maturity, leakage, policy feedback, monitoring, fairness, cost, rollback, and human review.

Prerequisites

  • cohort-retention
  • censoring-survival
  • probability-basics

Learning objectives

  • Define churn, survival, margin, horizon, discounting, and acquisition cost for contractual and noncontractual businesses.
  • Estimate retention under right censoring and translate survival or repeat-purchase forecasts into discounted expected contribution value.
  • Validate LTV models chronologically with calibration, ranking, aggregate value, policy, and uncertainty metrics.
  • Distinguish predictive customer value from incremental value caused by a retention or acquisition action.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

LTV is expected discounted future contribution margin over a stated horizon, conditional on current information and policy. In subscriptions, churn may be an observed cancellation or nonrenewal; in noncontractual products, inactivity is latent and needs a repeat-purchase/dropout model or an operational lapse rule. I handle right censoring, customer heterogeneity, refunds and variable costs, validate on mature chronological cohorts, and report cohort calibration and uncertainty rather than only individual rank. CAC comparison uses incremental fully loaded acquisition cost. A high predicted LTV does not imply targeting will cause value; intervention decisions need treatment effects and costs.

What you must know

  • LTV is a horizon- and policy-dependent expectation
  • Contribution margin differs from revenue
  • Churn is observed only in some business settings
  • Censoring and heterogeneity are central, not edge cases
  • Predictive value and incremental intervention value are different estimands

Why this matters

Acquisition bidding, onboarding, account management, and financial planning depend on future economics rather than today's purchase. Simple LTV formulas can be useful sanity checks but often assume constant retention, constant margin, homogeneous customers, and infinite horizons. They overstate value when high-risk customers disappear early, costs scale with usage, or the model ignores refunds and support. Customer-base research emphasizes different probability models for contractual and noncontractual settings. Interviews test whether candidates connect retention, survival, uncertainty, and unit economics. Production models also influence who receives offers, changing future data and creating feedback loops.

Intuition

Picture each future period as a possible cash-flow box. The chance a customer is still active shrinks with time, and a discount factor makes distant margin worth less today. Expected LTV adds survival probability times expected contribution margin in each box. In a subscription, cancellation may reveal the event time. In retail, silence does not prove permanent death; a customer may buy again, so frequency and dropout are latent processes. Customers differ, and mixing them into one retention rate can produce a curve that represents nobody. A prediction describes expected value under current policy, not the causal gain from contacting that customer.

Contractual, noncontractual, and operational churn

In a contractual business, cancellation or failure to renew can define churn, though pauses, delinquency, upgrades, and reactivation need rules. In a noncontractual setting there is no observed termination; a 90-day lapse is an operational label, not proof the customer will never return. Buy-till-you-die models jointly represent purchasing while alive and latent dropout. Define entity, cohort, start, event, grace period, resurrection, horizon, and policy. Avoid deriving a churn label using future inactivity beyond the prediction cutoff without accounting for label maturity. Different products or regions may require distinct definitions rather than one global threshold.

Retention, hazard, and censoring

Survival S(t)=P(T>t) is the probability the event time exceeds t; hazard describes event risk among those still at risk. Kaplan-Meier multiplies conditional survival across observed event times and lets right-censored customers contribute until their last known follow-up. Its interpretation assumes censoring is independent of event time conditional on the analysis information; loss caused by treatment or data-source exit may violate this. Cohort retention at fixed periods is related but may define recurring activity rather than an absorbing event. Compare survival curves, hazards, and at-risk counts, and use Cox or parametric models only after checking proportionality or distributional assumptions.

Revenue, contribution margin, discounting, and CAC

Forecast incremental contribution, not gross revenue, when evaluating economics. Subtract variable fulfillment, payment, service, promotion, returns, fraud, and support costs according to ownership. For period t, expected value combines survival/activity probability, expected transactions or revenue while active, margin, and discount factor 1/(1+r)^t. Use a finite policy horizon unless a defensible terminal value is modeled. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) includes the incremental channel spend and allocated costs relevant to the decision; blended averages hide channel and marginal-cost differences. Payback time and downside risk often matter alongside mean LTV/CAC.

Models and chronological validation

Baselines include cohort curves, empirical Bayes shrinkage, and simple survival plus margin models. Contractual settings can use discrete-time hazard or survival regression; noncontractual repeat purchase may use Pareto/NBD or BG/NBD with a spend model under assumptions about frequency, dropout, and monetary value. Flexible ML can forecast horizon revenue but must respect censored labels and future leakage. Split by acquisition time, train only on information available at cutoff, and evaluate on mature future windows. Measure aggregate cohort calibration, MAE or deviance, quantile calibration, ranking, uncertainty coverage, and financial decision regret. Compare with simple recency-frequency-monetary baselines.

Interventions, feedback, and responsible use

High predicted value may identify customers who would remain anyway; high churn risk may identify users too late to help. Targeting should estimate incremental treatment effect or uplift, subtract contact and incentive cost, and honor eligibility and fairness constraints. Offers change observed retention and margin, so retraining on treated outcomes without policy features creates feedback. Maintain randomized holdouts or exploration to learn intervention effects. Avoid using value predictions to deny essential service or systematically exclude protected or low-income groups without governance. Report cohort-level economics and uncertainty, cap automated bids, and provide human review for material account actions.

Math / formal view

For discrete periods t=1..H, LTV=sum_t S(t) E[M_t|active at t]/(1+r)^t minus future incremental costs, where S(t) or purchase probability and margin M_t are model outputs. Kaplan-Meier is S_hat(t)=product_{u<=t}(1-d_u/n_u), with d_u events and n_u at risk just before u. For constant retention q and margin m starting next period over an infinite horizon, LTV=m q/(1+r-q), but this strong homogeneous stationary approximation should be a sanity check, not a default truth.

From headline revenue to incremental contribution value

Estimate censored survival, apply period-specific margin and finite-horizon discounting, compare marginal CAC and payback, and test retention interventions rather than targeting on risk alone.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Implement Kaplan-Meier survival and finite-horizon discounted contribution LTV, compare grouped risk calculations with pandas, and verify censoring and monotonicity.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
def kaplan_meier(durations,events):
    times=sorted(set(durations)); survival=1.0; curve=[]
    for t in times:
        at_risk=sum(d>=t for d in durations); failures=sum(d==t and e for d,e in zip(durations,events))
        if failures:survival*=1-failures/at_risk
        curve.append((t,survival,at_risk,failures))
    return curve
def discounted_ltv(curve,margin,discount,horizon):
    by_time=dict((t,s) for t,s,_,_ in curve); last=1.0; value=0.0
    for t in range(1,horizon+1):
        if t in by_time:last=by_time[t]
        value+=last*margin/(1+discount)**t
    return value
durations=[1,2,2,3,4,4]; events=[1,1,0,1,0,1]
curve=kaplan_meier(durations,events); ltv=discounted_ltv(curve,12,0.01,4)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame({'duration':durations,'event':events})
summary=df.groupby('duration')['event'].agg(['sum','count']).rename(columns={'sum':'failures'})
pandas_failures=summary['failures'].to_dict()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Version event and censoring semantics, margin/cost and horizon assumptions, validate on mature chronological cohorts, monitor calibration and policy feedback, and fall back to conservative cohort economics when model or cost inputs fail.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
survivals=[s for _,s,_,_ in curve]
assert all(b<=a for a,b in zip(survivals,survivals[1:]))
assert curve[0][2]==6 and curve[-1][2]==2
assert pandas_failures=={1:1,2:1,3:1,4:1}
assert 0<ltv<12*4
no_events=kaplan_meier([1,2,3],[0,0,0])
assert all(s==1 for _,s,_,_ in no_events)
assert discounted_ltv(curve,12,0.05,4)<ltv

Common mistakes

  • Calling last activity the churn date

    In noncontractual settings dropout is latent; use a lapse definition or probabilistic repeat-purchase/dropout model and allow resurrection.

  • Using revenue as LTV

    Economic decisions need contribution margin after relevant variable costs, refunds, incentives, and service costs.

  • Dropping active customers from duration modeling

    They are right-censored and contribute known survival time; deleting them biases lifetime downward.

  • Targeting the highest predicted risk

    Risk is not treatment responsiveness; optimize incremental effect minus cost under policy and fairness constraints.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is right censoring?

    The event has not been observed by the cutoff, so lifetime is known only to exceed the observed follow-up; survival methods use that partial information.

  • How does LTV differ in contractual and noncontractual businesses?

    Contractual churn can often be observed, while noncontractual dropout is latent and repeat-purchase plus dropout processes must be modeled or operationally defined.

  • How do you validate LTV?

    Use chronological mature cohorts, aggregate and segment calibration, ranking and error, uncertainty coverage, financial baselines, and decision outcomes under the deployment policy.

Production / system-design connection

Version churn and resurrection rules, cohort/start, cutoff, horizon, margin and cost tables, discount rate, feature timestamps, model, policy, and calibration. Maintain censored duration data and label-maturity checks. Reconcile predicted aggregate value with realized cohort revenue and contribution, tracking refunds and service costs. Monitor survival calibration, hazard drift, channel mix, prediction intervals, ranking, LTV/CAC, payback, and targeting treatment effects. Use randomized holdouts to measure incremental interventions and prevent policy feedback. Protect financial and behavioral data, audit slice outcomes, and cap bids or incentives. On model or cost-pipeline failure, revert to conservative cohort baselines and prior bid caps while retaining predictions and decisions for audit.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Why is a current active subscriber not missing data?

    Show solution

    Their event time is right-censored: you know they survived through follow-up, which contributes information to survival estimation.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    Revenue is $100 and variable cost $40. Which enters contribution LTV?

    Show solution

    $60 before other relevant incremental costs and discounting, not the full $100 revenue.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Why can one constant retention rate mislead?

    Show solution

    Customer hazards vary with tenure and latent segment; averaging heterogeneity can distort both curve shape and long-horizon value.

14.10

Interference & Network Effects in Experiments

mediumverified
Roles: ds, da, as

Topic overview

Network experiments study treatments whose effects can spill across users, sellers, geographic areas, or shared resources, violating the usual no-interference assumption that each unit's outcome depends only on its own assignment. This chapter develops potential outcomes under exposure mappings, direct, spillover, total, and equilibrium effects; graph and cluster randomization; saturation and two-stage designs; switchbacks; marketplaces; contamination; cluster construction; variance and power; Horvitz-Thompson-style weighting; meta-experiments for detecting interference; and generalization to full rollout. You will learn why individual randomization can estimate a diluted mixture rather than the global policy effect, why cluster randomization reduces cross-arm edges but sacrifices independent units, how to define exposure without conditioning on realized outcomes, and how network evolution or hidden edges threaten identification. A worked messaging example contrasts direct and total effects. The lab simulates spillovers on a ring network, compares individual with cluster assignment, and verifies contamination, bias direction, and cluster-aware summaries. Production guidance covers graph snapshots, cluster versions, assignment, privacy, monitoring, safety, and rollback. The goal is to align the experiment's counterfactual worlds with how treatment actually propagates.

Prerequisites

  • experiment-design
  • trees-graphs-algorithms
  • causal-inference

Learning objectives

  • Define direct, spillover, total, and equilibrium estimands through treatment and neighborhood exposure mappings.
  • Choose individual, cluster, saturation, two-stage, or switchback assignment based on interference topology and policy target.
  • Analyze power and uncertainty using the actual independent randomization units and assignment probabilities.
  • Implement a spillover simulation and diagnose contamination and estimator mismatch under competing designs.
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Standard A/B inference assumes no interference: one unit's assignment does not affect another's outcome. In social networks, marketplaces, and shared-capacity systems that can fail. I define the target effect first - direct, spillover, or total effect under full rollout - and an exposure mapping describing relevant neighbors' assignments. Individual randomization has high power but can dilute effects through cross-arm exposure. Graph-cluster or market-level randomization reduces contamination at the cost of fewer independent units and possible cluster imbalance; saturation or two-stage designs estimate spillovers. I use graph snapshots and cluster-aware inference, measure exposure and leakage, and avoid claiming a full-rollout effect from an estimand the design cannot identify.

What you must know

  • Interference makes outcomes depend on assignment vectors
  • Direct and total rollout effects are different estimands
  • Individual randomization can be precise for the wrong mixed-exposure contrast
  • Clustering trades fewer cross-arm edges for fewer independent units
  • Graph, exposure, and assignment versions are part of the causal design

Why this matters

A treated user may invite control friends, a seller may change prices for all buyers, or a routing policy may alter congestion for both arms. In these settings, control is exposed indirectly and treatment effects can be amplified, diluted, or reversed. Research from large platforms documents network experiments and meta-experiments that detect bias from standard individual randomization. Interviews test whether candidates recognize Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) failure and redesign rather than merely clustering standard errors. Production designs also face incomplete graphs, rapidly changing edges, and privacy constraints.

Intuition

In an ordinary experiment, imagine each unit inside an isolated box. Network interference adds arrows between boxes, so flipping one treatment changes several outcomes. Individual randomization cuts many arrows between treatment and control, mixing their experiences. Cluster randomization groups strongly connected units and flips one coin per cluster, keeping more arrows within the same world. But if there are only twenty clusters, twenty is closer to the effective replication count than the millions of members. A full-rollout policy treats every node, an exposure condition rarely observed in a fifty-fifty individual experiment; extrapolation needs design or modeling support.

Potential outcomes and exposure mappings

Without interference, unit i has Y_i(1) and Y_i(0). With interference, Y_i may depend on the full assignment vector. An exposure mapping compresses it to conditions such as own assignment plus fraction of treated neighbors, treated household, market saturation, or shared-resource load. A direct effect compares own treatment at the same neighborhood exposure; a spillover effect compares neighborhood exposure holding own treatment; a total effect compares policy worlds such as all treated versus all control. Equilibrium effects may include adaptation over time. State the mapping before outcomes and acknowledge hidden or weighted edges. Misspecification changes the estimand and can create residual interference.

Individual, cluster, saturation, and switchback designs

Individual randomization supports direct contrasts but often creates mixed exposure. Graph-cluster randomization partitions nodes and randomizes clusters, aiming to maximize within-cluster edges while maintaining enough balanced clusters. Geographic or market clustering follows operational interactions. Two-stage designs randomize clusters to treatment saturation, then units within clusters, enabling direct and spillover contrasts under assumptions. Saturation designs vary treated fractions. Switchbacks alternate a shared market or service across time, useful for congestion or marketplace interference when carryover is short. A randomized meta-experiment can compare individual and cluster designs to test for interference bias.

Cluster quality, power, and effective sample size

Clustering reduces cross-arm edges but can create unequal cluster sizes, covariate imbalance, and few randomization units. Cluster construction should use a pre-treatment graph snapshot and be independent of outcomes. Balance volume, connectivity, geography, and operational constraints; rerandomization rules must be specified. Intracluster outcome correlation and cluster-size variation inflate variance. Analyze at cluster level or use design-consistent cluster-robust/randomization inference; user-level standard errors are anti-conservative. Exposure-aware estimators may have extreme inverse probabilities when some conditions are rare. Power simulations should use realistic topology, effects, graph evolution, and the exact assignment algorithm.

Exposure, estimators, and diagnostics

Log assignment separately from realized exposure. For a declared exposure condition, estimate means using design probabilities; Horvitz-Thompson or Hajek weighting can correct unequal exposure probabilities but may be noisy. Regression adjustment with pre-treatment cluster covariates can improve precision while preserving design. Report cluster counts, sizes, cross-arm edge fraction, exposure distribution, assignment probabilities, balance, attrition, and uncertainty. Compare intent-to-treat by cluster with exposure-response analyses, clearly labeling additional assumptions. Do not condition on post-treatment network changes such as new friendships without addressing mediation and selection. Test sensitivity to plausible alternative exposure mappings.

Dynamic networks, rollout, and operational safety

Graph snapshots become stale as edges form, disappear, or remain unobserved; treatment may itself change the network. Version snapshot time, edge definition, direction, weight, and clustering algorithm, and measure boundary leakage during the test. Full rollout can change equilibrium, capacity, prices, or content supply beyond observed saturations. Use saturation response, long-term holdouts, staged geographic rollout, structural assumptions, or conservative bounds for generalization. Protect graph relationships and suppress small clusters. Monitor harm and capacity globally because spillovers cross experiment arms. Rollback may itself have network carryover; define cooldown and measurement after treatment removal. Recompute estimates under plausible hidden-edge and cluster-boundary perturbations so conclusions expose sensitivity to an incomplete graph rather than treating observed adjacency as ground truth.

Math / formal view

Let Z be the assignment vector and G_i(Z) an exposure mapping. Potential outcome is Y_i(z_i,g). A direct effect at exposure g is E[Y_i(1,g)-Y_i(0,g)]; a spillover effect for controls compares E[Y_i(0,g_1)-Y_i(0,g_0)]; a total policy effect may compare E[Y_i(1,g_all)-Y_i(0,g_none)]. For exposure condition e with probability pi_i(e), a Horvitz-Thompson mean uses N^{-1}sum_i 1{E_i=e}Y_i/pi_i(e). Variance must follow the dependent assignment design.

Invitation spillovers dilute an individual A/B contrast

Map invitation edges, define direct and total effects, compare individual and cluster designs in a meta-experiment, and report leakage plus cluster-aware uncertainty before extrapolating to rollout.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate network spillovers, compare individual and cluster assignment, and verify contamination, contrast dilution, and cluster-aware summaries.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import random
def neighbors(i,n): return ((i-1)%n,(i+1)%n)
def outcome(i,z,direct=1.0,spill=1.5):
    exposure=sum(z[j] for j in neighbors(i,len(z)))/2
    return direct*z[i]+spill*exposure
def individual_assignment(n,seed):
    rng=random.Random(seed); return [rng.randrange(2) for _ in range(n)]
def cluster_assignment(n,cluster_size,seed):
    rng=random.Random(seed); clusters=[rng.randrange(2) for _ in range(n//cluster_size)]
    return [clusters[i//cluster_size] for i in range(n)]
def contrast(z):
    y=[outcome(i,z) for i in range(len(z))]
    return sum(v for v,a in zip(y,z) if a)/sum(z)-sum(v for v,a in zip(y,z) if not a)/(len(z)-sum(z))
def crossing_edges(z): return sum(z[i]!=z[(i+1)%len(z)] for i in range(len(z)))
n=200; zi=individual_assignment(n,7); zc=cluster_assignment(n,10,7)
individual_effect=contrast(zi); cluster_effect=contrast(zc)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd
summary=pd.DataFrame([{'design':'individual','effect':individual_effect,'crossing':crossing_edges(zi)},{'design':'cluster','effect':cluster_effect,'crossing':crossing_edges(zc)}]).set_index('design')
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Freeze graph and clusters before assignment, log realized exposure and leakage, simulate design power, analyze independent clusters, monitor ecosystem-wide guardrails, and include cooldown and graph evidence in rollback.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert 0<sum(zi)<n and 0<sum(zc)<n
assert summary.loc['cluster','crossing']<summary.loc['individual','crossing']
assert cluster_effect>individual_effect
assert abs(individual_effect-1.0)<0.35
assert cluster_effect>2.0
all_control=[0]*n; all_treated=[1]*n
total_effect=sum(outcome(i,all_treated)-outcome(i,all_control) for i in range(n))/n
assert abs(total_effect-2.5)<1e-12
assert individual_effect<total_effect

Common mistakes

  • Only clustering standard errors

    That can address dependence but not bias from control units receiving treatment spillovers; redesign assignment or identify exposure effects.

  • Treating graph members as independent

    Inference follows cluster or structured assignment, and effective replication may be the number of clusters.

  • Defining exposure after seeing outcomes

    Outcome-driven exposure mappings create specification search; predefine and test sensitivity.

  • Calling the 50/50 contrast a full-rollout effect

    The observed exposure mixture may differ radically from all-treated equilibrium; state the identified estimand.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is interference?

    One unit's outcome depends on other units' assignments or treatments, so the usual isolated-unit potential-outcome model fails.

  • Why cluster-randomize a graph?

    It keeps more interacting units in the same arm, reducing cross-arm contamination and making policy-world contrasts more visible, at a power cost.

  • How can you detect network effects?

    Use domain evidence and exposure diagnostics, or randomize over assignment mechanisms and compare individual versus cluster estimates in a meta-experiment.

Production / system-design connection

Version the target estimand, exposure mapping, graph source and cutoff, edge semantics, cluster algorithm and map, assignment probabilities, balance constraints, treatment versions, and analysis plan. Store cluster assignment and unit membership immutably; log realized exposure and boundary interactions separately. Monitor cluster-size imbalance, cross-arm edge fraction, graph staleness, exposure support, attrition, capacity, and global safety metrics. Simulate power and estimator behavior on representative graph snapshots. Restrict graph access and publish only privacy-safe aggregates. Roll out gradually with capacity and ecosystem guardrails. On harm, stop treatment globally where spillovers require it, observe cooldown, and retain graph, assignment, and exposure evidence for reproducible rollback analysis.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 1 · practice

    Why can individual randomization underestimate a positive network effect?

    Show solution

    Control units receive spillover and treated units lack an all-treated neighborhood, shrinking the own-assignment contrast relative to full rollout.

  2. Exercise 2 · practice

    What is the main power cost of cluster randomization?

    Show solution

    Outcomes within clusters are correlated and the independent assignment count is clusters, often far smaller than users.

  3. Exercise 3 · practice

    Can a post-treatment friendship graph define exposure?

    Show solution

    It may be a mediator affected by treatment; using it naively conditions on a treatment consequence. Prefer a pre-treatment graph or explicit causal mediation assumptions.

15.1

Causal Inference vs Prediction

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Prediction asks what will happen; causal inference asks what would happen if we intervene. A predictive feature can be highly correlated with an outcome without being a valid lever. Causal answers require assumptions about treatment assignment, confounding and counterfactuals.

What you must know

  • prediction ≠ causation
  • treatment/outcome
  • counterfactual
  • identification assumptions

Why this matters

Data Scientists are often asked “will X happen?” and “will changing X cause Y?” Those are different questions and require different validation.

Intuition

For each unit, causality imagines two potential outcomes—under treatment and under control—but we can observe only one. Experimental randomization or credible identification assumptions help estimate the missing counterfactual.

Deep explanation

Randomized controlled trials balance confounders in expectation. With observational data, DAGs and designs such as matching, difference-in-differences or instrumental variables may identify effects under stronger assumptions.

Math / formal view

Individual treatment effect: Y_i(1)-Y_i(0), but only one potential outcome is observed for each unit.

Worked example

A churn model may find support calls predict cancellation. Reducing support calls is not necessarily a causal intervention; both could be caused by underlying product problems.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Simulate confounding to show prediction is not intervention.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); n=10000
ability=rng.normal(size=n)
training=(ability+rng.normal(size=n)>.3).astype(int)
salary=2*ability + 1.5*training + rng.normal(size=n)
naive=salary[training==1].mean()-salary[training==0].mean()
print('naive association',naive,'true treatment effect',1.5)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
# Adjust for the confounder with a simple regression.
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
X=np.c_[training,ability]; m=LinearRegression().fit(X,salary)
print('adjusted training coefficient',m.coef_[0])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Causal decisions should document assumptions and sensitivity; production recommendation/policy systems should not turn predictive correlations into interventions without evidence.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(m.coef_[0]-1.5)<.1
assert naive>m.coef_[0]

Common mistakes

  • Interpreting feature importance as causal effect.
  • Controlling for every available variable, including colliders or post-treatment variables.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does randomization help causal inference?
  • What is a confounder?

Production / system-design connection

Causal decisions should document assumptions and sensitivity; production recommendation/policy systems should not turn predictive correlations into interventions without evidence.

15.2

DAGs, Confounders & Colliders

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A causal DAG encodes assumptions about which variables cause which others. A confounder causes both treatment and outcome and often needs adjustment; a collider is caused by two variables and conditioning on it can create a spurious association.

What you must know

  • DAG
  • confounder
  • collider
  • backdoor paths

Why this matters

Choosing adjustment variables mechanically from correlation can bias causal estimates. DAG reasoning makes assumptions explicit before modeling.

Intuition

Imagine arrows as information about the data-generating process. Conditioning can close useful backdoor paths—but can also accidentally open a path through a collider.

Deep explanation

The backdoor criterion formalizes sets that block noncausal paths between treatment and outcome without blocking the causal effect itself. DAGs do not prove assumptions; they make them inspectable.

Worked example

Ability → Training and Ability → Salary makes Ability a confounder when estimating Training → Salary. If Hiring ← Ability and Hiring ← Network, conditioning on Hiring can associate Ability and Network even if they were independent.

Common mistakes

  • Calling every correlated variable a confounder.
  • Conditioning on a collider because “more controls must be better.”

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a backdoor path?
  • Can DAG structure be learned reliably from data alone?

Production / system-design connection

For experimentation/decision systems, keep causal assumptions versioned alongside the analysis and distinguish pre-treatment from post-treatment features.

Best references

  • Causal Inference: The MixtapeScott Cunningham · Free online textbook · Intermediate

    Applied causal inference with DAGs, potential outcomes and quasi-experimental designs backed by worked examples.

15.3

Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects

very highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Causal inference defines treatment effects through potential outcomes: what the same unit would experience under treatment versus control. Because both cannot be observed, identification requires randomization or assumptions/design.

What you must know

  • Fundamental problem: one potential outcome is missing.
  • ATE, ATT and CATE answer different questions.
  • Assignment mechanism is central.

Why this matters

Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Fundamental problem: one potential outcome is missing.

Deep explanation

Causal inference defines treatment effects through potential outcomes: what the same unit would experience under treatment versus control. Because both cannot be observed, identification requires randomization or assumptions/design. ATE, ATT and CATE answer different questions. Assignment mechanism is central. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Estimate the average effect of a pricing banner, not merely whether exposed users buy more.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

Likely follow-ups

  • What assumptions does Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects make?
  • How would you validate or debug Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects in practice?

Production / system-design connection

In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.

15.4

Backdoor Adjustment & Confounding Control

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

A valid adjustment set blocks noncausal backdoor paths between treatment and outcome without conditioning on colliders or descendants that introduce bias. DAGs make these assumptions explicit.

What you must know

  • Control confounders, not every available variable.
  • Conditioning on colliders can create associations.
  • Causal graph is an assumptions tool.

Why this matters

Backdoor Adjustment & Confounding Control appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Control confounders, not every available variable.

Deep explanation

A valid adjustment set blocks noncausal backdoor paths between treatment and outcome without conditioning on colliders or descendants that introduce bias. DAGs make these assumptions explicit. Conditioning on colliders can create associations. Causal graph is an assumptions tool. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Adjust for prior customer risk when studying intervention effect, but not for a post-treatment support interaction caused by the intervention.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

15.5

Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

The propensity score is the probability of treatment given observed covariates. Matching or inverse-probability weighting can balance observed confounders, but cannot repair unmeasured confounding or poor overlap.

What you must know

  • Check common support/positivity.
  • Assess covariate balance after adjustment.
  • Extreme weights increase variance.

Why this matters

Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Check common support/positivity.

Deep explanation

The propensity score is the probability of treatment given observed covariates. Matching or inverse-probability weighting can balance observed confounders, but cannot repair unmeasured confounding or poor overlap. Assess covariate balance after adjustment. Extreme weights increase variance. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Weight observational treatment records so measured pre-treatment characteristics resemble a randomized comparison.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

15.6

Difference-in-Differences

highsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Difference-in-differences compares outcome changes over time between treated and control groups. Its key identifying assumption is that, absent treatment, their trends would have evolved in parallel.

What you must know

  • Inspect pre-trends.
  • Treatment timing and anticipation matter.
  • Use clustered/appropriate uncertainty.

Why this matters

Difference-in-Differences appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Inspect pre-trends.

Deep explanation

Difference-in-differences compares outcome changes over time between treated and control groups. Its key identifying assumption is that, absent treatment, their trends would have evolved in parallel. Treatment timing and anticipation matter. Use clustered/appropriate uncertainty. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Compare sales change in regions receiving a policy versus similar untreated regions before and after rollout.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Compute a simple 2x2 difference-in-differences estimate.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
treated_pre=100; treated_post=130
control_pre=90; control_post=100
did=(treated_post-treated_pre)-(control_post-control_pre)
print('DiD',did)
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
df=pd.DataFrame({'y':[100,130,90,100],'treated':[1,1,0,0],'post':[0,1,0,1]})
fit=smf.ols('y ~ treated + post + treated:post',data=df).fit()
print(fit.params['treated:post'])
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

A real DiD study needs many units/time periods, pre-trend diagnostics, explicit treatment timing, robust/clustered uncertainty and sensitivity to composition changes.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert abs(did-20)<1e-9

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

15.7

Instrumental Variables

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

An instrumental variable affects treatment, is independent of unmeasured outcome causes under assumptions, and affects the outcome only through treatment. IV can identify causal effects when confounding remains, but valid instruments are hard to justify.

What you must know

  • Relevance, independence and exclusion restriction.
  • Weak instruments create unstable estimates.
  • Often estimates a local effect for compliers.

Why this matters

Instrumental Variables appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.

Intuition

Relevance, independence and exclusion restriction.

Deep explanation

An instrumental variable affects treatment, is independent of unmeasured outcome causes under assumptions, and affects the outcome only through treatment. IV can identify causal effects when confounding remains, but valid instruments are hard to justify. Weak instruments create unstable estimates. Often estimates a local effect for compliers. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.

Worked example

Use randomized encouragement as an instrument for actual program participation when not everyone complies.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
  • Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.

  • Check manipulation and continuity.
  • Do not extrapolate local effects broadly without justification.

16.1

Time-Series Splits & Backtesting

very highsummary
Roles: ds, mle, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Random train/test splitting is usually wrong for forecasting because it leaks the future into the past. I split chronologically and evaluate with rolling or expanding-window backtests that mimic how the model will actually be used.

What you must know

  • chronological split
  • rolling/expanding windows
  • no future leakage
  • match deployment horizon

Why this matters

Forecast validation is easy to make unrealistically optimistic. A model should only use information that would have existed at the prediction timestamp.

Intuition

Imagine standing at each historical date and pretending it is “today.” Train only on the past, forecast the next horizon, record the error, then move forward.

Deep explanation

Random cross-validation breaks temporal ordering. Use a final untouched future holdout for the last estimate, while rolling-origin validation compares models/hyperparameters. Feature engineering must also be point-in-time correct: rolling means, target encodings, and joins cannot peek ahead.

Worked example

For monthly demand, train Jan–Dec 2024 and validate Jan–Mar 2025; then train through Mar and validate Apr–Jun. Compare errors across windows instead of trusting one lucky split.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Backtest without future leakage using expanding windows.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
y=np.arange(30)+np.sin(np.arange(30))
errors=[]
for cutoff in range(15,27,3):
    train=y[:cutoff]; val=y[cutoff:cutoff+3]
    pred=np.repeat(train[-1],len(val)) # naive baseline
    errors.append(mean_absolute_error(val,pred))
print(errors, np.mean(errors))
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
for tr,va in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4).split(y):
    assert tr.max()<va.min()
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Backtests should mirror prediction cadence, horizon, retraining frequency and data availability. Production feature pipelines need event-time/point-in-time semantics.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert len(errors)==4
assert all(e>=0 for e in errors)

Common mistakes

  • Using random K-fold CV on dependent time-series observations.
  • Computing rolling features on the full dataset before splitting, which leaks future information.

Likely follow-ups

  • When is random splitting acceptable for temporal data?
  • How do you choose expanding vs sliding windows?

Production / system-design connection

Backtests should mirror prediction cadence, horizon, retraining frequency and data availability. Production feature pipelines need event-time/point-in-time semantics.

16.2

Stationarity, ACF & PACF

highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Stationarity means the statistical behavior of a series is stable enough over time for many classical models to learn consistent relationships. I inspect trend/seasonality and autocorrelation; differencing or transformation can help when the level is non-stationary.

What you must know

  • weak stationarity
  • autocorrelation
  • ACF/PACF
  • differencing

Why this matters

ARIMA-family methods rely on structure in lagged values and residuals. Understanding autocorrelation also helps diagnose leakage and seasonality.

Intuition

ACF asks “how correlated is the series with itself k steps ago?” PACF tries to isolate the direct lag-k relationship after accounting for shorter lags.

Deep explanation

Weak stationarity is typically about approximately constant mean/variance and covariance depending on lag rather than absolute time. ACF/PACF are diagnostics, not magical parameter selectors. Differencing can remove stochastic trends but over-differencing adds noise.

Math / formal view

ACF(k) = Corr(y_t, y_{t-k}). First difference: Δy_t = y_t - y_{t-1}.

Worked example

A monthly series with a rising level may show slow ACF decay. First differencing y_t-y_{t-1} can make the remaining dependence easier to model; a spike at lag 12 can suggest annual seasonality.

Common mistakes

  • Equating stationarity with “flat data.”
  • Blindly differencing until a statistical test passes without checking business meaning.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does an ACF spike at a seasonal lag mean?
  • What is over-differencing?

Production / system-design connection

Monitor residual autocorrelation after deployment; systematic temporal structure in errors often means the model is leaving forecastable signal unused.

16.3

ARIMA / SARIMA

highsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

ARIMA combines autoregression, differencing and moving-average error terms. The p,d,q orders control lagged values, differencing and lagged forecast errors; SARIMA adds seasonal equivalents. I use it as a strong interpretable baseline when temporal dependence is meaningful.

What you must know

  • AR(p)
  • I(d)
  • MA(q)
  • seasonal extension

Why this matters

ARIMA remains a valuable baseline: transparent, data-efficient and excellent for understanding whether complex models truly add value.

Intuition

ARIMA predicts the present from a cleaned-up version of the past: first make the series sufficiently stable, then explain it with previous values and previous surprises.

Deep explanation

AR terms model dependence on lagged observations; MA terms model dependence on lagged innovations/residuals. Model selection should combine diagnostics, validation and domain knowledge, not just minimize AIC. Seasonal structure can be represented explicitly with SARIMA.

Math / formal view

ARIMA(p,d,q): apply d differences, then model with p autoregressive lags and q lagged innovations.

Worked example

If weekly demand depends strongly on the previous two weeks and residual shocks persist one step, ARIMA(2,1,1) might be a candidate after differencing a trend. Validate it against naive seasonal baselines.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Fit an ARIMA baseline and inspect forecasts/residuals.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); y=np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=120))
train,test=y[:100],y[100:]
fit=ARIMA(train,order=(1,1,1)).fit(); pred=fit.forecast(len(test))
print(pred[:3])
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
naive=np.repeat(train[-1],len(test))
print('ARIMA MAE',mean_absolute_error(test,pred),'naive',mean_absolute_error(test,naive))
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

ARIMA is cheap to retrain and explain, making it a useful fallback/baseline even when a production stack later adopts boosted trees or neural forecasting.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert len(pred)==len(test)
assert np.isfinite(pred).all()

Common mistakes

  • Thinking MA(q) means moving-average smoothing of observations.
  • Selecting p,d,q only from ACF/PACF and skipping backtesting.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the difference between AR and MA?
  • Why can a seasonal naive baseline beat ARIMA?

Production / system-design connection

ARIMA is cheap to retrain and explain, making it a useful fallback/baseline even when a production stack later adopts boosted trees or neural forecasting.

16.4

Exponential Smoothing / ETS

mediumsummary
Roles: ds, da, as
45–60 SECOND INTERVIEW ANSWER

Exponential smoothing builds forecasts from recursively updated level, trend and seasonality components, giving more weight to recent observations. ETS models are excellent business-forecasting baselines, especially when patterns are smooth and recurring.

What you must know

  • level
  • trend
  • seasonality
  • recent observations weighted more

Why this matters

ETS often performs extremely well on operational forecasting with little tuning and has an intuitive decomposition for stakeholders.

Intuition

Instead of fitting one global regression line, keep updating a compact state of “where the series is now, where it is moving, and what season we are in.”

Deep explanation

Simple exponential smoothing models level only; Holt adds trend; Holt-Winters adds seasonality. Additive vs multiplicative components depend on whether seasonal amplitude stays constant or grows with the level.

Worked example

If monthly demand has a stable upward trend and December is consistently +20 units, additive seasonal ETS is natural. If the December uplift is about +20%, multiplicative seasonality may fit better.

RUNNABLE CODE LAB

Build it → Use it → Ship it → Verify it

Fit an ETS-style trend/seasonal forecast.

Open lab files
1 · Build itfrom first principles
import numpy as np
t=np.arange(72)
y=20+.2*t+3*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/12)+np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0,.4,len(t))
2 · Use itlibrary / production-style API
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
m=ExponentialSmoothing(y,trend='add',seasonal='add',seasonal_periods=12).fit()
f=m.forecast(12)
print(f)
3 · Ship itengineering artifact / production context

Keep a reproducible backtest by horizon; retrain only after the newest complete observations and compare against seasonal-naive before deployment.

4 · Verify itsanity checks / assertions
assert len(f)==12 and np.isfinite(f).all()

Common mistakes

  • Assuming exponential smoothing is just a moving average.
  • Using multiplicative seasonality when zeros/negative values make it inappropriate.

Likely follow-ups

  • Holt vs Holt-Winters?
  • Additive vs multiplicative seasonality?

Production / system-design connection

ETS is lightweight and reliable for batch forecasting, and is a strong champion model to compare with more expensive approaches.
